title: Irrigation and Drainage — practice questions
$comment: Answer positions were distributed while authoring, per the discipline recorded after the chapter 1 bank was found to key 55% of its questions to option (b). Numerical items were recomputed independently before keying.

questions.stem: The NET IRRIGATION REQUIREMENT of a crop differs from its CONSUMPTIVE USE in that the net irrigation requirement is:
options: The consumptive use multiplied by the irrigation efficiency
The consumptive use plus the conveyance losses in the canal system
Always equal to the consumptive use
The consumptive use less the effective rainfall and any contribution from the soil moisture store or the groundwater
questions.solution:
**The consumptive use LESS the EFFECTIVE RAINFALL and any contribution from the soil moisture store or the groundwater** — that is, only the part that irrigation must actually supply.

**The sequence of quantities, each derived from the one before:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **CONSUMPTIVE USE (evapotranspiration, ET)** ← | **The water the crop TRANSPIRES plus what EVAPORATES from the soil surface — the total demand, whatever supplies it** ← |
| **CROP WATER REQUIREMENT** ← | **ET plus any special requirements — puddling and land preparation for paddy, leaching, and losses in the field** ← |
| **NET IRRIGATION REQUIREMENT (NIR)** ← | **Crop water requirement MINUS effective rainfall, minus the contribution from soil moisture and from groundwater** ← |
| **FIELD irrigation requirement** ← | **NIR ÷ the field APPLICATION efficiency** ← |
| **GROSS irrigation requirement (GIR)** ← | **Field requirement ÷ the CONVEYANCE efficiency — the quantity that must be diverted at the head of the system** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION FROM THE FIRST ROW TO THE LAST IS THE WHOLE ARITHMETIC OF IRRIGATION PLANNING AND ITS DIRECTION IS WORTH NOTING: the quantity INCREASES at every step below the third, and DECREASES at the third.**

> **Rainfall reduces what irrigation must supply; inefficiency increases what must be diverted to supply it.**

> **So the gross requirement at the headworks can be two or three times the crop's actual consumptive use, and the difference is entirely rainfall on one side and losses on the other.**

> **Getting the direction of each step right is the commonest arithmetic error in the subject: dividing where one should multiply, or subtracting the rainfall from the gross rather than from the crop requirement, produces an answer wrong by a large factor.**

**THE SOIL MOISTURE AND GROUNDWATER CONTRIBUTIONS IN THE THIRD ROW ARE OFTEN NEGLECTED AND ARE SOMETIMES SUBSTANTIAL:**

| Contribution | Note |
|---|---|
| **Moisture stored in the ROOT ZONE from the previous season** ← | **Particularly at the start of the rabi season, following the monsoon — the soil profile is full, and the first weeks may need no irrigation at all** ← |
| **CAPILLARY RISE from a shallow water table** ← | **Where the water table is within 1 to 2 m of the root zone, it can supply a real fraction of the demand** ← |
| **Neither appears in a simple ET calculation** ← | **So a requirement computed without them OVERSTATES the irrigation needed** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW HAS A CONSEQUENCE THAT CUTS BOTH WAYS AND IT IS WORTH FOLLOWING: in a waterlogged area the shallow water table supplies much of the crop's need, so the irrigation requirement is genuinely lower.**

> **Continuing to irrigate at the full computed rate then adds water the crop does not need to a profile that is already too wet — which raises the water table further and worsens the waterlogging.**

> **So the failure to account for capillary contribution actively drives the waterlogging problem, and it is one of the mechanisms by which an irrigation scheme damages its own command.**

> **The remedy is to measure the water table and adjust the schedule, which requires observation wells and someone to read them — a modest provision that is regularly omitted.**

**AND THE PADDY EXCEPTION IN THE SECOND ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE DESERVES A NOTE, SINCE IT DOMINATES NEPALI IRRIGATION:**

> **Paddy is not irrigated to meet an evapotranspiration demand; it is PONDED, and the water requirement is dominated by PERCOLATION through the field's floor and by the puddling water used in land preparation.**

> **So a paddy field's requirement may be 1,000 mm or more against an evapotranspiration of perhaps 500 mm, and the difference is water going into the ground.**

> **That percolation is not entirely lost — it recharges the groundwater and may be pumped again downstream — which is why a basin-scale water accounting gives a very different picture of paddy's water use from a field-scale one.**

> **A field's efficiency of 40 per cent may correspond to a basin efficiency of 80 per cent, because most of the 'loss' returns to the system; and this is why the pursuit of field-level efficiency can be misdirected if the returns are not traced.**

examTip.trick: **ET → crop water requirement → SUBTRACT effective rainfall → NIR → DIVIDE by application efficiency → DIVIDE by conveyance efficiency → GIR.**
examTip.trap: **Rainfall is subtracted at the CROP requirement stage, not from the gross** — and the efficiencies DIVIDE. Getting either direction wrong is wrong by a large factor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Capillary rise from a shallow water table supplies real water** — ignoring it over-irrigates land that is already too wet, driving the waterlogging it suffers from.

questions.stem: A crop has a base period of 120 days and the duty of water for it is 1,800 hectares per cumec. The DELTA for the crop is:
questions.solution:
**57.6 cm.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The relation** | **Δ = 8.64 B / D, with Δ in metres, B in days and D in hectares per cumec** ← |
| **Substituting** | **= 8.64 × 120 / 1,800** ← |
| **Numerator** | **= 1,036.8** ← |
| **Δ** | **= 1,036.8 / 1,800 = 0.576 m** ← |
| **In centimetres** | **= 57.6 cm** ← |

> **So the delta is 57.6 cm, that is 576 mm of water depth over the whole base period.**

**THE CONSTANT 8.64 IS A PURE UNIT CONVERSION AND DERIVING IT MAKES THE FORMULA UNFORGETTABLE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **One cumec flowing for one DAY delivers 1 × 86,400 = 86,400 m³** ← | ← |
| **Spread over ONE HECTARE (10,000 m²), that is a depth of 8.64 m** ← | ← |
| **So 1 cumec for B days over D hectares gives a depth of 8.64 B / D metres** ← | **Which is the formula** ← |

> **Anyone who forgets whether the 8.64 goes on top or underneath can rebuild it in fifteen seconds from that observation, which is far more reliable than recalling the arrangement.**

> **And the derivation also settles the UNITS, which is where the other common error lies: the formula gives METRES, so an answer wanted in centimetres must be multiplied by 100, and one wanted in millimetres by 1,000.**

**THE THREE QUANTITIES AND HOW THEY RELATE:**

| Quantity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DUTY (D)** ← | **The AREA a unit discharge will irrigate — hectares per cumec. A HIGH duty is EFFICIENT: more land from the same water** ← |
| **DELTA (Δ)** ← | **The total DEPTH of water the crop needs over its base period** ← |
| **BASE PERIOD (B)** ← | **From the first watering to the last** ← |
| **Their relation** | **Δ = 8.64 B/D, equivalently D = 8.64 B/Δ** ← |

> **THE INVERSE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN DUTY AND DELTA IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE TO HOLD, AND IT FOLLOWS FROM COMMON SENSE: a thirsty crop with a large delta irrigates a small area from a given discharge, so its duty is low.**

> **Paddy has a delta of 1,000 to 1,250 mm and a correspondingly LOW duty; wheat has a delta of about 400 mm and a HIGH duty.**

> **So the two numbers say the same thing from opposite ends, and a candidate confusing them will conclude that paddy is the efficient crop.**

**WHAT MAKES THE DUTY VARY, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL SUBSTANCE:**

| Factor | Effect on duty |
|---|---|
| **The CROP** ← | **The dominant factor — paddy low, wheat and gram high** ← |
| **The CLIMATE** ← | **Hot, dry and windy conditions raise evapotranspiration and LOWER the duty** ← |
| **The SOIL** ← | **A sandy soil percolates heavily, lowering the duty; a clay soil retains water and raises it** ← |
| **The method of APPLICATION** ← | **Wild flooding gives a low duty; furrow, sprinkler and drip progressively higher** ← |
| **The condition of the CANAL** ← | **A lined canal delivers more of what it carries, so the duty AT THE HEAD is higher** ← |
| **Where the duty is MEASURED** ← | **Duty at the FIELD outlet is higher than duty at the canal HEAD, because the losses in between have not yet occurred** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE DISTINCTION THAT MUST BE STATED WHENEVER A DUTY IS QUOTED AND IT IS FREQUENTLY OMITTED: a duty figure is meaningless without saying WHERE it applies.**

> **Duty at the field is the crop's own requirement; duty at the outlet includes the distributary losses; duty at the head of the main canal includes everything.**

> **The three differ by a factor approaching two on a leaky system, so comparing a duty from one scheme with a duty from another without establishing the reference point compares nothing at all.**

> **A properly stated figure is therefore 'duty at the head of the distributary' or 'duty at the outlet', and a bare number should be treated with suspicion until its reference is established.**

examTip.trick: **Δ = 8.64 B/D = 8.64 × 120/1,800 = 0.576 m = 57.6 cm.** The formula gives METRES.
examTip.trap: **Derive the 8.64: one cumec for one day is 86,400 m³, over one hectare that is 8.64 m depth.** Then the arrangement is obvious rather than remembered.
examTip.mnemonic: **HIGH duty is efficient (more land per cumec), and delta is its inverse** — paddy has a big delta and a low duty. And always state WHERE the duty applies.

questions.stem: EFFECTIVE RAINFALL, in the context of irrigation planning, means:
options: The total rainfall recorded during the crop's growing season
That part of the rainfall which is actually stored in the root zone and available to the crop
The rainfall that falls only during the daytime
The rainfall measured at the nearest meteorological station
questions.solution:
**That part of the rainfall which is actually STORED IN THE ROOT ZONE and available to the crop** — excluding what runs off, what percolates below the root zone, and what falls when the soil is already at field capacity.

**What is lost from the total rainfall before it becomes effective:**

| Loss | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURFACE RUNOFF** ← | **Rain falling faster than the soil can absorb it runs off the field — the more intense the storm, the greater the fraction lost** ← |
| **DEEP PERCOLATION below the root zone** ← | **Water that passes beyond the roots is gone as far as the crop is concerned** ← |
| **Rain falling when the soil is already at FIELD CAPACITY** ← | **The profile cannot hold more, so all of it runs off or percolates** ← |
| **INTERCEPTION by the foliage, evaporating without reaching the soil** ← | **A few millimetres per storm** ← |
| **Rain falling OUTSIDE the growing season** ← | **Except so far as it recharges the profile for the season's start** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND IT EXPLAINS WHY THE MONSOON'S ENORMOUS RAINFALL IS SO LITTLE USE AGRICULTURALLY: rain is only effective if the soil has ROOM for it.**

> **A soil at field capacity can accept nothing, so a 100 mm storm falling on a saturated profile contributes essentially nothing to the crop.**

> **In Nepal, some 80 per cent of the rain falls in four months and much of it falls on ground already wet — so the effective fraction of the monsoon rainfall is far lower than the totals suggest, and the dry season's small rainfall may be almost entirely effective.**

> **This is why a scheme's water requirement cannot be estimated by subtracting the seasonal rainfall total from the seasonal crop requirement: the effective fraction must be computed month by month, or the requirement will be badly understated.**

**HOW EFFECTIVE RAINFALL IS ESTIMATED:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **A fixed PERCENTAGE of the total** ← | **Crude — 70 to 80 per cent is sometimes used, and it ignores the intensity and the soil's condition entirely** ← |
| **The USDA Soil Conservation Service method** ← | **A tabulated relationship between monthly rainfall, monthly ET and effective rainfall — the usual practical method** ← |
| **DEPENDABLE rainfall at a stated probability** ← | **Using the 75 or 80 per cent dependable rainfall rather than the average — since a scheme designed on average rainfall FAILS in one year out of two** ← |
| **A daily SOIL WATER BALANCE** ← | **The most accurate — tracking the profile day by day and counting only what it can absorb; laborious by hand and trivial by computer** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS A POINT OF PRINCIPLE THAT APPLIES WELL BEYOND EFFECTIVE RAINFALL AND IT IS WORTH STATING GENERALLY: designing to an AVERAGE means failing half the time.**

> **An irrigation scheme sized on average rainfall will be short of water in every year drier than average, which is half of them.**

> **So the design value is a DEPENDABLE one — typically the rainfall exceeded in 75 or 80 per cent of years — which means the scheme is adequate in four years out of five and short in the fifth.**

> **Choosing that probability is a real decision with a cost: a higher dependability means a larger and dearer scheme, and the appropriate level depends on what the crop is worth and what failure costs the farmer.**

> **For a subsistence crop where failure means hunger, a high dependability is warranted; for a supplementary irrigation improving an already viable rainfed crop, a lower one is rational.**

> **The same reasoning governs the choice of dependable FLOW for the source, and the two must be consistent — a scheme designed on 80 per cent dependable rainfall and 50 per cent dependable river flow has a weakest link that the rainfall assumption conceals.**

examTip.trick: **Only what is stored in the ROOT ZONE and available** — excluding runoff, deep percolation, interception and rain on an already-full profile.
examTip.trap: **Monsoon rain falls largely on wet ground, so its effective fraction is small** — subtracting the seasonal total from the seasonal requirement badly understates the need.
examTip.mnemonic: **Designing to an AVERAGE means failing half the time** — use 75 or 80 % dependable rainfall, and make the dependable FLOW assumption consistent with it.

questions.stem: In an irrigation system the CONVEYANCE efficiency is 70 per cent and the FIELD APPLICATION efficiency is 60 per cent. The OVERALL (project) efficiency is:
options: 65 per cent
130 per cent
42 per cent
10 per cent
questions.solution:
**42 per cent.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The efficiencies MULTIPLY, they do not average** ← | **Each acts on what survives the previous one** ← |
| **Overall = 0.70 × 0.60** | **= 0.42** ← |
| **That is** | **42 per cent** ← |

> **So of every 100 units diverted at the headworks, 42 reach the crop's root zone.**

**WHY THEY MULTIPLY IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION AND OPTION (a) IS THE ERROR IT GUARDS AGAINST:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Divert 100 units at the head** ← | ← |
| **Conveyance at 70 per cent delivers 70 to the field** ← | **30 lost in the canals and watercourses** ← |
| **Application at 60 per cent puts 42 of those 70 into the root zone** ← | **28 lost in the field** ← |
| **So 42 of the original 100 are used** ← | **And the average of 70 and 60 — that is 65 — is meaningless** ← |

> **THE COMPOUNDING IN THE THIRD ROW IS WHY IRRIGATION EFFICIENCY IS SO LOW OVERALL AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: two respectable-sounding efficiencies produce a poor combined result.**

> **And a real system has more than two stages — main canal, branch, distributary, watercourse, field channel, field — each with its own efficiency, all multiplying.**

> **Five stages at 90 per cent each give 0.9⁵ = 59 per cent, so a system in which no single element is bad can still be poor overall.**

> **This is the same multiplicative arithmetic met with fish passes in series, and it has the same implication: improving one stage while the others remain poor achieves proportionately little, and the gains come from raising the WORST stages.**

**THE EFFICIENCIES DEFINED, SINCE THEY ARE EASILY CONFUSED:**

| Efficiency | Definition | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **CONVEYANCE, η_c** ← | **Water delivered to the field ÷ water diverted at the head** ← | **60 to 80 per cent unlined; 85 to 95 lined** ← |
| **APPLICATION (farm), η_a** ← | **Water stored in the root zone ÷ water delivered to the field** ← | **40 to 60 per cent surface; 70 to 85 sprinkler; 85 to 95 drip** ← |
| **USE (water use), η_u** ← | **Water USED by the crop ÷ water delivered to the field** ← | ← |
| **DISTRIBUTION, η_d** ← | **A measure of how UNIFORMLY the water is spread over the field — high average depth with poor uniformity still leaves dry patches** ← | ← |
| **OVERALL (project), η_p** ← | **η_c × η_a — this question** ← | **30 to 50 per cent is common** ← |

> **THE DISTRIBUTION EFFICIENCY IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OMITTED AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE OF WHAT AVERAGES CONCEAL: a field can receive exactly the right average depth and still have parts under-irrigated.**

> **The farmer, seeing the dry patch, irrigates until THAT patch is wet — which over-irrigates everywhere else.**

> **So poor uniformity forces over-application, and the apparent application efficiency falls for a reason that has nothing to do with the quantity applied and everything to do with how evenly it was spread.**

> **Improving uniformity — by land levelling above all — therefore raises efficiency without any change to the water applied, and LAND LEVELLING is consistently among the most cost-effective irrigation improvements available.**

> **THE COMPARISON IN THE SECOND ROW BETWEEN SURFACE AND DRIP IS WORTH A CLOSING CAUTION, HOWEVER: the field-level gain from drip is real, and the BASIN-level gain may be much smaller.**

> **Water 'lost' to deep percolation from a surface-irrigated field largely recharges the aquifer and is pumped again; water not applied under drip was never diverted.**

> **So converting a scheme to drip saves less water at the basin scale than the field efficiencies suggest, and where the percolation was recharging wells the conversion can reduce the groundwater those wells depend on.**

> **That is a genuinely counter-intuitive result and it is well documented, and it means efficiency improvements should be assessed on a basin water balance rather than on field figures alone.**

examTip.trick: **Efficiencies MULTIPLY: 0.70 × 0.60 = 42 %.** Option (a), 65 %, is their average, which means nothing.
examTip.trap: **Five stages at 90 % each give 59 %** — a system with no single bad element can still be poor. Gains come from raising the WORST stage.
examTip.mnemonic: **Poor UNIFORMITY forces over-application** — the farmer irrigates until the dry patch is wet. Land levelling raises efficiency without changing the water applied.

questions.stem: In irrigation terminology, the CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA (CCA) is:
options: The total area lying within the irrigation boundary, including villages, roads and barren land
The area actually irrigated in a particular season
The area that could be irrigated if unlimited water were available
That part of the gross command area which is culturable — the gross area less the land not fit for cultivation, such as villages, roads, ponds, rock and forest
questions.solution:
**That part of the GROSS COMMAND AREA which is CULTURABLE** — the gross area less the land not fit for cultivation, such as villages, roads, ponds, rock and forest.

**The areas, from largest to smallest:**

| Area | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS COMMAND AREA (GCA)** ← | **The TOTAL area that the canal system could command by gravity — everything within its boundary, culturable or not** ← (option a) |
| **CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA (CCA)** ← | **GCA MINUS the unculturable land — villages, roads, ponds, rock outcrop, forest, barren ground** ← |
| **Culturable CULTIVATED area** ← | **The part of the CCA actually under cultivation** ← |
| **Culturable UNCULTIVATED area** ← | **Culturable but left fallow** ← |
| **INTENSITY OF IRRIGATION** ← | **The area actually IRRIGATED in a season, as a PERCENTAGE of the CCA** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION MATTERS BECAUSE EVERY IRRIGATION CALCULATION IS BASED ON THE CCA AND NOT THE GCA, AND CONFUSING THEM OVERSTATES THE DEMAND: the roads and villages within the command need no water.**

> **The difference is not trivial — the unculturable fraction may be 15 to 25 per cent of the gross area in a settled plain, and more in broken country.**

> **So a design based on the GCA sizes the canal a fifth too large, and one based on it for a benefit calculation overstates the area that will actually benefit.**

**THE INTENSITY OF IRRIGATION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE FIGURE THAT DECIDES THE CANAL'S SIZE AND IT REPAYS UNDERSTANDING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is the percentage of the CCA irrigated in a given SEASON** ← | **So there is a kharif intensity and a rabi intensity, and an annual total** ← |
| **It can EXCEED 100 per cent annually** ← | **Because the same land is irrigated in more than one season — 50 per cent in kharif and 50 in rabi gives an annual intensity of 100 per cent** ← |
| **A well-served command may reach 150 or 180 per cent annually** ← | **With two crops on most of the land and three on some** ← |
| **The canal is sized on the SEASONAL peak, not the annual total** ← | **Since the seasons do not overlap** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHERE THE CONFUSION USUALLY ARISES AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: an intensity above 100 per cent does not mean more land than exists.**

> **It means the same land is being cropped more than once a year, which is precisely what irrigation is for — converting a single rainfed monsoon crop into two or three irrigated ones.**

> **So the intensity is a measure of how INTENSIVELY the land is used through the year, and raising it is the scheme's principal benefit.**

> **A scheme that irrigates 100 per cent of its CCA in kharif and nothing in rabi has an annual intensity of 100 per cent and has achieved comparatively little, since kharif is the monsoon season when the crop would largely have grown anyway.**

> **A scheme irrigating 40 per cent in kharif and 60 in rabi has the same annual intensity and has done far more good, because the rabi crop would not have existed without it.**

> **WHICH IS WHY THE SEASONAL BREAKDOWN MATTERS MORE THAN THE ANNUAL TOTAL, AND IT IS THE FIGURE TO ASK FOR: the value of irrigation lies overwhelmingly in the DRY season, when it is the difference between a crop and no crop, rather than in the monsoon, when it is the difference between a crop and a slightly better one.**

> **This has a direct consequence for scheme design in Nepal: a run-of-river irrigation intake with abundant monsoon flow and little dry-season flow delivers water when it is least valuable and fails when it is most — the same seasonal mismatch that afflicts run-of-river hydropower, arising from the same hydrology.**

> **Storage, groundwater conjunctive use, or a source with a dependable dry-season yield are what convert such a scheme from a marginal benefit into a substantial one.**

examTip.trick: **CCA = GCA minus the unculturable land** — villages, roads, ponds, rock, forest. All irrigation calculations use the CCA.
examTip.trap: **Annual intensity can exceed 100 %** — the same land cropped twice. It measures how intensively the land is used through the year, not extra land.
examTip.mnemonic: **The DRY season is where irrigation's value lies** — the difference between a crop and none. A monsoon-only intake delivers when water is least valuable.

questions.stem: The AVAILABLE MOISTURE in a soil, from the point of view of irrigation, is the moisture held between:
options: Field capacity and the permanent wilting point
Saturation and field capacity
Saturation and the permanent wilting point
The hygroscopic coefficient and oven-dry condition
questions.solution:
**FIELD CAPACITY and the PERMANENT WILTING POINT** — the upper limit being what the soil retains against gravity, and the lower the point at which the plant can no longer extract water and does not recover.

**The soil moisture states, from wettest to driest:**

| State | Meaning | Available to the plant? |
|---|---|---|
| **SATURATION** ← | **All the pores full of water; no air** ← | **The excess drains away, and the soil is anaerobic while it lasts** ← |
| **FIELD CAPACITY (FC)** ← | **After free drainage has ceased, typically 1 to 3 days after wetting** ← | **The UPPER limit of useful storage** ← |
| **Between FC and PWP** ← | **Held in the smaller pores and as films** ← | **AVAILABLE — this is the range irrigation manages** ← |
| **PERMANENT WILTING POINT (PWP)** ← | **The plant wilts and does NOT recover even if placed in a humid atmosphere** ← | **The LOWER limit** ← |
| **HYGROSCOPIC water** | **Held so tightly by the soil particles that no plant can extract it** | **NOT available** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE REASON THE UPPER LIMIT IS FIELD CAPACITY AND NOT SATURATION, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION: water above field capacity does not stay.**

> **It drains away under gravity within a day or two, and while it is present the soil has no air in it — so the roots cannot respire and the crop is harmed rather than helped.**

> **So irrigating beyond field capacity achieves nothing except deep percolation, a temporary anaerobic condition and a contribution to the water table.**

> **That is the technical statement of why over-irrigation is wasteful AND damaging, and it explains the depth of irrigation calculation: the aim is to refill the profile to field capacity and no further.**

**THE READILY AVAILABLE MOISTURE, WHICH IS WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS SCHEDULING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A plant does NOT extract water equally easily across the whole available range** ← | ← |
| **Near field capacity the water is loosely held and easily taken** ← | ← |
| **Approaching the wilting point it is held ever more tightly, and the plant is under STRESS long before it wilts** ← | ← |
| **So irrigation is scheduled to refill the profile after only a FRACTION of the available moisture has been used** ← | **Commonly 40 to 60 per cent — the READILY available moisture** ← |
| **That fraction is the MANAGEMENT ALLOWED DEPLETION** ← | **And it is chosen by crop sensitivity and by the value of the crop** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL RULE AND IT IS WHY IRRIGATION IS NOT DELAYED UNTIL THE PLANT SHOWS DISTRESS: by the time wilting is visible, yield has already been lost.**

> **A crop under moisture stress closes its stomata, stops photosynthesising and stops growing, and it does so well before any visible symptom appears.**

> **So scheduling by observation of the crop is scheduling too late, and it is why soil moisture measurement — by tensiometer, by gypsum block, by feel and appearance, or by a computed water balance — is worth the trouble.**

> **The choice of depletion fraction also depends on the crop's stage: most crops have CRITICAL PERIODS — flowering and grain filling in particular — during which stress costs disproportionate yield, and a lower depletion is allowed then.**

**THE TYPICAL VALUES, WHICH GIVE THE RANGE ITS PRACTICAL SIZE:**

| Soil | Field capacity | Wilting point | Available moisture |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SAND** ← | **About 10 %** | **4 %** | **Only about 6 per cent by weight — a small reservoir, so frequent light irrigation is needed** ← |
| **LOAM** ← | **About 22 %** | **10 %** | **About 12 per cent — the most convenient** ← |
| **CLAY** ← | **About 38 %** | **22 %** | **About 16 per cent — a large reservoir, but the water is held tightly and infiltration is slow** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN WHY THE SOIL DETERMINES THE IRRIGATION SCHEDULE AS MUCH AS THE CROP DOES: a sandy soil holds little, so it must be irrigated often and lightly.**

> **A clay holds much, so it can be irrigated seldom and heavily — but its infiltration rate is low, so applying a heavy depth takes a long time and risks runoff.**

> **So the sandy soil is limited by its STORAGE and the clay by its INFILTRATION, and the irrigation method and interval follow from which limit applies.**

> **That is why a schedule cannot be transferred between fields of different soil, and why a soil survey is part of designing an irrigation scheme rather than an academic preliminary.**

examTip.trick: **Field capacity down to permanent wilting point.** Above field capacity the water drains away within days and the soil is anaerobic meanwhile.
examTip.trap: **Only 40-60 % of that range is READILY available** — the plant is stressed long before it wilts, so irrigation is scheduled on depletion, not on visible symptoms.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sand is limited by STORAGE (irrigate often and lightly); clay by INFILTRATION (seldom and heavily, but slowly).** The schedule follows the soil, not just the crop.

questions.stem: A soil has a field capacity of 22 per cent and a permanent wilting point of 10 per cent (both by weight), a dry density of 1.5 g/cm³, and the crop's root zone is 1.0 m deep. If irrigation is applied when 50 per cent of the available moisture has been used, the NET DEPTH of each irrigation is:
options: 180 mm
120 mm
90 mm
60 mm
questions.solution:
**90 mm.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Available moisture, as a fraction by weight** | **22 − 10 = 12 per cent = 0.12** ← |
| **Convert to a DEPTH: multiply by the dry density and the root zone depth** ← | **d = 0.12 × 1.5 × 1,000 mm** ← |
| **Total available moisture in the root zone** | **= 180 mm** ← |
| **Irrigating at 50 per cent depletion** | **= 0.50 × 180** ← |
| **NET depth of each irrigation** | **= 90 mm** ← |

> **So each irrigation must replace 90 mm of water in the root zone.**

**THE CONVERSION IN THE SECOND STEP IS WHERE ERRORS OCCUR AND IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT EXPLICITLY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The moisture contents are given BY WEIGHT, as a fraction of the dry soil's weight** ← | ← |
| **To convert to a DEPTH of water, multiply by the soil's DRY DENSITY (relative to water) and by the depth of soil** ← | **d = (θ_fc − θ_wp) × (γ_d/γ_w) × D** ← |
| **Here γ_d = 1.5 g/cm³, so γ_d/γ_w = 1.5** ← | **Dimensionless** ← |
| **And D = 1.0 m = 1,000 mm** ← | ← |
| **Omitting the dry density is the commonest error** ← | **It would give 120 mm instead of 180, and 60 instead of 90 — which is option (d)** ← |

> **THE PHYSICAL REASON THE DENSITY ENTERS IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN MEMORISING: the moisture content is a ratio of the water's weight to the SOIL's weight, and how much soil there is in a metre depth depends on how dense it is.**

> **A dense soil contains more soil per metre and therefore more water at the same moisture content by weight.**

> **So the density converts 'per unit weight of soil' into 'per unit volume of profile', which is what a depth of water is.**

**THE FREQUENCY OF IRRIGATION FOLLOWS DIRECTLY AND IS USUALLY THE NEXT PART OF THE QUESTION:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **If the crop's consumptive use is, say, 5 mm per day** ← | ← |
| **The 90 mm will be depleted in 90/5** | **= 18 days** ← |
| **So the irrigation INTERVAL is 18 days** ← | ← |
| **And the GROSS depth to be applied at each irrigation** ← | **= 90 ÷ the field application efficiency; at 60 per cent, that is 150 mm** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN AND IT MATTERS FOR THE CANAL'S DESIGN: the net depth is what the crop needs, and the GROSS depth is what must be delivered to the field.**

> **The difference is the application loss, and it can be half as much again — so a canal sized on the net depth will be substantially undersized.**

> **The sequence net depth, then gross depth, then discharge required, then canal capacity is the chain that connects the soil physics to the structure, and every step in it either multiplies or divides by an efficiency.**

> **A useful check on the whole calculation is the interval: 18 days is a plausible irrigation interval for a field crop on a loam.**

> **An interval of 2 days would suggest a sandy soil or an arithmetic error, and one of 60 days would suggest the root zone or the depletion fraction had been overstated.**

> **Knowing what a plausible answer looks like is worth as much as the calculation, because it catches the error that the arithmetic itself cannot.**

verification.notes: (0.22-0.10) x 1.5 x 1000 = 180 mm available; 50 per cent depletion gives 90 mm net.

examTip.trick: **(θ_fc − θ_wp) × dry density × root depth = 0.12 × 1.5 × 1,000 = 180 mm available; × 0.5 = 90 mm net.**
examTip.trap: **Omitting the DRY DENSITY is the commonest error** — it gives 60 mm, which is option (d). The density converts 'per weight of soil' into 'per volume of profile'.
examTip.mnemonic: **Then divide by the application efficiency for the GROSS depth**, and divide the net depth by the daily consumptive use for the INTERVAL. Check the interval is plausible.

questions.stem: The BLANEY-CRIDDLE method of estimating consumptive use differs from the PENMAN method in that Blaney-Criddle:
options: Requires measurements of solar radiation, humidity and wind speed
Requires only temperature and the day-length (latitude) data
Measures the consumptive use directly with a lysimeter
Applies only to paddy
questions.solution:
**It requires only TEMPERATURE and the day-length (latitude) data** — so it can be applied where little climatic data exists, at the cost of being less accurate.

**The methods, by the data they demand:**

| Method | Data required | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **BLANEY-CRIDDLE** ← | **Mean TEMPERATURE and the monthly percentage of annual DAYTIME HOURS (from latitude)** ← | **The least demanding; empirical; adequate for a preliminary estimate** ← |
| **THORNTHWAITE** ← | **Temperature only** ← | **Even simpler; developed for humid climates and poor in arid ones** ← |
| **RADIATION method** ← | **Temperature and SOLAR RADIATION or sunshine hours** ← | **Better** ← |
| **PENMAN and PENMAN-MONTEITH** ← | **Temperature, HUMIDITY, WIND speed and RADIATION** ← (option a) | **A physically based combination of the ENERGY BALANCE and the AERODYNAMIC terms — the most accurate, and the FAO standard** ← |
| **PAN EVAPORATION** ← | **A measured pan evaporation, multiplied by a pan coefficient** ← | **Simple and surprisingly good, if the pan is properly sited and maintained** ← |
| **LYSIMETER** ← | **A direct measurement of the water balance of an isolated block of soil with the crop growing in it** ← (option c) | **The reference against which the others are calibrated; expensive and used for research** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION DOWN THAT LIST IS ONE OF INCREASING DATA DEMAND AND INCREASING ACCURACY, AND THE CHOICE IS A PRACTICAL ONE RATHER THAN A THEORETICAL ONE: use the best method the available data supports.**

> **Applying Penman-Monteith with estimated humidity, assumed wind speed and radiation derived from sunshine hours that were themselves interpolated does not produce Penman-Monteith accuracy — it produces a precise-looking number resting on invented inputs.**

> **Blaney-Criddle with real temperature data may well be more reliable than Penman with fabricated ones, and it is more honest about its uncertainty.**

> **That is a general principle worth carrying: a sophisticated method fed with poor data is not better than a simple method fed with good data, and the appearance of rigour it lends can be actively misleading.**

**WHY PENMAN IS THEORETICALLY SUPERIOR, WHICH IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Evaporation requires ENERGY to change water from liquid to vapour** ← | **Supplied chiefly by solar radiation — the ENERGY BALANCE term** ← |
| **And it requires the vapour to be REMOVED from above the surface** ← | **By wind, into air that is not already saturated — the AERODYNAMIC term** ← |
| **Either can be the limiting factor** ← | **A still humid day limits by removal; a calm cool day limits by energy** ← |
| **Penman COMBINES both terms, weighted by their relative importance** ← | **Which is why it works across climates** ← |
| **A temperature-based method captures the energy term only, and that indirectly** ← | **So it performs poorly where wind and humidity dominate — in an arid, windy climate especially** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE INSIGHT THAT MAKES THE COMBINATION NECESSARY AND IT EXPLAINS WHERE SIMPLE METHODS FAIL: evaporation is limited sometimes by the supply of energy and sometimes by the removal of vapour.**

> **A method based on temperature alone assumes the energy term always governs, which is roughly true in a humid climate and quite false in a dry windy one — where a hot dry wind can drive evaporation far beyond what the radiation alone would support.**

> **This matters in Nepal because the country contains both conditions: the humid Terai in the monsoon and the dry, windy trans-Himalayan valleys of Mustang and Manang, where a temperature-based estimate would badly understate the demand.**

> **So the method's suitability varies within the country, and a national figure or a method chosen for the plains should not be applied to the northern valleys without checking.**

> **The CROP COEFFICIENT should also be mentioned, since it completes the calculation: all these methods estimate a REFERENCE evapotranspiration ET₀, for a standard grass surface, and the actual crop's use is ET_c = K_c × ET₀ — with K_c varying through the crop's growth stages from perhaps 0.3 at emergence to 1.15 at full cover and back down at maturity.**

examTip.trick: **Blaney-Criddle needs only temperature and latitude; Penman needs temperature, humidity, wind AND radiation.** Option (a) describes Penman.
examTip.trap: **Penman fed with invented humidity and wind is not more accurate than Blaney-Criddle fed with real temperatures** — sophistication with poor data is misleading precision.
examTip.mnemonic: **Evaporation needs ENERGY to vaporise and WIND to remove the vapour** — Penman combines both. Temperature-only methods fail in dry windy places like Mustang.

questions.stem: The KOR WATERING of a crop is:
options: The last watering given before harvest
The water applied during land preparation and puddling
The total water applied over the crop's whole base period
The first watering given after the plants have grown a few centimetres, applied within a limited kor period
questions.solution:
**The FIRST watering given after the plants have grown a few centimetres, applied within a limited KOR PERIOD** — and it is the watering that determines the canal's PEAK capacity, since the whole command demands it at nearly the same time.

**Why the kor watering governs the canal's design:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The kor watering must be given within a SHORT window — the kor period** ← | **Two to four weeks, depending on the crop** ← |
| **If it is delayed beyond that window, the crop's yield suffers** ← | **So it cannot be spread out at the operator's convenience** ← |
| **The whole command sows at about the same time, so it all needs the kor watering at about the same time** ← | ← |
| **The demand is therefore CONCENTRATED, and it is the season's peak** ← | ← |
| **The canal must be sized to deliver the kor depth over the whole area within the kor period** ← | **Which is the OUTLET DISCHARGE FACTOR calculation** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL POINT AND IT IS THE SAME SIMULTANEITY ARGUMENT MET IN WATER SUPPLY, HERE WORKING IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION: in a town, individual demands are staggered and the peak factor is modest.**

> **In an irrigation command, the demands are SYNCHRONISED by the agricultural calendar — everyone sows within days of one another and everyone needs the kor watering within the same fortnight.**

> **So there is no diversity to rely on, and the canal must carry very nearly the sum of all the individual peaks.**

> **This is why an irrigation canal's capacity is set by a single agronomic event rather than by an average demand, and why the kor period and the kor depth are the two figures that decide it.**

**THE KOR DEPTHS AND PERIODS, FOR REFERENCE:**

| Crop | Kor depth | Kor period |
|---|---|---|
| **RICE** ← | **190 mm** | **2 weeks** ← |
| **WHEAT** ← | **135 mm** | **4 weeks** ← |
| **SUGARCANE** | **165 mm** | **4 weeks** |
| **COTTON** | **100 mm** | **4 weeks** |
| **Maize** | **100 mm** | **4 weeks** |

> **RICE'S COMBINATION OF THE LARGEST DEPTH AND THE SHORTEST PERIOD IN THE FIRST ROW MAKES IT THE CROP THAT DICTATES CANAL CAPACITY WHEREVER IT IS GROWN, and the arithmetic shows why: 190 mm in 14 days demands twice the discharge that 135 mm in 28 days does.**

> **So a command with a substantial rice area needs a canal roughly twice the size that the same area under wheat would need, for that period alone.**

> **And since the canal is sized for its peak, that capacity sits largely unused for the rest of the year — which is one reason irrigation canals are so expensive relative to the water they deliver annually.**

**THE OUTLET DISCHARGE FACTOR CALCULATION, WHICH FOLLOWS DIRECTLY:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The outlet factor is the DUTY at the outlet during the kor period** ← | ← |
| **D = 8.64 × kor period in days ÷ kor depth in metres** ← | **The same relation as before, applied to the kor watering alone** ← |
| **For rice: D = 8.64 × 14 / 0.190 = 637 hectares per cumec** ← | ← |
| **For wheat: D = 8.64 × 28 / 0.135 = 1,792 hectares per cumec** ← | **Nearly three times as much land from the same discharge** ← |
| **The canal's capacity is then the area to be served divided by the weighted outlet factor** ← | ← |

> **The contrast between the third and fourth rows quantifies the point exactly: the same cumec serves 637 hectares of rice or 1,792 of wheat during the kor.**

> **So the CROPPING PATTERN determines the canal's size almost as directly as the area does, and a shift in the pattern after the canal is built changes what it can serve.**

> **This is the technical basis of the prescribed cropping pattern discussed earlier: it is not an interference for its own sake but the assumption on which the canal's capacity rests, and departing from it means the canal cannot deliver what the new pattern demands.**

verification.notes: Rice outlet factor 8.64 x 14/0.190 = 637 ha/cumec; wheat 8.64 x 28/0.135 = 1792 ha/cumec.

examTip.trick: **The FIRST watering after the plants appear, within a short kor period** — and the whole command needs it at once, so it sets the canal's peak.
examTip.trap: **No diversity to rely on** — unlike a town's demand, an irrigation command's demands are SYNCHRONISED by the agricultural calendar.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rice: 190 mm in 2 weeks. Wheat: 135 mm in 4.** So one cumec serves 637 ha of rice or 1,792 of wheat — the cropping pattern sizes the canal.

questions.stem: Compared with SURFACE (flood, border or furrow) irrigation, DRIP irrigation:
options: Applies water slowly and directly to the root zone of each plant
Requires a larger volume of water for the same crop
Cannot be used on sloping ground
Wets the whole soil surface uniformly
questions.solution:
**It applies water SLOWLY and DIRECTLY to the root zone of each plant**, so evaporation, deep percolation and weed growth between rows are all reduced — at the cost of a high capital outlay and a susceptibility to CLOGGING of the emitters.

**The methods of application compared:**

| Method | Application efficiency | Suited to |
|---|---|---|
| **WILD FLOODING** ← | **30 to 40 per cent — the least efficient** ← | **Flat land, abundant water, low-value crops** ← |
| **BORDER strip** | **50 to 60 per cent** | **Close-growing crops on gently graded land** ← |
| **CHECK BASIN** ← | **50 to 70 per cent** | **PADDY, and orchards — the standard Nepali method** ← |
| **FURROW** ← | **55 to 70 per cent** | **Row crops — maize, cotton, vegetables, potatoes** ← |
| **SPRINKLER** ← | **70 to 85 per cent** | **Undulating land, sandy soils, and where land levelling is impracticable** ← |
| **DRIP (trickle)** ← | **85 to 95 per cent — the highest** ← | **High-value row and orchard crops, scarce water, saline water** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION IS ONE OF INCREASING CONTROL AND INCREASING COST, AND THE CHOICE IS ECONOMIC AS MUCH AS TECHNICAL: drip's efficiency is worth paying for when the water is scarce or the crop is valuable, and not otherwise.**

> **A drip system costing several times a furrow system's capital, installed for a low-value cereal in a command with abundant monsoon water, will not repay its cost however efficient it is.**

> **So the appropriate method follows from the value of the water and the value of the crop, and both must be considered.**

**DRIP'S ADVANTAGES BEYOND EFFICIENCY, WHICH ARE OFTEN THE REAL REASONS FOR CHOOSING IT:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **The land BETWEEN the rows stays DRY** ← | **So weeds do not germinate there, saving weeding labour and herbicide — often a larger saving than the water** ← |
| **FERTILISER can be applied through the system (fertigation)** ← | **Placed precisely at the root, in the right quantity at the right time — a substantial agronomic gain** ← |
| **The soil is never SATURATED, so aeration is maintained continuously** ← | **Which many crops respond to markedly** ← |
| **SALINE water can be used more safely** ← | **The continuous slow application keeps the salts moving away from the root zone rather than concentrating there** ← |
| **It works on STEEP and irregular land** ← | **With pressure-compensating emitters** ← (so option c is wrong) |
| **Foliage stays DRY, reducing fungal disease** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS TOGETHER OFTEN JUSTIFY DRIP WHERE THE WATER SAVING ALONE WOULD NOT, AND THEY ARE WORTH RAISING IN ANY COMPARISON: the weeding labour saved and the fertiliser efficiency gained can exceed the value of the water.**

> **A farmer weighing drip against furrow is comparing total costs and total returns, not water use — so an argument made on water efficiency alone may fail to persuade even where the system is a good investment.**

**AND THE CLOGGING PROBLEM, WHICH IS DRIP'S CHARACTERISTIC FAILURE:**

| Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **PHYSICAL — sand, silt and organic particles** ← | **FILTRATION is essential — sand, screen or disc filters, cleaned regularly** ← |
| **CHEMICAL — precipitation of calcium carbonate and iron** ← | **Acid injection periodically; and it is worse with hard or iron-bearing groundwater** ← |
| **BIOLOGICAL — algae, bacterial slime and roots entering the emitters** ← | **Chlorination periodically; and keeping light off the lines to prevent algae** ← |
| **A blocked emitter is INVISIBLE** ← | **The plant it served simply dies, and by then the damage is done** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHY CLOGGING IS SO SERIOUS RATHER THAN MERELY INCONVENIENT AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS: nothing shows that an emitter has blocked until the plant it feeds is visibly suffering.**

> **With a furrow system a blockage is obvious — the water does not reach the end of the furrow — and it is corrected within minutes.**

> **With drip, each plant depends on its own emitter, and one blocked emitter kills one plant with no warning to anyone.**

> **So the FILTRATION and the maintenance regime are not accessories to a drip system but the thing that determines whether it works — and a system installed without adequate filtration, or with filters nobody cleans, degrades steadily and invisibly until a substantial fraction of the field is failing.**

> **That is the commonest reason drip installations disappoint, and it is a maintenance failure rather than a technical one — which makes it the more important to design for, since the technology cannot compensate for it.**

examTip.trick: **Slow application direct to the root zone** — less evaporation, less percolation, fewer weeds between rows. High capital cost and clogging are its price.
examTip.trap: **The weeding saving and fertigation often justify it where the water saving alone would not** — a farmer compares total costs, not water use.
examTip.mnemonic: **A blocked emitter is INVISIBLE and kills one plant silently** — unlike a blocked furrow, which is obvious at once. Filtration and maintenance decide whether drip works.

questions.stem: In the agricultural calendar of Nepal and northern India, the RABI season is:
options: The monsoon season, from June to October
The short hot-weather season between the other two
The winter season, sown about October or November and harvested in March or April
The season during which the land is left fallow
questions.solution:
**The WINTER season, sown about October or November and harvested in March or April** — the season in which irrigation is most valuable, since there is little rain.

**The three cropping seasons:**

| Season | Period | Character | Typical crops |
|---|---|---|---|
| **KHARIF (monsoon)** ← | **Sown June-July with the monsoon's onset, harvested September-October** ← | **Abundant rain; irrigation SUPPLEMENTS it** ← (option a) | **PADDY above all; maize, millet, jute, cotton, sugarcane** ← |
| **RABI (winter)** ← | **Sown October-November on the residual monsoon moisture, harvested March-April** ← | **LITTLE rain; irrigation is essential and its value is greatest** ← | **WHEAT, barley, gram, mustard, lentil, potato, winter vegetables** ← |
| **ZAID (hot weather, spring)** ← | **March-April to June — the short season between rabi and kharif** ← (option b) | **HOT and dry; entirely dependent on irrigation, and the water is scarcest** ← | **Melons, cucurbits, fodder, summer vegetables, spring maize** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FACT IN IRRIGATION PLANNING FOR THE REGION AND IT IS WORTH STATING AS A CONCLUSION: irrigation earns its keep in RABI, not in kharif.**

> **In kharif the monsoon supplies most of the crop's need, and irrigation makes the difference between a good crop and a slightly better one — or provides insurance against a break in the rains, which is real but intermittent value.**

> **In rabi there is almost no rain, so irrigation makes the difference between a crop and no crop at all.**

> **A scheme that delivers reliably in rabi transforms its command; one that delivers only in kharif adds comparatively little.**

> **And this is exactly where the hydrology is least helpful, since the rivers are lowest in the dry season — which is the central difficulty of surface irrigation in Nepal and the reason so many schemes' actual benefit falls short of their appraisal.**

**THE SOIL MOISTURE POINT IN THE RABI ROW DESERVES ITS OWN NOTE, SINCE IT IS OFTEN THE MARGIN OF VIABILITY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Rabi is sown into a profile FILLED by the monsoon** ← | ← |
| **So the first weeks may need no irrigation at all** ← | **The crop lives on stored moisture** ← |
| **The requirement builds as the profile is depleted and the crop grows** ← | ← |
| **A rabi crop in a good soil may need only two or three irrigations** ← | **Which a modest source can supply** ← |
| **The same crop on a SANDY soil, which stores little, needs many more** ← | **And may be unviable on the same source** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW EXPLAINS WHY A SMALL AND UNRELIABLE SOURCE CAN STILL BE WORTH DEVELOPING FOR RABI: two or three well-timed irrigations of a wheat crop can be the difference between a failure and a full yield.**

> **That is a much smaller volume than a kharif paddy crop would demand, and it falls at a time when the alternative is nothing.**

> **So a scheme too small to support paddy may be entirely viable as a rabi supplement — which is a conclusion that a design starting from paddy's requirement would never reach, and it is why the cropping pattern must be chosen to suit the water available rather than the water sized to suit an assumed pattern.**

> **THE ZAID SEASON IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST DEMANDING AND THE LEAST OFTEN PLANNED FOR, AND IT IS WORTH A CAUTION: it is entirely irrigation-dependent, it falls when the rivers are at their absolute minimum, and its crops are high in value.**

> **So the demand and the scarcity coincide exactly, and a scheme that permits zaid cropping without having the dry-season water to sustain it creates a conflict — the zaid crop competes with the rabi crop's final irrigations and with domestic and downstream needs.**

> **Whether to permit zaid cropping at all is therefore a real allocation decision for a scheme with a limited dry-season source, and one that should be settled deliberately rather than by whoever opens the gate first.**

examTip.trick: **Rabi is the WINTER season — October/November to March/April.** Kharif is the monsoon (a) and zaid the hot weather between (b).
examTip.trap: **Irrigation earns its keep in RABI, not kharif** — the difference between a crop and none, rather than between a good crop and a slightly better one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rabi is sown into a monsoon-filled profile**, so two or three irrigations may suffice — which makes a small source viable for rabi though useless for kharif paddy.

questions.stem: In a canal system, SEEPAGE losses are distinguished from EVAPORATION losses in that seepage:
options: Occurs only in lined canals
Is much the larger of the two
Is negligible compared with evaporation in a hot climate
Occurs only when the canal is running at full supply
questions.solution:
**It is much the LARGER of the two — commonly accounting for the great majority of the total conveyance loss** — and much of the seeped water is not truly lost but recharges the groundwater.

**The two losses compared:**

| Loss | Magnitude | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **SEEPAGE (percolation through the bed and banks)** ← | **The great majority — commonly 80 to 90 per cent of the total loss** ← | **Depends on the soil's permeability, the wetted perimeter, the depth of flow and the depth to the water table** ← |
| **EVAPORATION from the water surface** ← | **A small fraction — typically 1 to 2 per cent of the flow, and under 20 per cent of the total loss** ← | **Depends on the surface area, the temperature, the humidity and the wind** ← |

> **THE DOMINANCE OF SEEPAGE IS WORTH FIXING BECAUSE THE INTUITION RUNS THE OTHER WAY IN A HOT COUNTRY: evaporation is visible, is associated with heat, and feels as though it should matter most.**

> **In fact a canal's water surface is narrow relative to its length and the evaporation from it is a few millimetres a day, which against a substantial depth of flow is a small proportion.**

> **Seepage acts over the whole wetted perimeter — bed and both banks — continuously, and through an unlined alluvial bed it can be very large indeed.**

> **So a measure that reduces evaporation, such as covering a canal, addresses the smaller loss at greater cost, while LINING addresses the larger one — which is why lining is the standard remedy and covering is not.**

**THE QUALIFICATION IN THE ANSWER — THAT SEEPED WATER IS NOT ALL LOST — IS THE MORE INTERESTING POINT AND IT DESERVES DEVELOPING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water seeping from a canal enters the GROUNDWATER** ← | ← |
| **It is therefore available to be PUMPED from wells in the command** ← | **And in many commands it is a major source of recharge** ← |
| **So at the BASIN scale it has not left the system** ← | **Only at the canal's own accounting boundary** ← |
| **Lining a canal REDUCES that recharge** ← | **And in a command dependent on wells, lining the canals can lower the water table and reduce well yields** ← |
| **Which is a genuine and documented consequence rather than a theoretical one** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE RESULT AND IT PARALLELS THE DRIP IRRIGATION POINT EXACTLY: an efficiency improvement at one scale can be a loss at another.**

> **The canal authority lines its canals and reports a large saving; the well owners in the command find their water table falling and their pumping costs rising.**

> **The water 'saved' was water they were using.**

> **This does not make lining wrong — the seepage may be recharging a saline aquifer, or causing waterlogging, or emerging uselessly downstream — but it does mean the saving must be assessed on a BASIN water balance rather than on the canal's own losses.**

> **The question to ask of any claimed water saving is: where was that water going before, and who was using it?**

> **If the answer is 'into a saline aquifer' or 'to the sea', the saving is real; if it is 'to the wells in the command', it is a transfer rather than a saving.**

**WHERE SEEPAGE IS UNAMBIGUOUSLY HARMFUL, WHICH IS WHERE LINING IS UNAMBIGUOUSLY RIGHT:**

| Case | Note |
|---|---|
| **Where it causes WATERLOGGING of the adjoining land** ← | **A canal in embankment across a flat command raises the water table around it, and the land beside the canal is often the first to waterlog** ← |
| **Where the water table is already high** ← | **Any addition is harmful** ← |
| **Where the groundwater is SALINE** ← | **So the recharge cannot be used, and raising the table brings salt to the surface** ← |
| **Where the seepage causes SLOPE INSTABILITY** ← | **A canal on a hillside — the Nepali case — where seepage saturates the slope below and triggers landslides** ← |
| **And where the water is genuinely scarce and the recharge is not recovered** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DECISIVE CASE IN NEPAL'S HILLS AND IT IS DIFFERENT IN KIND FROM THE PLAINS ARGUMENT: a hill canal's seepage does not recharge a usable aquifer, it saturates the slope it is cut into.**

> **The consequence is not a lost resource but a landslide, which takes the canal with it and often the land and houses below.**

> **So lining a hill canal is a SLOPE STABILITY measure as much as a water conservation one, and the case for it is far stronger than the water saving alone would suggest — which is worth arguing when the lining is questioned on cost.**

examTip.trick: **Seepage is 80-90 % of the conveyance loss; evaporation is a small fraction** — despite the intuition in a hot climate. Hence lining, not covering.
examTip.trap: **Seeped water largely RECHARGES the groundwater** — so lining can lower the water table and reduce well yields. Assess savings on a basin balance, not the canal's own.
examTip.mnemonic: **In the hills, canal seepage saturates the SLOPE and triggers landslides** — so lining there is a stability measure, and the case is far stronger than water saving alone.

questions.stem: WARABANDI is a system of distributing irrigation water in which:
options: Each farmer takes water whenever the canal is running
Water is sold by volume through a meter at each outlet
Water is delivered continuously to every field at a small rate
Each landholding receives the water of the whole outlet for a fixed turn of a fixed duration on a fixed day of a weekly cycle
questions.solution:
**Each landholding receives the water of the whole outlet for a FIXED TURN of a fixed duration on a fixed day of a weekly cycle**, the turn's length being proportional to the holding's area.

**How the system works:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The outlet runs CONTINUOUSLY at its designed discharge whenever the distributary is running** ← | ← |
| **The whole of that flow goes to ONE farmer at a time** ← | **Not shared simultaneously** ← |
| **Each farmer's TURN is a fixed number of hours per week** ← | **Proportional to his area — so many minutes per hectare** ← |
| **The turns follow a fixed ROSTER, published and known to all** ← | **Same day, same hours, every week** ← |
| **The cycle is typically SEVEN days** ← | ← |
| **The farmer takes his turn whether he needs it or not** ← | **And gets nothing outside it** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL DESIGN IDEA AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY IT MATTERS: giving one farmer the whole flow for a short time is far better than giving every farmer a share of it continuously.**

> **A large flow for a short period fills the field channels quickly, reaches the far end of the field, and wets the land efficiently.**

> **A trickle to every field continuously loses most of itself in the channels, never reaches the tail of the field, and irrigates nothing properly.**

> **So concentrating the flow in time is a genuine efficiency gain, and it is the same principle as running canals in rotation rather than all at part supply.**

**WHAT WARABANDI ACHIEVES, WHICH IS MORE ABOUT EQUITY THAN EFFICIENCY:**

| Achievement | Note |
|---|---|
| **EQUITY — every farmer gets a share proportional to his LAND, regardless of his influence** ← | **Which is its principal purpose** ← |
| **PREDICTABILITY — a farmer knows exactly when his water will come** ← | **So he can prepare his field, arrange labour and plan his sowing** ← |
| **It requires NO measurement, NO gates at each field and NO official present** ← | **The roster and the clock do the whole job** ← |
| **And it distributes a SHORTAGE fairly** ← | **When the supply falls, every turn is shortened proportionally rather than the head-enders taking all of it** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHY THE SYSTEM HAS SURVIVED AND SPREAD, AND IT IS AN IMPORTANT PRACTICAL VIRTUE: warabandi requires almost no institutional capacity.**

> **There are no meters to read, no valves to set, no water charges to compute by volume, and no official to be present or to be bribed.**

> **A written roster and a functioning clock are sufficient, and the farmers themselves enforce it because each one's turn is threatened by anyone who overruns.**

> **In a setting where the irrigation department cannot be present at every outlet every day — which is every setting — that self-enforcing quality is worth more than any technically superior arrangement that depends on supervision.**

**ITS LIMITATIONS, WHICH ARE REAL AND WORTH STATING:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is INFLEXIBLE — the turn comes when it comes, not when the crop needs water** ← | **A farmer whose crop needs water on Tuesday and whose turn is Friday must wait** ← |
| **It takes NO account of the crop, the soil or the weather** ← | **Everyone gets the same rate per hectare whether they grow paddy or gram** ← |
| **Which discourages high-value and water-sensitive crops** ← | **Since their requirements cannot be met on a fixed schedule** ← |
| **It assumes the supply is RELIABLE enough for the roster to mean anything** ← | **A roster nobody can rely on is worse than none** ← |
| **And it can entrench the disadvantage of TAIL-enders** ← | **If the channel losses mean the tail's turn delivers less water than the head's** ← |

> **THE FIRST THREE ROWS TOGETHER DESCRIBE THE TRADE THAT WARABANDI MAKES AND IT IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT: it purchases EQUITY and SIMPLICITY at the cost of FLEXIBILITY.**

> **A demand-based system in which farmers order water when they need it is agronomically superior and requires an institutional capacity — measurement, communication, scheduling, enforcement — that few systems possess.**

> **So warabandi is the right answer where that capacity is absent, and it becomes the wrong answer as agriculture intensifies and diversifies toward crops whose value justifies a more responsive service.**

> **That transition is where many South Asian systems now find themselves, and it is a difficult one — because the institutional arrangements that a flexible service requires cannot simply be declared, and abandoning warabandi before they exist gives neither equity nor flexibility.**

examTip.trick: **The whole outlet flow to one farmer at a time, for a fixed turn proportional to his area, on a fixed weekly roster.**
examTip.trap: **A large flow for a short time beats a trickle continuously** — it reaches the field's far end instead of being lost in the channels. Concentration in time is an efficiency gain.
examTip.mnemonic: **It is SELF-ENFORCING and needs no meters, gates or officials** — which is why it survives. It buys equity and simplicity at the cost of flexibility.

questions.stem: CONJUNCTIVE USE of surface water and groundwater in an irrigated command means:
options: Managing the two sources together as a single resource
Using groundwater only where surface water is unavailable
Mixing canal water and well water before application to improve its quality
Abandoning surface irrigation in favour of tube wells
questions.solution:
**Managing the two sources TOGETHER as a single resource** — using surface water when it is plentiful and pumping groundwater when it is not, so that the aquifer acts as a natural reservoir and the water table is controlled.

**Why the combination is more than the sum of its parts:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **The AQUIFER acts as a RESERVOIR** ← | **Storing the monsoon's surplus underground, where it does not evaporate, needs no dam, floods no land and displaces nobody** ← |
| **Surface water is used in the WET season when it is abundant** ← | **And it recharges the aquifer as it goes, through canal seepage and field percolation** ← |
| **Groundwater is pumped in the DRY season when the rivers are low** ← | **From the store that the wet season built up** ← |
| **The pumping LOWERS the water table, which controls WATERLOGGING** ← | **So the drainage problem and the dry-season supply problem solve one another** ← |
| **And the combined system is far more RELIABLE than either alone** ← | **Groundwater covers a failed monsoon; surface water covers a power failure** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ELEGANT PART OF THE ARRANGEMENT AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: the two great problems of a surface-irrigated command are a shortage of water in the dry season and a rising water table causing waterlogging.**

> **Conjunctive use addresses both with a single measure, because pumping the groundwater is simultaneously a supply and a drainage operation.**

> **The water that was causing the waterlogging becomes the water that irrigates the rabi crop.**

> **That is a genuinely satisfying resolution — two problems that would each require expensive works are cancelled against one another — and it is why conjunctive use is so strongly advocated for the Indo-Gangetic commands.**

**THE STORAGE COMPARISON IN THE FIRST ROW IS WORTH QUANTIFYING, SINCE IT IS THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT:**

| Aspect | SURFACE reservoir | AQUIFER storage |
|---|---|---|
| **Evaporation loss** | **LARGE — metres per year from the surface** ← | **NONE** ← |
| **Land submerged** | **A great deal** ← | **NONE** ← |
| **People displaced** | **Often many** ← | **None** ← |
| **Sedimentation** | **Progressive loss of capacity** ← | **Not applicable** ← |
| **Capital cost** | **Very high** ← | **Nil — the aquifer exists** ← |
| **Recovery cost** | **Nil, gravity** ← | **PUMPING energy, continuously** ← |
| **Distribution** | **Requires a canal network** ← | **The well is where the water is needed** ← |

> **THE TRADE IS IN THE LAST TWO ROWS AND IT IS A CLEAR ONE: a surface reservoir costs a great deal to build and nothing to draw from, and an aquifer costs nothing to build and a permanent energy bill to draw from.**

> **So the balance depends on the cost and reliability of ENERGY, which is precisely the variable that is unfavourable in Nepal and much of the region.**

> **Where power is expensive, unreliable or absent, groundwater's advantages are heavily discounted — and where it is cheap and reliable, aquifer storage is superior to a dam in almost every respect.**

**THE FAILURE MODE OF CONJUNCTIVE USE, WHICH MUST BE GUARDED AGAINST:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The arrangement depends on the aquifer being RECHARGED as much as it is pumped** ← | ← |
| **If pumping exceeds recharge, the water table falls YEAR ON YEAR — MINING the aquifer** ← | ← |
| **Which is not conjunctive use but the consumption of a stock** ← | ← |
| **The consequences are rising pumping costs, wells running dry, land SUBSIDENCE, and in coastal areas SALINE INTRUSION** ← | ← |
| **And the decline is invisible until it is far advanced** ← | **Since nobody sees the water table** ← |
| **So MONITORING of the water table is the indispensable requirement** ← | **A network of observation wells, read regularly, is what distinguishes management from extraction** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION AND IT IS THE ELEMENT MOST OFTEN ABSENT: conjunctive use requires knowing what the water table is doing, and that requires measuring it.**

> **Without observation wells, a command practising 'conjunctive use' is simply a command where people pump, and whether the aquifer is in balance or in decline is unknown to everyone.**

> **The measurement is cheap — a network of simple observation wells and a schedule of readings — and it is the difference between managing a resource and discovering, twenty years later, that it has gone.**

> **In the Terai, where tube well irrigation has expanded rapidly, that monitoring network is the single most valuable investment in groundwater management available, and it costs a fraction of one deep tube well.**

examTip.trick: **Manage both as ONE resource** — surface water in the wet season (recharging as it goes), groundwater in the dry, with the aquifer as the reservoir.
examTip.trap: **Pumping solves the dry-season shortage AND the waterlogging at once** — the water causing the problem becomes the water irrigating the rabi crop.
examTip.mnemonic: **Aquifer storage: no evaporation, no submergence, no displacement, no cost to build — but a permanent PUMPING bill.** The balance turns on energy cost.

questions.stem: A run-of-river irrigation intake is to be designed on a Himalayan river. The DESIGN DISCHARGE for the diversion should be based on:
options: The river's mean annual flow
The river's monsoon peak flow
The dependable dry-season flow at a stated exceedance probability
The flood of a 100-year return period
questions.solution:
**The DEPENDABLE dry-season flow at a stated exceedance probability** — since it is the MINIMUM available flow, not the average, that limits what the scheme can reliably serve.

**Which flow governs which element, since the question's options are all real design flows for something:**

| Flow | What it governs |
|---|---|
| **DEPENDABLE LOW flow (say 80 per cent exceedance in the driest month)** ← | **The AREA the scheme can reliably irrigate — this question** ← |
| **MEAN annual flow** ← | **Little directly; it is a resource statistic, not a design value** ← (option a) |
| **The MONSOON high flow** ← | **The capacity of the intake's silt excluder and the settling arrangements** ← (option b) |
| **The DESIGN FLOOD, 50 to 100 years** ← | **The WEIR, the barrage, the guide banks, the flood protection and the founding levels** ← (option d) |
| **The maximum probable flood** ← | **The safety check for a large structure** ← |

> **THE POINT OF THE QUESTION IS THAT A SINGLE STRUCTURE IS DESIGNED AGAINST SEVERAL DIFFERENT FLOWS, AND EACH ELEMENT TAKES THE ONE THAT THREATENS IT:**

> **The intake's CAPACITY is limited by the least flow available.**

> **The weir's STABILITY is threatened by the greatest.**

> **The sediment works are sized for the flow that carries the most sediment, which is neither extreme but the rising monsoon flow.**

> **So a design that adopts one flow throughout has got most of the structure wrong, and the first step in any headworks design is to establish the several design flows and assign each to what it governs.**

**WHY THE MEAN FLOW IS PARTICULARLY MISLEADING IN A HIMALAYAN RIVER, WHICH IS WORTH QUANTIFYING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The monsoon flow may be TWENTY to FIFTY times the dry-season flow** ← | **Or more on a smaller, rain-fed catchment** ← |
| **So the MEAN is dominated by the monsoon and bears no relation to the dry-season minimum** ← | ← |
| **A scheme sized on the mean has several times the water it will actually have in April** ← | ← |
| **And its command, developed on that basis, then fails in the season irrigation matters most** ← | **Which is the rabi and zaid conclusion reached earlier** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES A FAILURE PATTERN COMMON ENOUGH TO BE WORTH NAMING AND IT IS AN APPRAISAL FAILURE RATHER THAN AN ENGINEERING ONE: the scheme is built, the command is developed, the farmers plant a rabi crop, and there is not enough water.**

> **The works are sound and the hydrology was wrong, or rather the right hydrology was computed and the wrong statistic was used from it.**

> **The consequence falls on the farmers, who have invested in a cropping pattern the scheme cannot sustain, and it is not correctable — the river has the flow it has.**

**WHAT DEPENDABILITY LEVEL TO CHOOSE, WHICH IS A REAL DECISION:**

| Level | Meaning | Appropriate to |
|---|---|---|
| **50 per cent (the median)** ← | **Available in half the years** ← | **Nothing; a scheme fails every other year** ← |
| **75 to 80 per cent** ← | **Available in 3 or 4 years out of 5** ← | **The usual irrigation standard** ← |
| **90 per cent and above** ← | **Available in 9 years out of 10** ← | **Domestic supply, and high-value or perennial crops where failure is very costly** ← |

> **THE CHOICE IS AN ECONOMIC ONE AND IT SHOULD BE MADE EXPLICITLY: a higher dependability means a smaller command served more reliably, and a lower one means a larger command that fails more often.**

> **Neither is right in the abstract — it depends on what the crop is worth, what a failure costs the farmer, and whether he has an alternative.**

> **A subsistence farmer with no other source needs high dependability, because a failure means hunger; a farmer with a well as a backup can accept a lower level from the canal, because his fallback exists.**

> **Which returns to the conjunctive use argument from a different direction: the presence of groundwater does not merely add water, it allows the surface scheme to be designed to a lower dependability and therefore to serve a larger area — and that interaction is missed entirely if the two sources are planned by separate agencies, as they usually are.**

examTip.trick: **The dependable DRY-SEASON flow** — the minimum available limits what the scheme can serve. The mean and the flood govern other things.
examTip.trap: **Every option is a real design flow for SOMETHING** — the flood sizes the weir, the monsoon sizes the sediment works, the low flow sizes the command.
examTip.mnemonic: **Monsoon flow can be 20-50 times the dry-season flow**, so the mean says nothing about April. A scheme sized on the mean fails in the season that matters.

questions.stem: The CROP FACTOR (crop coefficient) K_c used with a reference evapotranspiration ET₀:
options: Is a constant for each crop throughout its growing season
Varies through the crop's growth stages
Applies only to the reference grass crop
Converts the actual evapotranspiration into the reference value
questions.solution:
**It VARIES through the crop's growth stages** — low at emergence when the ground is bare, rising to a maximum at full canopy cover, and falling again as the crop matures and senesces.

**The four growth stages and their coefficients:**

| Stage | Description | Typical K_c |
|---|---|---|
| **INITIAL** ← | **From sowing to about 10 per cent ground cover; the soil is mostly bare and the loss is chiefly EVAPORATION from the soil surface** ← | **0.3 to 0.5** ← |
| **CROP DEVELOPMENT** ← | **From 10 per cent cover to full cover; K_c rises steadily** ← | **Rising** ← |
| **MID-SEASON** ← | **Full canopy, through flowering to early maturity; TRANSPIRATION dominates and the demand is at its greatest** ← | **1.05 to 1.20 — the MAXIMUM** ← |
| **LATE SEASON** ← | **Ripening and senescence; the leaves die back and the crop is often deliberately dried before harvest** ← | **Falling to 0.3 to 0.6** ← |

> **THE PHYSICAL REASON FOR THE SHAPE IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING AND IT MAKES THE CURVE PREDICTABLE FOR ANY CROP: K_c measures how much water the crop and its soil lose relative to a full grass cover.**

> **At the initial stage there is almost no crop, so the loss is soil evaporation from a mostly bare field — much less than a full grass sward would transpire, hence K_c well below 1.**

> **At mid-season the crop covers the ground completely and is transpiring at full rate, often exceeding the short reference grass — hence K_c above 1.**

> **At the end the leaves are dying and transpiring little — hence a fall.**

> **So the curve's shape follows the crop's LEAF AREA, and a crop's K_c curve can be sketched from knowing how its canopy develops, without looking anything up.**

**THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR SCHEDULING, WHICH IS THE POINT OF USING K_c AT ALL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **ET_c = K_c × ET₀** ← | **The crop's actual water need is the reference value scaled by the coefficient** ← |
| **So the requirement CHANGES through the season even if the weather does not** ← | ← |
| **A schedule based on a single average K_c OVER-irrigates early and UNDER-irrigates at mid-season** ← | ← |
| **The mid-season under-irrigation is the damaging half** ← | **Because mid-season includes FLOWERING and grain filling, the stages most sensitive to stress** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE REASON THE VARIATION MATTERS AGRONOMICALLY RATHER THAN JUST ARITHMETICALLY: the peak demand and the peak sensitivity coincide.**

> **A crop's need is greatest at exactly the growth stage where a shortage costs the most yield, so an averaged schedule fails in the worst possible way.**

> **This is why irrigation scheduling is stated by growth stage rather than by a uniform interval, and why the CRITICAL PERIODS of each crop — for wheat, crown root initiation, flowering and grain filling; for maize, tasselling and silking — are identified and protected even when the water is short.**

> **If a supply must be rationed, the correct response is not to reduce every irrigation proportionally but to protect the critical stages and accept a shortfall at the insensitive ones — which is DEFICIT IRRIGATION applied deliberately, and it can produce nearly the full yield on substantially less water.**

> **THE FIRST STAGE'S HIGH SOIL EVAPORATION IN THE FIRST ROW ALSO POINTS AT A PRACTICAL MEASURE WORTH NOTING: early in the season most of the loss is from a bare soil surface, and it is entirely unproductive.**

> **MULCHING the surface — with straw, residues or plastic — suppresses that evaporation almost completely, and the water saved is water the crop never had access to anyway.**

> **So mulching is one of the few measures that saves water without any agronomic penalty, and its benefit is concentrated in exactly the stage where K_c shows the loss to be least useful.**

examTip.trick: **Low at emergence, peak at full canopy (1.05-1.20), falling at senescence** — the curve follows the crop's LEAF AREA.
examTip.trap: **ET_c = K_c × ET₀** — K_c scales the reference upward or downward. Option (d) has the conversion backwards.
examTip.mnemonic: **Peak demand and peak SENSITIVITY coincide at mid-season** — so if water must be rationed, protect the critical stages rather than cutting every irrigation equally.

questions.stem: A canal outlet (module) described as RIGID or NON-MODULAR:
options: Delivers a constant discharge regardless of the water levels on either side of it
Delivers a discharge proportional to the distributary's discharge
Automatically closes when the field is fully irrigated
Delivers a discharge that varies with the water levels both upstream and downstream
questions.solution:
