**It delivers a discharge that VARIES with the water levels BOTH upstream and downstream** — such as a simple pipe or an open sluice, which is cheap but gives the cultivator no protection against fluctuation and can be tampered with.

**The classification of outlets:**

| Type | Discharge depends on |
|---|---|
| **NON-MODULAR** ← | **BOTH the upstream and downstream water levels — a simple submerged pipe or open sluice** ← |
| **SEMI-MODULE (flexible module)** ← | **The UPSTREAM level only — the downstream level having no effect, provided the outlet runs free** ← |
| **RIGID MODULE** ← | **NEITHER — the discharge is CONSTANT within a range of levels** ← (which is option a) |

> **THE QUESTION'S PHRASING DELIBERATELY PAIRS TWO TERMS THAT ARE OFTEN CONFUSED, AND THE DISTINCTION MATTERS: 'rigid module' and 'non-modular' are OPPOSITES, not synonyms.**

> **A rigid module gives a fixed discharge; a non-modular outlet gives a discharge that varies with everything.**

> **The word 'module' refers to the outlet's ability to MODULATE — to hold its discharge steady against changing conditions — so 'non-modular' means it does not, and 'rigid module' means it does so completely.**

**THE PRACTICAL BEHAVIOUR OF EACH, WHICH DECIDES WHERE IT IS USED:**

| Type | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| **NON-MODULAR (pipe outlet)** ← | **Cheap, simple, no moving parts, easily built and repaired locally** ← | **Discharge varies with both levels, so the share is unpredictable; easily TAMPERED with by damming the watercourse below** ← |
| **SEMI-MODULE (open flume, orifice semi-module)** ← | **Discharge independent of the downstream level, so tampering below is ineffective; still simple** ← | **Varies with the distributary's level, so the share falls when the canal runs low** ← |
| **RIGID MODULE (Gibb's module)** ← | **Constant discharge whatever the levels — the fairest** ← | **Complex, expensive, needs maintenance, and it takes NO account of the distributary's actual availability** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CONTAINS A DISADVANTAGE OF THE RIGID MODULE THAT IS EASILY MISSED AND IS DECISIVE IN A SHORTAGE: a constant-discharge outlet takes its full share even when the canal is short of water.**

> **So the head-end outlets draw their full entitlement and the tail of the distributary receives nothing at all.**

> **A SEMI-MODULE, whose discharge falls as the distributary's level falls, distributes the shortage automatically — every outlet gets proportionally less, and the tail still gets something.**

> **That self-adjusting property makes the semi-module the preferred type in practice despite the rigid module's theoretical superiority, and it is a good example of a device that performs worse under ideal conditions and better under real ones.**

**THE TAMPERING POINT DESERVES ITS OWN NOTE BECAUSE IT DRIVES THE CHOICE MORE THAN ANY HYDRAULIC CONSIDERATION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A non-modular outlet's discharge rises if the downstream level is LOWERED** ← | **By deepening or clearing the watercourse** ← |
| **And it rises if the upstream level is RAISED** ← | **By placing an obstruction in the distributary just below the outlet** ← |
| **Both are easily done with a shovel and are hard to detect** ← | **The obstruction is removed before the inspector arrives** ← |
| **The water gained comes directly from the outlets DOWNSTREAM** ← | **So tampering is not a victimless act; it is a transfer from the tail-enders** ← |
| **A semi-module removes half the opportunity and a rigid module all of it** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHY OUTLET DESIGN IS AS MUCH A SOCIAL QUESTION AS A HYDRAULIC ONE AND IT IS WORTH SEEING CLEARLY: in a canal running short of water, every litre one farmer takes above his share is a litre another farmer does not get.**

> **The outlet is the point at which that competition is either governed or left open, and a design that can be manipulated will be.**

> **So the case for the more expensive outlet is not hydraulic elegance but the protection of the tail-enders, who are invariably the poorest and least able to protest — and that is an argument that should be made in those terms rather than in terms of discharge coefficients.**

examTip.trick: **Non-modular: depends on BOTH levels. Semi-module: upstream only. Rigid module: NEITHER — constant discharge.** Option (a) is the rigid module.
examTip.trap: **'Rigid module' and 'non-modular' are OPPOSITES, not synonyms** — 'module' means the ability to hold discharge steady, so 'non-modular' means it cannot.
examTip.mnemonic: **A rigid module takes its full share even in a shortage, starving the tail** — a semi-module's discharge falls with the canal, distributing the shortage automatically.

questions.stem: A canal aligned along the RIDGE (watershed) line of a tract, as distinct from a contour canal, has the advantage that it:
options: Can irrigate the land on both sides by gravity, and it requires no CROSS-DRAINAGE works
Follows a shorter route between two points
Requires less excavation than any other alignment
Can be aligned without any survey
questions.solution:
**It can irrigate the land on BOTH SIDES by gravity, and it requires NO CROSS-DRAINAGE works, since no natural drainage crosses a watershed.**

**The three alignments:**

| Alignment | Description | Suited to |
|---|---|---|
| **RIDGE (watershed) canal** ← | **Follows the watershed between two drainages** ← | **The PLAINS, where a ridge line can be followed — the ideal alignment** ← |
| **CONTOUR canal** ← | **Follows a contour, with the land falling away on one side** ← | **HILLY country, where no usable ridge exists** ← |
| **SIDE SLOPE canal** ← | **Runs down the slope, roughly at right angles to the contours, parallel to the natural drainage** ← | **Where the canal must descend; it crosses no drainage but commands little** ← |

> **THE TWO ADVANTAGES OF THE RIDGE ALIGNMENT ARE BOTH CONSEQUENCES OF ONE FACT AND IT IS WORTH SEEING THE FACT FIRST: a watershed is, by definition, the line from which water flows AWAY in both directions.**

> **So a canal on it commands the land falling away on either side, which doubles the area served per kilometre of canal.**

> **And no natural stream can cross it, because water does not flow uphill onto a watershed — so there is nothing to be carried over, under or through.**

> **Both advantages follow from the definition, which is why the ridge alignment is sought wherever the topography permits.**

**THE COST OF CROSS-DRAINAGE WORKS IS THE LARGER OF THE TWO SAVINGS AND IT IS WORTH QUANTIFYING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A CONTOUR canal cuts across every stream and gully on the hillside** ← | ← |
| **Each crossing needs an AQUEDUCT, a SUPER-PASSAGE, a SIPHON or a LEVEL CROSSING** ← | **Each a substantial structure** ← |
| **A long contour canal may need dozens of them** ← | **And they can be the greater part of its cost** ← |
| **Each is also a maintenance liability and a point of failure** ← | **Blocked by debris in a flood, or breached** ← |
| **A ridge canal needs NONE of them** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE OPERATIONAL POINT AS WELL AS THE CAPITAL ONE: cross-drainage structures are where a hill canal fails.**

> **A monsoon flood in a side stream arrives with boulders and debris, blocks the super-passage or overtops the aqueduct, and breaches the canal — and the canal is then out of service until it is repaired, which may be weeks.**

> **So every cross-drainage work avoided is both a capital saving and a removed vulnerability, and the alignment that avoids them is worth going some distance out of the way for.**

**IN NEPAL, HOWEVER, THE RIDGE ALIGNMENT IS OFTEN UNAVAILABLE AND IT IS WORTH SAYING WHY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A ridge canal requires a ridge that is at a suitable LEVEL relative to the source** ← | **The water must reach the ridge, and in hill country the ridges are high** ← |
| **In the Terai, ridge alignments are used and work well** ← | **The classic plains arrangement** ← |
| **In the hills, the source is a river in a valley and the land is on the slopes above it** ← | **So the canal must be a CONTOUR canal, running along the hillside from an intake upstream** ← |
| **And it therefore crosses every gully** ← | ← |
| **So Nepali hill irrigation is dominated by contour canals with many cross-drainage works** ← | **Which is why such schemes are expensive per hectare and vulnerable in the monsoon** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW EXPLAINS A GREAT DEAL ABOUT THE ECONOMICS OF HILL IRRIGATION IN NEPAL AND IT SHOULD BE STATED PLAINLY: a hill scheme's cost is dominated by the conveyance, not by the headworks or the command.**

> **A canal contouring for ten kilometres along a hillside to reach a hundred hectares of terraces is a great deal of structure for a small command, and it must cross a gully every few hundred metres.**

> **This is why HDPE pipe has displaced open canal for many small hill schemes: a pipe crosses a gully on a simple support or in a shallow trench, needs no aqueduct, loses nothing to seepage, cannot be blocked by a landslide falling into it, and can follow the ground's undulations without a structure at every dip.**

> **The pipe costs more per metre and eliminates most of the structures, and on a small scheme in broken country that trade is decisively favourable — which is a case of a modern material changing the appropriate design rather than merely substituting for an old one.**

examTip.trick: **Commands both sides AND needs no cross-drainage** — both follow from the definition of a watershed: water flows away from it in both directions.
examTip.trap: **Cross-drainage works can be the greater part of a contour canal's cost** — and they are where it fails in a monsoon flood.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepal's hills force CONTOUR alignments**, so hill schemes are conveyance-dominated — which is why HDPE pipe, needing no aqueducts, has displaced open canals on small schemes.

questions.stem: KENNEDY'S theory of the design of a stable alluvial canal is based on the concept of:
options: A regime perimeter determined by the discharge alone
A critical velocity that neither silts nor scours
The tractive force exerted by the flow on the bed particles
The maximum permissible velocity for the lining material
questions.solution:
**The CRITICAL VELOCITY — the velocity that will just keep the silt in suspension without either depositing it or scouring the bed** — which he related to the DEPTH of flow.

**Kennedy's proposition:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **He observed canals on the Upper Bari Doab that had run for years WITHOUT silting or scouring** ← | **And reasoned that their velocity must be the 'right' one** ← |
| **He called that the CRITICAL VELOCITY, V₀** ← | ← |
| **And found it depended on the DEPTH of flow: V₀ = 0.55 m y^0.64** ← | **y being the depth in metres and m the CRITICAL VELOCITY RATIO for the silt's coarseness** ← |
| **m = 1.0 for the silt of the Upper Bari Doab** ← | **Greater than 1 for coarser silt, less for finer** ← |
| **The eddies that keep silt in suspension rise from the BED, so their strength depends on the depth** ← | **Which is his physical justification for depth rather than the hydraulic radius** ← |

> **THE DEPENDENCE ON DEPTH IN THE THIRD ROW IS KENNEDY'S DISTINCTIVE CONTRIBUTION AND HIS REASONING FOR IT IS WORTH KNOWING: he argued that the silt is held up by eddies generated at the BED, which rise through the water column.**

> **A deeper channel generates stronger eddies over a longer rise, so it can support a higher silt load at a given velocity — or equivalently needs a higher velocity to be in balance.**

> **That is a physical argument rather than a curve fit, and it is why the relation uses the depth rather than the hydraulic radius or the area.**

> **Whether it is correct in detail is another matter, and Lacey's later work took a different view — but the reasoning is sound enough to be worth understanding rather than dismissing.**

**THE PROCEDURE, AND ITS WEAKNESS:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **ASSUME a depth y** ← | ← |
| **Compute V₀ from Kennedy's relation** ← | ← |
| **Compute the area A = Q/V₀** ← | ← |
| **Assume a side slope and a B/y ratio, and find B** ← | ← |
| **Compute the velocity from KUTTER'S or Manning's formula with an assumed BED SLOPE** ← | ← |
| **Compare with V₀; if they differ, assume a new depth and repeat** ← | **A trial-and-error solution** ← |

> **THE WEAKNESS IS IN THE FOURTH AND FIFTH STEPS AND IT IS THE CENTRAL CRITICISM OF THE METHOD: Kennedy gives ONE equation and the problem has THREE unknowns — the bed width, the depth and the slope.**

> **So two of them must be ASSUMED, and the answer depends on what is assumed.**

> **The B/y ratio comes from experience or from tables, and the bed slope from the available ground slope or from a rule of thumb.**

> **Two designers using Kennedy's method on the same problem can therefore produce different canals, both satisfying the theory.**

> **That indeterminacy is what Lacey's regime theory set out to remove, by providing enough independent relations to fix all three unknowns from the discharge and the silt grade alone.**

**THE COMPARISON WITH LACEY, WHICH IS THE STANDARD EXAMINATION PAIRING:**

| Aspect | KENNEDY | LACEY |
|---|---|---|
| **Basis** | **Critical velocity related to DEPTH** ← | **A REGIME condition relating perimeter, area and slope to discharge and silt** ← |
| **Silt characterised by** | **Critical velocity ratio m** ← | **SILT FACTOR f** ← |
| **Number of independent relations** | **ONE — so B, y and S cannot all be determined** ← | **Enough to fix them ALL** ← |
| **Resistance formula** | **KUTTER'S, applied separately** ← | **Built into the regime relations** ← |
| **Shape** | **Trapezoidal, assumed** ← | **A SEMI-ELLIPSE is the true regime shape, approximated by a trapezoid** ← |
| **Slope** | **Assumed** ← | **DERIVED — S = f^(5/3)/(3340 Q^(1/6))** ← |
| **Silt transport** | **Considered only through the critical velocity** | **Considered through the whole regime concept** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND SIXTH ROWS ARE THE SUBSTANCE OF LACEY'S ADVANCE AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT: Lacey's method DETERMINES the bed slope, and Kennedy's requires it to be assumed.**

> **That matters practically because the slope is the parameter a designer has least freedom over — it is largely fixed by the ground — so a method that tells you what slope the canal REQUIRES lets you check whether the ground provides it.**

> **If Lacey's required slope is flatter than the ground, the surplus must be taken up in falls; if it is steeper, the canal cannot be in regime at that discharge and will scour.**

> **That is a genuinely useful design check, and Kennedy's method cannot make it.**

examTip.trick: **Critical velocity V₀ = 0.55 m y^0.64** — the velocity that neither silts nor scours, related to DEPTH because the suspending eddies rise from the bed.
examTip.trap: **Kennedy gives ONE equation for THREE unknowns (B, y, S)** — so two must be assumed, and different designers get different canals. That indeterminacy is what Lacey removed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacey DERIVES the bed slope; Kennedy assumes it** — which lets Lacey's method check whether the ground actually provides the slope the canal needs.

questions.stem: In Lacey's regime theory, the SILT FACTOR f is related to the average particle size m (in millimetres) by f = 1.76√m. For a silt of average size 0.5 mm, the silt factor is:
questions.solution:
**1.24.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **f = 1.76 √m, with m in millimetres** ← | ← |
| **√0.5** | **= 0.7071** ← |
| **f = 1.76 × 0.7071** | **= 1.244, about 1.24** ← |

> **So the silt factor is about 1.24 — a slightly coarse silt, since f = 1.0 corresponds to the standard Kennedy silt.**

**THE SILT FACTOR'S ROLE IN THE REGIME RELATIONS, WHICH IS WHY IT IS COMPUTED FIRST:**

| Relation | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Silt factor** | **f = 1.76 √m** ← |
| **Regime VELOCITY** | **V = (Q f² / 140)^(1/6)** ← |
| **Regime hydraulic RADIUS** ← | **R = 2.5 V²/(2f), that is R = 5V²/(2f)** ← |
| **Regime WETTED PERIMETER** ← | **P = 4.75 √Q** ← |
| **Regime SCOUR depth** ← | **R = 0.47 (Q/f)^(1/3)** ← |
| **Regime bed SLOPE** ← | **S = f^(5/3) / (3340 Q^(1/6))** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST STRIKING OF THESE RELATIONS AND IT IS WORTH NOTING FOR WHAT IT DOES NOT CONTAIN: the wetted perimeter depends on the DISCHARGE ALONE.**

> **The silt factor does not appear in it at all.**

> **So a channel carrying 100 cumec has a wetted perimeter of 4.75 × 10 = 47.5 m whether it flows through fine silt or coarse sand — the material affects the depth, the velocity and the slope but not the perimeter.**

> **That is a genuinely surprising result and it is one of the reasons Lacey's theory was taken seriously: it makes a strong, simple, testable claim, and the claim holds reasonably well across a wide range of alluvial channels.**

> **It also has a practical use in river work: the regime perimeter is what determines the WATERWAY to be provided at a bridge or a barrage, and it can be computed from the design flood alone without knowing anything about the bed material.**

**THE PHYSICAL MEANING OF THE SILT FACTOR IS WORTH STATING, SINCE IT IS OTHERWISE AN OPAQUE COEFFICIENT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **f increases with the COARSENESS of the material** ← | **From about 0.4 for very fine silt to 1.0 for standard silt and above 2 for coarse sand and gravel** ← |
| **A HIGH f means a coarse bed, which requires a STEEPER slope and a HIGHER velocity to stay in regime** ← | **Which the relations show: S rises with f^(5/3), and V with f^(1/3)** ← |
| **And a coarse bed gives a SHALLOWER, wider channel** ← | **Since R falls as f rises** ← |
| **So the silt factor governs the channel's SHAPE and SLOPE, and the discharge governs its SIZE** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE CLEANEST SUMMARY OF WHAT THE THEORY SAYS AND IT IS WORTH CARRYING: DISCHARGE sets how big the channel is, and the BED MATERIAL sets what shape and slope it takes.**

> **That division is intuitively reasonable — a bigger river is a bigger channel, and a gravel-bed river is steeper and wider than a silt-bed river of the same discharge — and it is exactly what one observes in the field.**

> **A Himalayan gravel-bed river and a Gangetic silt-bed river carrying the same flood look entirely different, and the difference is the silt factor.**

> **A caution to close on: Lacey's relations were derived from stable irrigation canals in the Indo-Gangetic alluvium, carrying a limited silt load in a narrow range of materials.**

> **Applying them to a Himalayan boulder-bed river, whose f would be far outside the range of the data, is an extrapolation well beyond their basis — and the answers, while they can be computed, should be treated as indicative rather than as design values.**
tags: wetted perimeter depends only on Q
discharge sets size and silt sets shape

examTip.trap: **P = 4.75√Q contains NO silt factor** — the wetted perimeter depends on discharge alone, which is why it gives the waterway at a bridge without knowing the bed material.
examTip.mnemonic: **Discharge sets the SIZE; silt factor sets the SHAPE and SLOPE.** And Lacey came from Gangetic canals — applying it to a boulder-bed river is far outside its basis.

questions.stem: Using Lacey's relation R = 0.47 (Q/f)^(1/3), the normal SCOUR DEPTH for a discharge of 30 cumec in a bed of silt factor 1.0 is about:
questions.solution:
**About 1.46 m.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Q/f** | **= 30/1.0 = 30** ← |
| **The cube root of 30** | **= 3.107** ← |
| **R = 0.47 × 3.107** | **= 1.460 m** ← |

> **So the normal scour depth is about 1.46 m below the high flood level.**

**WHAT THIS DEPTH MEANS AND WHAT IT IS USED FOR, WHICH MATTERS MORE THAN THE ARITHMETIC:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **R is the normal scour depth measured BELOW the HIGH FLOOD LEVEL, not below the bed** ← | **A frequent and serious error** ← |
| **It is the depth at which an alluvial channel in regime would naturally sit** ← | ← |
| **It is the BASE from which all the foundation depths at a bridge or a headworks are computed** ← | ← |
| **Each location has its own MULTIPLE of R, depending on how severely the flow attacks it** ← | ← |

> **THE MULTIPLES ARE THE PRACTICAL CONTENT AND THEY WERE MET EARLIER IN THE GUIDE BANK CONTEXT:**

| Location | Scour depth |
|---|---|
| **A straight reach, unobstructed** ← | **1.0 R** ← |
| **A moderate bend** ← | **1.5 R** ← |
| **A severe bend** ← | **1.75 R** ← |
| **A right-angled bend, or a severe attack** ← | **2.0 R** ← |
| **The NOSE of a guide bank** ← | **2.0 to 2.5 R — the deepest** ← |
| **Around a bridge PIER** ← | **2.0 R** ← |
| **Downstream of an apron or a floor** ← | **1.25 to 1.75 R** ← |

> **AND THE FOUNDATION RULE THAT FOLLOWS: a foundation must be taken to a depth BELOW the anticipated scour, with a further margin.**

> **For a bridge pier that margin is commonly 2 m below the computed scour level; for a floor's cut-off, it is enough to prevent the scour hole undermining the floor's edge.**

> **So the sequence is: compute R from Lacey, multiply by the factor for the location, and found below that — and each step must be done deliberately rather than by adopting a customary depth.**

**THE FIRST ROW OF THE SECOND TABLE DESERVES REPEATING AS A WARNING BECAUSE THE ERROR IS SO CONSEQUENTIAL: R is measured from the HIGH FLOOD LEVEL downward.**

> **If the high flood level is 3 m above the existing bed and R is 1.46 m, then the scour level is 1.46 m below the flood level — which is 1.54 m ABOVE the existing bed, and there is no scour at all at that section.**

> **Conversely if the flood level is 6 m above the bed, the scour level is 4.54 m below the bed, and the foundation must go deeper still.**

> **So the same R gives entirely different founding depths depending on the flood's depth over the bed, and a designer who treats R as a depth below the bed will be badly wrong in one direction or the other.**

> **A useful sanity check is that R should be comparable with the river's own flow DEPTH in flood — because a regime channel's hydraulic radius is what R represents.**

> **If a computed R comes out at a small fraction of the observed flood depth, or several times it, either the discharge or the silt factor is wrong — and checking that comparison catches the error before it reaches a foundation drawing.**
tags: R measured below high flood level

examTip.trick: **R = 0.47(Q/f)^(1/3) = 0.47 × 3.107 = 1.46 m.** Option (c) is the cube root without the 0.47.
examTip.trap: **R is measured BELOW THE HIGH FLOOD LEVEL, not below the bed** — so the founding depth depends on how deep the flood is over the bed. Treating it as a depth below bed is badly wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **Multiply by the location factor: 1.0 straight, 1.5 moderate bend, 2.0 pier or right-angle, 2.0-2.5 guide bank nose** — then found below that with a margin.

questions.stem: The TRACTIVE FORCE approach to designing a stable channel is based on:
options: The shear stress that the flowing water exerts on the bed and banks
The mean velocity of flow, compared with a critical velocity
The regime relations derived from stable canals
The discharge alone
questions.solution:
**The SHEAR STRESS that the flowing water exerts on the bed and banks, which must not exceed the value at which the boundary material begins to move** — the permissible shear being a property of the material rather than of the channel.

**The basis of the method:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **The average boundary shear stress is τ₀ = γ R S** ← | **Unit weight of water × hydraulic radius × slope** ← |
| **The material has a CRITICAL (permissible) shear stress at which its grains begin to move** ← | **A property of the grain size, shape and cohesion** ← |
| **A stable channel is one in which τ₀ is less than that critical value everywhere** ← | ← |
| **The shear is NOT uniform round the perimeter** ← | **It is greatest on the BED (about 0.97 γyS) and less on the SIDES (about 0.75 γyS)** ← |
| **But the SIDE grains are also acted on by GRAVITY down the slope** ← | **So they are less stable, and a reduction factor is applied to the permissible shear on the sides** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE FEATURE THAT MAKES THE METHOD PHYSICALLY SOUND AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: a particle on a sloping bank is already partly displaced by its own weight.**

> **A particle on the flat bed must be moved by the flow alone; a particle on a 2:1 side slope has a component of gravity urging it downslope, so a smaller additional force from the water will dislodge it.**

> **The steeper the side slope, the greater that component and the less shear the bank can withstand — and as the slope approaches the material's ANGLE OF REPOSE, the permissible shear approaches zero.**

> **So the tractive force method automatically links the channel's side slope to the material's angle of repose, which neither Kennedy's nor Lacey's method does.**

> **That is a genuine advance in physical reasoning and it is why the method is preferred for designing channels in coarse, non-cohesive material where the bank stability actually governs.**

**THE THREE APPROACHES COMPARED, WHICH IS THE USEFUL SUMMARY:**

| Approach | Criterion | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **PERMISSIBLE VELOCITY (Kennedy)** ← | **The mean velocity must lie in a range** ← | **Alluvial canals carrying silt; the traditional Indian method** ← |
| **REGIME (Lacey)** ← | **The channel adopts a determinate shape and slope for a given Q and f** ← | **Alluvial canals in fine material, in true regime** ← |
| **TRACTIVE FORCE** ← | **The boundary shear must not exceed the material's critical value** ← | **Channels in COARSE, non-cohesive material — gravel and cobbles — and LINED channels** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW'S APPLICATION IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS IN NEPAL AND IT IS WORTH DRAWING OUT: a canal cut in the boulder and gravel deposits of a Himalayan valley is not an alluvial silt canal.**

> **Its bed material is far coarser than anything in Lacey's data, it carries a coarse bed load rather than a suspended silt load, and its stability is a question of whether individual stones are moved rather than of whether a silt load is transported in balance.**

> **Those are precisely the conditions the tractive force method addresses and the regime method does not.**

> **So for a hill canal in gravel, the tractive force approach is the appropriate one, and applying Lacey's relations because they are the ones taught for canal design is a category error.**

> **THE METHOD'S OWN LIMITATION SHOULD ALSO BE STATED: it is a threshold criterion, addressing whether the boundary MOVES.**

> **It says nothing about whether the channel can TRANSPORT the sediment load arriving from upstream, which is the question the regime approach addresses.**

> **A channel can be perfectly stable by the tractive force criterion — its own boundary immobile — and silt up completely because it cannot carry the load delivered into it.**

> **So the two criteria answer different questions, and a canal carrying a substantial sediment load needs both: enough shear to move the incoming load through, and not so much as to erode its own boundary.**

> **That is the same pair of limits as the self-cleansing and non-scouring velocities in a sewer, arrived at from a more fundamental direction.**
tags: angle of repose and side slopes

examTip.trick: **τ₀ = γRS must stay below the material's critical shear** — a property of the grains, not of the channel.
examTip.trap: **Bank grains are less stable than bed grains** — gravity already pulls them downslope, so the permissible shear falls as the side slope approaches the angle of repose.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tractive force suits COARSE material (Himalayan gravel); Lacey suits fine alluvium.** And the two answer different questions: boundary stability against load transport.

questions.stem: The FREEBOARD provided in an irrigation canal above its full supply level is intended to guard against:
options: Loss of water by evaporation
The canal running below its full supply level
Wave action, a temporary rise from a sudden gate closure or an unforeseen inflow, settlement of the banks, and accumulated silt raising the bed
Erosion of the canal's bed
questions.solution:
**WAVE action, a temporary rise from a sudden gate closure or an unforeseen inflow, SETTLEMENT of the banks, and accumulated silt raising the bed** — any of which could otherwise overtop and breach the bank.

**What the freeboard covers:**

| Cause of a rise | Note |
|---|---|
| **WAVES raised by wind on a wide canal** ← | ← |
| **A SURGE when a gate downstream is closed** ← | **The flow is stopped and the water backs up, exactly as in a pipeline but with a free surface** ← |
| **An unforeseen INFLOW — storm runoff entering the canal from the adjoining land** ← | **A real and common cause of breaches in a monsoon** ← |
| **SETTLEMENT of a bank built on soft ground** ← | **Which lowers the bank rather than raising the water, with the same result** ← |
| **Accumulated SILT raising the bed** ← | **So the same discharge flows at a higher level** ← |
| **Operational error — the canal run above its design discharge** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE THAT CAUSES MOST BREACHES IN PRACTICE AND IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT: a canal running along a hillside or across a slope INTERCEPTS the runoff from the land above it.**

> **In a heavy storm, that runoff enters the canal along its whole length, and the canal — which was sized for its irrigation discharge — receives a flow it was never designed for.**

> **It overtops at the lowest point of the bank and breaches, and the breach then discharges the whole canal's flow onto the land below, causing far more damage than the storm itself.**

> **So the freeboard is one defence, and the more important one is a CATCH DRAIN on the uphill side to intercept the runoff before it reaches the canal, together with ESCAPES to shed a surplus deliberately.**

> **A hill canal without a catch drain will be breached, and the only question is when.**

**THE FREEBOARD ALLOWANCES, WHICH VARY WITH THE CANAL'S SIZE:**

| Discharge | Freeboard |
|---|---|
| **Up to 0.75 cumec** | **0.30 m** ← |
| **0.75 to 1.5 cumec** | **0.45 m** ← |
| **1.5 to 85 cumec** | **0.60 m** ← |
| **Above 85 cumec** | **0.75 to 0.90 m** ← |

> **THE OTHER ELEMENTS OF A CANAL'S CROSS-SECTION ARE WORTH LISTING ALONGSIDE, SINCE THEY ARE OFTEN ASKED TOGETHER:**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **BERM — a horizontal shelf between the cutting's slope and the bank** ← | **Absorbs any slips from the cutting so they do not enter the canal; distributes the bank's load; and allows the canal to widen naturally as it silts** ← |
| **SERVICE ROAD (inspection road) on one bank** ← | **For maintenance, inspection and the movement of the desilting plant** ← |
| **DOWLA — a small bank along the edge of the service road** ← | **Preventing vehicles running into the canal, and keeping road runoff out** ← |
| **SPOIL BANK — surplus excavated material placed outside the bank** ← | **With gaps left so that the natural drainage is not blocked** ← |
| **BORROW PIT — where fill is taken for the banks** ← | **Kept a specified distance from the toe, so it does not weaken the bank or provide a seepage path** ← |
| **CATCH (drainage) DRAIN on the uphill side** ← | **As discussed** ← |

> **THE GAPS IN THE SPOIL BANK IN THE FOURTH ROW ARE A DETAIL WORTH NOTING BECAUSE THEIR OMISSION CAUSES A PREDICTABLE PROBLEM: a continuous spoil bank alongside a canal is an embankment across the natural drainage.**

> **Water that used to drain across the alignment now ponds behind it, waterlogging the land, and eventually finds a way through — often through the canal bank itself.**

> **So the spoil must be placed in discontinuous lengths with gaps at the natural drainage lines, which costs nothing if it is planned and is impossible to correct once the spoil has been dumped along the whole length.**

> **It is a good example of a decision made by a machine operator, in the absence of instruction, that quietly creates a drainage problem nobody later connects with the canal's construction.**

examTip.trick: **Waves, surges, unforeseen inflow, bank settlement and silt accumulation** — anything that raises the water relative to the bank.
examTip.trap: **Storm runoff entering a hill canal is the commonest cause of breaches** — and the real defence is a CATCH DRAIN uphill plus escapes, not freeboard alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Leave GAPS in the spoil bank at the natural drainage lines** — a continuous spoil bank dams the drainage, waterlogs the land, and eventually breaches the canal itself.

questions.stem: The BALANCING DEPTH in the design of a canal's cross-section is the depth of cutting at which:
options: The canal's velocity is exactly self-cleansing
The seepage loss is a minimum
The canal runs exactly at full supply level
The volume of excavation from the cutting exactly equals the volume of fill required for the two banks
questions.solution:
**The depth at which the volume of EXCAVATION from the cutting exactly equals the volume of FILL required for the two banks** — so that no material need be borrowed and none disposed of.

**Why it matters:**

| Situation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Cutting SHALLOWER than the balancing depth** ← | **Not enough excavated material for the banks, so fill must be BORROWED and hauled — an extra cost, and it leaves borrow pits** ← |
| **Cutting DEEPER than the balancing depth** ← | **Surplus material that must be DISPOSED of as spoil — an extra cost, and it creates the spoil bank problems noted earlier** ← |
| **Cutting AT the balancing depth** ← | **The earthwork balances; the cheapest section** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE IS SIMPLY THAT MOVING EARTH COSTS MONEY AND MOVING IT TWICE COSTS MORE, AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING HOW LARGE THAT COST IS IN A CANAL: earthwork is the dominant item in an unlined canal's construction.**

> **A canal is a linear structure hundreds of kilometres long, and the earthwork quantity per kilometre is large.**

> **So a section that balances saves both the borrowing and the disposal along that whole length, and the saving is substantial.**

> **Equally, the balancing depth is a design target rather than a rule — the ground level varies along the alignment, so the actual cutting depth varies, and the aim is to balance the earthwork over a REACH rather than at every cross-section.**

**HOW IT IS USED IN PRACTICE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The canal's SECTION — bed width, depth, side slopes, bank widths — is fixed first** ← | **From the hydraulic design** ← |
| **The balancing depth then follows from the geometry** ← | **The depth of cutting at which the cut area equals the fill area** ← |
| **The canal's BED LEVEL is then set, where the ground permits, so that the cutting is at about that depth** ← | ← |
| **Over a long reach, the ground rises and falls, so the canal alternates between deeper cutting and higher embankment** ← | ← |
| **The MASS HAUL diagram is used to plan the movement of material along the alignment** ← | **Balancing a surplus in one reach against a deficit in the next, and minimising the haul distance** ← |

> **THE MASS HAUL DIAGRAM IN THE LAST ROW IS THE TOOL THAT TURNS THE PRINCIPLE INTO A CONSTRUCTION PLAN AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: it plots the CUMULATIVE volume of cut minus fill along the alignment.**

> **Where the curve rises there is a surplus; where it falls, a deficit.**

> **A horizontal line drawn across the curve gives a reach over which the earthwork balances, and the area between the line and the curve measures the HAUL — the volume times the distance it must be moved.**

> **So the diagram lets the engineer see at a glance where material should be taken from and where it should go, how far it must be hauled, and where borrowing or disposal is unavoidable.**

> **It is the same tool used in road earthwork, and the reasoning is identical.**

**A CAUTION ON THE MATERIAL ITSELF, WHICH THE BALANCING CALCULATION DOES NOT ADDRESS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The balancing depth is a VOLUME calculation** ← | **It assumes the excavated material is SUITABLE for the banks** ← |
| **It frequently is not** ← | **Rock, gravel, organic soil, or a highly permeable sand may be excavated where a low-permeability bank material is wanted** ← |
| **And the volumes are not equal in any case, since material BULKS on excavation and COMPACTS in the fill** ← | **A bulking factor and a compaction factor both apply, and they do not cancel** ← |
| **So a nominal balance in bank measure may be a real surplus or deficit** ← | ← |

> **The third row is a routine source of error in earthwork estimating generally: a cubic metre of soil in the ground is not a cubic metre in the truck nor a cubic metre in the compacted embankment.**

> **Soil typically bulks 20 to 30 per cent on excavation and then compacts to perhaps 90 per cent of its in-situ volume in a well-compacted fill — so roughly 1.1 cubic metres of excavation is needed for each cubic metre of embankment.**

> **Ignoring that gives a systematic shortfall of fill of around 10 per cent along the whole length, discovered when the banks are being built and material has to be found from somewhere.**

examTip.trick: **Cut volume equals fill volume** — so nothing is borrowed and nothing disposed of. Earthwork dominates an unlined canal's cost.
examTip.trap: **Balance over a REACH, not at every section** — the ground level varies, so use a MASS HAUL diagram to plan where material moves and how far.
examTip.mnemonic: **Soil BULKS on excavation and COMPACTS in the fill, and the two do not cancel** — about 1.1 m³ of cut per m³ of embankment. Ignoring it short-changes the fill by 10 %.

questions.stem: In a LINED canal, an important design provision that is unnecessary in an unlined canal is:
options: A self-cleansing velocity
Adequate freeboard
A service road along the bank
Pressure relief
questions.solution:
**PRESSURE RELIEF — weep holes or a drainage layer beneath the lining** — to release any water pressure that builds up behind the lining, which would otherwise lift and destroy it when the canal is emptied.

**The uplift mechanism, which is the lining's characteristic failure:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water gets BEHIND the lining** ← | **Through cracks and joints, from rainfall on the banks, from the surrounding groundwater, or from leakage at structures** ← |
| **While the canal is FULL, the water inside balances that pressure** ← | **So nothing happens and the problem is invisible** ← |
| **When the canal is EMPTIED — for maintenance, or at the end of the season — the internal pressure disappears** ← | ← |
| **The external water pressure is then unbalanced, and it acts UPWARD on the lining** ← | ← |
| **A concrete lining is thin and has almost no weight to resist it** ← | **So it lifts, cracks, and breaks up** ← |
| **The damage occurs during the DRAWDOWN and is discovered when the canal is inspected** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CRITICAL MOMENT AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: a canal lining is most at risk when the canal is EMPTY, not when it is full.**

> **This is counter-intuitive — the lining looks unloaded when there is no water in it — and it is why linings are so often damaged during the annual closure, which is precisely when the maintenance was supposed to be done.**

> **It is also why RAPID DRAWDOWN is prohibited: emptying the canal slowly gives the water behind the lining time to drain away, so the pressure difference never develops.**

> **A canal emptied quickly by opening the escapes fully can lose its lining over a long reach in a few hours, and the damage is entirely self-inflicted.**

**THE PROVISIONS AGAINST IT:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **WEEP HOLES through the lining, with a filter behind them** ← | **Letting the external water in rather than allowing it to build pressure — and the filter prevents the soil washing through** ← |
| **A DRAINAGE LAYER of granular material beneath the lining** ← | **Collecting the seepage and leading it to an outlet** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL and TRANSVERSE drains under the lining in a high water table** ← | ← |
| **Controlled, SLOW drawdown** ← | **An operating rule rather than a construction provision, and it costs nothing** ← |
| **PRESSURE RELIEF VALVES in the lining of large canals** ← | **Flap valves that open under external pressure** ← |
| **Adequate lining WEIGHT where uplift cannot be avoided** ← | **A thicker slab, which is expensive** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW EMBODIES A PRINCIPLE WORTH GENERALISING: rather than resisting the water pressure, LET THE WATER THROUGH.**

> **A weep hole deliberately breaches the lining's watertightness in order to preserve the lining, accepting a small leak to prevent a total failure.**

> **That is the same reasoning as the drainage behind a retaining wall, the drainage gallery in a gravity dam and the filter beneath a revetment — in each case the structure is protected not by resisting the water but by giving it a path.**

> **Recognising it as one principle across four applications is worth doing, because the instinct in each case is to seal more thoroughly, and the correct answer is the opposite.**

**THE OTHER MATTERS PARTICULAR TO LINED CANALS, FOR COMPLETENESS:**

| Matter | Note |
|---|---|
| **A lined canal can run at a HIGHER velocity** ← | **So it is smaller for the same discharge, and needs less land** ← |
| **Its Manning's n is lower and CONSTANT with age** ← | **Unlike an unlined canal, which deteriorates** ← |
| **JOINTS must be provided and sealed** ← | **To accommodate thermal and shrinkage movement; and the sealant deteriorates and must be renewed** ← |
| **The lining must be protected from VEGETATION** ← | **Roots penetrating a joint will lift a slab** ← |
| **And from LIVESTOCK and vehicles crossing it** ← | **Which requires designed crossings, or the lining is broken at every informal crossing point** ← |
| **Repairs must be made PROMPTLY** ← | **A small crack admits water behind the lining and grows into a lifted slab; a lining deteriorates rapidly once it begins** ← |

> **The last row is the operating discipline that determines a lining's life, and it follows directly from the uplift mechanism: every crack is a route for water to get behind, and behind is where the damage is done.**

> **So a lined canal is not a maintenance-free canal — it is a canal whose maintenance is different, consisting of prompt crack sealing and joint renewal rather than desilting and weed clearance.**

> **A scheme that lines its canals and then reduces its maintenance budget on the strength of it will find the lining failing within a decade, and replacing a lining costs more than laying it.**

examTip.trick: **Water behind the lining lifts it when the canal is EMPTIED** — the lining is most at risk when it looks unloaded.
examTip.trap: **Rapid drawdown destroys linings** — emptying slowly lets the water behind drain away first. An operating rule that costs nothing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Let the water THROUGH, don't resist it** — weep holes here, drainage behind a retaining wall, a gallery in a dam, a filter under a revetment. One principle, four applications.

questions.stem: When an alluvial canal is taken round a CURVE, the characteristic consequence is that:
options: Silt is deposited on the inside (convex) bank while the outside (concave) bank is scoured
Silt is deposited uniformly around the curve
The outside bank silts and the inside bank scours
The curve has no effect on the distribution of silt
questions.solution:
**SILT is deposited on the INSIDE (convex) bank while the OUTSIDE (concave) bank is SCOURED** — because the spiral secondary flow carries the bed material inward along the bed.

**The mechanism, which is the same as in a natural river bend:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water moving round a curve is thrown OUTWARD by centrifugal effect** ← | **So the water surface is higher on the outside** ← |
| **That superelevation drives a return flow along the BED, INWARD** ← | ← |
| **The result is a SPIRAL (helical) secondary current** ← | **Outward at the surface, inward along the bed** ← |
| **The bed current carries the SEDIMENT toward the INSIDE** ← | **Where it is deposited** ← |
| **And the outside bank, attacked by the faster surface flow, is SCOURED** ← | ← |

> **THIS IS EXACTLY THE MECHANISM THAT MAKES A RIVER MEANDER, AND RECOGNISING IT AS THE SAME PHENOMENON IS USEFUL: the outer bank erodes and the inner bank builds, so the bend migrates outward and downstream, and a slight initial curvature amplifies itself.**

> **In a canal that self-amplification is prevented by the banks, but the deposition and scour still occur — so a curved reach silts on one side and erodes on the other, and both are problems.**

> **The silting reduces the section and the scour threatens the bank, and neither is self-correcting.**

**THE DESIGN CONSEQUENCES FOR A CANAL:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **Use a GENEROUS radius — the flatter the curve, the weaker the secondary flow** ← | **Minimum radii of 3 to 7 times the bed width for small canals, and 10 to 15 times or more for large ones** ← |
| **PROTECT the outer bank with pitching through the curve and for a distance beyond it** ← | **The scour continues downstream of the bend's end** ← |
| **Expect and plan for DESILTING on the inside** ← | ← |
| **Avoid taking an OUTLET off the inside of a curve** ← | **It would draw the silt-laden bed water and silt up continuously** ← |
| **And prefer to take an offtake from the OUTSIDE of a curve** ← | **Where the surface water is cleaner — the same principle as a river intake on the outer bank** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER GIVE A PRACTICAL RULE OF REAL VALUE AND IT IS THE SAME RULE MET AT A RIVER INTAKE: draw water from the OUTSIDE of a bend, where the flow is deep and the sediment has moved away.**

> **An offtake on the inside of a curve is drawing from precisely the place where the secondary current is depositing, so it takes a disproportionate share of the silt load and its own channel silts up.**

> **This is a siting decision that costs nothing to get right at the design stage and is very difficult to correct afterwards, and it explains why some distributaries silt persistently while others on the same canal do not.**

> **THE SAME SECONDARY FLOW IS ALSO EXPLOITED DELIBERATELY IN SILT CONTROL, WHICH IS WORTH NOTING AS A CLOSING POINT: if the bed current carries sediment toward the inside of a curve, then a curve can be used to CONCENTRATE the sediment where it can be removed.**

> **That is the principle of the vortex tube and of several silt ejector arrangements, and it is why a silt excluder at a headworks is sometimes placed on a deliberately curved approach.**

> **A phenomenon that is a nuisance in a canal alignment becomes a tool when it is arranged intentionally — which is a good instance of the general point that understanding a mechanism lets you use it rather than merely avoid it.**

examTip.trick: **Surface flow outward, BED flow inward** — so the sediment is carried to the INSIDE and deposited there, while the outside is scoured.
examTip.trap: **Never take an offtake from the INSIDE of a curve** — it draws from where the silt is depositing. Take it from the OUTSIDE, as at a river intake.
examTip.mnemonic: **The same spiral that makes rivers meander** — and it can be exploited deliberately, which is how vortex tubes and some silt excluders work.

questions.stem: Lacey's relation for the regime WETTED PERIMETER of an alluvial channel, P = 4.75 √Q, is notable because:
options: It depends on the discharge alone
It applies only to lined channels
It gives the perimeter in terms of the silt factor only
It is valid only for discharges below 10 cumec
questions.solution:
**It depends on the DISCHARGE ALONE — the silt factor does not appear in it** — so the waterway required at a bridge or a barrage can be estimated without knowing the bed material.

**The relation and its use:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **P = 4.75 √Q, with P in metres and Q in cumec** ← | ← |
| **For Q = 100 cumec, P = 47.5 m** ← | ← |
| **For Q = 10,000 cumec, P = 475 m** ← | **A tenfold increase in the perimeter for a hundredfold increase in discharge** ← |
| **In a wide shallow channel, P is very nearly the WIDTH** ← | **Since the depth is small relative to the width, the two side slopes add little** ← |
| **So the relation effectively gives the channel's WIDTH from its discharge** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE WHY THE RELATION IS SO USEFUL IN RIVER ENGINEERING, AND IT IS ITS PRINCIPAL PRACTICAL APPLICATION: it gives the WATERWAY that a bridge or a barrage should provide.**

> **A river confined to less than its regime width will scour deeply and attack the structure; one given more than its regime width will deposit shoals within the waterway and concentrate its flow unpredictably against one part of it.**

> **So the regime width is the right width — the one the river would adopt for itself — and providing it is the way to obtain a stable arrangement.**

> **This is called Lacey's waterway, and it is the starting point for the waterway at any major crossing of an alluvial river.**

**THE SQUARE-ROOT FORM DESERVES A MOMENT'S ATTENTION BECAUSE IT SHAPES RIVERS' PROPORTIONS:**

| Observation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **P grows as √Q, so QUADRUPLING the discharge only DOUBLES the width** ← | ← |
| **The area must grow in proportion to Q at constant velocity** ← | ← |
| **So the DEPTH must grow too — roughly as √Q as well** ← | ← |
| **Which is why large rivers are both wider AND deeper than small ones, in comparable proportion** ← | **Rather than merely wider** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW MATCHES OBSERVATION AND IS WORTH NOTING AS A CHECK ON THE THEORY: rivers do not become indefinitely wide and shallow as they grow.**

> **A great river is deep as well as broad, and its width-to-depth ratio is not wildly different from a small one's in the same material.**

> **That the relations predict this correctly is part of why Lacey's regime theory earned its standing, despite being empirical and despite its limited data base.**

**THE PRACTICAL CAUTION IN APPLYING IT TO A BRIDGE, WHICH IS WORTH STATING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The Q to use is the DESIGN FLOOD, not the mean flow** ← | ← |
| **A waterway LESS than the regime width causes AFFLUX and deep scour at the piers** ← | **And the afflux then has its own consequences upstream, as discussed for marginal bunds** ← |
| **A waterway GREATER than the regime width is not safe either** ← | **The river shoals within it, its flow concentrates in a part of the opening, and the concentrated flow attacks whatever it is aimed at** ← |
| **So the waterway should be close to the regime value, with GUIDE BANKS to make the river use all of it** ← | ← |
| **In a BOULDER-bed Himalayan river, the relation is outside its data range** ← | **And the waterway must be judged from the river's own observed behaviour and its braided width, not from the formula** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE POINT THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT: a generous waterway is not a safe waterway.**

> **The instinct is that a wider opening is more conservative, and for the hydraulics of passing the flood it is.**

> **But a river given more room than it needs does not spread evenly across it; it forms shoals and threads a deep channel through part of the opening, and that channel can move from one span to another between floods.**

> **So an over-wide bridge has a wandering deep channel somewhere within it, attacking piers that were founded on the assumption of a distributed flow.**

> **The remedy is the guide bank, whose purpose is precisely to make the river use the whole waterway centrally and consistently — which is why waterway and guide banks are designed together and neither makes sense without the other.**

The silt factor does not appear in it — so the waterway required at a bridge or a barrage can be estimated without knowing the bed material.

examTip.trick: **P = 4.75√Q contains no silt factor** — so the regime waterway follows from the design flood alone, without knowing the bed material.
examTip.trap: **An OVER-WIDE waterway is not safe** — the river shoals within it and threads a deep channel through part of the opening, which wanders between floods.
examTip.mnemonic: **Quadrupling Q only doubles the width** — so big rivers are deeper as well as wider. And waterway and GUIDE BANKS are designed together.

questions.stem: A CANAL ESCAPE is provided in an irrigation system in order to:
options: Allow the cultivators an additional point of offtake
Measure the discharge passing down the canal
Dispose of surplus water from the canal into a natural drainage
Raise the water level upstream so that offtakes can command
questions.solution:
**To dispose of SURPLUS water from the canal into a natural drainage** — protecting the canal from breaching when the demand falls suddenly, allowing it to be emptied for maintenance, and shedding storm water that has entered it.

**When an escape is needed:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Rain falls over the command, and the cultivators stop taking water** ← | **The canal's flow has nowhere to go and the level rises** ← |
| **An outlet or a distributary is closed unexpectedly** ← | ← |
| **A BREACH or a blockage downstream stops the flow** ← | **And the water backs up behind it** ← |
| **STORM RUNOFF enters the canal from the adjoining land** ← | **Adding a flow the canal was not designed for** ← |
| **The canal must be EMPTIED for maintenance or for a repair** ← | ← |
| **The head regulator cannot be closed quickly enough** ← | **Or the canal is a long way from the headworks and the water already in it must go somewhere** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE COMMONEST AND IT IS AN INSTRUCTIVE SITUATION: rain over an irrigated command REDUCES the demand to nothing within hours.**

> **The canal, however, is still running — it was set days earlier at the headworks, and the water already in transit takes hours or days to arrive.**

> **So a canal full of water arrives at a command that no longer wants any of it, and unless there is somewhere for that water to go, the canal rises and breaches.**

> **This is the irrigation equivalent of load rejection in a hydropower scheme, and it is dealt with the same way: a controlled route for the surplus, provided in advance.**

> **A breach, by contrast, is an uncontrolled escape at the weakest point, and it damages the canal, floods the land below and interrupts the supply for weeks.**

**THE TYPES OF ESCAPE:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURPLUS WATER escape (weir type)** ← | **A side weir set at full supply level; it operates AUTOMATICALLY whenever the level rises above FSL, with no operator** ← |
| **SCOURING (tail) escape** ← | **Gated, and set at BED level, so it can empty the canal completely and also scour out the silt** ← |
| **A tail escape at the canal's end** ← | **Which also keeps a flow moving at the tail, preventing stagnation and silting there** ← |

> **THE AUTOMATIC OPERATION OF THE WEIR-TYPE ESCAPE IN THE FIRST ROW IS ITS GREAT VIRTUE AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: it requires nobody to be present and nobody to make a decision.**

> **The level rises above full supply, water spills over the side weir, and the level is held.**

> **A gated escape, by contrast, requires an operator to recognise the situation and open the gate — and the situation typically arises at night, in heavy rain, when nobody is there.**

> **So the automatic escape is what actually protects the canal, and the gated escape is for the planned operations of emptying and scouring.**

> **Providing only the gated type is a common economy that leaves the canal unprotected in exactly the circumstance that threatens it.**

**WHERE AN ESCAPE MUST BE SITED, WHICH IS THE CONSTRAINT THAT GOVERNS:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Where a natural DRAINAGE is available to receive the discharge** ← | **Which is the limiting factor — an escape needs somewhere to escape TO** ← |
| **The drainage must be able to take the flow WITHOUT damage** ← | **A large canal's surplus discharged into a small nala will scour it and flood the land along it** ← |
| **At intervals along the canal, and immediately upstream of any long reach without one** ← | ← |
| **Just upstream of a major structure or a critical reach** ← | **So the reach can be protected** ← |
| **With ENERGY DISSIPATION at the discharge point** ← | **The escaped water falls from canal level to the drainage and will scour if it is not controlled** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE ONES MOST OFTEN NEGLECTED AND THEY CREATE A PROBLEM DOWNSTREAM RATHER THAN AT THE CANAL: an escape discharging a substantial flow into a small watercourse transfers the canal's problem to somebody else's land.**

> **The receiving nala is sized by nature for its own catchment's runoff, and the escape can deliver several times that.**

> **So it scours, its banks fail, and the land alongside floods — and the cause is a structure built to protect the canal.**

> **The escape channel between the canal and the drainage therefore needs its own design — a lined channel or a chute with energy dissipation, and an assessment of what the receiving watercourse can accept — and it is not simply an opening in the bank.**

examTip.trick: **Shed surplus water into a natural drainage** — protecting against a breach when demand falls, allowing emptying, and taking storm inflow.
examTip.trap: **A weir-type escape works AUTOMATICALLY; a gated one needs an operator** — and the crisis comes at night in heavy rain, when nobody is there.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rain stops the demand within hours, and the canal is still running** — the irrigation version of load rejection. And design the escape CHANNEL, or you flood someone else.

questions.stem: Lacey's regime bed slope relation S = f^(5/3) / (3340 Q^(1/6)) shows that, for a given silt factor, a channel's regime slope:
options: Increases with the discharge
Is independent of the discharge
Decreases as the discharge increases
Depends only on the silt factor
questions.solution:
**It DECREASES as the discharge increases** — so a large canal or river requires a FLATTER slope than a small one in the same material.

**Reading the relation:**

| Term | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Q appears in the DENOMINATOR, to the power 1/6** ← | **So S falls as Q rises — but SLOWLY, since a sixth power is a weak dependence** ← |
| **f appears in the NUMERATOR, to the power 5/3** ← | **So S rises STEEPLY with the coarseness of the material** ← |
| **A 64-fold increase in Q halves the slope** ← | **64^(1/6) = 2** ← |
| **A doubling of f multiplies the slope by 2^(5/3) = 3.17** ← | **More than threefold** ← |

> **THE COMPARISON BETWEEN THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE FEATURE OF THE RELATION AND IT MATCHES OBSERVATION EXACTLY: the BED MATERIAL controls the slope far more strongly than the discharge does.**

> **A gravel-bed mountain stream is steep and a silt-bed plains river is flat, and the difference is enormous — a slope of 1 in 100 against 1 in 10,000, a factor of a hundred.**

> **The discharge, meanwhile, varies over an even larger range between them and contributes only a factor of a few.**

> **So if one is asked why a river is steep, the answer is almost always its bed material rather than its size, and the relation says so quantitatively.**

**THE PRACTICAL USE OF THE SLOPE RELATION IN CANAL DESIGN:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Lacey's relations give the slope the canal REQUIRES to be in regime** ← | ← |
| **The GROUND provides whatever slope it provides** ← | ← |
| **If the ground is STEEPER than the regime slope, the surplus must be taken up in FALLS** ← | **Which is the usual case, and it is why canal falls exist** ← |
| **If the ground is FLATTER than the regime slope, the canal cannot be in regime** ← | **It will silt, and the alignment must be reconsidered or the canal accepted as one requiring desilting** ← |
| **So the comparison of required slope with available slope is the first check on an alignment** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE NORMAL SITUATION IN THE INDO-GANGETIC PLAIN AND IT EXPLAINS THE CHARACTERISTIC FORM OF ITS CANAL SYSTEMS: the country falls at perhaps 1 in 2,000 and the canal needs 1 in 6,000, so two-thirds of the available fall is surplus.**

> **That surplus is concentrated in falls at intervals, and the reaches between them run at the regime slope.**

> **The falls are then convenient sites for regulators, bridges, metering and even small hydropower — which is why a canal fall is so often a combined structure.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MORE DIFFICULT CASE AND IT ARISES ON A VERY FLAT COMMAND OR AT THE TAIL OF A LONG SYSTEM: the ground simply does not fall fast enough for the canal to carry its silt.**

> **The options are then to reduce the silt entering the canal at the headworks — which is what silt excluders and ejectors are for — to line the canal so that a higher velocity is permissible on a given slope, to accept a programme of desilting, or to reduce the canal's size so that its regime slope is steeper.**

> **That last option is worth noting because it is counter-intuitive: a SMALLER canal needs a STEEPER slope, so splitting a flow between two smaller canals raises the slope each requires and may bring both within the available fall.**

> **That is a genuine design option and it follows directly from the Q^(1/6) in the denominator — an example of a relation's algebraic form suggesting a solution that would not otherwise occur to one.**
tags: slope rises steeply with silt factor

verification.notes: 64^(1/6) = 2, so a 64-fold Q increase halves S; 2^(5/3) = 3.17 for a doubling of f.

examTip.trick: **Q is in the denominator to the 1/6 power, so a bigger channel needs a FLATTER slope** — but weakly: a 64-fold Q increase only halves it.
examTip.trap: **f is in the numerator to the 5/3 power** — the bed MATERIAL controls the slope far more strongly than the discharge. That is why gravel streams are steep.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compare required slope with available ground slope first** — surplus goes into FALLS, and a deficit means silting. Splitting the flow raises the required slope of each.

questions.stem: Among the types of canal lining, an EARTH or COMPACTED CLAY lining is chosen in preference to concrete chiefly because it:
options: Withstands higher velocities than concrete
Is much cheaper and can be built with local material and unskilled labour
Requires no maintenance
Prevents weed growth entirely
questions.solution:
**It is much CHEAPER and can be built with LOCAL material and unskilled labour** — accepting that it reduces seepage only partly, cannot resist high velocities, and is damaged by weeds and by burrowing animals.

**The lining types compared:**

| Lining | Seepage reduction | Permissible velocity | Cost | Life |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Compacted EARTH or CLAY** ← | **PARTIAL — perhaps 50 to 70 per cent** ← | **LOW** ← | **Lowest** ← | **Short; needs regular repair** ← |
| **Brick or stone MASONRY** ← | **Good** | **Moderate** | **Moderate; labour-intensive, which suits where labour is cheap** ← | **Long, with pointing renewed** ← |
| **CONCRETE, cast in situ** ← | **Very good — 90 per cent and more** ← | **HIGH** ← | **High** ← | **Long** ← |
| **Precast concrete or tiles** | **Good; many joints** | **High** | **High** | **Long** |
| **Shotcrete** | **Good; thin and quick** | **High** | **Moderate to high** | **Moderate** |
| **Plastic or geomembrane, buried** ← | **EXCELLENT — nearly complete** ← | **The MEMBRANE itself takes none; it must be COVERED and the cover takes the flow** ← | **Moderate** ← | **Long if protected, and destroyed at once if exposed or punctured** ← |
| **Boulder lining / dry stone pitching** ← | **Little** ← | **High — it is an EROSION protection rather than a seepage barrier** ← | **Low where stone is at hand** ← | **Long** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS SHOW THAT 'LINING' COVERS TWO DIFFERENT OBJECTIVES AND CONFUSING THEM IS A REAL ERROR: some linings stop SEEPAGE and some resist EROSION.**

> **A geomembrane is a superb seepage barrier and has no resistance to flow at all — it must be buried beneath a protective layer that does the hydraulic work.**

> **A boulder pitching resists high velocities admirably and stops almost no seepage.**

> **A concrete lining does both, which is why it is the default, and it pays for both whether both are needed or not.**

> **So the first question in selecting a lining is which problem is being solved — and where the objective is purely erosion protection on a steep hill canal in stable ground, a stone pitching is the right answer and concrete is an expensive way to obtain a seepage reduction that was not required.**

**THE EARTH LINING'S PLACE, WHICH IS NARROWER THAN ITS CHEAPNESS SUGGESTS:**

| Suitable where | Unsuitable where |
|---|---|
| **A low-velocity canal in a mild climate** ← | **Velocities above about 0.7 m/s** ← |
| **Suitable clay is available LOCALLY** ← | **No clay within an economic haul** ← |
| **Labour is cheap and skills limited** ← | **The seepage must be nearly eliminated** ← |
| **A partial seepage reduction is worthwhile** ← | **Burrowing animals are prevalent** ← |
| **Regular maintenance is realistically available** ← | **Maintenance will not happen** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IN BOTH COLUMNS IS THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL CONSIDERATION AND IT IS WORTH GENERALISING BEYOND LININGS: the appropriate technology is the one whose MAINTENANCE will actually be performed.**

> **An earth lining that is repaired each year performs well for decades; the same lining unmaintained degrades within a few seasons to no better than an unlined canal, and the money is wasted.**

> **A concrete lining tolerates neglect longer, degrades more slowly, and is far more expensive to repair when it does fail.**

> **So the choice depends on the maintenance institution as much as on the hydraulics — and where a water users' association exists and functions, the cheaper maintainable option is genuinely better; where it does not, the more durable option may be the only one that survives.**

> **That is a judgment about institutions rather than materials, and it is one an engineer is often reluctant to make explicitly — but it is unavoidable, because choosing a technology is choosing a maintenance requirement, and a requirement that will not be met is a design defect.**

examTip.trick: **Cheap, local material, unskilled labour** — at the cost of partial seepage reduction, low permissible velocity and vulnerability to weeds and burrows.
examTip.trap: **'Lining' serves TWO different objectives** — stopping SEEPAGE and resisting EROSION. A geomembrane does one and a boulder pitching the other; concrete does both and charges for both.
examTip.mnemonic: **The right technology is the one whose MAINTENANCE will actually happen** — an unmaintained earth lining is no better than no lining within a few seasons.

questions.stem: In Lacey's regime theory, a channel is said to be in TRUE REGIME when:
options: Its discharge, its silt grade and its silt charge are constant, its boundary is composed of the same material as the sediment it transports, and it has adjusted its width, depth and slope so that it neither silts nor scours over a period
Its velocity everywhere exceeds the critical velocity
It is fully lined so that its boundary cannot change
Its bed slope equals the natural ground slope
questions.solution:
**When its discharge, its silt grade and its silt charge are constant, its boundary is composed of the SAME material as the sediment it transports, and it has adjusted its width, depth and slope so that it neither silts nor scours over a period.**

**The conditions Lacey specified for true regime:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The DISCHARGE is constant** ← | ← |
| **The flow is UNIFORM** ← | ← |
| **The SILT CHARGE — the quantity of sediment carried — is constant** ← | ← |
| **The SILT GRADE — the size of that sediment — is constant** ← | ← |
| **The channel flows through material that it has ITSELF DEPOSITED, and which is the same as what it transports** ← | **An INCOHERENT alluvium** ← |
| **The channel is free to adjust its WIDTH, DEPTH and SLOPE** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS ARE THE CONDITIONS THAT ARE HARDEST TO SATISFY AND THEY DEFINE THE THEORY'S LIMITS, so they deserve attention:**

> **The channel must be able to change all three of its dimensions — so a channel with fixed banks, a rock bed or a lining is not free to reach regime and the theory does not apply to it.**

> **And it must flow through the same material it carries — so a canal excavated in stiff clay and carrying fine silt is not in regime material, and nor is a channel on a rock bed or in gravel it cannot move.**

> **Those two conditions exclude a great many real channels, and Lacey himself distinguished TRUE regime — which is a theoretical ideal rarely fully realised — from INITIAL and FINAL regime.**

**THE THREE STATES LACEY DISTINGUISHED, WHICH ARE WORTH KNOWING:**

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **INITIAL regime** ← | **The channel has adjusted its DEPTH and its SLOPE but not yet its WIDTH — because the banks are still resisting, being of cohesive material or newly cut** ← |
| **FINAL (true) regime** ← | **All three — width, depth and slope — have adjusted, and the channel is fully self-formed** ← |
| **A channel in initial regime is APPARENTLY stable** ← | **But its dimensions are not those the regime relations predict, and it may move to final regime later** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A PRACTICAL WARNING WORTH HEEDING AND IT EXPLAINS SOME PUZZLING FIELD OBSERVATIONS: a newly cut canal may appear stable for years and then begin to widen.**

> **Its banks, initially firm from being freshly cut in cohesive material, gradually soften, are undercut, and slump — and the channel widens toward its true regime width.**

> **So a canal that has behaved perfectly for a decade is not necessarily in equilibrium, and the widening when it comes is not a failure of maintenance but the channel completing an adjustment that was always going to occur.**

> **Designing to the regime width from the start avoids that adjustment, which is one of the practical arguments for using the theory even where the conditions are imperfectly met.**

**AND THE HONEST ASSESSMENT OF THE THEORY, WHICH IS WORTH MAKING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is EMPIRICAL — a set of relations fitted to observations of Indian canals** ← | **Not derived from mechanics** ← |
| **Its data base was narrow — a particular range of discharges, in a particular alluvium, carrying a particular silt load** ← | ← |
| **Within that range it works remarkably well** ← | **Which is why it has been used for a century** ← |
| **Outside it — coarse beds, heavy sediment loads, steep slopes, rock — it is an extrapolation with no basis** ← | ← |
| **And it says nothing about the sediment TRANSPORT mechanics that a modern analysis would address** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER GIVE THE RIGHT ATTITUDE TO IT: Lacey's theory is a good and useful piece of empirical engineering within its domain, and it should be neither dismissed as unscientific nor applied beyond its evidence.**

> **For a canal in the Gangetic alluvium it remains an excellent starting point.**

> **For a channel in Himalayan gravel it is being used far outside its basis, and a tractive force analysis or a sediment transport computation is the appropriate tool — a point worth remembering in a country where most of the rivers are of the second kind and most of the teaching is of the first.**

examTip.trick: **Constant discharge, silt charge and silt grade; boundary of the same material it carries; free to adjust width, depth AND slope.**
examTip.trap: **INITIAL regime has adjusted depth and slope but not WIDTH** — so a canal stable for a decade may still widen later as its banks soften. Not a maintenance failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Empirical, from Gangetic canals, and excellent within that range** — but a Himalayan gravel-bed channel is far outside its evidence. Use tractive force there.

questions.stem: A canal running along a steep HILLSIDE, as is usual in Nepal, faces a hazard that a plains canal does not, namely that:
options: Its velocity is too low to be self-cleansing
Evaporation losses are excessive at altitude
The canal cannot be given an adequate freeboard
The slope above it may deliver landslide debris into the canal
questions.solution:
**The SLOPE above it may deliver LANDSLIDE debris into the canal, blocking it or breaching it — and the canal's own SEEPAGE may saturate the slope below and trigger a slide that carries the canal away.**

**The two directions of the hazard:**

| Direction | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **FROM ABOVE** ← | **Debris, rockfall and slide material from the slope above enters the canal; it blocks the section, the canal overtops, and the overtopping water erodes the outer bank and breaches it** ← |
| **FROM THE CANAL ITSELF** ← | **Seepage from the canal saturates the slope BELOW; the increased pore pressure reduces the slope's stability; and the slope fails, taking the canal with it** ← |

> **THE SECOND MECHANISM IS THE MORE INSIDIOUS AND IT DESERVES PARTICULAR ATTENTION BECAUSE THE CANAL CAUSES ITS OWN DESTRUCTION: an unlined canal on a hillside is a linear source of infiltration along the whole length of a slope.**

> **The water enters the ground, raises the pore pressure in the slope below, and reduces the effective stress on which the slope's friction depends.**

> **A slope that was marginally stable becomes unstable, and it fails — usually in the monsoon, when the canal is running full and the ground is already wet from rainfall.**

> **The failure removes a length of the canal, and the debris often blocks or destroys whatever is below.**

> **So a hill canal can be the CAUSE of the landslide that destroys it, which is a self-inflicted failure of a kind not met in the plains.**

**THE DESIGN RESPONSES, WHICH ARE MOSTLY ABOUT WATER:**

| Response | Note |
|---|---|
| **LINE the canal** ← | **The single most effective measure — it removes the seepage that destabilises the slope, and the case for it is slope stability more than water conservation** ← |
| **A CATCH DRAIN above the canal, properly lined and outletted** ← | **Intercepting the hillside runoff before it enters the canal, and carrying it to a designed crossing** ← |
| **CROSS-DRAINAGE at every gully, sized for a debris-laden flood** ← | **Not merely for the water — a super-passage that a boulder flow will block is no protection** ← |
| **ESCAPES at intervals, so a blockage does not cause a breach** ← | ← |
| **Avoid the alignments across ACTIVE slide zones and old slide debris** ← | **Which requires an engineering geological assessment of the whole alignment, not merely a survey of its level** ← |
| **Provide for INSPECTION and prompt clearance during the monsoon** ← | **A blockage cleared within hours is an inconvenience; one left for a day is a breach** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MEASURE WITH THE LARGEST EFFECT AND THE ONE MOST OFTEN OMITTED FROM THE INVESTIGATION: the alignment should be chosen with the slope's stability in mind, and that requires someone competent to walk it and read the ground.**

> **Old slide scars, hummocky ground, tension cracks, seepage lines, tilted trees and springs at the toe are all visible to a trained eye, and they mark the lengths where a canal will cause or suffer a failure.**

> **A survey that establishes the level and the length, without an engineering geological appraisal, will produce an alignment that is hydraulically correct and passes through three active slide zones.**

> **And realigning after construction is impossible — the canal is where it is — so the geological input has value only if it comes at the alignment stage.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE OPERATIONAL COROLLARY AND IT IS WORTH STATING BECAUSE IT IS CHEAP: a hill canal needs to be WALKED during the monsoon, frequently.**

> **A small slip that has half-blocked the section, cleared the same day, costs an hour's labour.**

> **The same slip left until the canal overtops costs a breach, a suspended supply, and often a much larger slide initiated by the escaping water.**

> **So the difference between a canal that survives a monsoon and one that does not is frequently a matter of whether anyone walked it — which is an institutional provision rather than an engineering one, and it should be written into the scheme's operating arrangements at design rather than left to be discovered.**

examTip.trick: **Debris in from above, and seepage out below destabilising the slope** — the canal can cause the landslide that destroys it.
examTip.trap: **Lining a hill canal is a SLOPE STABILITY measure first and a water-saving one second** — which makes the case far stronger than the seepage saving alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Walk the alignment with someone who can read the ground** — old scars, tension cracks, seepage lines and tilted trees. After construction it cannot be moved.

questions.stem: The advantage of a canal running with its bed BELOW the surrounding ground level (in cutting), as against one in EMBANKMENT above it, is that a canal in cutting:
options: Can command a larger area by gravity
Requires less excavation
Is easier to line
Cannot breach catastrophically
questions.solution:
**It cannot BREACH catastrophically — since there is no head of water above the surrounding ground to escape**, whereas a breached embankment discharges the whole canal onto the land below.

**The two conditions compared:**

| Aspect | In CUTTING | In EMBANKMENT |
|---|---|---|
| **Consequence of a bank failure** | **Minor — the water is at or below ground level and cannot run away** ← | **CATASTROPHIC — the canal's whole flow pours out onto the land below** ← |
| **Area commanded** | **LESS — the water surface is low relative to the land** ← (so option a favours embankment) | **More** ← |
| **Earthwork** | **EXCAVATION, which must be disposed of if surplus** ← | **FILL, which must be borrowed if there is a deficit** ← |
| **Seepage** | **Into the ground, raising the local water table** ← | **Out through the banks, which also THREATENS the banks' stability** ← |
| **Drainage of the adjoining land** | **The canal may INTERCEPT the drainage, acting as a drain** ← | **The canal BLOCKS the natural drainage, ponding water behind it** ← |
| **Bank stability** | **The cutting's slopes may slip inward** ← | **The banks may fail outward, and they are loaded by the water** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DECISIVE SAFETY CONSIDERATION AND IT IS WORTH STATING IN TERMS OF WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS: a breach in a canal running in embankment across a plain is a serious event.**

> **The canal may be carrying tens of cumecs, and once the bank is cut the whole of it discharges through the gap.**

> **The escaping flow rapidly enlarges the breach by erosion, so the discharge grows, and it floods the land below — which is often the land the canal was built to irrigate.**

> **Crops are destroyed, houses may be lost, and the canal is out of service until the breach is closed, which in a large canal is a substantial work.**

> **A canal in cutting cannot do this, because there is no head available: the water is below the surrounding ground and has nowhere to go.**

**WHY CANALS ARE NEVERTHELESS BUILT IN EMBANKMENT, WHICH IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE ARGUMENT:**
