| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **To COMMAND the land** ← | **The whole purpose of an irrigation canal is to deliver water at a level from which it can flow onto the fields — and that requires the canal to be HIGH** ← |
| **A canal in deep cutting commands nothing** ← | **The water cannot get out of it onto the land** ← |
| **So the canal's level is set by the COMMAND requirement, not by the earthwork** ← | ← |
| **And in a flat country, maintaining command over a long distance requires embankment** ← | **Since the canal's gentle slope soon leaves the falling ground behind** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW STATES THE GOVERNING CONSTRAINT AND IT RESOLVES THE APPARENT CONFLICT: the canal is not free to run in cutting.**

> **Its bed level is dictated by the level at which its outlets must deliver water, and that is fixed by the land they serve.**

> **So the designer's choice is not between cutting and embankment but between commanding the land and not commanding it — and where command requires embankment, embankment it must be.**

> **What the designer CAN do is recognise the consequence and provide for it: adequate bank width and freeboard, well-compacted banks, escapes to shed a surplus, inspection to catch a burrow or a seepage before it becomes a breach, and a service road so that a developing failure can be reached.**

> **THE PARTIAL CUTTING AND PARTIAL EMBANKMENT SECTION IS THE USUAL COMPROMISE AND IT IS WORTH NOTING: most canals run partly in cutting and partly in bank, which balances the earthwork (the balancing depth) and limits the head available to escape in a breach.**

> **The depth of water above the surrounding ground is then modest, so a breach discharges less and does so more slowly — and the difference between a canal whose water surface is half a metre above the ground and one where it is three metres is the difference between a manageable failure and a disaster.**

> **So minimising the height of the water above the ground, consistent with maintaining command, is a real design objective and not merely an earthwork economy.**

examTip.trick: **No head above the surrounding ground, so no catastrophic breach.** An embanked canal discharges its whole flow through a breach, enlarging it as it goes.
examTip.trap: **But a canal in cutting commands nothing** — the water cannot reach the fields. The bed level is dictated by COMMAND, not by earthwork economy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Minimise the height of water ABOVE the ground, consistent with command** — half a metre versus three metres is a manageable failure versus a disaster.

questions.stem: In designing a canal by Kennedy's method, the CRITICAL VELOCITY RATIO m is introduced in order to:
options: Convert the velocity from metres per second to other units
Account for the fact that the silt in a particular canal may be coarser or finer than that of the Upper Bari Doab canals on which Kennedy's original relation was based
Allow for the canal's side slopes
Correct for the canal's bed slope
questions.solution:
**To account for the fact that the silt in a particular canal may be COARSER or FINER than that of the Upper Bari Doab canals on which Kennedy's original relation was based** — m exceeding 1 for coarser silt and falling below 1 for finer.

**The values of m:**

| Silt | m |
|---|---|
| **Fine silt (light sandy soil)** ← | **0.7** ← |
| **Fine light sandy soil** | **1.0 — the Upper Bari Doab standard** ← |
| **Coarse light sandy soil** ← | **1.1** ← |
| **Sandy loam / coarse silt** ← | **1.2** ← |
| **Fine to medium sand** | **1.3** |
| **Coarse sand** ← | **1.5 and above** ← |

> **THE LOGIC OF THE FACTOR IS STRAIGHTFORWARD AND WORTH STATING: coarser silt is HARDER to keep in suspension, so it requires a HIGHER velocity to be transported without deposition.**

> **Kennedy's original relation V₀ = 0.55 y^0.64 was fitted to canals carrying a particular silt.**

> **A canal carrying coarser material needs a higher velocity than that relation gives, so m exceeds 1 and multiplies the velocity up.**

> **A canal carrying finer material needs less, so m falls below 1.**

> **The factor is therefore a straightforward calibration of an empirical relation to material other than the one it was derived from — an honest device rather than a fudge.**

**ITS PRACTICAL DIFFICULTY, WHICH IS THE HONEST CRITICISM OF KENNEDY'S METHOD:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **m must be CHOSEN by the designer, from experience or from a table** ← | ← |
| **And it enters the velocity DIRECTLY, so the whole design scales with it** ← | ← |
| **A choice of 1.0 against 1.2 changes the velocity by 20 per cent and the section correspondingly** ← | ← |
| **There is no independent way to determine it from a measurement of the silt** ← | **Unlike Lacey's f, which is computed from the particle size by a stated formula** ← |
| **So Kennedy's method has TWO subjective inputs — m and the assumed B/y ratio — plus an assumed slope** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE SUBSTANTIVE ADVANTAGE OF LACEY'S TREATMENT AND IT IS WORTH THE COMPARISON: Lacey's silt factor is f = 1.76√m with m the particle size in millimetres, so it follows from a laboratory measurement.**

> **Kennedy's critical velocity ratio is a judgment.**

> **A judgment informed by experience of similar canals is not worthless — it may be better than a laboratory figure from a single sample — but it is not reproducible, and two competent designers can reasonably differ.**

> **That is the difference between an empirical relation with a measurable parameter and one with a judged parameter, and it is why Lacey's method displaced Kennedy's for new design while Kennedy's remains useful for checking existing canals whose behaviour is known.**

> **A NOTE ON THE UNFORTUNATE COLLISION OF SYMBOLS IS WORTH ADDING BECAUSE IT CAUSES REAL CONFUSION IN EXAMINATIONS: 'm' means the CRITICAL VELOCITY RATIO in Kennedy's method and the PARTICLE SIZE in Lacey's silt factor formula.**

> **They are entirely different quantities that happen to share a letter, and a candidate who substitutes a particle size into Kennedy's relation, or a critical velocity ratio into Lacey's, will produce an answer that is not merely wrong but meaningless.**

> **Writing out what each symbol stands for before substituting is the defence, and it is worth the ten seconds it takes on any question involving both theories.**

examTip.trick: **m calibrates Kennedy's relation to silt other than the Upper Bari Doab's** — above 1 for coarser, below 1 for finer, since coarse silt needs more velocity to stay up.
examTip.trap: **m is a JUDGMENT; Lacey's f is COMPUTED from the particle size.** That reproducibility is the substantive advantage of Lacey's treatment.
examTip.mnemonic: **'m' is the critical velocity RATIO in Kennedy and the particle SIZE in Lacey's f = 1.76√m** — different quantities sharing a letter. Write out the symbols before substituting.

questions.stem: Among the components of a diversion headworks, the UNDERSLUICES are the:
options: Gated openings in the canal head regulator
Gated bays of the weir
Openings beneath the impervious floor for relieving uplift
Sluices provided in the guide banks
questions.solution:
**The gated bays of the weir, adjacent to the CANAL HEAD REGULATOR and with their crest LOWER than the rest of the weir** — which maintain a deep channel toward the regulator, pass the low flow, and scour the silt that accumulates in the pocket.

**The components of a diversion headworks:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **WEIR or BARRAGE** ← | **Raises the river's level so that water can enter the canal, and passes the flood** ← |
| **UNDERSLUICES (scouring sluices)** ← | **Low-crested gated bays next to the regulator — this question** ← |
| **DIVIDE WALL** ← | **Separates the undersluice pocket from the main weir, creating a still pocket in front of the regulator** ← |
| **CANAL HEAD REGULATOR** ← | **Controls the canal's intake and excludes silt** ← |
| **SILT EXCLUDER** ← | **Tunnels in the undersluice pocket floor, drawing the silt-laden bottom water away** ← |
| **FISH LADDER** ← | **Allowing fish to pass the obstruction** ← |
| **GUIDE BANKS, marginal bunds and river training** ← | **Confining the river and protecting the approaches** ← |
| **Impervious FLOOR, cut-offs and energy dissipation** ← | **The foundation of the whole structure** ← |

> **THE UNDERSLUICES' THREE FUNCTIONS ARE WORTH SEPARATING, SINCE THEY EXPLAIN WHY THEIR CREST IS LOWER THAN THE WEIR'S:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Maintain a DEEP, well-defined channel toward the head regulator** ← | **So the canal can draw water even in the lowest flow, and the river does not wander away from the intake** ← |
| **Pass the DRY WEATHER flow without spilling over the weir** ← | **Keeping the weir crest dry, which allows it to be inspected and repaired** ← |
| **SCOUR the silt deposited in the pocket in front of the regulator** ← | **By opening the gates and letting a concentrated flow sweep the pocket clean** ← |
| **And they pass a share of the FLOOD** ← | **Typically about twice the canal's discharge in capacity, or more** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE OPERATION THAT KEEPS THE HEADWORKS FUNCTIONING AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING AS A ROUTINE RATHER THAN AS A CAPABILITY: silt deposits in the pocket continuously, because the pocket is a still area beside the main flow.**

> **Left alone it fills, and once it has filled to the regulator's sill the canal draws silt directly.**

> **So the undersluice gates are opened periodically — typically at the start and end of the flood season and after any heavy silt-laden flow — and the concentrated discharge through them sweeps the accumulated deposit downstream.**

> **A headworks whose undersluices are never operated, or whose gates have seized, silts up in front of its own regulator and delivers silt into the canal from then on.**

> **That is a maintenance failure with a permanent consequence, since the silt in the canal then has to be dealt with along its whole length.**

**THE ARRANGEMENT'S GEOMETRY IS WORTH PICTURING, SINCE IT ALL FITS TOGETHER:**

| Element | Position |
|---|---|
| **The CANAL HEAD REGULATOR is on the bank, at right angles to the river or at an oblique angle to it** ← | ← |
| **The UNDERSLUICES occupy the bays of the weir immediately in FRONT of it** ← | ← |
| **The DIVIDE WALL runs upstream and downstream, separating that pocket from the main weir** ← | ← |
| **So the pocket is a still, deep bay in front of the regulator, isolated from the main flow** ← | ← |
| **And the SILT EXCLUDER tunnels run along the pocket's floor, drawing the bottom water into the undersluices and away** ← | ← |

> **THE PURPOSE OF THAT WHOLE ARRANGEMENT IS SILT EXCLUSION AND IT IS WORTH SEEING AS ONE SYSTEM: the divide wall creates a pocket, the pocket is kept deep by the undersluices, the excluder draws the silty bottom water out of it, and the regulator draws the cleaner surface water off the top.**

> **Each element is useless without the others: an excluder with no pocket has no still water to work in, a pocket with no undersluices silts up, and a regulator with neither draws the river's full silt load.**

> **So a headworks is not a collection of independent structures but an arrangement in which the silt is managed by geometry — and understanding the arrangement as a whole is more useful than knowing what each part is called.**

examTip.trick: **Low-crested gated bays next to the head regulator** — keeping a deep channel to the intake, passing the low flow, and scouring the pocket.
examTip.trap: **They must actually be OPERATED** — a headworks whose undersluices are never opened silts up in front of its own regulator and feeds silt into the canal permanently.
examTip.mnemonic: **Divide wall makes a pocket, undersluices keep it deep, excluder takes the silty bottom water, regulator takes the clean surface water.** One system, not four structures.

questions.stem: BLIGH'S CREEP THEORY for the design of an impervious floor on a permeable foundation assumes that:
options: Seepage occurs only beneath the vertical cut-offs
The uplift pressure is uniform beneath the whole floor
The seeping water creeps along the contact surface between the floor and the soil
The seepage path is a series of concentric circles
questions.solution:
**The seeping water CREEPS along the contact surface between the floor and the soil, and the head is lost UNIFORMLY along that path** — with VERTICAL and HORIZONTAL creep treated as EQUALLY effective.

**Bligh's propositions:**

| Proposition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The water travels along the contact surface, following its every rise and fall** ← | **Down a cut-off, along the floor, up the other side, and so on** ← |
| **The total CREEP LENGTH is the sum of all those vertical and horizontal distances** ← | ← |
| **The head is lost UNIFORMLY along that length** ← | **So the hydraulic gradient is constant** ← |
| **The required creep length is L = C × H** ← | **C being BLIGH'S COEFFICIENT for the soil and H the head** ← |
| **And the uplift at any point follows from the fraction of the creep length travelled** ← | ← |

> **THE ASSUMPTION IN THE FIRST ROW OF THE ANSWER — THAT VERTICAL AND HORIZONTAL CREEP ARE EQUALLY EFFECTIVE — IS BLIGH'S PRINCIPAL ERROR AND IT IS THE ONE LANE CORRECTED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Alluvial soil is STRATIFIED, deposited in horizontal layers** ← | ← |
| **So its permeability is much GREATER horizontally than vertically** ← | **Often by a factor of several, and sometimes by an order of magnitude** ← |
| **Water therefore travels far more easily along a horizontal path than down a vertical one** ← | ← |
| **So a metre of VERTICAL creep dissipates MORE head than a metre of horizontal creep** ← | ← |
| **Bligh treated them as equal, which OVERSTATES the effectiveness of horizontal creep** ← | **And therefore understates the length of floor required, or overstates the value of a long floor relative to a deep cut-off** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE AND IT IS WHY BLIGH'S THEORY IS UNSAFE IN ONE SPECIFIC RESPECT: it encourages the designer to obtain creep length cheaply, by extending the floor horizontally, when a vertical cut-off would have been far more effective.**

> **A long floor is a large area of concrete; a deep cut-off is a narrow wall.**

> **Bligh's arithmetic makes them equivalent per metre, so the designer builds the floor — and the structure has less protection than the calculation suggests.**

> **Several weirs designed on Bligh's theory failed by piping, which is what prompted the reassessment.**

**LANE'S WEIGHTED CREEP THEORY IS THE DIRECT CORRECTION AND IT IS WORTH STATING ALONGSIDE:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Lane WEIGHTED the horizontal creep by ONE THIRD** ← | **L_w = ⅓ (horizontal creep) + (vertical creep)** ← |
| **So a metre of vertical cut-off counts as much as THREE metres of floor** ← | ← |
| **Lane's coefficients C₁ are correspondingly different from Bligh's** ← | **And the two sets must not be interchanged** ← |
| **The theory is still empirical and still assumes a uniform loss of head** ← | **It corrects Bligh's weighting without changing his framework** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A TRAP WORTH FLAGGING EXPLICITLY: Bligh's C and Lane's C₁ are different numbers for the same soils, because the creep lengths they are applied to are computed differently.**

> **Using Bligh's coefficient with Lane's weighted creep length, or the reverse, gives an answer with no meaning — and the two tables look similar enough for the substitution to be made without noticing.**

> **The safeguard is to state which theory is being used at the top of the calculation and to take the coefficient from that theory's own table.**

**AND KHOSLA'S THEORY, WHICH SUPERSEDED BOTH, DIFFERS IN KIND RATHER THAN IN DEGREE:**

> **Khosla showed by analysis and by experiment that the head is NOT lost uniformly along the creep path at all.**

> **The flow beneath a floor is a two-dimensional potential flow, and the pressure distribution follows from solving that flow — not from measuring a path length.**

> **Most of the head is lost near the ENDS of the floor and near the cut-offs, and comparatively little along the middle of a long floor — which is why extending a floor's middle length achieves so much less than Bligh's theory suggests.**

> **So Khosla did not adjust Bligh's weighting; he replaced the whole conception, and his method gives the pressure at defined KEY POINTS from a theoretically derived set of curves rather than from a proportion of a path.**

examTip.trick: **Creep along the contact surface with UNIFORM head loss, vertical and horizontal counted EQUALLY.** L = C × H.
examTip.trap: **Treating them equally overstates horizontal creep** — alluvium is far more permeable horizontally. Lane weights the horizontal by ⅓, so 1 m of cut-off equals 3 m of floor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bligh's C and Lane's C₁ are DIFFERENT numbers** — never mix a coefficient from one theory with a creep length from the other. State the theory at the top of the calculation.

questions.stem: The EXIT GRADIENT at the downstream end of an impervious floor is important because, if it becomes too steep:
options: The floor will crack from thermal movement
The upstream water level will rise excessively
The floor will be lifted by uplift pressure
The seeping water emerging at the downstream end will dislodge the surface soil particles
questions.solution:
**The seeping water emerging at the downstream end will DISLODGE the surface soil particles, and the resulting erosion works progressively BACKWARD beneath the floor** — the phenomenon of PIPING, which undermines and destroys the structure.

**The mechanism of piping:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water seeping beneath the floor emerges at the downstream end, flowing UPWARD** ← | ← |
| **That upward flow exerts a SEEPAGE FORCE on the soil grains, opposing their weight** ← | ← |
| **If the exit gradient is steep enough, the seepage force EXCEEDS the submerged weight and the grains are lifted** ← | **The QUICK condition** ← |
| **Once grains are removed, the seepage concentrates through the resulting hollow** ← | **So the gradient there rises further** ← |
| **The erosion works BACKWARD, forming a PIPE beneath the floor** ← | **Toward the upstream side** ← |
| **When the pipe reaches the upstream water, the flow becomes unrestricted and the structure collapses** ← | ← |

> **THE PROGRESSIVE, SELF-ACCELERATING CHARACTER IN THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS IS WHAT MAKES PIPING SO DANGEROUS AND IT IS THE SAME PATTERN MET IN HYDRAULIC JACKING AND IN SEVERAL BIOLOGICAL UPSETS: the failure creates the condition that worsens it.**

> **A small amount of erosion shortens the seepage path, which steepens the gradient, which erodes more.**

> **So piping does not stabilise at a new equilibrium; once it begins it runs to completion, and it can do so in hours.**

> **And it begins invisibly, beneath the structure, with the only outward sign being a small quantity of sand appearing in the water downstream — which is why sand boils downstream of a weir or an embankment are treated as an emergency rather than as an observation.**

**THE CRITICAL GRADIENT AND THE FACTOR OF SAFETY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The CRITICAL exit gradient, at which grains are just lifted, is i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e)** ← | **G being the specific gravity of the grains and e the void ratio** ← |
| **For typical values — G = 2.65, e = 0.6 — that gives i_c ≈ 1.0** ← | **A gradient of unity** ← |
| **A FACTOR OF SAFETY of 4 to 6 is applied** ← | **A large factor, reflecting how sudden and complete the failure is** ← |
| **So the permissible exit gradient is about 1/4 to 1/7, depending on the soil** ← | **1/4 to 1/5 for shingle, 1/5 to 1/6 for coarse sand, 1/6 to 1/7 for fine sand** ← |

> **THE MAGNITUDE OF THE FACTOR IN THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH NOTING AND IT IS UNUSUALLY LARGE FOR A GEOTECHNICAL CHECK: four to six, against the two to three used for bearing capacity.**

> **The reason is the character of the failure: a bearing capacity failure gives warning by settlement and is progressive over time, while piping is sudden, complete and unrecoverable.**

> **Where a failure is brittle and catastrophic, the factor of safety is larger — the same reasoning that gives rupture a larger partial factor than yielding in steel design, and shear a larger margin than flexure in concrete.**

> **Recognising that as a general principle is more useful than remembering the specific numbers.**

**HOW THE EXIT GRADIENT IS CONTROLLED, WHICH IS THE DESIGN RESPONSE:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **A DOWNSTREAM CUT-OFF (sheet pile) at the floor's end** ← | **The most effective single measure — it forces the water to travel deeper and emerge further from the floor, flattening the gradient** ← |
| **A LONGER impervious floor** ← | **Increasing the seepage path, though less effective than depth, as Khosla showed** ← |
| **An INVERTED FILTER at the downstream end** ← | **Graded material that lets the water out and holds the soil in — the same filter criteria as everywhere else** ← |
| **A LOADED APRON of concrete blocks over the filter** ← | **Adding weight to resist the uplift on the emerging grains** ← |
| **Reducing the HEAD, where that is possible** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS DECISIVE AND IT FOLLOWS FROM KHOSLA'S ANALYSIS: the exit gradient is governed almost entirely by the DEPTH of the downstream cut-off, and hardly at all by the floor's length.**

> **Khosla's expression for the exit gradient contains the head, the floor length and the cut-off depth, and the cut-off depth dominates it — an exit gradient that cannot be brought within limits by any practicable floor length is brought within them by a modest increase in the cut-off's depth.**

> **So the downstream cut-off is not an optional refinement but the principal defence against piping, and a headworks designed with a long floor and a shallow end cut-off has spent its money in the wrong place.**

> **That conclusion is a direct product of Khosla's replacement of the uniform-creep assumption, and it is the clearest practical demonstration of why the theory mattered.**

examTip.trick: **Emerging seepage lifts the grains, and the erosion works BACKWARD as a pipe** until it reaches the upstream water and the structure collapses.
examTip.trap: **The factor of safety is 4 to 6, far larger than for bearing capacity** — because the failure is sudden, complete and unrecoverable rather than progressive.
examTip.mnemonic: **The DOWNSTREAM CUT-OFF's depth governs the exit gradient, not the floor's length** — which is Khosla's most important practical finding. Sand boils are an emergency.

questions.stem: The thickness of the impervious floor of a weir at a point where the residual UPLIFT head is 3.0 m, taking the specific gravity of the floor material as 2.24, must be at least:
questions.solution:
**2.42 m.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The floor must WEIGH enough to balance the uplift beneath it** ← | ← |
| **Uplift pressure per unit area = γ_w × h** | **= γ_w × 3.0** ← |
| **Weight of the floor per unit area = γ_w × G × t** | **= γ_w × 2.24 × t** ← |
| **But the floor is SUBMERGED, so its BUOYANT weight resists** ← | **γ_w (G − 1) t** ← |
| **Equating: γ_w (G − 1) t = γ_w h** | **So t = h/(G − 1)** ← |
| **t = 3.0 / (2.24 − 1) = 3.0/1.24** | **= 2.42 m** ← |

> **So the floor must be at least 2.42 m thick at that point — and a factor of safety of about 4/3 is commonly applied, giving about 3.2 m in practice.**

**THE (G − 1) IN THE DENOMINATOR IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG AND ITS REASON IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The floor sits in water, with water above it and uplift below** ← | ← |
| **So its EFFECTIVE weight is its buoyant weight — its own weight less the weight of water it displaces** ← | ← |
| **Which is γ_w (G − 1) t, not γ_w G t** ← | ← |
| **Using G instead of (G − 1) gives 3.0/2.24 = 1.34 m — option (b) — which is a 45 per cent UNDER-estimate** ← | **And an unsafe one** ← |

> **THE ERROR IS THEREFORE UNSAFE RATHER THAN CONSERVATIVE, WHICH IS WHY IT MATTERS: a floor designed by the wrong formula is thinner than it needs to be, and it will be lifted.**

> **The physical check is simple: a floor made of a material with G = 1 would weigh exactly what the water it displaces weighs, and could resist NO uplift at all — so the formula must give an infinite thickness at G = 1.**

> **t = h/(G − 1) does exactly that; t = h/G does not.**

> **Testing a formula at a limiting case in that way is a good general habit and it catches this class of error immediately.**

**WHERE THE UPLIFT HEAD h COMES FROM, WHICH IS THE HARDER PART OF THE PROBLEM:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The uplift at a point is the residual seepage head there, ABOVE the floor level at that point** ← | ← |
| **It is obtained from Bligh's proportion of the creep length, or from KHOSLA'S key point pressures** ← | ← |
| **Khosla's method gives the percentage pressure at defined key points from a set of curves** ← | **The junctions of the cut-offs with the floor, and the floor's ends** ← |
| **Corrections are then applied for the floor's THICKNESS, for MUTUAL INTERFERENCE of the piles, and for the floor's SLOPE** ← | **Three corrections, each with its own sign convention** ← |
| **And the uplift is greatest at the DOWNSTREAM end of the floor, where the floor is thinnest in the sloping glacis arrangement** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CONTAINS THE DESIGN TENSION THAT GOVERNS THE FLOOR'S PROFILE AND IT IS WORTH SEEING: the residual head is greatest at the downstream end, and that is also where the floor is under the stilling basin and cannot easily be made very thick.**

> **So the downstream floor thickness frequently governs the design, and the ways of relieving it are to lengthen the creep path upstream, to deepen the cut-offs, or to provide DRAINAGE holes through the floor with a filter beneath — which relieves the uplift by letting the water out rather than by resisting it.**

> **That last measure is the same principle as the weep holes in a canal lining and the drainage gallery in a gravity dam, and it is used in the downstream floor of many barrages for exactly this reason.**

> **A caution goes with it: a drainage hole beneath a stilling basin is at the point of greatest turbulence, so its filter must be robust and it must not become a route for the basin's own water to be forced downward into the foundation, which would defeat its purpose.**
tags: t equals h over G minus 1

examTip.trick: **t = h/(G − 1) = 3.0/1.24 = 2.42 m.** The floor is submerged, so its BUOYANT weight resists the uplift.
examTip.trap: **Using G instead of (G − 1) gives 1.34 m — a 45 % UNDER-estimate and unsafe.** Check the formula at G = 1: it must give infinite thickness, and t = h/G does not.
examTip.mnemonic: **Uplift is greatest at the DOWNSTREAM end, where the floor can least easily be thickened** — so lengthen the creep path, deepen the cut-off, or provide relief holes with a filter.

questions.stem: KHOSLA'S theory differs fundamentally from Bligh's in that Khosla showed that:
options: The seepage beneath a floor is a two-dimensional potential flow whose pressure distribution must be solved, not assumed
Seepage occurs only through the upstream half of the floor
The creep length should be weighted, with vertical creep counted three times
The exit gradient is independent of the cut-off depth
questions.solution:
**The seepage beneath a floor is a two-dimensional POTENTIAL FLOW whose pressure distribution must be SOLVED, not assumed** — so the head is not lost uniformly along the creep path, and the intermediate sheet piles are far less effective than the end ones.

**What Khosla established:**

| Finding | Note |
|---|---|
| **The flow beneath a floor obeys LAPLACE'S equation** ← | **So it is a potential flow problem with a determinate solution, not an empirical path length** ← |
| **The head is lost NON-uniformly** ← | **Most of it near the cut-offs and the floor's ends, and comparatively little along a long floor's middle** ← |
| **The OUTER (end) cut-offs are far more effective than INTERMEDIATE ones** ← | **An intermediate pile in the middle of a floor contributes remarkably little** ← |
| **The exit gradient depends chiefly on the DOWNSTREAM cut-off's depth** ← | **And on the floor length only weakly** ← (so option d is inverted) |
| **Undermining of the floor begins at the DOWNSTREAM end** ← | **Where the exit gradient is** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE FINDING WITH THE GREATEST PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE AND IT OVERTURNED EXISTING PRACTICE: intermediate sheet piles, which Bligh's theory credited with their full length of vertical creep, were shown to be largely ineffective.**

> **Under Bligh's theory a designer could add creep length cheaply by driving a pile anywhere along the floor, and each metre of pile counted.**

> **Khosla's analysis showed that a pile in the middle of a long floor sits where the pressure gradient is already gentle, so it dissipates very little additional head.**

> **The piles that matter are the ones at the ENDS, where the flow is converging and the gradients are steep.**

> **So the design conclusion is: TWO deep end cut-offs, and intermediate piles only where they are needed for another reason — such as protecting the floor against scour or providing a construction cut-off.**

**KHOSLA'S METHOD IN PRACTICE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The actual profile is broken into a set of SIMPLE STANDARD FORMS** ← | **A straight floor with a pile at one end, at the other end, or in the middle — each of which Khosla solved** ← |
| **The percentage pressure at defined KEY POINTS is read from his curves** ← | **The key points being the pile's top and bottom and the floor's junctions** ← |
| **THREE CORRECTIONS are then applied** ← | ← |
| **(i) For the floor's THICKNESS** ← | **Since the curves assume a floor of negligible thickness, and the key point is really at the floor's underside** ← |
| **(ii) For MUTUAL INTERFERENCE of the piles** ← | **Each pile affects the pressure at the others** ← |
| **(iii) For the SLOPE of the floor** ← | **Where a glacis is involved** ← |
| **The corrected pressures give the uplift, and hence the floor thickness at each point** ← | ← |

> **THE 'BREAKING INTO SIMPLE FORMS' IN THE FIRST STEP IS THE METHOD'S PRACTICAL DEVICE AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING AS AN ENGINEERING APPROACH: the exact solution for a complicated real profile is intractable, and the exact solutions for a few simple profiles are obtainable.**

> **So the real profile is decomposed into simple ones, each solved exactly, and the results combined with corrections for the interactions.**

> **That is a general technique — solve the tractable idealisations and correct for their interaction — and it recurs throughout engineering analysis wherever an exact solution to the real problem is out of reach.**

> **THE SIGN CONVENTIONS OF THE THREE CORRECTIONS ARE THE PRACTICAL DIFFICULTY IN APPLYING THE METHOD AND THEY DESERVE A WARNING: each correction can be positive or negative depending on which key point is being corrected and where the interfering pile lies.**

> **The thickness correction is applied toward the interior of the floor; the interference correction depends on whether the neighbouring pile is upstream or downstream; and the slope correction's sign depends on whether the floor descends or ascends in the direction of flow.**

> **Getting a sign wrong produces a pressure that is plausible in magnitude and wrong in direction, and the resulting floor thickness may be too small at the point that matters.**

> **The defence is to sketch the profile, mark the key points, and reason out each correction's direction physically before applying its magnitude — rather than taking the signs from a remembered rule.**

examTip.trick: **A potential flow to be SOLVED, not a path length to be measured** — so head is lost mostly near the cut-offs and ends, not uniformly.
examTip.trap: **INTERMEDIATE piles are largely ineffective; the END cut-offs do the work.** Bligh's theory credited every pile equally, which is why it misdirected design.
examTip.mnemonic: **Decompose into simple solved forms, read the key point pressures, apply three corrections — thickness, interference, slope.** Reason each correction's SIGN physically.

questions.stem: A SILT EXCLUDER at a diversion headworks differs from a SILT EJECTOR in that the excluder:
options: Removes silt from the canal after it has entered, at a point some distance downstream
Is a settling basin provided in the canal's first reach
Chemically flocculates the silt so that it settles
Is placed in the river, in the undersluice pocket upstream of the canal head regulator, and prevents the silt-laden bottom water from entering the canal at all
questions.solution:
**It is placed in the RIVER, in the undersluice pocket UPSTREAM of the canal head regulator, and prevents the silt-laden BOTTOM water from entering the canal at all** — whereas an ejector is placed IN the canal, downstream of the regulator, and removes silt that has already entered.

**The two devices compared:**

| Aspect | SILT EXCLUDER | SILT EJECTOR (extractor) |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | **In the RIVER, in the undersluice pocket, UPSTREAM of the regulator** ← | **In the CANAL, downstream of the regulator** ← |
| **Principle** | **PREVENTS the silty bottom water from entering** ← | **REMOVES silt that has already entered** ← |
| **Arrangement** | **A set of horizontal TUNNELS on the pocket floor, discharging through the undersluices** ← | **A tunnel or a diaphragm across the canal bed, with an escape channel to a drainage** ← |
| **Water used** | **River water that would have gone downstream anyway** ← | **CANAL water, which is diverted supply and is therefore LOST** ← |
| **Effectiveness** | **Good for the coarser fraction** | **Good, and it can be placed after the silt has had a reach to settle toward the bed** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL DIFFERENCE AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: the excluder costs the river's water and the ejector costs the CANAL's water.**

> **An excluder draws the silty bottom water off in the pocket and discharges it through the undersluices, back into the river — where it would have gone in any case.**

> **An ejector takes water that has already been diverted into the canal, has been paid for in head and in entitlement, and throws it away with the silt — typically 10 to 20 per cent of the canal's discharge.**

> **So the excluder is preferable wherever it can be made to work, and the ejector is the remedy where exclusion has proved insufficient.**

> **Many headworks have both: the excluder removes what it can at the intake, and the ejector removes what got past it a few kilometres down the canal.**

**HOW THE EXCLUDER WORKS, WHICH IS AN ELEGANT PIECE OF HYDRAULICS:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sediment concentration is greatest near the BED and least at the surface** ← | **The whole basis of the device** ← |
| **A set of horizontal tunnels is built on the pocket's floor, with their tops at about the regulator's sill level** ← | ← |
| **The tunnels draw off the BOTTOM layer of water — the most silt-laden** ← | ← |
| **And discharge it through the undersluices back to the river** ← | ← |
| **The regulator, whose sill is above the tunnels' roof, draws the cleaner SURFACE water** ← | ← |
| **The tunnels are made of DECREASING size away from the undersluices** ← | **So the velocity in each is maintained and none of them silts up** ← |

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE DESIGN DETAIL THAT MAKES THE DEVICE WORK RATHER THAN MERELY EXIST AND IT IS WORTH NOTING: a set of tunnels of uniform size would carry unequal flows, and the furthest would run slowly and silt up.**

> **Tapering them maintains the velocity in each, so each stays clear.**

> **That is the same reasoning as the graded barrels of an inverted siphon and the tapered flocculator — matching the geometry to the varying duty rather than adopting a uniform section — and it is a recurring mark of competent hydraulic design.**

**THE LIMITATION OF BOTH DEVICES SHOULD BE STATED AS A CLOSING POINT, SINCE IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED:**

> **Both work on the COARSER sediment, which travels near the bed and can be separated by drawing off the bottom layer.**

> **The FINE suspended fraction is distributed nearly uniformly through the depth, so drawing off the bottom water removes very little of it.**

> **So an excluder and an ejector together may remove most of the sand and very little of the silt — and if the canal's problem is fine silt deposition in its lower reaches, neither device will solve it.**

> **The remedy for the fine fraction is a SETTLING BASIN with a long detention, which is the hydropower solution, and it is far larger and more expensive than either device.**

> **Knowing which fraction is causing the problem is therefore the first step, and it requires the canal's sediment to be sampled and graded rather than assumed — a modest investigation that determines whether the expensive remedy is necessary or whether the cheap one will serve.**

examTip.trick: **Excluder: in the RIVER, before the regulator, keeps silt OUT. Ejector: in the CANAL, after the regulator, takes silt out.**
examTip.trap: **An excluder spends river water; an ejector spends CANAL water** — 10-20 % of the diverted supply. So exclude first and eject only what got past.
examTip.mnemonic: **Both work on the COARSE fraction near the bed** — fine suspended silt is spread through the depth and neither removes it. That needs a settling basin.

questions.stem: Using Bligh's creep theory with a coefficient C of 12 for fine sand, the total creep length required beneath a weir working under a head of 4 m is:
options: 3 m
questions.solution:
**48 m.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Bligh's relation** | **L = C × H** ← |
| **Substituting** | **= 12 × 4** ← |
| **L** | **= 48 m** ← |

> **So the total creep length — the sum of all the vertical and horizontal travel along the contact surface — must be at least 48 m.**

**BLIGH'S COEFFICIENTS, WHICH MUST BE TAKEN FROM HIS OWN TABLE AND NOT LANE'S:**

| Soil | Bligh's C |
|---|---|
| **Light sand and mud** ← | **18** ← |
| **Fine micaceous sand** ← | **15** ← |
| **Coarse-grained sand** ← | **12** ← |
| **Boulders, gravel and sand** ← | **5 to 9** ← |

> **THE PATTERN IS THAT FINER SOILS NEED LONGER CREEP AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING WHY, SINCE IT SEEMS BACKWARDS AT FIRST: a fine soil is LESS permeable, so one might expect it to need less protection.**

> **But the danger is not the quantity of seepage, it is the EROSION of the grains at the exit.**

> **Fine grains are light and are dislodged by a much gentler gradient than coarse ones, so the permissible exit gradient in fine sand is far lower — and a lower permissible gradient means a longer path for the same head.**

> **So the coefficient is governed by the soil's ERODIBILITY rather than by its permeability, and once that is seen the ordering of the table is obvious rather than arbitrary.**

**HOW THE CREEP LENGTH IS THEN DISTRIBUTED, WHICH IS THE DESIGN STEP THAT FOLLOWS:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The 48 m must be made up of vertical and horizontal creep** ← | ← |
| **Vertical creep comes from the CUT-OFFS — twice their depth each, since the water goes down one face and up the other** ← | **A 3 m cut-off contributes 6 m** ← |
| **Horizontal creep comes from the FLOOR's length** ← | ← |
| **The upstream and downstream cut-off depths are usually fixed first, from the SCOUR consideration** ← | **Lacey's R, times the appropriate factor** ← |
| **The remaining creep is then made up by the floor's LENGTH** ← | ← |
| **And the floor's length is disposed so that most of it is DOWNSTREAM** ← | **Where it is also needed for energy dissipation** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN IMPORTANT ORDERING POINT AND IT IS WORTH STATING: the cut-off depths are set by SCOUR, not by seepage.**

> **A cut-off must go below the anticipated scour level or the river will simply undermine it, and that requirement usually gives a greater depth than the seepage calculation alone would demand.**

> **So the sequence is: compute the scour depth from Lacey, set the cut-offs below it, compute the creep those cut-offs provide, and make up the balance with the floor.**

> **A designer who sizes the cut-offs for seepage and then finds them shallower than the scour has done the calculation in the wrong order and will have to start again.**

> **A FINAL CAUTION ON USING BLIGH AT ALL IS WORTH ADDING, SINCE THE QUESTION USES IT: Bligh's theory is superseded and is retained in teaching because it is simple and because it introduces the concepts.**

> **A modern design uses Khosla's method for the uplift pressures and the exit gradient, and Bligh's creep length at most as a preliminary check on the overall floor length.**

> **Designing a real weir on Bligh's theory alone would be indefensible, and the failures that prompted Khosla's work are the reason — so a candidate should be able to apply Bligh's arithmetic and should also be able to say why it is not used for design.**

examTip.trick: **L = C × H = 12 × 4 = 48 m.** Option (a) is H × H and (b) is C/H — both inversions of the relation.
examTip.trap: **Finer soils need LONGER creep** — not because they are more permeable but because their grains are lighter and are dislodged at a gentler exit gradient. Erodibility, not permeability.
examTip.mnemonic: **Set the cut-off depths from SCOUR first (Lacey's R), then make up the creep with the floor** — doing it the other way round means starting again.

questions.stem: The DIVIDE WALL at a diversion headworks is provided principally to:
options: Divide the canal's discharge between two branches
Separate the undersluice pocket from the weir proper
Support the roadway carried over the barrage
Divide the river's flood between two channels
questions.solution:
**To SEPARATE the undersluice pocket from the weir proper** — creating a still pocket in front of the canal head regulator, preventing cross-currents, and confining the scouring action of the undersluices to that pocket.

**Its several functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Creates a STILL POCKET in front of the head regulator** ← | **So the water the canal draws is quiet, and its coarser sediment has settled out** ← |
| **Prevents CROSS-CURRENTS between the undersluices and the weir bays** ← | **Which would otherwise form as the two discharge at different rates, and would scour the floor** ← |
| **Confines the SCOURING action of the undersluices to the pocket** ← | **So the scour is concentrated where it is wanted** ← |
| **Separates the two stilling basins, which are at different levels** ← | **The undersluice floor being lower than the weir's** ← |
| **Provides a working platform, and often carries the silt excluder tunnels' discharge** ← | ← |
| **Extends UPSTREAM to create the pocket and DOWNSTREAM to keep the two flows apart until they have both slowed** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE FUNCTION THAT PROTECTS THE STRUCTURE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: the undersluices and the weir bays beside them are discharging at very different rates and under different conditions.**

> **The undersluices, with a lower crest and gates, pass a concentrated deep flow; the weir bays pass a shallower flow over a higher crest.**

> **Where the two meet, the difference in velocity and direction creates a strong transverse current and an eddy.**

> **That cross-current attacks the floor, the aprons and the divide wall's own foundations, and it can scour a hole at the junction that undermines both.**

> **The divide wall keeps the two flows apart until they have both decelerated in their respective stilling basins, by which time the difference between them no longer matters.**

**ITS DOWNSTREAM EXTENSION IN THE LAST ROW DESERVES A NOTE, SINCE ITS LENGTH IS A REAL DESIGN QUESTION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Upstream, the wall extends far enough to form the pocket and to guide the flow into the undersluices** ← | ← |
| **Downstream, it must extend beyond the END of the stilling basins** ← | **Or the two flows meet while one is still fast and turbulent** ← |
| **A wall that stops too soon allows the cross-current to form at its end** ← | **Where it scours a hole and then undermines the wall itself from the tip backward** ← |
| **The tip is therefore founded DEEP and protected with a launching apron** ← | **The same treatment as a guide bank's nose, and for the same reason** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESCRIBES A FAILURE THAT HAS OCCURRED AND IT FOLLOWS THE FAMILIAR PATTERN: a structure ends, the flow concentrates at its end, the scour begins there, and it works backward.**

> **The guide bank's nose, the divide wall's tip, the end of a launching apron and the end of an impervious floor are all instances of the same thing — a boundary between a protected region and an unprotected one, at which the attack concentrates.**

> **Recognising that as one principle is worth doing, because the design response is the same in each case: found the end deep, protect it heavily, and give it launching material to fall into the hole that will form.**

> **THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE POCKET DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE ON SILT, SINCE IT IS THE POCKET'S REASON FOR EXISTING: a still pocket is a settling basin, and a settling basin fills.**

> **So the pocket accumulates the very sediment it was created to drop out of the canal's supply, and it must be scoured regularly through the undersluices.**

> **A pocket that is not scoured fills to the regulator's sill and then delivers silt into the canal continuously — at which point the divide wall, the pocket and the excluder are all working against a bed of accumulated sand and achieving nothing.**

> **The structure therefore requires an OPERATING regime to function, and the regime is as much part of the design as the geometry: the gates must be opened, in the right sequence, at the right times, and someone must be responsible for doing it.**

examTip.trick: **Separates the undersluice pocket from the weir** — creating a still pocket, preventing cross-currents, and confining the scour to the pocket.
examTip.trap: **It must extend DOWNSTREAM beyond the stilling basins** — otherwise the fast and slow flows meet at its tip, scour a hole, and undermine the wall from the end backward.
examTip.mnemonic: **Every structure's END is where the attack concentrates** — guide bank nose, divide wall tip, apron end, floor end. Found deep, protect heavily, provide launching material.

questions.stem: The CANAL HEAD REGULATOR at a diversion headworks is usually aligned at an angle of about 90 to 110 degrees to the axis of the weir, rather than in line with the river's flow, because this alignment:
options: Reduces the length of the regulator
Helps to exclude silt
Makes the gates easier to operate
Allows a longer bridge to be built over it
questions.solution:
**It helps to EXCLUDE SILT — the flow must turn to enter the canal, and the heavier silt-laden bottom water, having greater momentum, tends to continue downstream rather than turning.**

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water entering the canal must turn through a large angle** ← | ← |
| **Turning requires a force, supplied by a pressure gradient across the flow** ← | ← |
| **The SURFACE water is lighter and slower, and turns readily** ← | ← |
| **The BOTTOM water, denser with suspended sediment and carrying the bed load, has greater momentum and resists turning** ← | ← |
| **So it tends to continue straight on, past the regulator and toward the undersluices** ← | ← |
| **And the canal draws preferentially from the cleaner upper layer** ← | ← |

> **THIS IS THE SAME PRINCIPLE AS THE SIDE INTAKE ON A RIVER BEND AND AS THE SILT EXCLUDER, AND IT IS WORTH SEEING THE THREE TOGETHER: in every case the aim is to draw the SURFACE water and let the BOTTOM water go past.**

> **The bend does it by secondary circulation, the excluder by physically drawing off the bottom layer, and the oblique regulator by exploiting the momentum difference in a turn.**

> **Three different mechanisms serving one objective, and a well-designed headworks uses all three at once.**

> **That redundancy is deliberate: no single measure excludes silt completely, and their effects are broadly additive.**

**THE OTHER FUNCTIONS OF THE HEAD REGULATOR, FOR COMPLETENESS:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **REGULATE the canal's discharge** ← | **By its gates — admitting the required supply and no more** ← |
| **EXCLUDE silt, as above** ← | ← |
| **Prevent the river's FLOOD from entering the canal** ← | **By closing the gates entirely when the river is in flood** ← |
| **Provide a means of MEASURING the discharge admitted** ← | **Often by a metering flume or by the gate opening and head** ← |
| **And it must resist the differential water pressure when closed against a flood** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE FUNCTION THAT MATTERS MOST DURING AN EXTREME EVENT AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: when the river is in high flood, the last thing wanted is a canal drawing its full supply.**

> **The flood water is at its most silt-laden, so the canal would fill with sediment along its whole length.**

> **And the flood level may exceed what the canal's banks can safely contain, so the canal itself could be overtopped and breached from the head.**

> **So the standard operating rule is to CLOSE the head regulator during a major flood and reopen it when the river has fallen and cleared — accepting a short interruption of supply to avoid a long one.**

> **That rule requires the gates to WORK, which requires them to be exercised, greased and maintained in the dry season when nothing seems urgent.**

> **A regulator whose gates have seized cannot be closed when the flood comes, and the canal then receives the flood's full sediment load and, in the worst case, its flood level too — which is a maintenance failure with a consequence out of all proportion to the neglect.**

> **THE SILL LEVEL OF THE REGULATOR IS THE OTHER SILT-EXCLUDING PROVISION AND IT SHOULD BE MENTIONED: the sill is set WELL ABOVE the undersluice floor, typically 1.2 to 1.5 m above it.**

> **That raised sill means the canal draws from the upper part of the water column, above the layer where the coarse sediment travels.**

> **It is the simplest and most effective silt-exclusion measure of all, it costs nothing, and it is fixed permanently at design — so getting the sill level right is more valuable than any device installed later.**

examTip.trick: **The flow must TURN to enter the canal, and the heavy bottom water resists turning** — so it continues downstream and the canal draws cleaner surface water.
examTip.trap: **Three mechanisms serve one objective** — the bend's secondary flow, the excluder's tunnels, and the oblique regulator's momentum effect. Use all three.
examTip.mnemonic: **Close the head regulator during a major flood** — the water is at its most silt-laden and the level may exceed the canal's banks. Which requires the gates to have been maintained.

questions.stem: A BARRAGE is preferred to a WEIR at a diversion headworks principally because a barrage:
options: Controls the upstream water level by gates on a low crest
Costs less to build
Requires no impervious floor
Needs no operating staff
questions.solution:
**It controls the upstream water level by GATES on a LOW crest** — so the pond level can be held at any stage, and the gates can be opened fully in a flood to pass it at a much SMALLER AFFLUX than a weir of the same pond level.

**The two structures compared:**

| Aspect | WEIR | BARRAGE |
|---|---|---|
| **Crest level** | **HIGH — the pond level is obtained by the crest's height** ← | **LOW, near the river bed — the pond level is obtained by GATES** ← |
| **Control of the pond level** | **NONE, or limited by shutters** ← | **FULL — the gates can hold any level at any flow** ← |
| **AFFLUX in a flood** | **LARGE — the flood must pass OVER the high crest** ← | **SMALL — the gates are raised clear and the flood passes at nearly its natural level** ← |
| **Marginal bunds and land submerged** | **EXTENSIVE, because of the afflux** ← | **Much less** ← |
| **Silt** | **Deposits upstream, since the pond is permanent** ← | **Can be SLUICED through by opening the gates** ← |
| **Capital cost** | **LOWER** ← (so option b favours the weir) | **HIGHER — gates, hoists, piers, a bridge and machinery** ← |
| **Operation** | **None required** ← (option d favours the weir) | **Continuous — gates must be operated with the river's stage** ← |
| **A road or rail crossing** | **Not usually** | **Usually provided over the piers, which offsets part of the cost** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER CONTAIN THE DECISIVE ARGUMENT AND IT IS AN ECONOMIC ONE RATHER THAN A HYDRAULIC ONE: the barrage costs more as a structure and far less in its CONSEQUENCES.**

> **A weir holding the same pond level must pass its flood over a high crest, which raises the flood level upstream by a substantial afflux.**

> **That afflux extends for kilometres upstream as a backwater, submerging land, requiring marginal bunds along both banks for that whole distance, and requiring drainage sluices through those bunds.**

> **A barrage passes its flood with the gates raised, at very nearly the river's natural level, so the afflux is small and the marginal bunds are short or unnecessary.**

> **In flat country, where a small afflux extends a long way, the land and the bunds saved can far exceed the barrage's extra cost — which is why virtually all modern headworks on large rivers are barrages.**

**THE SILT ADVANTAGE IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE OTHER MAJOR CONSIDERATION AND IT IS OFTEN DECISIVE ON A SEDIMENT-LADEN RIVER:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A weir creates a PERMANENT pond, in which the river's sediment settles** ← | ← |
| **That pond fills over years, and the deposition extends upstream** ← | **Raising the bed, which raises the flood levels further** ← |
| **A barrage can be OPENED during the flood, drawing the pond down** ← | **So the river flows through nearly at its natural level and carries its sediment straight through** ← |
| **This is SLUICING, and it is the same operation as reservoir sluicing** ← | ← |
| **So a barrage's pond can be maintained indefinitely, and a weir's fills** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS AN OPERATION RATHER THAN A PROPERTY, WHICH IS THE QUALIFICATION WORTH ADDING: a barrage only sluices its sediment if its gates are actually opened during the flood.**

> **That requires the gates to work, the hoists to be maintained, the power supply to be available, and the operators to be present and to open them at the right time — which is during the flood, at night, in the rain.**

> **A barrage whose gates are not opened behaves like a weir and silts up like one, and it has cost more to build.**

> **So the barrage's advantages are conditional on an operating capability that the weir does not require, and where that capability is doubtful the comparison is less one-sided than the table suggests.**

> **This is the same consideration met in choosing between a trickling filter and an activated sludge plant, and between an earth lining and concrete: the technically superior option is superior only if it is operated and maintained as its design assumes.**

examTip.trick: **Low crest with gates** — the pond level is controlled, and the flood passes with the gates raised at a much smaller afflux than a weir gives.
examTip.trap: **The barrage costs MORE as a structure and far less in CONSEQUENCES** — the afflux a weir causes needs marginal bunds for kilometres, and that land usually exceeds the gate cost.
examTip.mnemonic: **A barrage only sluices if its gates are OPENED — during the flood, at night, in the rain.** Unopened, it silts up like a weir and cost more.

questions.stem: A FISH LADDER at a diversion headworks must be designed so that:
options: The head is dissipated in a series of small steps or baffles
The water drops through it in a single fall
The velocity through it is as high as possible, to attract the fish
It operates only during the flood season
questions.solution:
**The head is dissipated in a SERIES OF SMALL STEPS or baffles, each with a velocity and a drop that the local species can negotiate, with resting pools between** — and its entrance must be placed where the fish will FIND it, close to the main flow they are following.

**The requirements of a working fish pass:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Small individual DROPS, within the species' leaping or swimming ability** ← | **Typically 150 to 300 mm per step for the species of the region** ← |
| **Velocities the fish can SWIM AGAINST** ← | **Which depends on the species and its size — a figure of 2 m/s or less is usual, with slower resting areas** ← |
| **RESTING pools between the steps** ← | **Deep enough and still enough for a fish to recover before the next effort** ← |
| **A continuous ATTRACTION FLOW at the entrance** ← | **Enough discharge for the fish to detect it against the river's main flow** ← |
| **The ENTRANCE placed where migrating fish naturally congregate** ← | **Close against the structure, at the downstream end, where they follow the main current and are stopped** ← |
| **Operation throughout the MIGRATION season** ← | **Which may not coincide with the flood season** ← (so option d is wrong) |
| **An EXIT upstream placed where the fish are not swept back over the weir** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE REQUIREMENT MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG AND IT DETERMINES WHETHER THE STRUCTURE WORKS AT ALL: a fish pass that fish cannot FIND is useless however well its hydraulics are designed.**

> **Migrating fish follow the strongest current upstream until they are stopped by the obstruction, and they then search along the barrier's face.**

> **A ladder placed at the far bank, or set back from the structure, or discharging a trickle into a slack area, will not be found — the fish congregate below the spillway or the undersluices where the main flow is, and they stay there.**

> **So the entrance must be immediately adjacent to the main discharge, and it must have enough flow of its own to be detectable as a route.**

> **Many fish ladders in the region have been built and are not used by fish, and the commonest reason is the entrance's position rather than any failing in the ladder itself.**

**THE TYPES OF FISH PASS:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **POOL AND WEIR (pool type)** ← | **A staircase of pools separated by small weirs — the traditional and commonest form** ← |
| **DENIL (baffle) pass** ← | **A steep chute with closely spaced baffles that create a slow zone near the bed — compact, and suited to strong swimmers** ← |
| **VERTICAL SLOT pass** ← | **Pools separated by walls with a full-depth vertical slot — it works over a range of water levels, which is a real advantage** ← |
| **NATURE-LIKE BYPASS channel** ← | **A gently graded rocky channel around the structure, resembling a natural stream — the most effective for a wide range of species, and it needs space** ← |
| **Fish LOCK or LIFT** ← | **A mechanical device for high structures** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW'S ADVANTAGE IS WORTH NOTING BECAUSE IT ADDRESSES A REAL LIMITATION OF THE POOL TYPE: a river's level varies, and a pool-and-weir ladder is designed for one range of levels.**

> **Outside that range it either drowns out, losing its steps, or the drops become too great.**

> **A vertical slot pass has a slot running the full depth, so it functions similarly at any level within a wide range — which suits a river whose stage varies greatly, as Himalayan rivers do.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS INCREASINGLY THE PREFERRED SOLUTION WHERE SPACE ALLOWS AND IT IS WORTH ADVOCATING: a nature-like bypass is a rocky, vegetated, gently sloping channel that passes around the structure and looks like a stream.**

> **It passes not only the strong-swimming target species but the whole range of the river's fauna — small fish, juveniles, invertebrates and bottom-dwellers — which a steep engineered ladder does not.**

> **That matters because a conventional fish ladder is designed for one or two species of commercial interest and is impassable to most of the river's biota, so it maintains a fishery while leaving the ecological barrier substantially in place.**

> **Where the objective is the river's ecology rather than a single fishery, the bypass channel is the honest answer — and its requirement is land and gradient rather than money, which is sometimes available and sometimes not.**

examTip.trick: **Small steps with resting pools, velocities the fish can manage, and an ENTRANCE they will find** — beside the main flow they are following.
examTip.trap: **The entrance's position decides whether it works** — fish search along the barrier where the main current is. A ladder set back or at the far bank is never found.
examTip.mnemonic: **A VERTICAL SLOT pass works over a range of river levels; a NATURE-LIKE BYPASS passes the whole biota**, not just the one strong-swimming species a ladder targets.

questions.stem: The energy of the water passing over a weir is dissipated downstream principally by:
options: Friction along the downstream apron
Gradual widening of the channel
Forming a hydraulic jump on the downstream glacis or in a stilling basin
Allowing the water to fall freely into a plunge pool in every case
questions.solution:
**Forming a HYDRAULIC JUMP on the downstream glacis or in a stilling basin** — the supercritical flow reverting to subcritical with a large loss of energy in the turbulence of the jump.

**Why a jump is the chosen mechanism:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water passing over a weir arrives at the toe with a high velocity and a small depth — SUPERCRITICAL flow** ← | ← |
| **The river downstream is flowing slowly and deeply — SUBCRITICAL** ← | ← |
| **The transition from supercritical to subcritical CANNOT be gradual** ← | **It occurs as an abrupt HYDRAULIC JUMP** ← |
| **The jump is intensely turbulent, and that turbulence DISSIPATES the energy as heat** ← | **Efficiently — 50 to 85 per cent of the incoming energy for a strong jump** ← |
| **So the jump is not a nuisance to be avoided but the DEVICE by which the energy is destroyed** ← | ← |
| **The design problem is to make it occur WHERE it can be contained** ← | **On the protected floor, not on the erodible riverbed beyond it** ← |

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE WHOLE OF STILLING BASIN DESIGN AND IT IS WORTH STATING AS THE OBJECTIVE: the jump will happen somewhere, and the design's task is to fix where.**

> **If it forms on the concrete floor, its energy is dissipated harmlessly and the water leaves at a modest velocity.**

> **If it is swept downstream onto the riverbed, the supercritical flow scours a hole, and the hole works back toward the structure and undermines it.**

> **So the position of the jump is the design criterion, and it depends on the TAILWATER depth: a jump forms where the available tailwater matches the sequent depth required for the incoming supercritical flow.**

**THE TAILWATER PROBLEM, WHICH IS THE CENTRAL DIFFICULTY:**

| Situation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Tailwater depth EQUALS the sequent depth** ← | **The jump forms exactly at the toe — the ideal, and it occurs at only one discharge** ← |
| **Tailwater depth GREATER than sequent depth** ← | **The jump is DROWNED and moves upstream; it dissipates less energy, and the fast water may travel along the surface** ← |
| **Tailwater depth LESS than sequent depth** ← | **The jump is SWEPT DOWNSTREAM, off the floor and onto the erodible bed — the dangerous case** ← |
| **And the tailwater depth varies with the DISCHARGE, which varies enormously** ← | **So the ideal condition can hold at only one flow** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHY STILLING BASIN DESIGN IS DIFFICULT AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: the designer must produce a basin that works over the whole range of discharges, and the jump's requirements change with every one of them.**

> **The usual solution is to DEPRESS the floor — building the basin below the riverbed level — so that the depth of water over it exceeds the natural tailwater depth.**

> **That converts a deficiency of tailwater into a sufficiency, and it is why stilling basins are excavated below bed level rather than laid on it.**

> **A SLOPING GLACIS is used for the same reason: the jump can form at whatever point along the slope suits the discharge, so the basin accommodates a range of conditions rather than one.**

**THE APPURTENANCES THAT STABILISE THE JUMP:**

| Device | Function |
|---|---|
| **CHUTE BLOCKS at the basin's entrance** ← | **Split the incoming jet and spread it, thickening the flow and helping the jump to form** ← |
| **BAFFLE (friction) BLOCKS on the floor** ← | **Obstruct the flow, dissipating energy directly and holding the jump in place** ← |
| **An END SILL, solid or dentated** ← | **Lifts the outgoing flow away from the bed and helps to hold the jump within the basin** ← |
| **A depressed floor** ← | **As above** ← |
| **A launching APRON of loose stone beyond the basin** ← | **Which is the acknowledgment that some scour will occur anyway** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE HONEST PROVISION AND IT IS WORTH ENDING ON: however well the basin is designed, the flow leaving it is not the same as the natural river flow, and some scour will occur at the transition.**

> **So a flexible protection is provided beyond the rigid floor — loose stone, or blocks on a filter — which launches into the scour hole as it forms and armours its face.**

> **The rigid structure is thereby protected by a flexible one that is designed to be deformed, which is the same principle as the launching apron at a guide bank.**

> **Attempting instead to extend the rigid floor until no scour occurs is both expensive and futile, because the transition simply moves to the new end — and the flexible apron accepts the scour rather than trying to prevent it.**

examTip.trick: **A hydraulic jump — supercritical to subcritical — dissipating 50-85 % of the energy in turbulence.** The transition cannot be gradual.
examTip.trap: **The jump WILL happen; the design fixes WHERE.** Too little tailwater sweeps it downstream onto the erodible bed, and the scour works back to the structure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Depress the basin floor below bed level** to manufacture the tailwater depth the jump needs. And accept some scour beyond it with a launching apron.

questions.stem: The UPSTREAM sheet pile (cut-off) at a weir serves a different primary purpose from the DOWNSTREAM one, in that the upstream pile chiefly:
options: Controls the exit gradient and prevents piping
Provides the working platform for construction
Supports the weir's crest structure
Reduces the uplift pressure beneath the floor by lengthening the seepage path at its start
questions.solution:
**It reduces the UPLIFT pressure beneath the floor by lengthening the seepage path at its start** — whereas the downstream pile's chief function is to control the EXIT GRADIENT and to protect against undermining by scour.

**The division of duties:**

| Pile | Primary function | Secondary functions |
|---|---|---|
| **UPSTREAM cut-off** ← | **Reduces the UPLIFT pressure under the floor** ← | **Protects against upstream scour; reduces the total seepage; provides a construction cut-off** ← |
| **DOWNSTREAM cut-off** ← | **Controls the EXIT GRADIENT — the piping check** ← (which is option a) | **Prevents undermining by the downstream scour hole; anchors the floor's end** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE piles** ← | **Little hydraulically, as Khosla showed** ← | **Break the floor into panels; provide a barrier if one panel fails; assist during construction** ← |

> **THE REASON THE TWO ENDS DO DIFFERENT JOBS FOLLOWS FROM WHERE THE SEEPAGE IS IN ITS JOURNEY AND IT IS WORTH REASONING THROUGH:**

> **At the UPSTREAM end the water is entering, and it still carries almost its full head — so anything that dissipates head there reduces the pressure under everything downstream of it.**

> **A deep upstream cut-off therefore lowers the whole uplift diagram, and the floor can be thinner throughout.**

> **At the DOWNSTREAM end the water is leaving, and the concern is no longer pressure but the VELOCITY with which it emerges and whether it will carry grains with it.**

> **A deep downstream cut-off forces the water to travel further down and emerge further out, flattening the gradient at the exit.**

> **So the same device serves two quite different purposes according to where it is placed, and the depths required for the two purposes are computed differently.**

**WHICH GOVERNS IN PRACTICE, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The DOWNSTREAM cut-off's depth is usually the governing one** ← | **Because the exit gradient requirement is demanding and the factor of safety is large** ← |
| **It is also constrained by SCOUR — it must go below the anticipated scour level** ← | **Which is often deeper than the seepage requirement** ← |
| **The upstream cut-off is generally shallower** ← | **Its uplift benefit being useful but less critical** ← |
| **Both must go below the scour level appropriate to their position** ← | **Upstream scour is less severe than downstream scour** ← |
| **So the sequence is: compute both scour depths, set the piles below them, then check the exit gradient and the uplift, and deepen the downstream pile if the gradient requires** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE DESIGN SEQUENCE AND IT IS WORTH FOLLOWING IN THAT ORDER, because the scour requirement is absolute — a pile above the scour level will be exposed and undermined whatever its hydraulic merit.**

> **The seepage requirements are then checked against a geometry already fixed by scour, and only the downstream pile is likely to need deepening beyond it.**

> **Reversing the order — designing for seepage and then discovering the scour requires more — wastes the calculation.**

**AND THE INTERMEDIATE PILE'S CONTINUING USEFULNESS DESERVES A NOTE, SINCE KHOSLA SHOWED IT TO BE HYDRAULICALLY WEAK:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulically it contributes little, which is Khosla's finding** ← | ← |
| **But it acts as a BARRIER if a panel of the floor is damaged or lifted** ← | **Confining the failure rather than letting the whole floor be undermined** ← |
| **And it stiffens the floor and provides a construction joint** ← | ← |
| **So it is retained for structural and robustness reasons rather than for seepage** ← | ← |

> **The second row is a good example of a provision whose justification changed while the provision remained: intermediate piles were originally driven for their creep length under Bligh's theory, and Khosla showed that reason to be largely mistaken.**

> **They continued to be provided because a different and better reason existed — the containment of a local failure — which is a case of a practice being right for a reason other than the one that established it.**

> **That is worth recognising because the opposite also occurs: a practice may survive after its original justification has been disproved and no better one exists, and distinguishing the two requires asking what the provision actually does rather than why it was first adopted.**

examTip.trick: **Upstream pile: reduces UPLIFT. Downstream pile: controls the EXIT GRADIENT.** The water carries full head at one end and is emerging at the other.
examTip.trap: **Both must first go below the SCOUR level for their position** — a pile above it is undermined whatever its hydraulic merit. Scour first, then seepage.
examTip.mnemonic: **Intermediate piles do little hydraulically (Khosla) but confine a local floor failure** — retained for a better reason than the one that established them.

questions.stem: The INVERTED FILTER provided at the downstream end of a weir's impervious floor consists of graded material laid so that:
options: The coarsest material is at the bottom, against the foundation soil, and the finest at the top
The finest material is at the bottom and the coarsest at the top
All the layers are of uniform grading
It is impermeable, to prevent any seepage emerging
questions.solution:
**The FINEST material is at the bottom, against the foundation soil, and the COARSEST at the top.**

**Why the grading is in that order, which is what makes it 'inverted':**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The purpose is to let the seeping WATER out while holding the foundation SOIL in** ← | **The two filter criteria, once again** ← |
| **The layer immediately against the soil must be FINE enough to retain it** ← | **Or the soil washes through and the piping the filter was built to prevent occurs within the filter itself** ← |
| **Each successive layer upward is COARSER, retaining the layer below it** ← | ← |
| **The topmost layer is coarse stone, which is permeable and heavy** ← | ← |
| **The arrangement is called INVERTED because a normal filter, as in a water treatment plant, is graded the other way — coarse at the bottom** ← | **The name records the contrast** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW EXPLAINS THE NAME AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE THE TERM IS OTHERWISE PUZZLING: a rapid sand filter has its coarse gravel at the bottom, over the underdrains, and its fine sand on top, because the water flows DOWNWARD through it.**

> **Here the water flows UPWARD, out of the foundation, so the grading is reversed — fine at the bottom where the water enters, coarse at the top where it leaves.**

> **The principle is identical in both: the fine layer is placed where the fine material is, and the grading coarsens in the direction of flow.**

> **So the two are not different rules but one rule applied to flows in opposite directions, and remembering the flow direction determines the grading without any need to recall which is called 'inverted'.**

**WHAT THE INVERTED FILTER ACHIEVES AT A WEIR:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **RELIEVES the uplift at the floor's downstream end** ← | **By letting the seepage out, so no pressure accumulates beneath the floor's edge** ← |
| **PREVENTS the emerging seepage from carrying soil with it** ← | **Which is the piping mechanism** ← |
| **Its WEIGHT resists the uplift on the soil grains** ← | **Adding to their stability against the exit gradient** ← |
| **It is FLEXIBLE, so it can settle into a scour hole without cracking** ← | **Unlike a rigid floor** ← |
| **And it is usually covered with CONCRETE BLOCKS with open joints** ← | **Which hold the filter in place against the flow while letting the water through** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS A NECESSARY COMPLICATION AND IT ADDRESSES AN OBVIOUS OBJECTION: a graded filter of loose material laid in a river would be washed away by the first flood.**

> **So it is protected by a layer of concrete blocks, laid with deliberate gaps between them.**

> **The blocks are heavy enough to stay put and the gaps let the water through, so the filter beneath is retained while continuing to function.**

> **The gaps are essential — blocks laid tight, or grouted, would seal the filter and defeat it entirely, converting a pressure-relieving arrangement into a pressure-accumulating one.**

> **That is a construction detail that a bricklayer or a mason would naturally get wrong, since the instinct is to lay blocks close and neat, and it must therefore be specified explicitly and inspected.**

> **THE COMBINATION OF FUNCTIONS IN THIS ARRANGEMENT IS WORTH APPRECIATING AS A CLOSING POINT: the inverted filter with its block cover simultaneously relieves pressure, retains soil, adds weight, remains flexible and resists the flow.**

> **Each of those is a distinct requirement, and a single well-considered detail satisfies all five — which is characteristic of a mature engineering solution that has been refined by experience of the ways it can fail.**

> **A designer meeting the detail for the first time may see it as unnecessarily elaborate; each element is there because its omission caused a failure somewhere, and understanding which failure each prevents is the way to know what may safely be simplified and what may not.**

examTip.trick: **Finest at the BOTTOM against the soil, coarsening upward** — because the water flows UPWARD out of the foundation. 'Inverted' relative to a sand filter.
examTip.trap: **Coarsen in the DIRECTION OF FLOW** — that one rule gives both a rapid sand filter's grading and an inverted filter's, without remembering which is called what.
examTip.mnemonic: **The covering blocks must have OPEN JOINTS** — laid tight or grouted they seal the filter and turn pressure relief into pressure accumulation. Specify and inspect it.

questions.stem: The POND LEVEL that a diversion headworks must maintain is determined by:
options: The maximum flood level of the river
The natural bed level of the river at the site
The height of the guide banks
The level required at the canal's head to command its designed area
questions.solution:
**The LEVEL required at the canal's head to command its designed area** — that is, the canal's full supply level at its head plus the head loss through the regulator, with a small margin.

**How the pond level is arrived at, working backwards from the command:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Start at the FURTHEST and HIGHEST field the canal must command** ← | **The critical point of the command** ← |
| **Add the depth of water needed on that field, and the head loss in the field channel and the outlet** ← | ← |
| **Work back UP the canal, adding the head loss along every reach** ← | **The canal's own slope, plus the losses at every structure — falls, regulators, crossings** ← |
| **This gives the FULL SUPPLY LEVEL required at the canal's head** ← | ← |
| **Add the head loss through the HEAD REGULATOR itself** ← | **The working head across it** ← |
| **Add a small MARGIN** ← | ← |
| **The result is the POND LEVEL the weir or barrage must maintain** ← | ← |

> **THE DIRECTION OF THAT CALCULATION IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION AND IT IS WORTH STATING EXPLICITLY: the pond level is determined by the COMMAND, working backwards, and not by the river.**

> **The river's bed level, its flood level and its natural water level are all facts about the site; they do not determine what the headworks must achieve.**

> **What the headworks must achieve is to deliver water at a level from which it can reach the highest field at the far end of the command, and everything else follows from that.**

> **So the design begins at the tail of the command and works upstream to the headworks — the reverse of the direction in which the water flows, and the reverse of the order in which the works are built.**

**WHY THIS MATTERS, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A HIGHER pond level commands MORE land** ← | **So there is a temptation to raise it** ← |
| **But a higher pond level means a higher weir crest or higher gates** ← | **A larger structure** ← |
| **And a greater AFFLUX, hence longer marginal bunds and more submergence** ← | ← |
| **And a greater head across the structure, hence more seepage, more uplift and a longer floor** ← | ← |
| **So every metre of pond level is expensive, and it must be JUSTIFIED by the command it adds** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ECONOMIC DISCIPLINE THAT SHOULD GOVERN THE DECISION AND IT IS FREQUENTLY ABSENT: the pond level is often set by taking the command as given and computing what level it needs, without asking whether the last few hundred hectares are worth what they cost.**
