> **The marginal land — the highest and furthest — is the most expensive to command, because it sets the pond level for the whole scheme and every consequence of that level follows from it.**

> **Excluding a small area of high land at the tail can sometimes lower the pond level by half a metre, which shortens the marginal bunds by kilometres, reduces the submergence, and shortens the impervious floor.**

> **So the boundary of the command is a design variable and not a datum, and it should be examined rather than accepted — which requires the engineer to question the command's extent, a question that is often treated as belonging to somebody else.**

> **THE OTHER LEVELS AT A HEADWORKS ARE WORTH LISTING ALONGSIDE, SINCE THEY ARE EASILY CONFUSED:**

| Level | Determined by |
|---|---|
| **POND level** ← | **The command, as above** ← |
| **CREST level of a weir** ← | **The pond level (the crest IS at pond level for a weir without shutters)** ← |
| **Crest level of a BARRAGE** ← | **Set LOW, near the bed — the pond level being obtained by the gates** ← |
| **HIGH FLOOD level** ← | **The design flood, passed over the structure** ← |
| **AFFLUXED high flood level** ← | **The high flood level plus the afflux, which sets the marginal bunds and the guide banks' top** ← |
| **Downstream floor and cistern level** ← | **The hydraulic jump requirement and the scour depth** ← |

examTip.trick: **Work BACKWARDS from the highest, furthest field** — adding every head loss up the canal, then through the regulator, to get the pond level.
examTip.trap: **The river's bed and flood levels are facts about the site, not determinants of the pond level** — the COMMAND determines it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Every metre of pond level costs a bigger structure, more afflux, longer bunds and a longer floor** — so the command's boundary is a design variable worth questioning.

questions.stem: A LAUNCHING APRON of loose stone is laid beyond the rigid floor of a weir. Its stone quantity is computed so that:
options: It covers the riverbed to a uniform thickness over the whole downstream reach
It weighs enough to resist the uplift beneath the floor
There is sufficient material to pave the whole face of the scour hole
It fills the anticipated scour hole completely
questions.solution:
**There is sufficient material to PAVE the whole face of the SCOUR HOLE, at the required thickness, when the apron LAUNCHES into it as the hole develops.**

**How a launching apron works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The apron is laid HORIZONTALLY on the bed beyond the rigid floor** ← | **A layer of loose stone of designed thickness and length** ← |
| **A flood scours a hole beyond the floor's end** ← | ← |
| **The apron's outer edge is UNDERMINED and the stone SLIDES down the face of the developing hole** ← | ← |
| **It comes to rest on that face, ARMOURING it** ← | **At its natural angle of repose, roughly 2:1** ← |
| **The hole can then deepen no further, and the structure is protected** ← | ← |
| **The apron has 'launched' — it has moved from horizontal to sloping** ← | ← |

> **THE MECHANISM IS DELIBERATE AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING AS A DESIGN PHILOSOPHY: the apron is designed to be DESTROYED in its original form.**

> **It is not intended to stay where it is laid; it is intended to fall into a hole that has not yet formed, and to line that hole when it does.**

> **So a launching apron that has moved is not damaged — it is working as intended, and an inspection finding the apron displaced into a scour hole should record a success rather than a defect.**

> **That distinguishes it from every rigid element of the structure, where movement means failure, and it is why a launching apron and a concrete floor must be understood as different kinds of protection rather than as more and less of the same thing.**

**THE QUANTITY CALCULATION, WHICH FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM THE MECHANISM:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Determine the anticipated SCOUR DEPTH D below the bed** ← | **From Lacey's R times the factor for that location** ← |
| **The slope of the launched apron is taken as 2 horizontal to 1 vertical** ← | **The stone's angle of repose under water** ← |
| **So the LENGTH of the launched face is √(D² + (2D)²) = D√5 ≈ 2.24 D** ← | ← |
| **The launched THICKNESS is taken as about 1.25 times the laid thickness** ← | **Because the stone loosens as it falls** ← |
| **So the VOLUME required per metre run is 2.24 D × 1.25 t** ← | **t being the thickness required on the slope** ← |
| **And that volume is laid horizontally as an apron of length L and thickness T such that L × T equals it** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW'S FACTOR OF 2.24 IS THE ONE TO REMEMBER AND IT COMES STRAIGHT FROM THE GEOMETRY: a 2:1 slope descending D has a sloping length of D√5.**

> **So an apron protecting a 6 m scour needs to pave 13.4 m of slope face, and it must contain enough stone to do so at the required thickness.**

> **Underestimating that quantity is the classic failure: the apron launches, runs out of stone part way down the slope, and the unprotected lower part of the hole continues to deepen — after which the whole apron slides in and the floor's end is undermined.**

> **So the quantity is not a nominal allowance but the thing that determines whether the protection works, and it must be computed from the anticipated scour rather than adopted from a standard drawing.**

**THE STONE'S SIZE IS THE OTHER REQUIREMENT AND IT DESERVES A NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The individual stones must be heavy enough not to be carried away by the flow** ← | **Before they have launched and interlocked** ← |
| **Their size is related to the velocity, by a relation such as the one giving the required weight as proportional to the sixth power of the velocity** ← | **So the required weight rises extremely steeply with velocity** ← |
| **Where stone of the required size is unavailable, WIRE CRATES (gabions) are used** ← | **Binding smaller stones into units of adequate weight** ← |
| **Gabions launch well and are flexible, but the wire CORRODES and abrades** ← | **Particularly in a boulder-carrying Himalayan river, where the wire is cut by the moving bed load within a few seasons** ← |

> **The last row is a real limitation in Nepal and it is worth stating: gabions are widely used because suitable large stone is often unavailable and wire crates are cheap and easily made.**

> **In a river carrying gravel and boulders in flood, the wire is abraded and cut, the crates burst, and the stone is dispersed — sometimes within two or three monsoons.**

> **So a gabion protection in such a river is a temporary measure requiring regular replacement, and treating it as permanent protection is a mistake that appears a few years after construction, when the budget for replacement no longer exists.**

verification.notes: Launched face on 2:1 slope over depth D has length D*sqrt(5) = 2.236 D.

examTip.trick: **Enough stone to PAVE the scour hole's face when it launches** — 2.24 D of slope length at a 2:1 repose slope, with 1.25 times the laid thickness.
examTip.trap: **A displaced launching apron is WORKING, not damaged** — it is designed to fall into a hole that has not yet formed. Unlike every rigid element, where movement means failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Running out of stone part way down the slope is the classic failure** — compute the quantity from the anticipated scour, never from a standard drawing.

questions.stem: Khosla's method requires three CORRECTIONS to the key point pressures read from his curves. These corrections are for:
options: Temperature, humidity and wind
The floor's thickness, the mutual interference of the sheet piles, and the slope of the floor
Discharge, velocity and depth
Uplift, scour and seepage
questions.solution:
**The floor's THICKNESS, the MUTUAL INTERFERENCE of the sheet piles, and the SLOPE of the floor.**

**Each correction and why it is needed:**

| Correction | Reason |
|---|---|
| **THICKNESS of the floor** ← | **Khosla's curves are derived for a floor of NEGLIGIBLE thickness, with the key points on the floor's upper surface; the pressure is actually wanted at the floor's UNDERSIDE, which is lower and therefore at a different point on the pressure gradient** ← |
| **MUTUAL INTERFERENCE of piles** ← | **The curves are derived for a SINGLE pile in an infinite floor; a real structure has two or three piles, and each alters the flow field around the others** ← |
| **SLOPE of the floor** ← | **The curves assume a HORIZONTAL floor; a glacis is inclined, and the correction accounts for it** ← |

> **THE PATTERN IS THAT EACH CORRECTION UNDOES ONE OF THE IDEALISATIONS IN THE ORIGINAL SOLUTION, WHICH IS WORTH SEEING AS THE METHOD'S LOGIC: Khosla solved simple, idealised cases exactly, and the corrections carry those exact solutions toward the real geometry.**

> **That is a general technique in engineering analysis — solve what can be solved and correct toward what cannot — and it is why the corrections must be applied rather than treated as refinements that can be omitted.**

> **Omitting them does not give a slightly less accurate answer; it gives the answer to a different structure.**

**THE SIGNS AND MAGNITUDES, WHICH ARE WHERE THE DIFFICULTY LIES:**

| Correction | Sign and magnitude |
|---|---|
| **THICKNESS** ← | **Always applied TOWARD the interior of the floor — that is, it moves the pressure toward the value at the next key point in the direction of the floor's body; its magnitude is proportional to the floor's thickness relative to the pile's depth** ← |
| **INTERFERENCE** ← | **NEGATIVE for the point on a pile's side FACING the interfering pile if that pile is downstream, and positive in the reverse case; computed from a formula involving both piles' depths and their spacing** ← |
| **SLOPE** ← | **Applied only to the key point at the junction of the SLOPING floor with a pile; POSITIVE for a DOWN slope in the direction of flow and negative for an up slope; it is proportional to the slope's steepness** ← |

> **THE SIGN CONVENTIONS ARE THE PRACTICAL TRAP AND THEY DESERVE A METHOD RATHER THAN A RULE TO REMEMBER: the reliable approach is to sketch the profile, mark the key points, and ask physically which way each effect should push the pressure.**

> **A thicker floor puts the underside deeper into the flow field, where the pressure is closer to the value at the next point along — so the correction moves it that way.**

> **A pile downstream of the point in question intercepts some of the flow, reducing the pressure at that point.**

> **A floor sloping downward in the direction of flow shortens the effective path to the exit at that point, so the pressure there is higher than a horizontal floor would give.**

> **Reasoning each one out takes a minute and is far more reliable than recalling a table of signs, and it also catches the case where the geometry is unusual and the remembered rule does not apply.**

**AND A NOTE ON WHY THE METHOD IS STILL USED, DESPITE COMPUTERS BEING ABLE TO SOLVE THE FLOW DIRECTLY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A finite element or finite difference seepage analysis solves the real geometry exactly, with no corrections at all** ← | **And it takes minutes** ← |
| **So Khosla's curves and corrections are, strictly, unnecessary for a new design** ← | ← |
| **They remain valuable as a CHECK on a computed result** ← | **A hand calculation that agrees with the software confirms both** ← |
| **And they make the physics VISIBLE in a way a contour plot does not** ← | **The designer who has applied the corrections understands which pile is doing the work and why** ← |
| **Which is what allows a computed result to be judged rather than merely accepted** ← | ← |

> **The last two rows are the honest justification for still learning the method, and it is the same argument made for Hardy Cross: the value is not in performing the calculation but in understanding what the software is computing.**

> **An engineer who can only run the program cannot tell when the program has been given the wrong problem — and being given the wrong problem, rather than solving it incorrectly, is how modern analysis most often goes astray.**

examTip.trick: **Thickness, mutual interference, slope** — each undoing one idealisation in Khosla's exact solutions for simple cases.
examTip.trap: **Omitting a correction gives the answer to a DIFFERENT structure**, not a slightly less accurate one. They are not optional refinements.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reason each SIGN out physically from a sketch** — a thicker floor sits deeper in the field, a downstream pile intercepts flow, a down-slope shortens the path to the exit.

questions.stem: RIVER TRAINING works are undertaken with several objectives. Works classified as HIGH WATER training are those intended chiefly to:
options: Improve the river for navigation at low flows
Concentrate the low-flow channel for an intake
Provide safe passage of the flood discharge and to protect the adjoining land from inundation
Reduce the river's sediment load
questions.solution:
**To provide safe passage of the FLOOD discharge and to protect the adjoining land from inundation** — chiefly by embankments and levees.

**The three classes of river training, by the flow they address:**

| Class | Objective | Principal works |
|---|---|---|
| **HIGH WATER training (flood control)** ← | **Pass the FLOOD safely and keep it off the land** ← | **LEVEES and marginal embankments** ← |
| **MEAN WATER training (channel training)** ← | **Efficient SEDIMENT transport, and a stable, well-defined channel** ← | **GROYNES, spurs, bank pitching, guide banks** ← |
| **LOW WATER training** ← | **Concentrate the low flow into a single deep channel** ← (option b, and option a for navigation) | **Bandalling, dykes, closing subsidiary channels** ← |

> **THE THREE CLASSES ADDRESS DIFFERENT FLOWS AND THEIR REQUIREMENTS CAN CONFLICT, WHICH IS THE POINT WORTH TAKING FROM THE CLASSIFICATION:**

> **High water training confines the flood, which raises its level and its velocity within the confinement.**

> **Mean water training seeks a channel that is in equilibrium with its sediment load.**

> **Low water training concentrates the small flow, which requires narrowing the section that the flood needs wide.**

> **So a work that serves one objective may work against another, and a training scheme must be clear about which flow it is designed for — a point that is easily lost when 'river training' is treated as a single activity.**

**THE OBJECTIVES OF RIVER TRAINING GENERALLY, WHICH IS THE FULLER LIST:**

| Objective | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevent the river from CHANGING its course** ← | **Which on an alluvial river is a real and continuing tendency** ← |
| **Protect the banks from EROSION** ← | ← |
| **Confine the flood and protect the land from INUNDATION** ← | ← |
| **Direct the flow at a bridge, a barrage or an intake so that it approaches CENTRALLY and axially** ← | ← |
| **Improve the channel's SEDIMENT-carrying capacity, so it does not aggrade** ← | ← |
| **Provide a stable channel for NAVIGATION** ← | **Of limited relevance in Nepal** ← |
| **Prevent OUTFLANKING of a structure** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE FUNDAMENTAL ONE ON AN ALLUVIAL RIVER AND IT IS WORTH BEING REALISTIC ABOUT: a river in alluvium moves because that is what alluvial rivers do.**

> **It erodes one bank and deposits on the other, its meanders migrate, and in a braided reach the channels shift wholesale between floods.**

> **Training works do not stop that tendency; they constrain it locally, at a cost, for as long as they are maintained.**

> **So a training scheme is a permanent commitment rather than a one-time construction, and a scheme built and then unmaintained will be outflanked or destroyed and the river will resume its behaviour.**

> **That is worth stating plainly at the appraisal stage, because the maintenance obligation is a real cost that is frequently omitted from the comparison with the alternative of not building at all.**

**AND THE ALTERNATIVE OF NOT TRAINING DESERVES ITS OWN CONSIDERATION, WHICH IS OFTEN NOT GIVEN:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A river allowed to occupy its natural floodplain spreads its flood, so the peak downstream is LOWER** ← | ← |
| **It deposits its sediment on the floodplain, which is how the floodplain was built and how its fertility is maintained** ← | ← |
| **Confining it raises the flood level and velocity WITHIN the confinement, and passes the flood downstream faster** ← | **Increasing the peak there** ← |
| **And the sediment that would have spread over the floodplain is deposited in the confined channel instead** ← | **Raising its bed — the perched river problem** ← |
| **So training a reach transfers a problem downstream and stores one up locally** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE HONEST ASSESSMENT AND IT SHOULD BE MADE BEFORE THE WORKS ARE DESIGNED RATHER THAN AFTER THEY HAVE FAILED: embanking a river is not a neutral act with only local effects.**

> **The land protected is genuinely protected, and the flood it no longer spreads onto arrives somewhere else, faster and higher.**

> **In a basin where every reach embanks itself in turn, the cumulative result can be worse for everyone than no embankment at all — which is a cumulative-impact problem of exactly the kind discussed under environmental assessment, and it requires the same basin-scale rather than project-scale view.**
tags: high mean and low water training

examTip.trick: **High water = flood passage and levees. Mean water = sediment transport and channel stability. Low water = concentrating the small flow.**
examTip.trap: **The three objectives can CONFLICT** — low water training narrows what the flood needs wide. A scheme must state which flow it is designed for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Training constrains the river locally for as long as it is maintained** — and it passes the flood downstream faster and higher. A basin-scale question, not a reach-scale one.

questions.stem: A SPUR (groyne) projecting into a river from its bank is classified as REPELLING, ATTRACTING or DEFLECTING according to:
options: The angle at which it is set to the bank
The material of which it is built
Its length relative to the river's width
Whether it is submerged or not
questions.solution:
**The ANGLE at which it is set to the bank** — one pointing UPSTREAM repels the flow away from the bank, one pointing DOWNSTREAM attracts the flow toward it, and one at right angles merely deflects it locally.

**The three orientations:**

| Type | Angle | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **REPELLING spur** ← | **Pointing UPSTREAM, at 60 to 75 degrees to the bank measured downstream** ← | **Throws the flow AWAY from the bank — the usual choice for bank protection** ← |
| **DEFLECTING spur** ← | **At right angles to the bank** ← | **Deflects the flow locally without moving the main current far** ← |
| **ATTRACTING spur** ← | **Pointing DOWNSTREAM** ← | **Draws the flow TOWARD the bank — used deliberately where the flow must be brought to a particular point, such as an intake** ← |

> **THE REPELLING ORIENTATION IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE ONE USED FOR BANK PROTECTION AND ITS GEOMETRY IS WORTH PICTURING: a spur angled upstream presents an inclined face to the oncoming flow.**

> **The flow striking that face is turned away from the bank, and a zone of slack water and deposition forms in the angle behind the spur.**

> **So the bank downstream of the spur is sheltered, and it silts up rather than eroding.**

> **A spur angled downstream does the opposite: the flow is guided along its face toward the bank, and the bank beyond it is attacked — which is why an attracting spur is used only where the flow is wanted at the bank, and never for protection.**

> **Setting a protective spur at the wrong angle therefore makes the erosion worse, and it is an error that is easy to make on the ground where the flow direction is not obvious at low water.**

**THE OTHER FEATURES OF A SPUR SYSTEM:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **SPACING between spurs** ← | **Typically 2 to 2.5 times their length; too far apart and the flow attacks the bank between them** ← |
| **A T-HEAD or hockey-stick head** ← | **An arm at the spur's nose, parallel to the flow, which spreads the attack and protects the nose** ← |
| **The NOSE is where the scour is deepest** ← | **Requiring the heaviest protection and a launching apron, exactly as at a guide bank's nose** ← |
| **They may be IMPERMEABLE (solid) or PERMEABLE** ← | **A permeable spur — piles, timber, bamboo screens — slows the flow and induces deposition rather than deflecting it sharply** ← |
| **The FIRST spur of a series faces the most severe attack** ← | **Since the flow arrives at it undisturbed** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW'S DISTINCTION IS WORTH DEVELOPING BECAUSE THE TWO KINDS WORK QUITE DIFFERENTLY:**

| Type | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **IMPERMEABLE (solid) spur** ← | **DEFLECTS the flow bodily; effective and severe, and it creates a strong eddy and deep scour at its nose** ← |
| **PERMEABLE spur** ← | **Lets the water through while SLOWING it; the reduced velocity causes DEPOSITION, which gradually builds the bank out** ← |
| **Permeable spurs are cheaper, use local material, and cause less scour** ← | **But they act slowly and are ineffective against a severe attack** ← |
| **They are well suited to a sediment-laden river** ← | **Since they work BY deposition, and a river with little sediment gives them nothing to work with** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CONDITION THAT DECIDES WHETHER A PERMEABLE SPUR IS APPROPRIATE AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED: a permeable spur protects a bank by encouraging the river to deposit sediment in front of it.**

> **On a heavily sediment-laden river — which most Nepali rivers are in the monsoon — that works well and quickly.**

> **On a clear river it does nothing, because there is no sediment to deposit, and the structure simply stands in the flow being slowly destroyed.**

> **So the sediment load is a design input for a permeable structure in a way it is not for a solid one, and bamboo and timber porcupines, bandalling and similar works are effective in the Terai for exactly this reason and would not be elsewhere.**

> **They also have the merit of being buildable by the community from local material at low cost, which for a village protecting its own land is often decisive — and a permeable work that the community can build and rebuild each year may protect more land over a decade than a solid work that is built once and then outflanked.**

examTip.trick: **Pointing UPSTREAM repels, downstream attracts, at right angles deflects.** Protective spurs point upstream at 60-75°.
examTip.trap: **A spur set at the wrong angle makes the erosion WORSE** — an attracting spur guides the flow onto the bank it was meant to protect.
examTip.mnemonic: **Permeable spurs work BY deposition**, so they need a sediment-laden river. Useless in a clear one — but buildable by the community from local material each year.

questions.stem: LEVEES (marginal embankments) built along a river to contain its floods produce, over time, a characteristic and dangerous consequence, namely that:
options: They erode away within a few seasons
The river's bed AGGRADES between them
The river's flood peak is reduced downstream
The groundwater beneath the protected land falls
questions.solution:
**The river's bed AGGRADES between them — because the sediment that would have spread over the floodplain is deposited in the confined channel — so the bed and the flood level RISE progressively, and the river becomes PERCHED above the land it is protecting.**

**The mechanism, step by step:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **An unconfined river in flood SPREADS over its floodplain** ← | **And deposits much of its sediment there, which is how a floodplain is built** ← |
| **Levees CONFINE the flood to the channel** ← | ← |
| **The sediment that would have gone onto the floodplain now stays in the channel** ← | ← |
| **And the channel's capacity to carry it is limited, so it DEPOSITS** ← | **The bed rises** ← |
| **A higher bed means a higher flood level for the same discharge** ← | ← |
| **So the levees must be RAISED to maintain the same protection** ← | ← |
| **Which confines the river further, and the cycle repeats** ← | ← |
| **Eventually the riverbed is ABOVE the surrounding land** ← | **A perched river** ← |

> **THE CYCLE IN THE SIXTH AND SEVENTH ROWS IS WHAT MAKES THIS SO SERIOUS AND IT IS ANOTHER SELF-REINFORCING FAILURE OF THE KIND MET SEVERAL TIMES: the remedy for the problem creates more of the problem.**

> **Each raising of the levee buys a few more years and makes the eventual situation worse.**

> **And the situation it builds toward is genuinely dangerous: a river flowing several metres above the surrounding country, held in by earth embankments.**

> **When such a levee fails — and earth embankments do fail — the water does not merely spill over; it pours out under a head, scours a breach, and floods the country to a depth it could never have reached naturally.**

> **So the protected land is safer in most years and far more exposed in the year the levee fails, which is a transfer of risk from frequent small floods to rare catastrophic ones.**

**THE OTHER CONSEQUENCES OF EMBANKING, WHICH COMPOUND THE FIRST:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **DRAINAGE CONGESTION behind the levee** ← | **The levee blocks the land's own drainage to the river, so local rainfall ponds behind it — and the sluices through it cannot discharge while the river is high** ← |
| **Loss of the floodplain's SILT and its fertility** ← | **The annual deposit that renewed the soil no longer arrives** ← |
| **Loss of the floodplain's groundwater RECHARGE** ← | ← |
| **A HIGHER flood peak DOWNSTREAM** ← | **Since the flood is passed on rather than stored on the floodplain** ← (so option c is inverted) |
| **Loss of the fishery and the wetland ecology that the flooding sustained** ← | ← |
| **And a false sense of security, which attracts SETTLEMENT into the protected area** ← | **So the population and the assets at risk increase** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST INSIDIOUS AND IT IS WELL DOCUMENTED WHEREVER FLOOD EMBANKMENTS HAVE BEEN BUILT: protection encourages development, and the development increases the damage when the protection eventually fails.**

> **Land that flooded every few years was used for grazing or for a monsoon crop and carried few permanent buildings.**

> **Protected by a levee, it is built on — and when the levee is overtopped or breached, the losses are far greater than any the unprotected land would have suffered.**

> **This is called the LEVEE EFFECT or the safe development paradox, and it means that a flood protection work's benefit must be assessed against the development it will induce rather than against the present land use.**

> **THE ALTERNATIVES ARE WORTH STATING, SINCE THE PICTURE IS OTHERWISE UNRELIEVEDLY NEGATIVE:**

| Alternative | Note |
|---|---|
| **Set the levees FURTHER BACK, giving the river room** ← | **The flood spreads, the sediment is deposited on a designated floodplain, and the aggradation is slower — 'room for the river'** ← |
| **RING bunds around settlements rather than continuous levees** ← | **Protecting what matters and leaving the floodplain to flood** ← |
| **Flood-PROOFING — raised platforms, raised houses, plinth levels above the flood** ← | ← |
| **Land use control and flood ZONING** ← | **The cheapest measure and the hardest politically** ← |
| **Early warning and evacuation** ← | ← |

> **The first row is increasingly the preferred approach internationally and it is worth knowing by name: rather than confining the river more tightly, the levees are set well back and the land between is accepted as floodplain.**

> **The flood spreads, its peak is attenuated, its sediment is deposited where it does good rather than in the channel, and the aggradation cycle is broken — at the cost of the land within the setback, which is used for purposes compatible with occasional flooding.**

examTip.trick: **Confined sediment raises the bed, which raises the flood, which requires raising the levee** — a self-reinforcing cycle ending in a perched river.
examTip.trap: **Downstream peaks RISE, not fall** — the flood is passed on rather than stored on the floodplain. Option (c) is inverted.
examTip.mnemonic: **The LEVEE EFFECT: protection attracts settlement, so the eventual failure costs far more.** Assess the benefit against the development induced, not the present land use.

questions.stem: BANDALLING, a traditional low water training technique used on rivers of the region, consists of:
options: Constructing a series of low masonry weirs across the channel
Dredging a navigation channel and maintaining it
Planting vegetation along the bank to resist erosion
Placing a series of bamboo screens
questions.solution:
**Placing a series of BAMBOO SCREENS, inclined to the flow and supported on poles, which obstruct the SURFACE flow while allowing the BOTTOM flow through** — so that sediment is deposited behind them and the main channel is scoured deeper.

**How bandalling works, which is a genuinely clever piece of traditional engineering:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A screen of bamboo matting is hung from poles, extending from the water surface DOWNWARD, but not to the bed** ← | **So it blocks the upper part of the flow and leaves the lower part open** ← |
| **The screens are set at an angle to the flow, in a line along the channel** ← | ← |
| **The obstructed SURFACE flow is deflected toward the main channel** ← | ← |
| **The BOTTOM flow passes beneath the screens into the sheltered area behind them** ← | ← |
| **That bottom flow is the most SEDIMENT-LADEN, and behind the screen it is slow** ← | **So it DEPOSITS its sediment there** ← |
| **Meanwhile the main channel, now carrying a greater share of the flow, SCOURS deeper** ← | ← |
| **So the subsidiary channel silts up and the main channel deepens — which is exactly what low water training seeks** ← | ← |

> **THE ARRANGEMENT IN THE FIRST AND FIFTH ROWS IS THE INGENIOUS PART AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: the screen is deliberately made to block the CLEAN water and pass the DIRTY water.**

> **That is the reverse of what an intake tries to do, and it is the right way round for this purpose.**

> **An intake wants clean water, so it draws from the surface and lets the bottom water pass.**

> **A bandal wants to DEPOSIT sediment behind it, so it admits the bottom water and blocks the surface water.**

> **Both exploit the same fact — that sediment concentration is greatest near the bed — and they use it in opposite directions for opposite purposes, which is a nice illustration of a principle being a tool rather than a rule.**

**ITS PRACTICAL MERITS, WHICH EXPLAIN ITS LONG USE:**

| Merit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Built entirely of LOCAL material — bamboo, matting and poles** ← | **No cement, no steel, no machinery** ← |
| **Erected by local labour, quickly** ← | ← |
| **Cheap enough to be rebuilt each season** ← | **Which is necessary, as the floods remove them** ← |
| **It works WITH the river's sediment rather than against its force** ← | **Inducing deposition rather than resisting flow** ← |
| **And it can be adjusted or moved as the channel responds** ← | **An adaptive rather than a fixed intervention** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CHARACTERISTIC THAT DISTINGUISHES THIS WHOLE FAMILY OF TRADITIONAL WORKS FROM ENGINEERED ONES AND IT IS WORTH DRAWING OUT: bandalling, permeable spurs, porcupines and brushwood fences all work by SLOWING water and letting it deposit, rather than by resisting its force.**

> **A solid structure opposes the river and must be strong enough to survive the opposition; a permeable one lets the river through and uses the river's own sediment to build the protection.**

> **The second requires far less material and far less strength, and it fails gracefully — a damaged bamboo screen is replaced, whereas a breached concrete spur is a construction project.**

> **Its limitations are equally clear: it works only where there is sediment, it acts slowly, it cannot resist a severe attack, and it requires annual attention.**

> **So it suits a sediment-laden river, a community that can maintain it, and a problem that can be addressed gradually — which describes a great deal of the Terai and very little of a major structure's protection.**

> **THE HONEST CONCLUSION IS THAT THE TWO APPROACHES ARE COMPLEMENTARY RATHER THAN COMPETING: the engineered work protects the structure that must not fail, and the traditional work protects the agricultural land where a gradual and renewable intervention is adequate and affordable.**

> **Dismissing the traditional technique as primitive, or proposing it where a structure's safety depends on the protection, are opposite errors and both are made.**

examTip.trick: **Bamboo screens hanging from the surface DOWNWARD, not reaching the bed** — blocking the clean surface flow and admitting the silty bottom flow to deposit behind.
examTip.trap: **It deliberately does the OPPOSITE of an intake** — an intake takes surface water and passes the bottom; a bandal blocks the surface and admits the bottom. Same fact, opposite purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **Permeable works use the river's SEDIMENT to build the protection**, rather than opposing its force. Cheap, renewable, gradual — and useless in a clear river.

questions.stem: A CUT-OFF, either natural or artificially made across the neck of a meander loop:
options: Shortens the river's course between two points, thereby steepening its slope over that reach
Lengthens the river's course and reduces its slope
Has no effect on the river's gradient
Reduces the river's discharge
questions.solution:
**It SHORTENS the river's course between two points, thereby STEEPENING its slope over that reach** — which increases the velocity and can start a wave of erosion travelling UPSTREAM and of deposition travelling downstream.

**The consequences of a cut-off:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The same fall is now accomplished over a SHORTER length** ← | **So the slope is steeper — often by a factor of two or three at a well-developed meander** ← |
| **A steeper slope means a HIGHER velocity and more erosive power** ← | ← |
| **The reach scours, and its bed LOWERS** ← | ← |
| **The lowered bed steepens the reach UPSTREAM of it, which then scours too** ← | **So the erosion propagates UPSTREAM — a knickpoint or headward erosion** ← |
| **All that eroded material is carried DOWNSTREAM and deposited where the slope flattens again** ← | **So deposition propagates downstream** ← |
| **The river adjusts over years or decades toward a new profile** ← | ← |

> **THE UPSTREAM PROPAGATION IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CONSEQUENCE THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT ONE TO ANTICIPATE: an intervention at one point causes changes far upstream of it.**

> **The instinct is that a river's behaviour is determined from upstream downward, so an intervention affects only what is below it.**

> **For the WATER that is broadly true; for the BED it is not.**

> **Lowering the bed at a point lowers the base level for everything upstream, and the upstream reach then erodes to match — so bridges, intakes, bank protection and structures for kilometres upstream can be undermined by a cut-off made downstream of them.**

> **This is a genuinely important principle in river engineering and it applies equally to dredging, to sand mining and to the lowering of a bed by any means.**

**NATURAL AND ARTIFICIAL CUT-OFFS:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **NATURAL cut-off** ← | **A meander loop grows until its neck is narrow, and a flood breaks through — leaving an OXBOW LAKE** ← |
| **ARTIFICIAL cut-off** ← | **Excavated deliberately, usually as a small PILOT CHANNEL which the river then enlarges itself** ← |

> **THE PILOT CHANNEL TECHNIQUE IN THE SECOND ROW IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS SO ECONOMICAL: the engineer does not excavate the full channel.**

> **A modest pilot cut is made across the neck — perhaps a tenth of the eventual section — and the river, finding a shorter and steeper route, does the rest of the excavation itself during the next flood.**

> **The river's own erosive power, which is the problem in most river work, is here harnessed to do the work.**

> **The pilot's alignment, its section and the timing of its opening are the design decisions, and once the river takes it the process is not controllable — so the consequences must be anticipated before rather than managed after.**

**WHY A CUT-OFF MIGHT BE MADE DELIBERATELY, AND THE CAUTION THAT GOES WITH IT:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **To prevent a meander loop from ERODING into a settlement, a road or a railway** ← | ← |
| **To improve a river's flood-carrying capacity by shortening and steepening it** ← | ← |
| **To straighten a channel for navigation** ← | ← |
| **To move the river away from a threatened structure** ← | ← |
| **BUT the upstream and downstream adjustments must be assessed and provided for** ← | **And they extend far beyond the cut-off itself** ← |
| **And a cut-off in a series of meanders may trigger others** ← | **Since the steepened reach attacks its neighbours' necks** ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE THE REASON CUT-OFFS ARE MADE CAUTIOUSLY AND SOMETIMES NOT AT ALL: the intervention is easy to start and impossible to stop.**

> **Once the river has taken the new course, the old loop silts up and cannot be restored, the adjustment propagates in both directions, and the engineer has committed the reach to a new regime whose full extent was estimated rather than known.**

> **So a cut-off is among the more consequential interventions available in river engineering, and it deserves an assessment of the whole reach rather than of the loop being cut — which is again the basin-scale rather than the site-scale view.**

examTip.trick: **A shorter course over the same fall means a STEEPER slope** — faster flow, scour in the reach, and adjustment propagating in both directions.
examTip.trap: **The erosion travels UPSTREAM** — lowering the bed lowers the base level for everything above, so structures kilometres upstream can be undermined. Also true of dredging and sand mining.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cut a small PILOT channel and let the river excavate the rest** — economical, and uncontrollable once it takes. Anticipate before, because you cannot manage after.

questions.stem: BIOENGINEERING, as applied to the protection of riverbanks and slopes in Nepal, uses vegetation in ways that depend on the plants':
options: Ornamental value and their contribution to the landscape
Mechanical and hydrological functions
Ability to be harvested as a commercial crop
Capacity to absorb pollutants from the water
questions.solution:
**Mechanical and hydrological functions — ROOTS reinforcing and anchoring the soil, stems ARMOURING the surface and slowing the flow, foliage intercepting rainfall, and the whole system transpiring water and so reducing pore pressures.**

**The engineering functions of vegetation, which are the basis of the technique:**

| Function | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **REINFORCE** ← | **Roots add tensile strength to a soil that has almost none — the same principle as reinforcing concrete or soil nailing, at a smaller scale** ← |
| **ANCHOR** ← | **Deeper roots tie a surface layer to firmer material beneath** ← |
| **ARMOUR** ← | **Stems and a dense turf protect the surface from raindrop impact and from scouring flow** ← |
| **CATCH and FILTER** ← | **Vegetation traps sediment and debris moving down a slope or along a bank, building the surface up** ← |
| **DRAIN and DEWATER** ← | **Transpiration removes soil water, lowering pore pressures and raising effective stress — the bio-drainage effect** ← |
| **INTERCEPT rainfall** ← | **Reducing the rain reaching the surface and its erosive energy** ← |
| **SUPPORT** ← | **Established woody stems can act as small buttresses and piles** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE TWO THAT ACT ON SLOPE STABILITY IN THE PROPER GEOTECHNICAL SENSE AND THEY DESERVE TO BE STATED IN THOSE TERMS: root reinforcement adds an apparent COHESION to the soil, and transpiration reduces the PORE PRESSURE.**

> **Both raise the shear strength on a potential failure surface — the first by adding to c, the second by increasing the effective stress through which φ acts.**

> **So vegetation's contribution to stability is not vague or merely surficial; it enters the same equation as any other stabilising measure and can be quantified, if roughly.**

> **The qualification is that root reinforcement acts only to the depth the roots reach — typically the top metre or two — so it stabilises SHALLOW failures and does nothing for a deep-seated one.**

> **Which means bioengineering addresses surface erosion, shallow slips and gully development, and does not address a deep landslide — a distinction that must be made honestly, because bioengineering is sometimes proposed where the mechanism is beyond it.**

**THE TECHNIQUES USED, WHICH ARE WORTH KNOWING BY NAME:**

| Technique | Note |
|---|---|
| **GRASS PLANTING in lines, contour or diagonal** ← | **The commonest and cheapest; slips of a fast-rooting grass planted in rows** ← |
| **BRUSH LAYERING** ← | **Live cuttings laid in trenches across the slope, which root and grow — providing both reinforcement and a surface barrier** ← |
| **PALISADES and WATTLE FENCES** ← | **Live stakes driven in lines, woven with branches, which trap material and root** ← |
| **LIVE CHECK DAMS in gullies** ← | ← |
| **Vegetated GABIONS and stone works** ← | **Combining a structural element with planting** ← |
| **JUTE or coir GEOTEXTILE with seeding** ← | **The fabric holds the surface while the vegetation establishes, and then rots away** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW EMBODIES THE ESSENTIAL IDEA OF COMBINING THE TWO APPROACHES AND IT IS WORTH GENERALISING: a biological system takes TIME to establish and a structural one works immediately.**

> **So the structural element carries the load during the establishment period, and the vegetation takes over as the structure decays.**

> **A jute net holds the soil for the two seasons the grass needs to root; a gabion holds the toe while the planting above it establishes; a brushwood check dam traps sediment until the vegetation growing in it can hold the gully itself.**

> **That handover from the temporary structure to the permanent vegetation is the design's central idea, and it fails if the vegetation does not establish — in which case the structure decays and nothing replaces it.**

> **So the SPECIES selection, the PLANTING SEASON and the AFTERCARE are not horticultural details but the determinants of whether the engineering works, and they require the involvement of someone who knows the local plants rather than a specification copied from elsewhere.**

> **In Nepal that knowledge exists locally and in the Department of Soil Conservation's practice, and the successful schemes have generally been those that used local species, planted at the start of the monsoon, with the community responsible for protecting the planting from grazing during establishment — the last being the requirement most often overlooked and the most common cause of failure.**

examTip.trick: **Reinforce, anchor, armour, catch, drain, intercept, support** — mechanical and hydrological functions, not amenity.
examTip.trap: **Roots reach only a metre or two, so bioengineering addresses SHALLOW failures** — surface erosion, shallow slips and gullies. It does nothing for a deep-seated landslide.
examTip.mnemonic: **The structure carries the load while the vegetation establishes, then hands over** — jute net, gabion, brushwood dam. And protect the planting from GRAZING, or it fails.

questions.stem: CHECK DAMS built across a gully as part of watershed management are intended primarily to:
options: Store water for irrigation
Generate small quantities of hydropower
Reduce the gully's gradient by trapping sediment behind each dam
Provide crossings for livestock and people
questions.solution:
**To REDUCE the gully's gradient by trapping sediment behind each dam** — so the flow's velocity and erosive power fall, the gully's deepening is arrested, and vegetation can establish on the accumulated material.

**How a series of check dams works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A small dam across the gully traps the sediment moving down it** ← | ← |
| **The deposit builds up behind the dam, forming a level or gently sloping surface** ← | ← |
| **The gully's effective gradient over that length is thereby REDUCED** ← | **From the gully's own steep slope to the flat surface of the deposit** ← |
| **A gentler gradient means a LOWER velocity and much less erosive power** ← | **Erosive power rising steeply with velocity** ← |
| **So the gully stops deepening, and its sides begin to stabilise at their angle of repose** ← | ← |
| **VEGETATION establishes on the trapped sediment, which is moist and fine** ← | **And the vegetation then holds it permanently** ← |
| **A SERIES of dams is used, each backing up to the toe of the one above** ← | **Converting a continuous steep gully into a staircase of flat reaches** ← |

> **THE SEVENTH ROW DESCRIBES THE CORRECT SPACING RULE AND IT IS THE DESIGN'S KEY DIMENSION: each dam's deposit should reach the FOOT of the dam above it.**

> **If the dams are further apart, a length of steep unprotected gully remains between the head of one deposit and the toe of the dam above — and that length continues to erode.**

> **So the spacing follows from the dam's effective height and the gully's slope: spacing = height ÷ (gully slope − deposit slope), roughly.**

> **A steeper gully therefore needs the dams closer together, and a series with too few dams achieves proportionately less than its numbers suggest, because the unprotected lengths between them continue to feed sediment down.**

**THE DESIGN REQUIREMENTS OF AN INDIVIDUAL CHECK DAM, WHICH ARE OFTEN NEGLECTED:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **A SPILLWAY or notch at the centre** ← | **So the flow passes over the middle and not round the ends — the single most important detail** ← |
| **The ends KEYED well into both banks** ← | **Or the flow outflanks the dam, which is the commonest failure** ← |
| **The foundation taken BELOW the gully bed** ← | **Or the dam is undermined by the scour at its own toe** ← |
| **An APRON or a stilling arrangement below the notch** ← | **The water falling over the dam scours a hole at its foot, which then undermines it** ← |
| **PERMEABILITY, so water passes through and pressure does not build behind** ← | **Which is why loose stone, gabions and brushwood are used rather than an impermeable wall** ← |
| **A modest HEIGHT — 1 to 2 m** ← | **A series of small dams is far better than one large one, and much less likely to fail** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS TOGETHER ACCOUNT FOR THE GREAT MAJORITY OF CHECK DAM FAILURES AND THEY ARE BOTH GEOMETRIC RATHER THAN STRUCTURAL: the dam does not break, the water goes round it.**

> **A dam built level across a gully with no notch will be overtopped at whichever point is lowest — which is usually at one end, where the construction met the bank.**

> **The flow then concentrates there, erodes the abutment, and cuts a new channel round the dam, leaving it standing in the middle of a widened gully doing nothing.**

> **A central notch ensures the overflow occurs where it is intended, over the dam's strongest and best-protected part, and the keying into the banks ensures the water cannot find a way round.**

> **Both cost nothing and both are routinely omitted by an untrained builder, which is why check dam construction is one of the activities where a small amount of supervision produces a large difference in outcome.**

> **THE SIXTH ROW'S PREFERENCE FOR SMALL DAMS DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE: a series of six 1 m dams achieves the same total gradient reduction as one 6 m dam, at less cost, with far less risk, and with any single failure affecting only one sixth of the length.**

> **A large check dam, by contrast, impounds a substantial mass of saturated sediment, and its failure releases that as a debris flow down the gully — turning a soil conservation work into the hazard it was built to prevent.**

examTip.trick: **Trap sediment to FLATTEN the gully's gradient** — lower velocity, arrested deepening, and a moist surface where vegetation can establish.
examTip.trap: **Each dam's deposit must reach the FOOT of the one above** — otherwise a steep unprotected length remains between them and continues to erode.
examTip.mnemonic: **A central NOTCH and ends KEYED into the banks** — most failures are the water going ROUND the dam, not through it. And many small dams beat one large one.

questions.stem: The CHURE (Siwalik) range is of particular concern in Nepal's watershed management because it:
options: Is the highest and most glaciated range in the country
Is composed of ancient, hard crystalline rock that resists erosion
Contains the country's principal hydropower reservoirs
Consists of young, weakly consolidated sandstone, mudstone and conglomerate, is steep and tectonically active
questions.solution:
**It consists of YOUNG, WEAKLY CONSOLIDATED sandstone, mudstone and conglomerate, is steep and tectonically active, and therefore erodes rapidly** — supplying enormous quantities of sediment to the Terai rivers and to the aquifer recharge zone below it.

**Why the Chure is so erodible:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **The rocks are GEOLOGICALLY YOUNG — the youngest in the Himalayan sequence** ← | **Deposited as the range's own erosion products, and only weakly cemented** ← |
| **They are WEAK — friable sandstone, soft mudstone, and conglomerate that disaggregates readily** ← | ← |
| **The range is being actively UPLIFTED** ← | **So it is steep, and streams cutting into it are steep and energetic** ← |
| **It receives INTENSE monsoon rainfall** ← | **Often the highest in the country, since it is the first barrier the monsoon meets** ← |
| **And it has been extensively DEFORESTED, quarried and cultivated** ← | **Removing the vegetation that held what cohesion the material had** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS ARE THE ESSENTIAL GEOLOGY AND THE POINT IS WORTH GRASPING RATHER THAN MEMORISING: the Chure is made of the eroded debris of the higher Himalaya, deposited, buried, weakly cemented, and then uplifted again.**

> **So it is, in effect, a range made of sediment that has been through the erosion process once already and is now going through it again.**

> **That material was never strong, and it has had no time to become so.**

> **Which is why the Chure supplies sediment out of all proportion to its area — it is not merely eroding, it is disintegrating.**

**WHY IT MATTERS DOWNSTREAM, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The Terai rivers carry enormous BED LOADS of Chure-derived gravel and sand** ← | **Which is why they are braided, aggrading and unstable** ← |
| **That sediment AGGRADES the riverbeds in the Terai** ← | **Raising flood levels and causing the channels to shift** ← |
| **It fills reservoirs, blocks intakes, buries irrigated land and destroys structures** ← | ← |
| **The BHABAR zone at the Chure's foot is the principal RECHARGE area for the Terai's aquifers** ← | **The coarse debris being highly permeable** ← |
| **So the Chure's condition affects both the SEDIMENT and the GROUNDWATER of the whole Terai** ← | ← |
| **And it is where much of the country's population and agriculture is** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER MAKE THE CONSERVATION CASE AND IT IS A DUAL ONE THAT IS SOMETIMES ARGUED ONLY ON THE SEDIMENT SIDE: the Chure and its Bhabar apron are the recharge zone for the aquifers that supply the Terai's drinking water and its tube well irrigation.**

> **Quarrying the riverbeds for construction aggregate, clearing the forest and converting the Bhabar to other uses affect the recharge as well as the erosion.**

> **So a measure that reduces the sediment yield may also be a measure that protects the groundwater, and the two benefits should be counted together — which strengthens a case that on sediment alone competes against the immediate value of the aggregate and the land.**

> **THE RIVERBED EXTRACTION POINT DESERVES ITS OWN NOTE BECAUSE IT IS AN ACUTE CURRENT ISSUE: the Chure rivers' gravel and sand are the country's principal source of construction aggregate, and demand has grown with construction.**

> **Extraction from the beds lowers them, which — by the headward erosion mechanism discussed for cut-offs — propagates upstream, undermining bridges, intakes and bank protection.**

> **It also lowers the water table in the adjoining land, since the river's bed is the local base level for the groundwater.**

> **So unregulated extraction damages infrastructure and water supply simultaneously, and the damage appears at some distance from the extraction and some years later — which makes it difficult to attribute and easy to permit.**

> **Regulating it requires knowing the river's sediment REPLENISHMENT rate and extracting no more than that, which is a measurable quantity and is very rarely measured.**

examTip.trick: **Young, weak, steep, tectonically active and heavily rained on** — a range made of the Himalaya's own eroded debris, weakly cemented and now eroding again.
examTip.trap: **It matters for GROUNDWATER as well as sediment** — the Bhabar apron at its foot is the Terai's principal aquifer recharge zone. Count both benefits in any conservation case.
examTip.mnemonic: **Riverbed extraction lowers the bed, and the erosion propagates UPSTREAM** — undermining bridges and intakes, and lowering the water table. Extract no more than the replenishment.

questions.stem: A BRAIDED river, characteristic of the Terai, is distinguished from a MEANDERING river in that a braided river:
options: Follows a single sinuous channel with a well-defined deep pool at each bend
Flows in a straight, stable channel
Divides into multiple interlacing channels separated by bars and islands
Has a bed of fine silt and cohesive banks
questions.solution:
**It divides into MULTIPLE interlacing channels separated by bars and islands, is generally WIDER, SHALLOWER and STEEPER, carries a heavy BED LOAD, and shifts its channels unpredictably between floods.**

**The two river types compared:**

| Property | MEANDERING | BRAIDED |
|---|---|---|
| **Planform** | **A single sinuous channel** ← (option a) | **Multiple interlacing channels around bars** ← |
| **Slope** | **Gentler** ← | **STEEPER** ← |
| **Width to depth ratio** | **Lower — relatively narrow and deep** ← | **HIGH — wide and shallow** ← |
| **Bank material** | **COHESIVE — silt and clay, which hold a steep bank** ← (option d) | **NON-COHESIVE — sand and gravel, which collapse readily** ← |
| **Sediment load** | **Chiefly SUSPENDED** ← | **Chiefly BED LOAD, and abundant** ← |
| **Stability** | **The channel migrates PREDICTABLY, by bend growth and cut-off** ← | **Channels shift WHOLESALE and unpredictably in each flood** ← |
| **Discharge variability** | **Moderate** | **HIGH — flashy, with a large ratio of flood to low flow** ← |

> **THE COMBINATION IN THE SECOND, FOURTH, FIFTH AND SEVENTH ROWS IS WHAT PRODUCES BRAIDING AND THE MECHANISM IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN LISTING: a river braids when it is supplied with more bed load than it can carry through, in banks that cannot hold a defined channel.**

> **The excess load is deposited as a bar in mid-channel.**

> **The flow divides around that bar, and each divided flow attacks its own bank.**

> **The banks, being non-cohesive sand and gravel, collapse readily, so the river widens.**

> **A wider river is shallower and slower, so it carries even less load and deposits more, forming further bars.**

> **The process is self-reinforcing, and the result is a wide shallow bed occupied by many shifting channels.**

> **So braiding is a SYMPTOM of an excess of bed load relative to transporting capacity, in erodible banks — which is precisely the condition where a Himalayan river debouches from the hills onto the Terai.**

**WHAT THIS MEANS FOR ENGINEERING WORKS, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL POINT:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The river's position is not fixed** ← | **A structure built on one channel may find the river elsewhere next monsoon** ← |
| **The 'width' to be spanned or protected is the whole BRAIDED BELT, not the current channel** ← | **Which may be kilometres wide** ← |
| **A bridge must span the belt, or be protected by GUIDE BANKS that force the river to a defined waterway** ← | ← |
| **Bank protection at one point simply moves the attack to another** ← | ← |
| **And the bed AGGRADES, so levels rise over time** ← | ← |
| **Scour is deep and its location unpredictable** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE DIMENSION THAT GOVERNS THE COST OF ANY CROSSING AND IT IS WHERE THE JUDGMENT LIES: spanning the whole braided belt is prohibitively expensive on a large river.**

> **So the alternative is to CONFINE the river to a chosen waterway with guide banks, and to accept the cost and the risk of that confinement.**

> **Lacey's waterway gives the width to confine to; the guide banks make the river use it; and their length is set so that the river cannot develop a loop tight enough to outflank them.**

> **That is the standard solution, and its weakness is that it depends entirely on the guide banks surviving — a braided river that outflanks its guide banks abandons the bridge, as has happened repeatedly.**

> **THE FIFTH ROW ADDS A LONG-TERM DIFFICULTY THAT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED: a braided river in the Terai is generally AGGRADING, so its bed level rises over the decades.**

> **A bridge built with adequate clearance in 1980 may have inadequate clearance in 2020, not because the floods have grown but because the bed beneath it has risen.**

> **And the same aggradation reduces the effectiveness of embankments, raises the flood levels for a given discharge, and progressively perches the river above its floodplain.**

> **So the design of any long-lived structure on such a river should consider not only the present bed level but the trend — which requires a record of past levels, and which is one of the more valuable things a survey department can maintain and one of the less commonly available.**

examTip.trick: **Multiple interlacing channels, wide and shallow, steep, heavy BED load, non-cohesive banks, unpredictable shifting.** Meandering is single, sinuous, cohesive-banked.
examTip.trap: **Braiding is a SYMPTOM of excess bed load in erodible banks** — a bar forms, the flow divides, the banks collapse, the river widens, and it deposits more. Self-reinforcing.
examTip.mnemonic: **The relevant width is the BRAIDED BELT, not today's channel** — so either span it or confine the river with guide banks to Lacey's waterway. And the bed is rising over decades.

questions.stem: In a river's sediment transport, BED LOAD is distinguished from SUSPENDED LOAD in that bed load:
options: Moves along the bed by rolling
Consists of the finest particles in the flow
Is measured routinely at most gauging stations
Travels faster than the water carrying it
questions.solution:
**It moves along the bed by ROLLING, SLIDING and SALTATION, remaining in substantially continuous contact with it** — whereas suspended load is held up in the body of the flow by turbulence and moves at nearly the water's own velocity.

**The components of a river's sediment load:**

| Component | Movement | Particle size |
|---|---|---|
| **BED LOAD** ← | **Rolling, sliding and SALTATION (bouncing) along the bed** ← | **The COARSER fraction — sand, gravel, cobbles, boulders** ← |
| **SUSPENDED LOAD** ← | **Held up by turbulence, distributed through the depth, moving with the water** ← | **Finer — silt and fine sand** ← |
| **WASH LOAD** ← | **A subset of the suspended load: material so FINE that it is carried straight through and is NOT found in the bed at all** ← | **Clay and the finest silt** ← |
| **DISSOLVED load** | **In solution** | **Not particulate** ← |

> **THE WASH LOAD DISTINCTION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE SUBTLEST AND IT IS WORTH GRASPING BECAUSE IT MATTERS FOR WHAT A RIVER CAN BE ASKED TO DO: wash load is material the river carries because it is SUPPLIED with it, not because it has the capacity to carry it.**

> **The river's capacity for wash load is effectively unlimited — the particles are so fine that any flow keeps them moving — so the quantity carried depends entirely on how much the catchment delivers.**

> **Bed load and the coarser suspended load are different: the river's capacity for them is limited by its hydraulics, and it carries what it can and deposits the rest.**

> **So catchment conservation reduces the WASH load directly, and it affects the bed load only by reducing the supply of coarse material — which is a slower and less certain effect.**

> **And a settling basin removes the coarse fraction and much of the suspended load, and removes wash load hardly at all — which is why a basin's outlet water is still turbid with clay while being free of sand.**

**THE MEASUREMENT PROBLEM, WHICH IS WHY OPTION (c) IS WRONG:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **SUSPENDED load is measured routinely** ← | **A depth-integrating sampler takes a sample through the water column, which is filtered and weighed** ← |
| **BED LOAD is very difficult to measure** ← | **It moves along the bed in surges, its rate varies enormously with time and across the section, and any sampler placed on the bed disturbs the very flow it is measuring** ← |
| **So bed load is rarely measured and usually ESTIMATED** ← | **As a percentage of the suspended load — commonly 10 to 20 per cent for a sand-bed river, and much more for a gravel-bed one** ← |
| **Those estimates are crude** ← | **And for a Himalayan gravel-bed river the bed load may exceed the suspended load, so the usual percentages are badly wrong** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN IMPORTANT CAUTION FOR NEPALI WORK AND IT AFFECTS RESERVOIR AND INTAKE DESIGN DIRECTLY: the conventional practice of estimating bed load as 10 to 20 per cent of the measured suspended load was developed for the sand-bed rivers of the plains.**

> **A steep boulder-bed river moves an enormous quantity of coarse material during floods, and that transport is invisible to a suspended sediment sampler.**

> **So a sediment yield computed from suspended measurements plus a conventional percentage can substantially understate the total — and the material it understates is precisely the coarse fraction that fills reservoirs, blocks intakes and destroys turbines.**

> **Where a design depends on the sediment yield, the coarse fraction should be assessed directly — from the volume accumulated in an existing reservoir, from a survey of a debris fan, or from the observed aggradation of the bed — rather than from a percentage rule.**

> **THE SALTATION MECHANISM IN THE FIRST ROW DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT EXPLAINS THE STEEP DEPENDENCE OF TRANSPORT ON FLOW: a grain at rest on the bed begins to move only when the flow exceeds a threshold.**

> **Once moving, it bounces, and each impact dislodges other grains.**

> **So bed load transport rises very steeply once the threshold is passed — commonly as a high power of the excess shear stress — which means almost all of a river's bed load is moved during the few days of the year when it is in flood.**

> **An intake or a settling basin designed on average conditions is therefore designed for conditions that do not matter, and the design case is the flood — which is the same conclusion reached about hydropower sediment and it has the same origin.**
tags: bed load underestimated in gravel rivers

examTip.trick: **Bed load rolls, slides and saltates in contact with the bed; suspended load is held up by turbulence and moves with the water.**
examTip.trap: **WASH LOAD is carried because it is SUPPLIED, not because the river has capacity** — so its quantity depends on the catchment, and a settling basin barely touches it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bed load is rarely measured and usually guessed at 10-20 % of suspended** — a plains rule that badly understates a Himalayan gravel river, where it may exceed the suspended load.

questions.stem: A STAGE-DISCHARGE (rating) curve for a river gauging station may exhibit a LOOP, in which the discharge for a given stage is greater on the rising limb of a flood than on the falling limb. This occurs because:
options: The gauge is read more accurately on the rising limb
The river's cross-section changes during the flood
On the rising limb the water surface slope is steeper than the bed slope (and flatter on the falling limb)
The sediment concentration is higher during the rise
questions.solution:
**On the RISING limb the water surface slope is STEEPER than the bed slope (and flatter on the falling limb), so the same depth conveys a greater discharge while the flood is rising.**

**The mechanism, which is a matter of unsteady flow:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A steady uniform flow has its water surface parallel to the bed** ← | **And the discharge follows from the depth and the bed slope** ← |
| **In a RISING flood, the water upstream is deeper than the water downstream** ← | **Because the flood wave has not yet arrived downstream** ← |
| **So the water surface slope is STEEPER than the bed slope** ← | ← |
| **A steeper energy slope gives a HIGHER velocity, so a greater discharge at the same depth** ← | ← |
| **On the FALLING limb the reverse holds — the water downstream is still deep while upstream has fallen** ← | **So the surface slope is FLATTER and the discharge less at the same depth** ← |
| **Plotting stage against discharge through a flood therefore traces a LOOP, anticlockwise** ← | ← |

> **THE PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE IS IN HOW A RATING CURVE IS USED AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT: a gauging station measures STAGE continuously and DISCHARGE only occasionally.**

> **The rating curve converts the continuous stage record into a continuous discharge record, and it is the basis of essentially all river flow data.**

> **If the true relation is a loop rather than a single curve, then a single-valued rating misestimates the discharge throughout every flood — too low on the rise and too high on the fall.**

> **The peak discharge, which is what matters most, is on the rising limb or near the peak, so a single-valued rating tends to UNDERSTATE the flood peak.**

> **The loop is significant on flat rivers with rapidly rising floods and negligible on steep ones, so the correction matters most in the Terai and least in the hills.**

**THE OTHER DIFFICULTIES WITH RATING CURVES, WHICH ARE WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE THEY AFFECT ALL RIVER DATA:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **EXTRAPOLATION beyond the measured range** ← | **Discharges are measured at the flows that can be gauged safely; the design flood is far larger, so the curve must be extended well beyond any measurement** ← |
| **A SHIFTING control** ← | **If the channel's bed or its downstream control scours or silts, the relation changes and the curve must be re-established** ← |
| **AGGRADING or DEGRADING beds** ← | **Which change the rating progressively over years** ← |
| **BACKWATER from a downstream structure or confluence** ← | **Which makes the stage depend on something other than the local discharge** ← |
| **Overbank flow at high stages** ← | **Where the section changes character abruptly and the curve has a break** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL FOR DESIGN AND IT DESERVES TO BE STATED PLAINLY: the flood discharge used in a design is almost always an EXTRAPOLATION.**

> **Gauging a river in flood is dangerous and difficult, so the measured points cluster in the range of ordinary flows.**

> **The design flood may be several times the largest measured discharge, and the discharge attributed to it comes from extending the curve — by a fitted equation, by a slope-area calculation, or by judgment.**

> **So a design flood figure carries an uncertainty that its precision conceals, and two competent hydrologists working from the same record can differ substantially.**

> **That is worth remembering when a design flood is quoted to three significant figures, and it is an argument for designing structures that fail gracefully when the estimate proves low — which returns to the point made about climate change and non-stationarity, arrived at from a different direction.**

> **A HIGH WATER MARK SURVEY after a large flood is the most valuable single addition to a rating curve's upper end, and it is cheap: marking and levelling the debris line and the stains on structures immediately after a flood, before they are lost, provides a stage that can be converted to a discharge by a slope-area computation — and one such point at the top of the range is worth many in the middle.**

examTip.trick: **Rising limb: surface slope steeper than the bed, so more discharge at the same depth.** Falling limb: flatter, so less. An anticlockwise loop.
examTip.trap: **A single-valued rating tends to UNDERSTATE the flood peak**, since the peak is near the rising limb. Significant on flat rivers, negligible on steep ones.
examTip.mnemonic: **The design flood is almost always an EXTRAPOLATION** beyond any measurement — so its precision conceals real uncertainty. Survey the high water marks after every big flood.

questions.stem: A flood of 100-year RETURN PERIOD has, in any single year, a probability of being equalled or exceeded of:
options: 1 in 100, and it therefore occurs exactly once in every 100 years
Zero until 100 years have elapsed since the last one
questions.solution:
**1 in 100 — but the events are INDEPENDENT**, so such a flood may occur in consecutive years, or not at all in 200, and the probability of it occurring at least once in a 100-year period is about 63 per cent.

**The arithmetic of return periods:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Probability of exceedance in any ONE year** | **p = 1/T** ← |
| **Probability of NON-exceedance in one year** | **1 − 1/T** ← |
| **Probability of NO exceedance in n years** | **(1 − 1/T)ⁿ** ← |
| **RISK — the probability of AT LEAST ONE exceedance in n years** ← | **R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ** ← |
| **For T = 100 and n = 100** | **R = 1 − (0.99)¹⁰⁰ = 1 − 0.366 = 0.634, that is 63 per cent** ← |

> **THE 63 PER CENT RESULT IS THE MOST USEFUL SINGLE FACT IN THIS SUBJECT AND IT SURPRISES ALMOST EVERYONE: a structure designed for the 100-year flood and standing for 100 years is MORE LIKELY THAN NOT to experience it.**

> **The intuition that a 100-year flood 'happens once in a hundred years' suggests it should be a marginal case, and the arithmetic says it is a two-in-three probability.**

> **And the figure is close to 63 per cent for any T when n equals T — because (1 − 1/T)^T approaches 1/e = 0.368 as T grows.**

> **So a 50-year design standing 50 years, or a 1,000-year design standing 1,000 years, each has about a 63 per cent chance of being exceeded.**

> **That is worth knowing as a single fact: designing for a return period equal to the design life gives roughly a two-thirds chance of exceedance.**

**THE MISCONCEPTIONS THE QUESTION'S OTHER OPTIONS EMBODY, EACH OF WHICH IS COMMON:**

| Misconception | The reality |
|---|---|
| **'It happens once every 100 years'** ← | **It has a 1 per cent annual chance; the intervals between occurrences are highly variable** ← (option a) |
| **'It cannot happen again soon'** ← | **The events are INDEPENDENT — last year's flood tells you nothing about this year's. Two 100-year floods in consecutive years is entirely possible and has occurred** ← (option d) |
| **'We have had ours, so we are safe'** ← | **The gambler's fallacy, applied to rivers** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MISCONCEPTION WITH THE MOST DAMAGING CONSEQUENCES AND IT AFFECTS PUBLIC AND OFFICIAL RESPONSE ALIKE: after a severe flood there is a widespread belief that the danger has passed for a generation.**

> **Reconstruction proceeds on that basis, warnings are discounted, and the protective measures that the flood demonstrated to be necessary are deferred.**

> **The probability, however, is unchanged — it is 1 per cent next year as it was last year — and the year after a great flood is exactly as dangerous as any other.**

> **Communicating that is genuinely difficult, and the phrase 'hundred-year flood' actively hinders it, which is why 'a 1 per cent annual chance' is increasingly preferred as the way of expressing the same thing.**

**AND THE CHOICE OF RETURN PERIOD FOR A DESIGN, WHICH FOLLOWS FROM THE RISK EQUATION:**

| Structure | Typical design return period |
|---|---|
| **Road cross-drainage, small culverts** | **10 to 25 years** ← |
| **Bridges on important roads** | **50 to 100 years** ← |
| **Barrages and weirs** | **50 to 100 years** ← |
| **Large dams — spillway** ← | **1,000 years or the probable maximum flood, according to the consequence of failure** ← |
| **Urban storm drainage** | **2 to 10 years** ← |

> **THE PATTERN IS THAT THE RETURN PERIOD RISES WITH THE CONSEQUENCE OF FAILURE RATHER THAN WITH THE STRUCTURE'S COST, and that is the correct basis: a culvert that is overtopped causes an inconvenience, and a dam that is overtopped may kill thousands.**

> **So the design standard is set by what happens when the design is exceeded, not by how much the structure is worth — and the risk equation makes the reasoning explicit, since it converts the return period into a probability of exceedance over the structure's actual life.**

> **A designer who states that probability, rather than the return period alone, has communicated something the decision-maker can weigh.**

But the events are INDEPENDENT, so such a flood may occur in consecutive years, or not at all in 200, and the probability of it occurring at least once in a 100-year period is about 63 per cent.

examTip.trick: **R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ.** For T = n = 100 that is 63 % — a structure designed for its own life's return period is MORE LIKELY THAN NOT to see it.
examTip.trap: **The events are INDEPENDENT** — two 100-year floods in consecutive years is entirely possible. 'We have had ours' is the gambler's fallacy applied to rivers.
examTip.mnemonic: **(1 − 1/T)^T → 1/e = 0.37, so R → 63 % whenever n = T.** One fact covering every return period. And quote the probability, not just the return period.

questions.stem: As a flood wave travels down a river reach, FLOOD ROUTING shows that the outflow hydrograph, compared with the inflow hydrograph:
options: Has a higher peak and arrives earlier
Is identical in shape and timing
Has a higher peak arriving later
Has a lower peak, arriving later and spread over a longer time
questions.solution:
**It has a LOWER peak, arriving LATER and spread over a LONGER time** — the reach's STORAGE absorbing part of the flood and releasing it gradually, which is ATTENUATION.

**What routing accounts for:**

| Effect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **ATTENUATION — the peak is reduced** ← | **Part of the inflow is stored in the reach as the flood rises, and released as it falls** ← |
| **TRANSLATION — the peak arrives later** ← | **The wave takes time to travel the reach** ← |
| **The hydrograph is BROADENED** ← | **Since the volume is conserved and the peak is lower, the base must be longer** ← |
| **The VOLUME under both hydrographs is the SAME** ← | **Nothing is lost, only redistributed in time — which is a useful check on any routing computation** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CHECK WORTH APPLYING TO ANY ROUTING RESULT AND IT CATCHES MOST ERRORS: the areas under the inflow and outflow hydrographs must be equal.**

> **Routing redistributes water in time; it does not create or destroy it.**

> **So if a computed outflow hydrograph encloses a different volume from the inflow, the computation is wrong — and the discrepancy usually indicates an error in the storage relation or in the time step.**

> **That check takes a minute with a planimeter or a simple summation and it should be made routinely.**

**THE STORAGE THAT PRODUCES THE ATTENUATION:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **PRISM storage** ← | **The volume in the reach corresponding to a uniform depth — a function of the outflow** ← |
| **WEDGE storage** ← | **The additional wedge-shaped volume when the surface is not parallel to the bed — POSITIVE on the rising limb and NEGATIVE on the falling** ← |
| **The MUSKINGUM method expresses the total as S = K[xI + (1 − x)O]** ← | **K being a travel time and x a weighting between inflow and outflow** ← |
| **x = 0 gives pure reservoir (level pool) storage — maximum attenuation** ← | ← |
| **x = 0.5 gives pure translation with NO attenuation** ← | ← |
| **Natural river reaches typically have x between 0.2 and 0.3** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS BRACKET THE BEHAVIOUR AND THEY ARE WORTH UNDERSTANDING PHYSICALLY: a RESERVOIR attenuates strongly and a CHANNEL translates with little attenuation.**

> **In a reservoir, the outflow depends only on the level, so a rising inflow raises the level slowly and the outflow lags and is much reduced.**

> **In a steep channel, the wave passes through with its shape nearly intact, delayed but not much flattened.**

> **A natural river reach lies between, and x measures where — a flat reach with a wide floodplain behaves more like a reservoir, and a confined steep reach more like a channel.**

> **So a river that has been EMBANKED, losing access to its floodplain, moves toward the channel end of that range — its x rises, its attenuation falls, and the flood is passed downstream more nearly intact.**

> **That is the quantitative expression of the point made earlier about levees increasing downstream peaks, and it is a satisfying convergence of two lines of reasoning on the same conclusion.**

**THE PRACTICAL USES OF ROUTING, WHICH ARE WORTH LISTING:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **FLOOD FORECASTING** ← | **A flood measured at an upstream gauge is routed down to predict the level and the timing at a town — which is the basis of a warning system** ← |
| **Designing a SPILLWAY** ← | **Routing the design flood through the reservoir gives the outflow the spillway must pass, which is less than the inflow because the reservoir attenuates** ← |
| **Assessing the effect of an EMBANKMENT or a channel change** ← | ← |
| **Sizing flood STORAGE or detention basins** ← | ← |
| **Estimating the flood at an ungauged point from a gauged one upstream** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A LARGE ECONOMY AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: a spillway need not pass the full inflow peak, because the reservoir's storage attenuates it.**

> **The attenuation depends on how much surcharge storage is available above the normal level and on the spillway's own characteristics, so the routing and the spillway design are interdependent and must be solved together.**

> **A larger spillway passes the flood at a lower surcharge and attenuates less; a smaller one surcharges more and attenuates more.**

> **So there is an economic optimum between spillway capacity and dam freeboard, and finding it requires the flood to be routed for each trial — which is why spillway design is an iterative computation rather than a direct one.**

examTip.trick: **Lower peak, later, broader** — storage absorbs part of the rise and releases it later. The VOLUME is unchanged, which is the check on any routing result.
examTip.trap: **Muskingum x = 0 is a reservoir (maximum attenuation), x = 0.5 is pure translation (none).** Natural reaches are 0.2-0.3; embanking pushes x up.
