examTip.mnemonic: **A spillway need not pass the full inflow peak** — the reservoir attenuates it. But routing and spillway size are interdependent, so the design is iterative.

questions.stem: The SEDIMENT DELIVERY RATIO of a catchment is:
options: The proportion of the gross erosion occurring within the catchment that actually reaches its outlet
The ratio of bed load to suspended load at the outlet
The proportion of the sediment that a reservoir traps
The ratio of the sediment concentration to the discharge
questions.solution:
**The proportion of the GROSS EROSION occurring within the catchment that actually reaches its outlet** — the remainder being deposited on slopes, in channels and on floodplains along the way — and it DECREASES as the catchment's area increases.

**Why the ratio is less than one, and why it falls with area:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Soil eroded from a field does not all reach the river** ← | **Much is deposited at the field's edge, in a hollow, at a change of slope, in a hedge or in a channel** ← |
| **The further the material must travel, the more opportunities there are for it to be deposited** ← | ← |
| **A LARGE catchment has longer travel paths, flatter lower reaches and more floodplain** ← | **So a smaller proportion of its gross erosion reaches the outlet** ← |
| **A SMALL steep catchment delivers most of what it erodes** ← | **Delivery ratios approaching 1 for a very small steep catchment** ← |
| **A large basin may have a delivery ratio of only 0.1 or less** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER PRODUCE A CONCLUSION THAT IS OFTEN MISUSED AND IS WORTH STATING CAREFULLY: the sediment yield measured at a basin's outlet is much LESS than the erosion occurring within it.**

> **So a measured yield cannot be converted into an erosion rate without the delivery ratio, and an erosion rate cannot be converted into a yield without it either.**

> **The two are routinely confused, and a soil loss figure per hectare — from a plot experiment or from the Universal Soil Loss Equation — multiplied by the catchment's area gives the GROSS erosion, which may be ten times the yield at the outlet.**

> **Quoting that figure as the sediment reaching a reservoir overstates the problem by an order of magnitude, and it is a mistake made often enough to be worth guarding against.**

**WHAT THIS MEANS FOR CATCHMENT CONSERVATION, WHICH IS THE PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT CONSEQUENCE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Conservation measures reduce EROSION at the source** ← | ← |
| **But only a fraction of the erosion prevented would have reached the outlet anyway** ← | **So the reduction in YIELD is a fraction of the reduction in erosion** ← |
| **In a large basin with a delivery ratio of 0.1, preventing 100 tonnes of erosion reduces the yield by about 10 tonnes** ← | ← |
| **So catchment treatment's effect on a downstream reservoir's silting is far SMALLER than the erosion figures suggest** ← | ← |
| **And the effect appears SLOWLY, as the sediment already in transit works through the system** ← | **Over decades** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE AN UNCOMFORTABLE FINDING AND THEY SHOULD BE STATED HONESTLY: catchment conservation is frequently proposed as the answer to reservoir sedimentation, and its effect on that particular problem is modest and slow.**

> **That does not make it worthless — conservation's benefits to the farmers whose soil is being lost, to the local water regime and to the productivity of the land are large and immediate, and they justify it on their own.**

> **But it is not a substitute for designing the reservoir to cope with the sediment it will receive, and a project appraisal that relies on catchment treatment to solve its sedimentation problem is relying on something that will not deliver within the project's life.**

> **So the two should be pursued together and justified separately: conservation for the catchment's own sake, and sediment management at the dam for the reservoir's.**

> **A FURTHER COMPLICATION IN THE HIMALAYA DESERVES MENTION: a large part of the sediment in a Himalayan river comes not from surface erosion of agricultural land but from LANDSLIDES, GLACIAL erosion, riverbank erosion and the wholesale mass wasting of a rapidly uplifting range.**

> **Those sources are largely natural and are not amenable to catchment treatment at all.**

> **So the fraction of the sediment yield that conservation could in principle address may be small before the delivery ratio is even considered — and studies in the region have repeatedly found the natural component to dominate.**

> **Which means the case for conservation in Nepal rests properly on protecting the land and the people living on it, and the sediment argument, though it is the one most often made to funders, is the weaker part of it.**

examTip.trick: **The fraction of gross erosion that reaches the outlet** — falling as the catchment grows, because longer paths give more chances to deposit.
examTip.trap: **A soil loss rate times the area gives GROSS EROSION, not yield** — which may be ten times what reaches the reservoir. A common order-of-magnitude error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Conservation's effect on reservoir silting is modest and slow** — and much Himalayan sediment is from landslides and mass wasting, not farmland. Justify conservation on its own merits.

questions.stem: A stone PITCHING (revetment) laid on a riverbank must be provided with a FILTER layer beneath it and a LAUNCHING APRON at its toe because:
options: The filter improves the pitching's appearance and the apron provides access
The filter increases the pitching's weight and the apron reduces the wave height
Without a filter the bank material is washed out through the pitching, which then settles and fails
Both are required only in tidal rivers
questions.solution:
**Without a FILTER the bank material is washed out THROUGH the pitching, which then settles and fails; and without a launching APRON the toe is undermined by scour, after which the whole pitching slides into the river.**

**The two failure mechanisms and their remedies:**

| Failure | Mechanism | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| **Loss of the bank material THROUGH the pitching** ← | **Water moving in and out of the bank — from waves, from the river's fluctuating level, and from groundwater seeping out — carries the fine bank material out through the gaps between the stones** ← | **A graded FILTER, or a geotextile, between the bank and the pitching** ← |
| **Undermining of the TOE** ← | **Scour at the bank's foot removes the material the pitching rests on** ← | **A LAUNCHING APRON of loose stone, or the toe founded below the scour level** ← |

> **THE FIRST MECHANISM IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT IS THE COMMONER CAUSE OF FAILURE IN PLACE: the pitching itself is undamaged and the bank behind it has gone.**

> **Water enters the bank when the river is high and drains out when it falls, and every cycle carries a little of the fine material out between the stones.**

> **The bank behind the pitching is progressively hollowed, the stones lose their support and settle into the voids, the pitching becomes irregular and open, and the process accelerates.**

> **An inspection sees a somewhat uneven pitching and no obvious damage, while the bank behind it is substantially gone — and the failure, when it comes, is sudden.**

> **So the filter is not a refinement beneath the visible work but the thing that determines whether the visible work has anything to sit on.**

**THE FILTER CRITERIA ARE THE SAME TWO CONDITIONS MET REPEATEDLY, AND THIS IS THEIR SIXTH APPEARANCE:**

| Criterion | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **RETENTION** | **Fine enough to hold the bank material** ← |
| **PERMEABILITY** | **Coarse enough to let the water out freely, so no pressure builds behind the pitching** ← |

> **THE SECOND CRITERION MATTERS PARTICULARLY HERE BECAUSE OF RAPID DRAWDOWN: when a flood falls quickly, the water in the bank cannot drain as fast as the river level falls.**

> **The bank is then left with a head of water inside it acting outward on the pitching — exactly the uplift condition that destroys a canal lining.**

> **A permeable filter lets that water out and the pressure never develops; an impermeable one, or a clogged filter, holds it in and the pitching is pushed off the bank.**

> **So the pitching must be free-draining, which is why it is laid dry rather than grouted — and grouting a stone pitching to make it look neat and permanent is a serious error that converts a drained revetment into a dam.**

**THE OTHER REQUIREMENTS OF A REVETMENT, FOR COMPLETENESS:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Stone SIZE adequate for the velocity** ← | **The required weight rising very steeply with velocity** ← |
| **A SLOPE no steeper than the stone will rest on** ← | **Commonly 2:1 or flatter** ← |
| **The pitching carried UP to above the highest flood level** ← | **Or the flow attacks the bank above it and works down behind the pitching** ← |
| **And carried along far enough at each END** ← | **Or the flow attacks the unprotected bank beyond the end and works back behind it — the outflanking failure again** ← |
| **Adequate THICKNESS — commonly 300 to 600 mm, or two stone layers** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS DESCRIBE THE SAME FAILURE AT DIFFERENT BOUNDARIES AND IT IS THE PATTERN NOTED SEVERAL TIMES: wherever protection stops, the attack concentrates and works back behind it.**

> **A revetment is therefore vulnerable at three places — its toe, its top and its two ends — and all four must be terminated properly.**

> **The toe gets a launching apron, the top is carried above the flood, and the ends are keyed into the bank or turned into it.**

> **A revetment that is beautifully built over its length and simply stops at each end will be flanked, and the length will then be undermined from behind — so the terminations are worth more attention than the length between them, and they are where the money should go if it is short.**

examTip.trick: **No filter and the bank washes out through the stones; no apron and the toe is undermined.** Two distinct failures needing two distinct provisions.
examTip.trap: **Never GROUT a stone pitching** — it must drain, or rapid drawdown leaves a head inside the bank that pushes the pitching off, exactly as it lifts a canal lining.
examTip.mnemonic: **Toe, top and both ends** — wherever protection stops the attack works back behind it. Terminations matter more than the length between them.

questions.stem: A community-based FLOOD EARLY WARNING SYSTEM on a Himalayan river faces a fundamental constraint, namely that:
options: The rivers do not flood predictably enough for any warning to be given
The lead time is very short
Satellite communication is unavailable in the mountains
Warnings cannot be issued at night
questions.solution:
**The LEAD TIME is very SHORT — the catchments are small and steep, so a flood may travel from the rainfall to the settlements in a few hours** — which determines what the warning can be expected to achieve.

**Why the lead time is short:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **The catchments are SMALL in area** ← | ← |
| **And very STEEP, so the runoff concentrates quickly** ← | **A short time of concentration** ← |
| **The rainfall is INTENSE and often localised** ← | ← |
| **So a flood can rise from nothing to its peak in a few hours** ← | **Or less on a small tributary** ← |
| **A gauge upstream may be only two or three hours' travel time above the settlement** ← | ← |
| **Which is the whole warning time available** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW DETERMINES WHAT THE SYSTEM CAN AND CANNOT ACHIEVE AND IT IS WORTH BEING REALISTIC ABOUT: two or three hours is enough to save LIVES and very little else.**

> **People can move to high ground, take their children and their livestock, and carry what they can lift.**

> **They cannot evacuate their houses' contents, move their grain stores, harvest a crop or protect their land.**

> **So the objective of such a system is the preservation of life, and measuring its success by property saved would misjudge it entirely.**

> **That is worth stating explicitly at the design stage, because a system justified on property protection will be judged to have failed when it saves lives and loses property — which is exactly what it was capable of doing.**

**WHAT MAKES SUCH A SYSTEM WORK, WHICH IS MOSTLY NOT TECHNICAL:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A rainfall or water level SENSOR upstream, with a reliable transmission link** ← | **The technical part, and the easiest** ← |
| **A defined THRESHOLD at which a warning is issued** ← | **Set from experience of past floods** ← |
| **A DISSEMINATION route that actually reaches people** ← | **Sirens, mobile phones, radio, and a chain of volunteers with a defined responsibility** ← |
| **A community that KNOWS what the warning means and what to do** ← | **Which requires drills, not merely information** ← |
| **Identified and accessible SAFE ground and routes to it** ← | **Marked, and known to everyone including children** ← |
| **MAINTENANCE of the equipment through years when no flood comes** ← | ← |
| **And TRUST — a community that has been warned wrongly several times will not respond** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND SEVENTH ROWS ARE THE ONES THAT DECIDE WHETHER THE SYSTEM SAVES ANYONE AND THEY ARE SOCIAL RATHER THAN TECHNICAL: a warning that reaches a community which does not know what to do achieves nothing.**

> **A siren that has sounded three times without a flood following will be ignored the fourth time, which is the one that matters.**

> **So the threshold must be set to give few false alarms — accepting that a lower threshold would give more warning — and the community must be involved in setting it and must understand the trade.**

> **A system designed and installed by an agency, without that involvement, typically works technically and fails in use, and the failure is attributed to the community rather than to the design.**

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE OTHER COMMON FAILURE AND IT IS AN INSTITUTIONAL ONE: a warning system's equipment sits unused for years.**

> **Batteries fail, sensors silt up, the radio link's license lapses, the trained volunteers move away, and the responsible official is transferred.**

> **Then a flood comes and nothing happens.**

> **So a warning system requires an institution with a continuing responsibility and a budget, and where that does not exist the system has a life of a few years regardless of its technical quality — which is an argument for the simplest system that will work, maintained locally, rather than the most capable one, maintained from the capital.**

> **The community-based systems on the Karnali and elsewhere in Nepal have worked partly because they are simple enough for the community itself to keep going, and that is a design decision as much as a social one.**

examTip.trick: **Small steep catchments give only a few hours** — enough to save lives, not property. Judge the system by that objective, not another.
examTip.trap: **A siren that has cried wolf will be ignored** — so the threshold must give few false alarms, and the community must understand the trade and help set it.
examTip.mnemonic: **The technical part is the easy part** — dissemination, drills, marked safe ground, maintenance and institutional continuity decide whether anyone is saved.

questions.stem: INTEGRATED WATERSHED MANAGEMENT is distinguished from a conventional sectoral approach chiefly by treating:
options: Only the forested portions of the catchment
The river channel alone, from source to outlet
Engineering structures as the sole means of intervention
The watershed as the planning unit, and its land, water, vegetation and people as one interacting system
questions.solution:
**The WATERSHED as the planning UNIT, and its land, water, vegetation and people as one interacting system** — so that upstream and downstream interests, and biophysical and social measures, are planned together rather than by separate agencies.

**Why the watershed is the right unit:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A watershed is defined by the WATER's own boundaries** ← | **Everything within it drains to one outlet, and nothing outside it does** ← |
| **So the effects of an action anywhere in it appear at the outlet** ← | **Which makes it the natural unit for accounting** ← |
| **Administrative boundaries — districts, municipalities, provinces — cut ACROSS watersheds** ← | **So a management unit defined administratively splits the system that is being managed** ← |
| **And sectoral agencies — forest, agriculture, irrigation, roads, water supply — each act on a part** ← | **Without seeing the whole** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER DESCRIBE THE PROBLEM THE APPROACH EXISTS TO SOLVE AND IT IS AN INSTITUTIONAL ONE RATHER THAN A TECHNICAL ONE: the system is one and the management is many.**

> **The forest department manages the forest, the agriculture department the farming, the roads department the road that is destabilising the slope, and the irrigation department the intake that is silting up because of all three.**

> **Each acts competently within its remit and the aggregate outcome is poor, because the interactions between them are nobody's responsibility.**

> **So integrated watershed management is chiefly a proposal about how to ORGANISE, and its technical content — terracing, check dams, plantation, waterways, improved cultivation — is largely the conventional content of each sector.**

> **That is worth being clear about, because it is often presented as a new set of techniques when it is a new arrangement of familiar ones.**

**THE UPSTREAM-DOWNSTREAM RELATIONSHIP, WHICH IS THE SUBSTANTIVE ISSUE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Actions UPSTREAM affect people DOWNSTREAM** ← | **Erosion, sediment, flood peaks, low flows and water quality all travel down** ← |
| **But the upstream community bears the COST of conservation and the downstream community receives the BENEFIT** ← | ← |
| **So there is no incentive for the upstream community to act** ← | **They are asked to farm less intensively, graze less and plant trees, for someone else's benefit** ← |
| **And they are usually the POORER of the two** ← | **Hill farmers upstream, irrigated plains or a city downstream** ← |
| **So a conservation programme that simply asks them to bear the cost will not be sustained** ← | ← |
| **Which is the argument for PAYMENT FOR ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES — the downstream beneficiary compensating the upstream provider** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE THE EQUITY PROBLEM AT THE HEART OF WATERSHED MANAGEMENT AND IT SHOULD BE STATED PLAINLY: the people asked to change their behaviour are the poorest and gain the least from doing so.**

> **A programme that treats their land use as the problem, and their compliance as the solution, is asking a subsistence farmer to reduce his production to protect a downstream reservoir he will never benefit from.**

> **Unsurprisingly, such programmes work while the project's payments continue and stop when they end.**

> **A programme that instead identifies measures which improve the upstream farmer's OWN productivity — terracing that raises his yield, water harvesting that lets him grow a second crop, fodder that feeds his livestock — obtains the same conservation as a by-product of something he wants anyway, and it continues after the project ends.**

> **That is the practical test of a watershed programme's design: does the upstream household benefit directly, or is it being asked to sacrifice?**

> **The first is sustainable and the second is not, and the difference is visible in the choice of measures rather than in the programme's stated objectives.**

> **NEPAL'S DEPARTMENT OF SOIL CONSERVATION AND WATERSHED MANAGEMENT HAS OPERATED ON THIS BASIS FOR DECADES, and the community forestry programme is the country's most successful instance of it — conservation achieved by giving the local users the ownership and the benefit, rather than by protecting the forest from them.**

examTip.trick: **The watershed as the unit, and land, water, vegetation and people as one system** — planned together rather than by separate agencies.
examTip.trap: **It is chiefly an INSTITUTIONAL proposal, not a new set of techniques** — the technical content is the conventional content of each sector, differently arranged.
examTip.mnemonic: **Upstream bears the cost and downstream gets the benefit, and upstream is poorer** — so choose measures that raise the upstream household's OWN yield, or it stops when the project does.

questions.stem: A DISTRIBUTARY HEAD REGULATOR and a CROSS REGULATOR are normally built as a PAIR at an offtake because:
options: Two structures share the cost of a single foundation
It allows the canal to be closed from either side
One structure would be too large to build
The head regulator admits the distributary's designed share
questions.solution:
**The head regulator ADMITS the distributary's designed share, while the cross regulator across the main canal just below it RAISES the upstream level** so that the head regulator can command that share even when the main canal runs at part supply.

**The two working together:**

| Structure | What it controls |
|---|---|
| **DISTRIBUTARY HEAD REGULATOR** ← | **The DISCHARGE entering the distributary** ← |
| **CROSS REGULATOR (across the main canal, just downstream of the offtake)** ← | **The LEVEL in the main canal upstream of itself** ← |
| **Together** ← | **The operator can set the distributary's discharge and the main canal's level INDEPENDENTLY** ← |

> **THE INDEPENDENCE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE WHOLE PURPOSE OF THE PAIRING AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY IT IS NEEDED: a head regulator's discharge depends on the HEAD across it, and that head depends on the main canal's level.**

> **When the main canal runs at full supply the level is high and the distributary gets its share.**

> **When the main canal runs at part supply — which it must whenever the river is low or the total demand is less than the design — the level falls and the distributary can no longer draw its share, however wide its gate is opened.**

> **A cross regulator, partly closed, backs the water up and restores the level, so the distributary is served regardless of what is passing down the main canal.**

> **Without it, the head-end distributaries would take what they could and the tail of the main canal would receive whatever was left — which is the outcome the pairing exists to prevent.**

**WHAT THE PAIR MAKES POSSIBLE OPERATIONALLY, WHICH IS THE LARGER BENEFIT:**

| Capability | Note |
|---|---|
| **ROTATIONAL operation of the distributaries** ← | **A group is run at FULL supply while others are closed, then the turn passes** ← |
| **Which keeps every running channel at its SELF-CLEANSING velocity** ← | **Rather than all of them running slowly and silting** ← |
| **And delivers a usable supply to the TAIL of each distributary during its turn** ← | **Rather than an inadequate supply to every tail all the time** ← |
| **Isolation of a reach for MAINTENANCE while the upstream offtakes continue** ← | ← |
| **And control of the SILT drawn into each offtake, by managing the level and the velocity in the reach** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER ARE THE ARGUMENT FOR ROTATION AND IT IS WORTH RESTATING BECAUSE IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE: when there is not enough water, giving everyone a little is worse than giving some people enough in turn.**

> **A channel running at a quarter of its design discharge runs at perhaps half its design velocity, which is below self-cleansing, so it silts — and its capacity falls further.**

> **Its water spreads thinly and never reaches the tail of the command, so the head-enders take it all and the tail-enders get nothing anyway.**

> **Rotation instead runs each channel properly for a shorter time: it stays clean, its water reaches the tail, and every cultivator gets a proper turn.**

> **The total water delivered is the same and the useful water delivered is far greater, and the difference is entirely in the arrangement.**

**THE PRACTICAL REQUIREMENT THIS IMPOSES SHOULD BE NOTED AS A CLOSING POINT: rotation requires the cross regulators to be OPERATED, on a schedule, by someone who knows the roster.**

> **A system with cross regulators that are never adjusted has the structures and not the benefit — the gates sit wherever they were last left, the levels are whatever they happen to be, and the distribution is determined by hydraulics rather than by policy.**

> **So the pairing of structures is a means to an operational end, and building them without establishing the operating arrangement produces the cost and not the result.**

> **That is a recurring theme in irrigation: the physical works are the smaller part of the system, and the arrangements for operating them are the larger part and the one that more often fails.**

examTip.trick: **Head regulator sets the distributary's DISCHARGE; cross regulator sets the main canal's LEVEL.** Together they can be set independently.
examTip.trap: **Without the cross regulator, a part-supply main canal cannot command its offtakes** — the head-enders take what they can and the tail gets nothing.
examTip.mnemonic: **When water is short, giving everyone a little is worse than giving some enough in TURN** — a channel at quarter supply silts and never reaches its tail anyway.

questions.stem: A pipe outlet 200 mm in diameter discharges under a working head of 0.6 m with a coefficient of discharge of 0.62 and is running SUBMERGED. Its discharge is about:
options: 67 litres per second
108 litres per second
42 litres per second
21 litres per second
questions.solution:
**About 67 litres per second.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Area of the pipe** | **A = πD²/4 = π × 0.2²/4 = 0.03142 m²** ← |
| **Velocity head term** | **√(2gH) = √(2 × 9.81 × 0.6) = √11.772 = 3.431 m/s** ← |
| **Q = C_d A √(2gH)** | **= 0.62 × 0.03142 × 3.431** ← |
| **Evaluating** | **= 0.0668 m³/s** ← |
| **In litres per second** | **= 66.8, about 67 l/s** ← |

> **So the outlet passes about 67 l/s under that head.**

**THE MEANING OF 'H' DIFFERS BETWEEN THE SUBMERGED AND THE FREE CASES, WHICH IS THE POINT TO GET RIGHT:**

| Condition | H is |
|---|---|
| **SUBMERGED (drowned) outlet** ← | **The DIFFERENCE in water level between the upstream and downstream sides** ← |
| **FREE (modular) outlet, discharging into air** ← | **The head from the upstream water surface to the CENTRE of the outlet** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION MATTERS BECAUSE THE TWO CONDITIONS BEHAVE QUITE DIFFERENTLY AND THE SAME OUTLET MAY BE IN EITHER, DEPENDING ON THE WATERCOURSE'S LEVEL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A SUBMERGED outlet is NON-MODULAR — its discharge depends on BOTH levels** ← | **So the cultivator can increase it by lowering the watercourse's level** ← |
| **A FREE outlet is a SEMI-MODULE — its discharge depends only on the upstream level** ← | **The downstream level being irrelevant so long as it stays below the outlet** ← |
| **So the same pipe outlet is non-modular when drowned and semi-modular when free** ← | ← |
| **Which means the DESIGN must establish which condition will obtain** ← | **And a free-flowing outlet is much to be preferred, since it cannot be manipulated from below** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL DESIGN CONCLUSION AND IT IS OFTEN ACHIEVABLE FOR LITTLE COST: setting the outlet high enough that it discharges FREELY into the watercourse, rather than being drowned by it, converts a non-modular outlet into a semi-modular one.**

> **That removes the cultivator's ability to increase his share by deepening the watercourse below the outlet — which is the commonest form of tampering, as noted earlier.**

> **The cost is a small loss of command, since the outlet must be set higher, and where the levels permit it that is a cheap improvement in equity.**

> **Where they do not permit it, the outlet is drowned and the design must accept the non-modular behaviour or provide a different type of module.**

**A CAUTION ON THE COEFFICIENT OF DISCHARGE IS WORTH ADDING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **C_d for a pipe outlet is typically 0.62 to 0.80** ← | **Depending on the entry's shape** ← |
| **A SHARP-edged entry gives about 0.62** ← | **The flow separates at the edge and contracts — the vena contracta** ← |
| **A BELL-MOUTHED or rounded entry gives 0.8 or more** ← | **Because the flow is not forced to turn a sharp corner and does not contract** ← |
| **So rounding the entry increases the discharge by nearly 30 per cent for the same pipe and head** ← | ← |

> **The fourth row is worth knowing because it is a free improvement in one direction and an unintended one in the other: a bell mouth added to an outlet increases its discharge substantially without any change to its diameter.**

> **A cultivator who rounds and smooths the entry to his outlet with a little mortar has increased his share by a quarter, and nothing about the outlet's stated dimensions has changed.**

> **So the entry's condition is part of what determines the discharge, and an outlet's calibration should be checked against its actual condition rather than assumed from its nominal size — which is one reason a fixed and inspectable module is preferable to a plain pipe where the water is contested.**

examTip.trap: **H is the LEVEL DIFFERENCE when submerged and the head to the outlet's CENTRE when free** — and the same pipe is non-modular drowned and semi-modular free.
examTip.mnemonic: **Set the outlet to discharge FREELY where the levels allow** — it then cannot be manipulated from below. And a rounded entry raises C_d from 0.62 to 0.8, a quarter more discharge.

questions.stem: A CANAL FALL is provided where:
options: The canal must cross a natural drainage
The canal's discharge must be measured
The natural ground falls more steeply than the canal's designed bed slope
The canal must be closed for maintenance
questions.solution:
**Where the NATURAL GROUND falls more steeply than the canal's designed bed slope** — so the accumulated surplus difference in level is taken up at one structure, allowing the reaches between falls to run at their proper gradient.

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A canal's bed slope is fixed by its REGIME requirement — perhaps 1 in 5,000** ← | **Steep enough to carry its silt, gentle enough not to scour** ← |
| **The country may fall at 1 in 1,000 or steeper** ← | ← |
| **So the canal, running flatter than the ground, rises steadily ABOVE the ground surface** ← | ← |
| **Continuing indefinitely, it would stand on an ever-higher embankment** ← | **Which is expensive and dangerous** ← |
| **A FALL drops the canal's bed at one point, bringing it back near the ground** ← | ← |
| **And the reach below starts again at the proper gradient** ← | ← |

> **THE ALTERNATIVE TO FALLS IS TO GIVE THE CANAL THE GROUND'S OWN SLOPE, AND THE COMPARISON IS THE DESIGN DECISION:**

| Option | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Canal at the GROUND's steep slope** ← | **Its velocity exceeds the non-scouring limit, so it must be LINED throughout — a cost per metre over the whole length** ← |
| **Canal at its REGIME slope, with FALLS** ← | **The canal is unlined, and the surplus level is taken up at discrete structures — a cost per structure** ← |
| **For most alluvial canals the second is far cheaper** ← | **A fall is a compact structure and lining is continuous** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE USUAL CONCLUSION AND IT EXPLAINS WHY FALLS ARE SO CHARACTERISTIC OF PLAINS CANAL SYSTEMS: a canal 100 km long across country falling at 1 in 1,000 must shed some 80 m of surplus level.**

> **Lining 100 km is an enormous expenditure; twenty falls of 4 m each is a modest one.**

> **So the system is designed as a series of gently graded reaches punctuated by drops, and the falls become convenient sites for other things.**

**THE SECONDARY FUNCTIONS A FALL COMMONLY SERVES, WHICH OFTEN JUSTIFY ITS POSITION:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **A ROAD or a footbridge over the canal** ← | **The structure is there, so the crossing is nearly free** ← |
| **A metering point, since the fall's crest is a WEIR of known characteristics** ← | **Giving the discharge from the upstream depth** ← |
| **A REGULATOR, if gates are added to the crest** ← | **Controlling the upstream level as well** ← |
| **A site for an OFFTAKE, taking advantage of the raised upstream level** ← | ← |
| **Small HYDROPOWER, using the head that is otherwise destroyed** ← | **Canal-fall micro-hydro schemes exist and are worthwhile where a grid connection is available** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WORTH NOTING BECAUSE IT INVERTS THE FALL'S PURPOSE: the fall exists to DESTROY surplus energy, and a turbine placed in it extracts that energy instead.**

> **The head is modest — a few metres — and the flow is substantial and steady during the irrigation season, which is a reasonable combination for a low-head turbine.**

> **The scheme's limitation is that the canal runs only when irrigation requires it, so the generation is seasonal and the plant is idle during the canal closure.**

> **But the civil works exist already, the water is already being managed, and the energy is genuinely free — so where a canal system has many falls and a grid to feed, the aggregate potential is real and it is one of the more attractive small hydropower opportunities available.**

> **THE POSITION OF A FALL ALONG THE CANAL IS THE REMAINING DESIGN QUESTION AND IT IS SETTLED BY BALANCING TWO THINGS: falls placed close together give small drops and many structures; falls placed far apart give large drops and few structures.**

> **Many small falls cost more in structures and less in earthwork, since the canal stays near the ground; few large falls cost less in structures and more in earthwork, since the canal runs deeper in cutting or higher in bank between them.**

> **The optimum is found by comparing the two costs over a range of spacings, and it commonly gives drops of 1 to 3 m — with the position of each adjusted to suit an offtake, a road crossing or a convenient site.**

examTip.trick: **The ground falls faster than the canal should** — so the surplus level is shed at discrete structures, letting the reaches between run at the regime slope.
examTip.trap: **The alternative is a steep LINED canal** — a cost per metre against a cost per structure. For long alluvial canals, falls win decisively.
examTip.mnemonic: **A fall destroys energy, so a turbine can extract it** — modest head, steady seasonal flow, and the civil works already exist. And falls host bridges, meters and regulators.

questions.stem: A TRAPEZOIDAL NOTCH FALL has an advantage over other types of canal fall in that its notches:
options: Require no energy dissipation downstream
Are cheaper to construct than any other form
Can be shaped so that the fall behaves as a proportional module
Allow boats to pass the fall
questions.solution:
**They can be shaped so that the fall behaves as a PROPORTIONAL module — passing the discharge in a nearly constant relationship to the upstream depth**, so the upstream water level is maintained at all discharges and the offtakes above it continue to command.

**The problem the trapezoidal notch solves:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A fall with a simple RECTANGULAR crest passes Q proportional to H^1.5** ← | **So a small discharge gives a small depth over the crest** ← |
| **The upstream water level therefore FALLS when the canal runs at part supply** ← | ← |
| **And the offtakes upstream lose their command** ← | **Which is the same problem the cross regulator addresses** ← |
| **A trapezoidal notch, correctly proportioned, gives Q nearly proportional to the DEPTH itself** ← | **Rather than to its 1.5 power** ← |
| **So the upstream depth varies with the discharge in the same proportion as the canal's own depth does** ← | ← |
| **And the fall behaves as a PROPORTIONAL MODULE — it takes its share without disturbing the level** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS CONTAIN THE DESIGN IDEA AND IT IS AN ELEGANT ONE: the notch's SHAPE is chosen so that its discharge relationship matches the canal's own.**

> **A rectangular notch is too steep a relationship and a triangular notch too shallow; a trapezoid, with the right side slope, falls between and can be tuned.**

> **The result is a fall that passes whatever the canal brings without either backing the water up or drawing it down — so the canal's regime is undisturbed by the presence of the fall, which is exactly what is wanted.**

> **This makes the trapezoidal notch fall a METERING device as well, since the relationship between depth and discharge is known and stable.**

**THE FAMILY OF FALLS, WHICH IS WORTH HAVING IN ORDER:**

| Fall | Character |
|---|---|
| **OGEE fall** ← | **A smooth crest following the nappe — the earliest, and it caused SCOUR because the energy was not dissipated** ← |
| **RAPID fall** ← | **A long masonry glacis down which the water runs — for small drops** ← |
| **STEPPED fall** ← | **A series of small drops, energy dissipated at each** ← |
| **TRAPEZOIDAL NOTCH fall** ← | **Notches in a wall, proportioned as above — this question** ← |
| **VERTICAL DROP (SARDA type) fall** ← | **A raised crest with a vertical drop into a cistern; the water cushion dissipates the energy** ← |
| **GLACIS fall — straight or parabolic** ← | **The MODERN type; energy dissipated by a HYDRAULIC JUMP on the glacis, whose position can be calculated** ← |
| **BAFFLE (Inglis) fall** ← | **A glacis with a baffle wall that stabilises the jump over a range of discharges** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION FROM THE FIRST TO THE LAST IS THE SAME AS FOR WEIRS AND FOR SPILLWAYS, AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING AS ONE HISTORY: the early forms passed the water smoothly and left its energy intact to scour the channel below.**

> **The later ones dissipate the energy deliberately, and the glacis type prevailed because the hydraulic jump's position and length can be COMPUTED rather than guessed.**

> **The baffle in the last row is the refinement that addresses the jump's weakness — that it forms in the right place at only one discharge — by providing an obstruction that holds it over a range.**

> **So the sequence is: ignore the energy, then dissipate it by impact, then dissipate it by a jump, then stabilise the jump.**

> **Each step responds to a shortcoming that experience revealed in the one before, which is how most families of hydraulic structures have developed and is why knowing the sequence is more useful than knowing the individual types.**

examTip.trick: **The notch's shape makes Q nearly proportional to the DEPTH**, so the upstream level is undisturbed at any discharge and the offtakes above keep their command.
examTip.trap: **A rectangular crest gives Q ∝ H^1.5**, so the upstream level drops at part supply. The trapezoid tunes the relationship to match the canal's own.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ogee → rapid → stepped → notch → Sarda → glacis → baffle** — ignore the energy, then dissipate by impact, then by a jump, then stabilise the jump.

questions.stem: Where a canal must cross a natural drainage, the work is called an AQUEDUCT when:
options: The drainage passes over the canal in a trough
The canal and the drainage are allowed to mix in a common pool
The drainage passes through barrels beneath the canal under pressure
The canal is carried over the drainage in a trough, with the drainage passing freely beneath it
questions.solution:
**The CANAL is carried OVER the drainage in a trough, with the drainage passing FREELY beneath it** — the canal's bed being above the drainage's high flood level.

**The six types of cross-drainage work:**

| Type | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** ← | **CANAL over the drainage; the drainage flows FREELY beneath, with clearance** ← |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** ← | **CANAL over the drainage, but the drainage passes beneath UNDER PRESSURE, its HFL being above the trough's soffit** ← (which is option c) |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** ← | **DRAINAGE over the canal in a trough; the canal flows FREELY beneath** ← (option a) |
| **CANAL SYPHON (syphon)** ← | **DRAINAGE over the canal, and the CANAL passes beneath under PRESSURE** ← |
| **LEVEL CROSSING** ← | **The two are allowed to MIX in a common pool, with regulators controlling what each takes onward** ← (option b) |
| **INLET and OUTLET** ← | **A small drainage is admitted INTO the canal at one point and let out at another** ← |

> **THE NAMING FOLLOWS ONE SIMPLE RULE AND IT IS WORTH FIXING BECAUSE THE SIX ARE OTHERWISE EASILY CONFUSED: the name describes what happens to the CANAL, and 'syphon' means something is under PRESSURE.**

| Element | Rule |
|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** ← | **From the Latin for carrying water — the CANAL is CARRIED over. So the canal is ON TOP** ← |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** ← | **The DRAINAGE passes over — 'super' meaning above, referring to the drainage. So the canal is BELOW** ← |
| **Adding 'SYPHON'** ← | **Means the LOWER of the two is flowing full and under pressure rather than freely** ← |
| **'SYPHON AQUEDUCT'** ← | **Canal on top (aqueduct), drainage below under pressure (syphon)** ← |
| **'CANAL SYPHON'** ← | **The CANAL is the one syphoning — so the canal is below and under pressure** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE PAIR MOST OFTEN CONFUSED AND THE RULE IN THE THIRD ROW RESOLVES THEM: in 'syphon aqueduct' the word aqueduct tells you the canal is on top, and syphon tells you the thing below is under pressure.**

> **In 'canal syphon' the word canal tells you which element is syphoning, and a syphoning element is the lower one — so the canal is below.**

> **Working the names out from that rule is more reliable than memorising four similar phrases, and it also makes the sixth type's name — level crossing — self-explanatory.**

**HOW THE CHOICE BETWEEN THEM IS MADE, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL QUESTION:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The RELATIVE LEVELS of the canal and the drainage decide most of it** ← | **Canal well above the drainage's HFL: aqueduct. Canal below the drainage's bed: super passage** ← |
| **Where the levels are close, a SYPHON of one kind or the other is unavoidable** ← | ← |
| **A SYPHON AQUEDUCT is generally preferred to a CANAL SYPHON** ← | **Because it is better to make the drainage flow under pressure occasionally in flood than to make the canal do so continuously** ← |
| **A canal syphon silts and is hard to clean** ← | **Being a depressed section carrying the canal's silt load permanently — the inverted siphon problem** ← |
| **A LEVEL CROSSING is used where the drainage is large and the levels are irreconcilable** ← | **It is cheap and it admits the drainage's silt and its floods into the canal, so it is a last resort** ← |
| **INLET and OUTLET suit a small drainage whose flow the canal can absorb** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER GIVE THE PREFERENCE THAT USUALLY DECIDES THE MATTER AND THE REASONING IS WORTH FOLLOWING: a syphon aqueduct puts the DRAINAGE under pressure, and the drainage flows only during storms.**

> **So the pressurised condition occurs for a few days a year, and between times the barrels are dry and can be inspected and cleaned.**

> **A canal syphon puts the CANAL under pressure, and the canal flows for most of the year carrying silt.**

> **So its barrels run full and silty continuously, they cannot be cleaned without shutting the canal, and they silt up.**

> **Given a choice, therefore, one makes the intermittent flow do the syphoning rather than the continuous one — which is a good instance of a design decision following from the OPERATING regime rather than from the hydraulics alone.**

examTip.trick: **Canal carried OVER, drainage free beneath.** Option (a) is a super passage, (c) a syphon aqueduct, (b) a level crossing.
examTip.trap: **'Aqueduct' means the canal is on top; 'syphon' means the LOWER one is under pressure.** So 'canal syphon' has the canal below. Work the names out, don't memorise them.
examTip.mnemonic: **Prefer a syphon AQUEDUCT to a canal syphon** — better the intermittent drainage flows under pressure than the continuous silt-laden canal, which would silt up unreachably.

questions.stem: In a SYPHON AQUEDUCT the drainage passes beneath the canal under pressure. The most important consequence for the design of the drainage barrels is that:
options: The barrel roof and the canal trough above are subject to uplift when the drainage runs under pressure
The barrels can be made smaller than for free flow
No energy dissipation is required downstream
The drainage's silt cannot enter the barrels
questions.solution:
**The barrel roof and the canal trough above are subject to UPLIFT when the drainage runs under pressure, and the barrel floor is subject to uplift from the drainage's seepage when the barrel is empty** — so both must be checked, and they are opposite cases.

**The two uplift conditions:**

| Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Barrels running FULL under pressure** ← | **The pressure inside acts UPWARD on the barrel's roof, and thence on the canal trough above; the trough's own weight and the water in it must resist it** ← |
| **Barrels EMPTY, with a high water table or the canal leaking** ← | **The external groundwater pressure acts UPWARD on the barrel's FLOOR, which may be lifted** ← |

> **THE TWO CASES ARE OPPOSITE AND EACH IS CRITICAL AT A DIFFERENT MOMENT, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THE STRUCTURE AWKWARD:**

> **The roof's worst case is when the drainage is in flood and the canal is EMPTY — maximum internal pressure below and minimum weight above.**

> **The floor's worst case is when the drainage is dry and the groundwater is high — maximum external pressure below and nothing inside to hold it down.**

> **So the two checks must be made at different combinations of the same variables, and a designer who considers only the 'full' condition has checked half the problem.**

> **The first case is the more commonly remembered and the second is the one that actually lifts floors, particularly where the canal above leaks into the surrounding ground and raises the water table locally.**

**THE OTHER FEATURES OF A SYPHON AQUEDUCT'S DESIGN:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The barrels are designed for the drainage's HIGH FLOOD discharge** ← | **With a velocity of 2 to 3 m/s, high enough to keep them clear of silt** ← |
| **TRANSITIONS are provided at the entry and exit of the drainage** ← | **Contracting into the barrels and expanding out, to limit the head loss** ← |
| **The AFFLUX upstream of the barrels must be computed and accommodated** ← | **Since the constriction raises the drainage's level upstream — which may flood land** ← |
| **An impervious FLOOR with cut-offs, exactly as for a weir** ← | **The head across the structure driving seepage beneath it** ← |
| **PROTECTION works upstream and downstream of the barrels** ← | **Launching aprons against the scour that the accelerated flow causes** ← |
| **And the CANAL's own trough, with its transitions** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CONSEQUENCE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT AFFECTS PEOPLE OTHER THAN THE CANAL'S OWNER: forcing a drainage through barrels constricts it, and a constriction raises the water level upstream.**

> **The land along the drainage above the crossing therefore floods more than it did, and to a greater depth.**

> **On a flat command that afflux can extend a considerable distance and affect a substantial area — and the people affected are not the canal's beneficiaries.**

> **So the barrels' capacity is not merely a hydraulic question but one of how much upstream flooding is being imposed, and providing generous waterway is cheaper than the compensation and the ill-will that a serious afflux causes.**

> **THE VELOCITY IN THE FIRST ROW IS A DELIBERATE CHOICE AND IT IS WORTH NOTING WHY IT IS SET HIGH: a barrel is a confined, inaccessible space that carries a flood-borne load of silt, gravel and debris.**

> **If it silts, clearing it requires entry into a confined space beneath a canal — a difficult and hazardous operation.**

> **So the barrels are sized for a velocity high enough that they scour themselves clear during each flood, accepting the greater head loss that implies.**

> **That is the same reasoning as the graded barrels of an inverted siphon, and it reflects the same underlying principle: where a structure cannot readily be cleaned, it must be designed not to need cleaning.**

examTip.trick: **Roof uplift when the barrels run full; FLOOR uplift when they are empty and the groundwater is high.** Two opposite cases, both critical.
examTip.trap: **The roof's worst case is drainage in flood with the canal EMPTY** — maximum pressure below and minimum weight above. Check the combinations, not just 'full'.
examTip.mnemonic: **Constricting the drainage causes AFFLUX upstream, flooding people who are not the canal's beneficiaries.** And keep the barrel velocity at 2-3 m/s: they cannot be cleaned.

questions.stem: A LEVEL CROSSING, in which a canal and a natural drainage are allowed to meet in a common pool with regulators on each outgoing channel, is adopted:
options: As the preferred solution wherever a canal crosses a drainage
As a last resort
Only where the drainage is very small
Where the canal must be carried well above the drainage
questions.solution:
**As a LAST RESORT — where the drainage is large and the levels of the two cannot be reconciled** — accepting that the drainage's silt and its floods will enter the canal and must be managed by the regulators.

**The arrangement:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **The canal and the drainage are led into a COMMON POOL** ← | **Where their waters mix** ← |
| **A CROSS REGULATOR on the canal, downstream of the pool** ← | **Admits to the canal only its designed discharge** ← |
| **A HEAD REGULATOR or a weir on the drainage, downstream of the pool** ← | **Passes the surplus down the drainage** ← |
| **So the pool is a junction, and the two regulators divide the combined flow** ← | ← |

> **ITS ADVANTAGES ARE FEW AND ITS DISADVANTAGES ARE MANY, WHICH IS WHY IT IS A LAST RESORT:**

| Advantage | Disadvantage |
|---|---|
| **CHEAP — no trough, no barrels, no long structure** ← | **The drainage's SILT enters the canal, and a flooded drainage carries a great deal of it** ← |
| **No difficulty with levels — the two simply meet** ← | **The drainage's FLOOD can enter the canal, overtopping and breaching it if the regulator is not closed in time** ← |
| **Simple to build** ← | **It requires ACTIVE OPERATION during every storm — someone must be present to work the gates** ← |
| ← | **Debris, and sometimes fish and other unwanted material, enter the canal** ← |
| ← | **And the canal's clean water is mixed with turbid drainage water** ← |

> **THE THIRD DISADVANTAGE IS THE DECISIVE ONE IN PRACTICE AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS: a level crossing is a structure that requires someone to operate it at the moment of danger.**

> **When the drainage comes down in flood, the canal's cross regulator must be closed promptly or the flood enters the canal.**

> **That moment is at night, in heavy rain, at a remote location — and if nobody is there, the canal receives the flood.**

> **The consequence is a breached canal, a flooded command below it, and a silted canal for kilometres.**

> **Every other type of cross-drainage work is PASSIVE — it does the right thing without anyone present — and that is worth a great deal more than the level crossing's lower capital cost.**

**SO WHEN IS IT NEVERTHELESS ADOPTED?**

| Circumstance | Note |
|---|---|
| **The drainage is LARGE — a substantial stream, not a minor nala** ← | **So a trough or barrels would be a major structure** ← |
| **The two beds are at nearly the SAME LEVEL** ← | **So neither can pass over the other without a great deal of earthwork** ← |
| **And there is no economic way to change either alignment or level** ← | ← |
| **The canal's discharge is large relative to the drainage's, so the dilution is tolerable** ← | ← |
| **And an operator can realistically be posted there** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CONDITION THAT USUALLY FORCES THE DECISION AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY IT IS SO CONSTRAINING: an aqueduct requires the canal's bed to be above the drainage's high flood level, and a super passage requires the drainage's bed to be above the canal's water surface.**

> **Between those two conditions lies a band of relative levels in which neither is possible without either raising the canal substantially — which affects its command and its earthwork for kilometres either side — or depressing one of them into a syphon.**

> **Where the syphon is also unattractive, because the drainage is large or the canal would silt, the level crossing is what remains.**

> **So it is chosen not because it is good but because the alternatives have been eliminated — and the honest presentation of such a decision states which alternatives were considered and why each was rejected, rather than presenting the level crossing as a positive choice.**
tags: silt and flood enter the canal

examTip.trick: **A last resort for a large drainage with irreconcilable levels** — the silt and the floods enter the canal and must be managed by gates.
examTip.trap: **It requires ACTIVE OPERATION at the moment of danger** — at night, in the rain, remotely. Every other cross-drainage work is passive, which is worth more than the capital saved.
examTip.mnemonic: **An aqueduct needs the canal above the drainage's HFL; a super passage needs the drainage above the canal.** Between those lies the band where nothing else works.

questions.stem: The TRANSITIONS provided at the entry and exit of an aqueduct's trough, where the canal contracts into the trough and expands out of it again, are shaped carefully because:
options: They carry the roadway across the structure
An abrupt change of section causes eddies and a large head loss
They are the cheapest part of the structure to build
They support the trough's side walls
questions.solution:
**An abrupt change of section causes eddies and a LARGE head loss — and the EXPANSION is the more critical, since a decelerating flow SEPARATES from the boundary readily while a contracting flow does not.**

**Why the two transitions differ in difficulty:**

| Transition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **CONTRACTION at the entry** ← | **The flow ACCELERATES; an accelerating flow is stable and follows the boundary readily, so a fairly abrupt contraction is tolerable** ← |
| **EXPANSION at the exit** ← | **The flow DECELERATES; a decelerating flow tends to SEPARATE from the boundary, forming eddies and losing energy** ← |

> **THE ASYMMETRY IS FUNDAMENTAL AND IT RECURS THROUGHOUT FLUID MECHANICS, SO IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN MEMORISING: a flow moving into a region of falling pressure is stable, and one moving into rising pressure is not.**

> **In a contraction the pressure falls in the direction of flow — a FAVOURABLE gradient — and the boundary layer is thinned and held against the wall.**

> **In an expansion the pressure rises in the direction of flow — an ADVERSE gradient — and the slow-moving fluid near the wall is decelerated to a standstill and then reversed, so the flow separates.**

> **Once separated, the expansion's added area is occupied by an eddy rather than by useful flow, and the energy is lost in turbulence.**

> **So an expansion must be GRADUAL — a total included angle of perhaps 1 in 3 to 1 in 5, against 1 in 2 for a contraction — and it is correspondingly longer and more expensive.**

**THE SAME ASYMMETRY APPEARS IN MANY PLACES AND RECOGNISING IT IS USEFUL:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **A DRAFT TUBE in a turbine** ← | **A gradual expansion, and its angle is limited for exactly this reason** ← |
| **A VENTURI meter** ← | **A short steep converging cone and a long gentle diverging one** ← |
| **A settling basin's INLET** ← | **The gradual expansion that prevents short-circuiting** ← |
| **A DIFFUSER of any kind** ← | ← |
| **And an aircraft wing's upper surface** ← | **Where the adverse gradient toward the trailing edge is what causes stall** ← |

> **THE VENTURI IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE CLEAREST ILLUSTRATION AND ITS SHAPE IS INSTANTLY RECOGNISABLE ONCE THE REASON IS KNOWN: the convergent cone is short and steep and the divergent cone is long and gentle.**

> **Anyone who has wondered why a venturi is not symmetrical has the answer in this asymmetry, and the same shape appears in a draft tube, a diffuser and an aqueduct's transitions for the identical reason.**

**THE FORMS OF TRANSITION USED IN CANAL WORK:**

| Form | Note |
|---|---|
| **STRAIGHT (wedge) transition** ← | **The simplest — plane walls at a fixed splay, commonly 1 in 2 in and 1 in 3 out** ← |
| **MITRA'S hyperbolic transition** ← | **Designed to keep the VELOCITY and hence the depth CONSTANT through the transition, for a horizontal bed** ← |
| **CHATURVEDI'S semi-cubical parabolic transition** ← | **A refinement of the same idea** ← |
| **HIND'S method** ← | **Which allows the bed level to vary as well, and computes the water surface profile through the transition** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW'S OBJECTIVE IS WORTH STATING BECAUSE IT EXPLAINS WHY A CURVED SHAPE IS USED AT ALL: if the velocity is held constant through the transition, there is no acceleration and therefore no pressure gradient along it.**

> **With no adverse gradient there is no tendency to separate, so the losses are minimal and the flow is smooth.**

> **Achieving that requires the width to vary in a particular way as the section changes — which is what the hyperbolic form provides.**

> **It is a good example of designing the geometry to eliminate the cause of a loss rather than accepting the loss and allowing for it, and where the head is scarce — as it always is on a long canal — that is worth the extra care in setting out.**

examTip.trick: **Accelerating flow is stable; decelerating flow SEPARATES.** So the expansion must be far more gradual than the contraction — 1 in 3 to 1 in 5 against 1 in 2.
examTip.trap: **Favourable pressure gradient in a contraction, ADVERSE in an expansion** — and an adverse gradient stalls the boundary layer. That is the whole reason.
examTip.mnemonic: **Same asymmetry as a venturi, a draft tube, a diffuser and a wing** — short steep in, long gentle out. Mitra's hyperbolic form holds the velocity constant so no gradient arises.

questions.stem: An INLET AND OUTLET arrangement for handling a small drainage crossing a canal consists of:
options: A pipe carrying the drainage beneath the canal
A trough carrying the drainage over the canal
A common pool with regulators on each outgoing channel
Admitting the small drainage into the canal at a suitable point
questions.solution:
**Admitting the small drainage INTO the canal at a suitable point, allowing its water to be carried along with the canal's, and releasing an equivalent quantity at an OUTLET further downstream into the drainage's continuation.**

**When the arrangement is suitable:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The drainage is SMALL — its discharge a modest fraction of the canal's** ← | **So the canal can absorb it without exceeding its capacity** ← |
| **Its water is reasonably CLEAN, or at least not heavily silt-laden** ← | **Since whatever enters is carried in the canal** ← |
| **The canal has spare CAPACITY, or an escape downstream** ← | ← |
| **And the drainage's continuation on the far side can receive the outlet's discharge** ← | ← |
| **The levels are such that the drainage can enter by gravity and leave by gravity** ← | ← |

> **ITS ATTRACTION IS SIMPLICITY AND CHEAPNESS AND IT IS WORTH NOTING WHAT IT AVOIDS: no trough, no barrels, no long structure, no transitions — merely an inlet and an outlet, each a modest opening in the canal's bank with some protection.**

> **For a small nala crossing a large canal, that is a sensible and proportionate solution, and building an aqueduct for such a crossing would be an absurdity.**

> **So the choice of cross-drainage type is scaled to the drainage, and the six types together cover the range from a field ditch to a major river.**

**ITS RISKS, WHICH LIMIT ITS USE:**

| Risk | Note |
|---|---|
| **The drainage may bring more water than expected in a storm** ← | **Its catchment's runoff having been under-estimated, or the storm exceptional** ← |
| **The canal is then over-supplied, and may overtop and breach** ← | ← |
| **The drainage brings SILT and DEBRIS into the canal** ← | ← |
| **And the canal's own regime is disturbed by the addition** ← | ← |
| **The inlet is a permanent opening, so it cannot be closed against a flood unless it is gated** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE PROVISION THAT MATTERS AND IT IS WORTH SPECIFYING DELIBERATELY: an inlet may be a simple opening or a gated one.**

> **A simple opening is cheaper and admits whatever the drainage brings.**

> **A gated inlet can be closed when the drainage is in flood, which protects the canal — but it then requires an operator, which reintroduces the level crossing's weakness on a smaller scale.**

> **The usual compromise is a simple inlet sized so that even the drainage's flood can be accommodated, together with a CANAL ESCAPE downstream capable of shedding the addition.**

> **That makes the arrangement passive: the drainage comes in, and the surplus goes out over the escape's weir without anyone doing anything, which is the arrangement's proper form.**

> **THE OUTLET'S FUNCTION DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS SOMETIMES MISUNDERSTOOD: the outlet is not there to return the same water that entered.**

> **It is there because the drainage's channel continues on the far side of the canal, and the land it drains still needs a route to it.**

> **Without an outlet, the canal has intercepted the drainage and its lower reach has lost its supply — while the land between the canal and the outlet has lost its drainage route entirely, and will waterlog.**

> **So the outlet serves the DRAINAGE's continuity rather than the canal's water balance, and its position is chosen where the drainage's channel can be resumed rather than where the canal finds it convenient.**

examTip.trick: **The drainage is admitted INTO the canal and an equivalent released downstream** — no trough, no barrels, for a small nala crossing a large canal.
examTip.trap: **Provide a canal ESCAPE downstream so the addition can be shed passively** — a gated inlet needs an operator, which reintroduces the level crossing's weakness.
examTip.mnemonic: **The outlet serves the DRAINAGE's continuity, not the canal's water balance** — without it the land between waterlogs and the lower drainage loses its route.

questions.stem: The impervious FLOOR of a canal regulator or a vertical drop is designed for uplift using the same seepage theory as a weir, but with one important difference in the governing condition, namely that:
options: The worst uplift occurs when the water is ponded to full supply level upstream and the downstream side is empty
The worst uplift occurs when both sides are at full supply level
Seepage theory does not apply to canal structures
The uplift is greatest during the monsoon flood
questions.solution:
**The worst uplift occurs when the water is PONDED to full supply level upstream and the downstream side is EMPTY** — the canal below having been dewatered for maintenance — which gives the greatest differential head across the structure.

**Why this condition governs:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The uplift depends on the DIFFERENTIAL head across the structure, not on the absolute level** ← | ← |
| **In normal operation both sides carry water and the differential is modest** ← | **Just the working head across the regulator** ← |
| **When the downstream reach is dewatered for maintenance, the differential becomes the FULL upstream depth** ← | ← |
| **And there is no water on the downstream floor to hold it down** ← | **So the uplift acts on an unloaded floor** ← |
| **Both effects worsen the condition at once** ← | **Maximum uplift and minimum counterweight** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS WHY THE CASE IS SO SEVERE AND IT IS THE SAME COMBINATION MET IN THE SYPHON AQUEDUCT'S ROOF: the worst loading and the least resistance coincide.**

> **That is a recurring pattern worth looking for in any structure subject to water pressure: the critical case is rarely the one with the most water, it is the one with the greatest DIFFERENCE and the least weight.**

> **A canal regulator carrying water on both sides is comfortably loaded; the same regulator with a dry reach below it is at its most vulnerable, and it is precisely then that people are working in the dry reach beneath the uplift.**

> **So the maintenance condition is both the structural worst case and the one during which people are present, which doubles its importance.**

**HOW THE CONDITION IS PROVIDED FOR:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **Design the floor's thickness for the FULL differential head** ← | **Using t = h/(G − 1) at each point, from the seepage pressure diagram** ← |
| **Provide DRAINAGE holes with an inverted filter through the downstream floor** ← | **Relieving the uplift rather than resisting it, as at a weir** ← |
| **Provide adequate CUT-OFFS to lengthen the creep path and reduce the pressures** ← | ← |
| **And, operationally, DEWATER SLOWLY and not fully where it can be avoided** ← | **Leaving a small depth on the downstream floor costs nothing and provides real counterweight** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS AN OPERATING PRECAUTION RATHER THAN A DESIGN ONE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT COSTS NOTHING: leaving 300 mm of water standing on the downstream floor during maintenance provides a useful counterweight and greatly reduces the net uplift.**

> **It is often perfectly possible — the work may be on the gates or the upstream side — and it is routinely not done because nobody has considered it.**

> **Where the floor itself must be worked on, the water must go, and then the design's provision is all there is — which is why the design must assume the fully dewatered case rather than relying on an operating practice.**

> **THE SAME REASONING APPLIES TO EVERY HYDRAULIC STRUCTURE WITH A REACH THAT CAN BE DEWATERED, AND IT IS WORTH LISTING WHERE IT ARISES: canal regulators, falls, cross-drainage works, lock gates, and the downstream floors of weirs and barrages.**

> **In each case there is a maintenance condition in which one side is emptied, and in each case that condition is more severe than any operating one.**

> **A designer who considers only the operating states has missed the governing case, and the failure — when it comes — occurs during maintenance with people in the structure.**

> **Which is why the maintenance condition should be listed explicitly among the design load cases rather than being assumed to be covered by the others.**
tags: maintenance as a design load case

examTip.trick: **Full supply upstream and DRY downstream** — the maximum differential head with no water above the floor to hold it down.
examTip.trap: **The worst case is rarely the one with the most water** — it is the one with the greatest DIFFERENCE and the least weight. Same pattern as a syphon aqueduct's roof.
examTip.mnemonic: **List the MAINTENANCE condition among the design load cases** — it is more severe than any operating state, and it is when people are inside the structure.

questions.stem: A STANDING WAVE FLUME or a PARSHALL FLUME installed in a canal measures the discharge by:
options: Timing a float over a measured length
Measuring the pressure difference across an orifice plate
Creating a CRITICAL-FLOW section
Measuring the velocity at a single point and multiplying by the area
questions.solution:
**Creating a CRITICAL-FLOW section — a contraction in which the flow passes through critical depth** — so that the discharge is a unique function of the UPSTREAM depth alone, independent of the downstream conditions.

**Why critical flow gives a unique measurement:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **At CRITICAL depth, the specific energy is a MINIMUM for a given discharge** ← | ← |
| **Equivalently, for a given specific energy the discharge is a MAXIMUM** ← | ← |
| **So at a critical section there is a one-to-one relationship between the depth and the discharge** ← | **Q = f(y) with no other variable** ← |
| **And a control is established: conditions DOWNSTREAM cannot influence the flow upstream of it** ← | **Because a disturbance cannot travel upstream through a critical or supercritical section** ← |
| **So the upstream depth alone determines the discharge, whatever happens below** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PROPERTY THAT MAKES THE DEVICE USEFUL AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING PHYSICALLY: a surface disturbance travels at a celerity √(gy) relative to the water.**

> **In subcritical flow the water is slower than that, so a disturbance can travel upstream and downstream conditions are felt upstream.**

> **At critical flow the water's velocity equals the wave celerity exactly, so a disturbance from downstream can make no headway.**

> **The section therefore isolates what is above it from what is below, which is what 'control' means in open channel hydraulics.**

> **A flume exploits that isolation: it forces the flow to pass through critical depth, and thereafter the upstream depth measures the discharge regardless of the tailwater, the canal's roughness or anything else downstream.**

**THE PRACTICAL ADVANTAGES OF A FLUME FOR CANAL MEASUREMENT:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **A single depth measurement gives the discharge** ← | **Read from a gauge on the wall — no instrument, no power, no calibration on site** ← |
| **It is INDEPENDENT of the downstream level, so it cannot be manipulated from below** ← | **Which matters where water is contested** ← |
| **It has no moving parts and needs no maintenance beyond keeping it clean** ← | ← |
| **It passes SILT and debris, unlike a weir, which ponds and deposits** ← | **Its floor being at or near the canal's bed** ← |
| **Its HEAD LOSS is small compared with a weir's** ← | **Since the flow recovers in the downstream expansion** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE ADVANTAGES OVER A WEIR AND THEY DECIDE THE CHOICE IN AN IRRIGATION CANAL: a sharp-crested weir is an excellent measuring device and a poor canal structure.**

> **It ponds the water upstream, so silt deposits behind it and the canal's regime is disturbed.**

> **It requires a substantial fall to operate, which on a canal short of head is unaffordable.**

> **And it traps floating debris, which must be cleared or the measurement is wrong.**

> **A flume avoids all three: its bed is at canal level so nothing deposits, its head loss is a fraction of a weir's, and debris passes through.**

> **So a weir is used where head is plentiful and a flume where it is not — which in a canal system is nearly always.**

**THE CONDITION THE FLUME REQUIRES DESERVES A CLOSING CAUTION: it must run in MODULAR (free) flow, with the critical section genuinely forming.**

> **If the tailwater rises high enough, the flume DROWNS — the jump downstream is submerged, the critical section is lost, and the upstream depth no longer determines the discharge alone.**

> **The device then behaves as a simple constriction, and readings taken from its gauge are wrong without anything appearing amiss.**

> **So a flume has a MODULAR LIMIT — a ratio of downstream to upstream head above which it drowns — and it must be set at a level, relative to the canal's downstream water surface, that keeps it below that limit at every discharge.**

> **A flume installed too low in a canal will read correctly at low flows and drown at high ones, which is exactly the wrong way round; and detecting it requires someone to check the downstream level against the modular limit rather than simply reading the gauge.**

examTip.trick: **A contraction forcing CRITICAL depth** — after which the upstream depth alone gives the discharge, whatever happens downstream.
examTip.trap: **At critical flow a disturbance cannot travel upstream** (water speed = wave celerity), which is why the section isolates upstream from downstream. That is what 'control' means.
examTip.mnemonic: **Preferred to a weir because it passes silt and costs little head** — but it must stay below its MODULAR LIMIT, or it drowns and reads wrong with nothing looking amiss.

questions.stem: A VERTICAL DROP structure in a canal dissipates the falling water's energy chiefly by:
options: The impact of the falling nappe into a cistern
Friction along the downstream apron
Gradual expansion of the channel below the drop
Aeration of the nappe as it falls
questions.solution:
**The IMPACT of the falling nappe into a CISTERN — a depressed floor holding a cushion of water** — the turbulence of that impact destroying the energy before the flow returns to the downstream channel.

**How the cistern works:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **The nappe falls freely from the crest** ← | **Gaining velocity as it falls** ← |
| **It plunges into the CISTERN — a floor DEPRESSED below the downstream bed** ← | ← |
| **The cushion of water in the cistern absorbs the impact** ← | **The jet's energy is destroyed in the turbulence of the plunge rather than on the floor** ← |
| **The cistern's DEPTH and LENGTH are given by empirical formulae** ← | **In terms of the drop and the discharge per metre width** ← |
| **And the flow leaves the cistern at a modest velocity, at the downstream bed level** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CISTERN'S PURPOSE AND IT IS WORTH BEING PRECISE ABOUT: the water cushion protects the FLOOR from the jet's impact and provides the mass in which the turbulence dissipates.**

> **A jet falling onto a bare concrete floor would erode it by direct impact and by the abrasion of any sediment it carries.**

> **Falling into standing water, the jet spreads, entrains air, and is broken up before it reaches the floor — so the floor experiences a distributed and much reduced loading.**

> **This is the same mechanism as a plunge pool below a ski-jump spillway, and it is why a natural waterfall scours a deep pool at its foot and then stops deepening: the pool it has created protects the rock beneath it.**

> **So the cistern is an artificial plunge pool, formed deliberately at a chosen depth rather than allowed to develop where the water chooses.**

**THE COMPARISON WITH THE GLACIS TYPE OF FALL, WHICH IS THE MODERN ALTERNATIVE:**

| Aspect | VERTICAL DROP with cistern | GLACIS fall with hydraulic jump |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanism** | **IMPACT into a water cushion** ← | **A hydraulic JUMP on the sloping glacis** ← |
| **Predictability** | **Empirical — the cistern's dimensions come from formulae fitted to experience** ← | **CALCULABLE — the jump's position and length follow from the hydraulics** ← |
| **Performance over a range of discharges** | **Reasonable** ← | **Good, since the jump can form at different points on the glacis** ← |
| **Suited to** | **SMALL drops and modest discharges** ← | **Larger drops and discharges, and where the tailwater varies** ← |
| **Construction** | **Simpler** ← | **More extensive** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE REASON THE GLACIS TYPE PREVAILED FOR LARGER STRUCTURES AND IT IS THE SAME REASON THAT RUNS THROUGH THIS WHOLE SUBJECT: a mechanism whose behaviour can be COMPUTED is preferable to one that must be judged.**

> **The hydraulic jump's sequent depth, its length and its energy loss all follow from the Froude number of the incoming flow, so a designer can place it, contain it and verify it.**

> **The impact cistern's performance is described by formulae fitted to observation, which serve well within the range of the observations and cannot be relied upon outside it.**

> **So the vertical drop remains appropriate for the small falls that make up most of a distributary system, and the glacis fall is used where the consequence of misjudging the dissipation would be serious.**

> **THE DOWNSTREAM PROTECTION IS REQUIRED IN BOTH CASES AND IT IS WORTH CLOSING ON: whatever the dissipation arrangement, the flow leaving it is more turbulent than the canal's normal flow and will scour the unprotected bed.**

> **So a length of pitching or an apron follows the cistern, and beyond that a launching apron of loose stone to accept whatever scour still occurs.**

> **The sequence — dissipation, then rigid protection, then flexible protection, then the natural bed — recurs at every energy-dissipating structure from a small canal drop to a major spillway, and its logic is the same at every scale: destroy what energy you can, protect against what remains, and provide for the scour you have not prevented.**

examTip.trick: **Impact into a water cushion in a depressed cistern** — the turbulence of the plunge destroys the energy before the flow reaches the downstream bed.
examTip.trap: **The cistern is an artificial PLUNGE POOL** — the same mechanism by which a natural waterfall scours a pool and then stops deepening, the pool protecting the rock.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dissipate, then rigid protection, then flexible protection, then natural bed** — the same sequence at every scale from a canal drop to a spillway.

questions.stem: The GATES of a canal regulator are commonly VERTICAL LIFT gates rather than radial gates on small structures because vertical lift gates:
options: Require less hoisting force for the same head and span
Are simple, cheap and easily fabricated and repaired locally
Do not require any seals
Can be operated without any hoisting arrangement
questions.solution:
**They are SIMPLE, cheap and easily fabricated and repaired locally** — though they need a greater hoisting force than a radial gate, since the whole water thrust must be lifted against the friction on the guides.

**The two gate types compared:**

| Aspect | VERTICAL LIFT gate | RADIAL (Tainter) gate |
|---|---|---|
| **Form** | **A flat plate sliding vertically in guides** ← | **A curved skin plate on radial arms, pivoting about a trunnion** ← |
| **Hoisting force** | **HIGH — the water thrust presses the gate against its guides, and that friction must be overcome as well as the gate's weight** ← | **LOW — the water thrust passes through the trunnion, so it exerts NO moment about the pivot, and only the gate's weight and the trunnion friction must be overcome** ← (so option a is inverted) |
| **Structure above** | **A tall hoist gantry, since the gate must lift its full height clear of the water** ← | **Lower, since the gate rotates upward rather than lifting** ← |
| **Cost and complexity** | **LOW — a plate, guides and a screw hoist** ← | **Higher — curved plate, arms, trunnions and their anchorages** ← |
| **Local fabrication and repair** | **Easy** ← | **Requires more skill and precision** ← |
| **Suited to** | **Small to medium spans and heads** ← | **Large spans and heads — barrage bays, spillways** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS THE RADIAL GATE'S ELEGANT PROPERTY AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING BECAUSE IT IS PURELY GEOMETRIC: the water pressure on a curved surface whose centre of curvature is the trunnion acts everywhere ALONG A RADIUS.**

> **A force along a radius passes through the centre, so it produces no moment about it.**

> **The entire water thrust is therefore carried by the trunnion and contributes nothing to the hoisting effort.**

> **So a radial gate of any size can be lifted with a modest hoist, and its hoisting force is nearly independent of the head — which is exactly what is wanted for a large barrage bay.**
