> **That is a genuinely clever piece of design and it follows entirely from the choice of a circular skin plate centred on the pivot.**

**WHY VERTICAL LIFT GATES NEVERTHELESS DOMINATE SMALL CANAL WORK:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The heads are SMALL, so the friction is manageable** ← | **A metre or two of head on a two-metre gate is a modest thrust** ← |
| **The gates are SMALL, so the hoist is small** ← | ← |
| **They can be made and repaired by any competent fabricator** ← | **Which matters where a specialist workshop is far away** ← |
| **Their guides and seals are simple and forgiving** ← | ← |
| **And a damaged plate can be replaced without disturbing anything else** ← | **Whereas a radial gate's trunnion anchorage is embedded in the structure** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL CONSIDERATION FOR A DISPERSED IRRIGATION SYSTEM AND IT IS THE SAME REASONING MET REPEATEDLY: a system has hundreds of gates scattered over a large area, most of them far from any workshop.**

> **A gate that a district fabricator can make, and that a canal inspector can free with a hammer and grease, will be kept working.**

> **A gate requiring precision components and a specialist to repair will, when it seizes, stay seized.**

> **So the simpler gate's slightly greater hoisting effort is a small price for its maintainability, and the choice reflects the system's dispersion rather than the hydraulics of any single structure.**

> **THE MAINTENANCE OF GATES DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT DETERMINES WHETHER ANY OF THE OPERATING ARRANGEMENTS DISCUSSED IN THIS SUBCHAPTER ACTUALLY HAPPEN: a rotational supply needs cross regulators that can be adjusted, a headworks needs undersluices that can be opened in flood, and a level crossing needs a gate that closes when the storm comes.**

> **Every one of those depends on a gate that has been greased, exercised and kept free.**

> **A gate that is operated twice a year and left for the other eleven months will seize, and it will be discovered to have seized at the moment it is needed.**

> **So exercising the gates during the canal closure — opening and closing every one, greasing the screws, freeing the guides — is among the highest-value maintenance activities in an irrigation system, and it is unglamorous, invisible and routinely deferred.**

examTip.trick: **Simple, cheap and locally repairable, at the cost of a greater hoisting force** — the thrust presses the gate against its guides and that friction must be lifted.
examTip.trap: **A RADIAL gate's thrust passes through the trunnion and exerts NO moment** — so its hoisting force is small and nearly independent of the head. Option (a) is inverted.
examTip.mnemonic: **A gate a district fabricator can repair stays working** — which for hundreds of scattered gates outweighs the hydraulics. And EXERCISE every gate during the closure.

questions.stem: A canal must cross a road or a railway. Where the canal passes BENEATH the road in a covered conduit running full, the structure is analogous to:
options: An aqueduct, with the canal carried over
A super passage
A canal syphon
A level crossing
questions.solution:
**A CANAL SYPHON — the canal being depressed beneath the obstruction and running under pressure** — with the same difficulties of silting and inaccessibility.

**Why the analogy holds and why it matters:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The canal is taken BELOW the obstruction and rises again beyond it** ← | ← |
| **In that reach it flows FULL, under pressure, with no free surface** ← | ← |
| **So it has no ventilation, no self-cleansing shallow fast flow, and no access** ← | ← |
| **Its velocity must be kept HIGH enough to be self-cleansing** ← | **Or the depressed section fills with the canal's silt** ← |
| **And it cannot be rodded or cleaned in the ordinary way** ← | ← |
| **All of which are exactly the inverted siphon's problems** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE GOVERNING DESIGN REQUIREMENT AND IT IS THE SAME ONE MET IN A SEWER SIPHON AND A CANAL SYPHON PROPER: the depressed section must run fast enough to carry its sediment through.**

> **A canal carries silt continuously, and a low point in its profile is a settling basin unless the velocity prevents it.**

> **So the barrel is sized for a velocity above the canal's own — typically 2 to 3 m/s — which means it is SMALLER in section than the canal, and the flow accelerates into it and decelerates out.**

> **That acceleration and deceleration cost head, which must be available in the canal's profile — so a syphon consumes head, and on a canal short of head that consumption may be unaffordable.**

**THE ALTERNATIVES FOR A ROAD CROSSING, WHICH ARE USUALLY PREFERABLE:**

| Alternative | Note |
|---|---|
| **Carry the ROAD OVER the canal on a BRIDGE** ← | **Much the commonest and simplest solution — the canal is undisturbed and the bridge is an ordinary structure** ← |
| **Carry the road over on a CULVERT, for a small canal** ← | **With the canal passing through a box or a pipe of adequate size, ideally with a free surface** ← |
| **A canal syphon beneath the road** ← | **Used where the road cannot be raised — an existing highway, or one whose level is fixed** ← |
| **And where the canal is small and the crossing short** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DEFAULT AND IT IS WORTH SAYING WHY: raising the road a metre or two over a canal is an ordinary piece of road construction, and it leaves the canal's hydraulics entirely undisturbed.**

> **Depressing the canal beneath the road, by contrast, introduces a permanent silting liability, consumes head, and creates a length of conduit that cannot be inspected.**

> **So the general rule is to move the ROAD rather than the CANAL, and a syphon is adopted only where the road's level cannot be changed.**

> **That rule generalises usefully: where two systems must cross, disturb the one whose behaviour is less sensitive — and a road tolerates a change of level far better than a canal tolerates a change of hydraulic regime.**

**A NOTE ON THE SMALL CROSSINGS THAT MAKE UP MOST OF THE NUMBER, SINCE THEY ARE OFTEN NEGLECTED IN DESIGN:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A canal system has a great many minor crossings — village paths, cattle tracks, field access** ← | ← |
| **If none is provided, people will make their own** ← | **By damming the canal with earth and stones to cross it, or by driving cattle through it** ← |
| **Which breaks the banks, damages any lining, and obstructs the flow** ← | ← |
| **So CATTLE CROSSINGS and footbridges at reasonable intervals are not amenities but protective works** ← | ← |
| **And they should be sited where people already cross, not where the drawing finds convenient** ← | ← |

> **The last two rows state a principle that applies well beyond canals and is worth carrying: if a facility people need is not provided, they will improvise one, and the improvisation will damage the works.**

> **Providing the crossing costs a fraction of repairing the damage, and providing it where people actually cross — which requires walking the alignment and asking — is what makes it used rather than bypassed.**
tags: move the road not the canal

examTip.trick: **The canal is depressed and runs under pressure — a canal syphon** — with all the inverted siphon's silting and access problems.
examTip.trap: **Move the ROAD, not the canal, wherever possible** — a road tolerates a change of level far better than a canal tolerates a change of hydraulic regime.
examTip.mnemonic: **Provide cattle crossings where people already cross** — if you do not, they will dam the canal with earth to get across, and repairing that costs far more.

questions.stem: In designing the impervious floor of a canal regulator, the LENGTH of the floor downstream of the crest is governed principally by:
options: The width of the roadway carried over the structure
The requirement to contain the hydraulic jump and the turbulence that follows it
The depth of the upstream cut-off
The number of gate bays provided
questions.solution:
**The requirement to contain the HYDRAULIC JUMP and the turbulence that follows it, together with the creep length needed for seepage** — the jump requirement usually governing.

**The two requirements the downstream floor must satisfy:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Contain the HYDRAULIC JUMP and the turbulent flow beyond it** ← | **So that the fast, turbulent water is over concrete and not over the erodible bed** ← |
| **Provide part of the CREEP LENGTH for seepage** ← | **Contributing to the uplift and exit gradient control** ← |
| **Of the two, the jump requirement is usually the LONGER** ← | ← |

> **THE JUMP'S LENGTH IS THE QUANTITY THAT DECIDES THE FLOOR AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING HOW IT IS ESTIMATED: the length of a hydraulic jump is commonly taken as 5 to 6 times its SEQUENT (post-jump) depth.**

> **So a jump rising to a downstream depth of 1.5 m occupies 7.5 to 9 m of floor.**

> **And the floor must extend beyond the jump's end, because the flow leaving a jump is still turbulent and still erosive for some distance — commonly a further length equal to the sequent depth or more.**

> **So the downstream floor is typically 6 to 8 times the sequent depth, and that figure comes from the hydraulics rather than from any seepage consideration.**

**WHY THE JUMP'S POSITION MUST ALSO BE FIXED, WHICH IS THE HARDER PART:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The jump forms where the tailwater depth matches the sequent depth of the incoming supercritical flow** ← | ← |
| **Both of those vary with the DISCHARGE** ← | ← |
| **And the regulator operates over a wide range of discharges and gate openings** ← | **Unlike a weir, which passes what the river brings** ← |
| **So the jump's position moves as the gates are operated** ← | ← |
| **The floor must contain it at EVERY operating condition** ← | **Including partial gate openings, which produce the most severe conditions** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE CONDITION THAT CATCHES DESIGNERS OUT AND IT IS PARTICULAR TO GATED STRUCTURES: a partly opened gate produces a high-velocity jet under a small opening, and that is a more severe condition than the fully open gate passing the same discharge.**

> **So the design must consider the range of gate openings, not merely the full discharge with the gates raised.**

> **And an unsymmetrical operation — some bays open and others closed, which happens constantly — produces a concentrated jet and lateral currents that the symmetric analysis does not reveal.**

> **That is why an operating rule for a gated structure usually requires the gates to be opened SYMMETRICALLY and in a defined sequence, and why departing from that rule can damage a floor that is perfectly adequate for the flows it is passing.**

**AND THE DEPRESSED FLOOR OR CISTERN, WHICH IS THE USUAL SOLUTION TO THE VARYING JUMP:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **Depress the downstream floor below the canal's bed** ← | **Manufacturing extra tailwater depth so the jump forms on the floor at low discharges too** ← |
| **Use a SLOPING GLACIS rather than a vertical drop** ← | **So the jump can form at different points along the slope as the discharge varies** ← |
| **Provide FRICTION BLOCKS and an END SILL** ← | **Holding the jump in place over a range of conditions** ← |
| **And a flexible protection beyond the rigid floor** ← | **For whatever escapes** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST EFFECTIVE PROVISION AND IT IS THE REASON THE GLACIS FORM IS SO WIDELY USED: a sloping approach gives the jump a range of positions to choose from.**

> **At a low discharge the jump forms high on the glacis where the depths suit it; at a high discharge it moves down toward the toe.**

> **A vertical drop offers only one position, so it can be right at one discharge and wrong at all others.**

> **So the glacis accommodates the variation inherently, which for a gated regulator operating across a wide range is precisely what is needed — and it is why the glacis type displaced the vertical drop for all but the smallest structures.**

verification.notes: Jump length commonly 5-6 times the sequent depth; floor typically 6-8 times.

examTip.trick: **Contain the jump and the turbulence beyond it** — about 5-6 sequent depths for the jump and 6-8 for the floor. The seepage creep is usually the lesser requirement.
examTip.trap: **A PARTLY OPENED gate is more severe than a fully open one passing the same discharge** — a high-velocity jet under a small opening. Check the range of openings.
examTip.mnemonic: **A GLACIS lets the jump choose its position as the discharge varies; a vertical drop offers only one.** Hence the glacis form for anything but the smallest structures.

questions.stem: A canal regulator's structure is founded on permeable alluvium and is subject to seepage. The provision that most effectively reduces the UPLIFT beneath its downstream floor, without lengthening the structure, is:
options: Increasing the floor's thickness
Widening the structure
Adding an intermediate sheet pile beneath the middle of the floor
Pressure relief holes through the floor, with an inverted filter beneath them
questions.solution:
**PRESSURE RELIEF HOLES through the floor, with an inverted filter beneath them** — which let the seepage OUT rather than resisting it, so no pressure can accumulate.

**Why relief is more effective than resistance:**

| Approach | Note |
|---|---|
| **RESISTING the uplift by thickening the floor** ← | **Requires t = h/(G − 1), so a 3 m head needs 2.4 m of concrete — enormously expensive over a large area** ← (option a) |
| **RELIEVING the uplift by letting the water out** ← | **A hole and a filter cost almost nothing, and the pressure simply does not develop** ← |
| **An INTERMEDIATE sheet pile** ← | **Contributes little, as Khosla showed** ← (option c) |
| **So relief is by far the most economical measure where it can be used** ← | ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE IS THE SAME ONE MET IN A CANAL LINING'S WEEP HOLES, A RETAINING WALL'S DRAINAGE, A DAM'S DRAINAGE GALLERY AND AN INVERTED FILTER, AND IT IS WORTH STATING AS A GENERAL RULE: where water pressure threatens a structure, giving the water a path is nearly always cheaper than resisting it.**

> **The instinct is to make the structure stronger or heavier; the better answer is usually to remove the reason for the load.**

> **A relief hole converts a pressure problem into a small flow, and a small flow through a filter is harmless.**

> **The cost is a permanent seepage — water is being let through rather than held back — but at a canal regulator the water lost is trivial and the structure saved is substantial.**

**THE CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH RELIEF IS APPROPRIATE, WHICH LIMIT ITS USE:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The seepage lost must be ACCEPTABLE** ← | **Which it is at a canal structure, and is not at a dam whose reservoir must be retained** ← |
| **A proper FILTER must be provided, or the relief holes pipe the foundation out** ← | **Turning a pressure relief into an erosion path — which would be worse than the pressure** ← |
| **The holes must not become BLOCKED** ← | **By sediment from above, or by the filter clogging from below — and a blocked relief hole restores the full uplift while appearing to be provided for** ← |
| **And they must be placed where the pressure actually is** ← | **Toward the DOWNSTREAM end of the floor, where the residual head is greatest and the floor is thinnest** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PROVISION'S WEAKNESS AND IT IS A REAL ONE: a relief hole is a small opening in a floor beneath turbulent water carrying sediment.**

> **It will tend to block, and its blockage is invisible.**

> **A floor designed on the assumption of relief, whose holes have blocked, has the uplift of an unrelieved floor and the thickness of a relieved one — which is the combination that lifts floors.**

> **So relief holes should be designed to be inspectable and clearable where that is possible, and the floor should retain some margin against the unrelieved case rather than relying entirely on the relief.**

> **That is a general principle for any provision whose failure is silent: do not let the structure's safety depend wholly on something whose functioning cannot be observed.**

> **THE ALTERNATIVE MEASURES DESERVE A CLOSING SUMMARY, SINCE THE QUESTION ASKED FOR THE MOST EFFECTIVE WITHOUT LENGTHENING:**

| Measure | Effect on uplift |
|---|---|
| **UPSTREAM cut-off, deepened** ← | **Reduces the pressure everywhere downstream of it — very effective** ← |
| **Relief holes with a filter** ← | **Eliminates the pressure locally — most effective and cheapest** ← |
| **A longer floor** ← | **Reduces the pressure, but the question excluded lengthening, and Khosla showed the middle of a long floor achieves little** ← |
| **Thickening** ← | **Does not reduce the uplift at all; it merely resists it** ← |
| **An intermediate pile** ← | **Little effect** ← |

> **The fourth row states a distinction worth being precise about: thickening the floor does not REDUCE the uplift, it resists it.**

> **The pressure beneath is unchanged; the floor is simply heavy enough to stay put.**

> **Every other measure in the list actually lowers the pressure, which is a different and better kind of solution — and confusing 'resisting a load' with 'removing a load' is a distinction worth keeping sharp in any design.**

examTip.trick: **Let the water OUT rather than resisting it** — a hole and a filter cost almost nothing, while resisting a 3 m head needs 2.4 m of concrete.
examTip.trap: **Thickening does not REDUCE the uplift, it resists it** — the pressure beneath is unchanged. Relief, cut-offs and floor length actually lower it.
examTip.mnemonic: **A blocked relief hole is a silent failure** — full uplift with a floor thinned on the assumption of relief. Keep a margin against the unrelieved case.

questions.stem: In a canal system, the term MODULE applied to an outlet means a device that:
options: Can be moved from one location to another
Is built from standard precast components
Serves exactly one hectare of command
Delivers a discharge that is independent of one or both of the water levels
questions.solution:
**A device that delivers a discharge that is INDEPENDENT of one or both of the water levels** — a semi-module being independent of the downstream level, and a rigid module of both.

**The classification restated, since the terminology is the whole point:**

| Type | Discharge depends on |
|---|---|
| **NON-MODULAR** ← | **BOTH the upstream and downstream levels** ← |
| **SEMI-MODULE (flexible module)** ← | **The UPSTREAM level only** ← |
| **RIGID MODULE** ← | **NEITHER — constant discharge within a working range** ← |

> **THE WORD 'MODULE' REFERS TO THE DEVICE'S ABILITY TO MODULATE ITS DISCHARGE AGAINST CHANGING CONDITIONS, AND ONCE THAT IS SEEN THE THREE TERMS ARE SELF-EXPLANATORY: no modulation, partial modulation, full modulation.**

> **The alternative reading — that a module is a standardised component — is the ordinary English meaning and is not what is meant here, which is why the term causes confusion.**

**THE DESIGN QUALITIES BY WHICH OUTLETS ARE JUDGED, WHICH ARE WORTH KNOWING AS A SET:**

| Quality | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **FLEXIBILITY** ← | **The ratio of the rate of change of the outlet's discharge to that of the parent channel — F = (dq/q)/(dQ/Q)** ← |
| **PROPORTIONALITY** ← | **Flexibility EQUAL TO 1 — the outlet's share changes in exact proportion to the canal's discharge, so every outlet keeps its share whatever the supply** ← |
| **HYPER-PROPORTIONAL** ← | **F greater than 1 — the outlet takes MORE than its share when the canal runs high and less when it runs low** ← |
| **SUB-PROPORTIONAL** ← | **F less than 1 — the outlet takes less than its share when the canal is high** ← |
| **SENSITIVITY** ← | **The rate of change of the outlet's discharge with the parent channel's water LEVEL** ← |
| **SETTING** ← | **The ratio of the outlet's sill level above the canal's bed to the canal's depth — which is what determines the flexibility** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE PROPERTY MOST DESIRED IN AN IRRIGATION SYSTEM AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING WHY: a PROPORTIONAL outlet takes the same FRACTION of the canal's discharge whatever that discharge is.**

> **So when the canal runs at half supply, every outlet gets half its designed share — and the shortage is distributed equally over the whole command without anyone having to do anything.**

> **That is exactly the equitable outcome that a canal operator would want to achieve manually, obtained automatically by the outlets' geometry.**

> **A hyper-proportional outlet, by contrast, takes more than its share in good times and less in bad — which favours whoever has one and disadvantages everyone else, and does so most in a shortage when it matters most.**

**AND THE SETTING IS WHAT DETERMINES WHICH BEHAVIOUR AN OUTLET HAS, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL LEVER:**

| Setting | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **A LOW sill, near the canal's bed** ← | **The outlet's head varies little as the canal's level falls, so it keeps taking nearly its full discharge — HYPER-proportional** ← |
| **A HIGH sill** ← | **The outlet's head falls sharply as the canal's level falls, so its discharge falls faster than the canal's — SUB-proportional** ← |
| **An intermediate setting** ← | **PROPORTIONAL** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW EXPLAINS WHY OUTLETS SET TOO LOW ARE SUCH A PROBLEM IN PRACTICE AND IT IS A COMMON DEFECT: a low sill also admits more SILT, as noted earlier, and it makes the outlet hyper-proportional.**

> **So an outlet lowered — whether by design, by the bed rising around it, or by a cultivator deepening its approach — takes more than its share and more than its share of silt, both at the expense of everyone downstream.**

> **The setting is therefore worth checking during any survey of a system that is distributing water inequitably, and it is frequently found to be the explanation.**

> **Restoring the sill to its designed level is a cheap intervention with an immediate effect on the distribution, and it does not require a new structure — merely a measurement, a rebuilt sill, and someone with the authority to insist on it.**

examTip.trick: **'Module' means the ability to MODULATE against changing levels** — semi-module independent of the downstream level, rigid module of both.
examTip.trap: **Flexibility F = (dq/q)/(dQ/Q), and F = 1 is PROPORTIONAL** — every outlet keeps its share automatically, which distributes a shortage equitably with no operator.
examTip.mnemonic: **A LOW sill makes an outlet hyper-proportional AND draws more silt** — so a lowered sill takes more than its share of both, at everyone else's expense.

questions.stem: Land is said to be WATERLOGGED, for agricultural purposes, when:
options: The water table rises so close to the ground surface that the root zone becomes saturated and the air in the soil is displaced
Water stands on the surface to a depth of more than 300 mm
The soil's moisture content exceeds its field capacity for more than a day
The land floods during the monsoon
questions.solution:
**When the WATER TABLE rises so close to the ground surface that the ROOT ZONE becomes saturated and the air in the soil is displaced** — so the roots cannot respire and the crop suffers, regardless of whether water stands on the surface.

**Why the definition is about the ROOT ZONE and not about standing water:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Plant roots need OXYGEN as much as they need water** ← | **They respire, and respiration requires air in the soil's pores** ← |
| **A saturated soil has NO air** ← | **Every pore is full of water** ← |
| **So the roots suffocate, even though there is no shortage of water** ← | **The plant may wilt while standing in saturated soil, which appears paradoxical** ← |
| **This happens when the water table is within the root zone, whether or not water is visible at the surface** ← | ← |
| **So waterlogging is diagnosed by the WATER TABLE's depth, not by appearances** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESCRIBES AN OBSERVATION THAT PUZZLES PEOPLE AND IS WORTH EXPLAINING: a crop in waterlogged ground can show the symptoms of drought.**

> **Its roots, deprived of oxygen, cannot function; they cannot take up water however much surrounds them; so the plant wilts.**

> **A farmer seeing a wilting crop and irrigating it makes the situation worse, and the mistake is entirely understandable.**

> **So the diagnosis requires an observation the eye cannot make — the depth to the water table — which is why OBSERVATION WELLS are the basic instrument of drainage work and why their absence leaves the problem undiagnosed.**

**THE CRITICAL DEPTH TO THE WATER TABLE, WHICH IS WHAT DRAINAGE AIMS TO ACHIEVE:**

| Crop | Water table depth required |
|---|---|
| **Shallow-rooted crops and vegetables** | **About 0.8 to 1.0 m** ← |
| **Most field crops — wheat, maize, cotton** ← | **1.0 to 1.5 m** ← |
| **Deep-rooted crops, orchards, sugarcane** ← | **1.5 to 2.0 m and more** ← |
| **PADDY** ← | **A special case — it is grown deliberately in saturated soil and tolerates it** ← |
| **Where SALINITY is a risk** ← | **DEEPER still, since capillary rise from a shallow table brings salt to the surface** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE CONSIDERATION THAT USUALLY GOVERNS AND IT LINKS THE TWO PROBLEMS TOGETHER: waterlogging and SALINITY are usually the same problem seen at two stages.**

> **A rising water table waterlogs the root zone.**

> **Where the climate is arid and the evaporation high, water rises from that shallow table by CAPILLARY action to the surface and evaporates — leaving its dissolved salts behind.**

> **So the surface accumulates salt, year on year, and the land becomes saline as well as waterlogged.**

> **The critical depth for salinity is therefore the depth below which capillary rise cannot reach the surface effectively — commonly taken as 1.5 to 2 m in a fine-textured soil — and it is deeper than the depth the crop's roots alone would require.**

**THE CAUSES OF WATERLOGGING, WHICH THE REMEDY MUST ADDRESS:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **SEEPAGE from unlined canals** ← | **A major contributor in any irrigated command** ← |
| **OVER-IRRIGATION — applying more than the crop can use** ← | **The excess percolating to the water table** ← |
| **Inadequate natural DRAINAGE** ← | **A flat command with no outfall** ← |
| **Obstruction of the natural drainage by ROADS, RAILWAYS, canals and spoil banks** ← | **Every embankment across a drainage line ponds water behind it** ← |
| **Heavy rainfall on land with a high water table** ← | ← |
| **And an impermeable layer beneath the root zone, perching the water** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CAUSE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT IS ONE THAT ENGINEERS THEMSELVES CREATE: an irrigated command is criss-crossed with linear embankments — canal banks, roads, railways, spoil banks — and every one of them is a dam across the natural drainage unless openings are provided.**

> **The openings are cheap at construction and impossible to add economically afterwards, and they are the first thing omitted when a contractor is economising.**

> **So a command can be waterlogged not by too much water but by water that cannot get out, and the culprit is a set of embankments each of which was built for a good reason by a different agency.**

> **Which returns to the integrated watershed argument: the drainage of a command is nobody's particular responsibility, and it is affected by everybody's works.**

examTip.trick: **The water table within the ROOT ZONE, displacing the soil air** — regardless of whether water stands on the surface. Roots need oxygen as well as water.
examTip.trap: **A waterlogged crop shows DROUGHT symptoms** — its roots cannot function, so it wilts in saturated soil. Irrigating it makes matters worse.
examTip.mnemonic: **Salinity needs a DEEPER table than the roots do** — 1.5-2 m, below the reach of capillary rise. Waterlogging and salinity are one problem at two stages.

questions.stem: SALINE and ALKALI (sodic) soils are distinguished in that a saline soil:
options: Has a high pH, above 8.5, and a poor physical structure
Has an excess of soluble salts
Cannot be reclaimed by any means
Is caused only by seawater intrusion
questions.solution:
**It has an EXCESS of soluble salts, a pH usually below 8.5, and a flocculated structure that remains PERMEABLE** — so it can be reclaimed by LEACHING alone, whereas an alkali soil's excess SODIUM has dispersed the clay, destroying its permeability, and it requires a chemical amendment such as GYPSUM before leaching can work.

**The two soil problems compared:**

| Property | SALINE soil | ALKALI (sodic) soil |
|---|---|---|
| **Principal problem** | **Excess SOLUBLE SALTS** ← | **Excess exchangeable SODIUM** ← |
| **Electrical conductivity** | **HIGH, above 4 dS/m** ← | **May be low** ← |
| **Exchangeable sodium percentage (ESP)** | **Below 15** ← | **ABOVE 15** ← |
| **pH** | **Usually BELOW 8.5** ← | **ABOVE 8.5, and often above 9** ← (option a) |
| **Soil STRUCTURE** ← | **FLOCCULATED and permeable — the salts hold the clay particles together** ← | **DISPERSED — the sodium forces the clay particles apart, and the soil becomes impermeable and structureless** ← |
| **Appearance** | **A WHITE crust of salt — 'white alkali'** ← | **A dark, greasy surface from dispersed organic matter — 'black alkali'** ← |
| **Reclamation** | **LEACHING with good water, plus drainage to carry the salt away** ← | **GYPSUM (calcium sulphate) first, to replace the sodium with calcium, THEN leaching** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE HEART OF THE DISTINCTION AND IT IS THE PROPERTY THAT DETERMINES THE REMEDY: a saline soil is PERMEABLE and an alkali soil is not.**

> **That is counter-intuitive — one would expect the soil with more salt to be the more damaged — and the chemistry explains it.**

> **Dissolved salts of any kind keep clay particles FLOCCULATED, clustered into aggregates with pores between them, so the soil drains.**

> **SODIUM in particular, when it occupies the clay's exchange sites, causes the particles to repel one another and DISPERSE, filling the pores and sealing the soil.**

> **So a saline soil can be washed clean, because water passes through it; and an alkali soil cannot, because water will not pass through it at all.**

> **The remedy for the alkali soil must therefore FIRST restore the permeability, and only then remove the sodium — which is exactly what gypsum does.**

**HOW GYPSUM WORKS, WHICH IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Gypsum is calcium sulphate, and it supplies CALCIUM ions** ← | ← |
| **Calcium displaces SODIUM from the clay's exchange sites** ← | **Calcium being more strongly held than sodium** ← |
| **The displaced sodium goes into solution as sodium sulphate** ← | ← |
| **The clay, now calcium-saturated, FLOCCULATES and the soil becomes permeable again** ← | ← |
| **Leaching then washes the sodium sulphate away** ← | ← |
| **And DRAINAGE carries it out of the area** ← | **Without which the salt merely moves down and returns** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE REQUIREMENT WITHOUT WHICH NOTHING ELSE WORKS AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS: leaching moves salt DOWNWARD, and unless the drainage removes it from the area it will return.**

> **Water applied to leach a saline soil carries the salt to the water table.**

> **If the water table is shallow and has no outlet, the salt accumulates there, the table rises further, and capillary action brings the salt back to the surface in the next dry season.**

> **So leaching without drainage is a temporary redistribution that makes the situation worse — it adds water to a command that is already waterlogged and returns the salt within months.**

> **DRAINAGE IS THEREFORE THE PRECONDITION FOR EVERY RECLAMATION MEASURE, and this is the point at which the salinity problem and the drainage problem become the same problem: you cannot fix the salt without removing the water, and you cannot remove the water without an outfall.**

> **Which is why the phrase used by drainage engineers — 'the salt must have somewhere to go' — is the whole of the subject in six words, and why a reclamation scheme with no outfall is not a scheme at all.**

examTip.trick: **Saline: soluble salts, pH under 8.5, PERMEABLE — leach it. Alkali: sodium, pH over 8.5, DISPERSED and impermeable — gypsum first, then leach.**
examTip.trap: **Salts FLOCCULATE clay and keep the soil permeable; SODIUM disperses it and seals it.** So the soil with more salt is the easier to fix.
examTip.mnemonic: **The salt must have somewhere to GO** — leaching without drainage moves it to the water table, which then rises and brings it back. Drainage is the precondition for everything.

questions.stem: In the design of a SUBSURFACE (tile) drainage system, the SPACING of the laterals is determined principally by:
options: The width of the fields and the convenience of cultivation
The diameter of the pipes available
The soil's hydraulic conductivity
The crop to be grown, alone
questions.solution:
**The SOIL's hydraulic conductivity, the DEPTH to the impermeable layer, the depth of the drains, and the rate at which the water table must be lowered** — related by a formula such as Hooghoudt's.

**The variables and how each affects the spacing:**

| Variable | Effect on spacing |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic CONDUCTIVITY k of the soil** ← | **A MORE permeable soil drains more readily, so the drains can be FURTHER apart** ← |
| **DEPTH to the impermeable layer** ← | **A deeper permeable layer gives more flow area beneath the drains, so they can be further apart** ← |
| **DEPTH of the drains** ← | **Deeper drains lower the water table over a wider zone, so they can be further apart** ← |
| **The DRAINAGE COEFFICIENT — the rate of water to be removed** ← | **A greater rate needs CLOSER spacing** ← |
| **The permitted water table height MIDWAY between the drains** ← | **A lower permitted level needs closer spacing** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT DESIGN LEVER AND IT IS WORTH QUANTIFYING BECAUSE THE ECONOMICS TURN ON IT: deepening the drains allows them to be spaced further apart, and spacing is what determines the cost.**

> **A drainage system's cost is dominated by the LENGTH of pipe per hectare, which is inversely proportional to the spacing.**

> **Halving the spacing doubles the pipe length and roughly doubles the cost.**

> **So a modest increase in depth, which costs a little more per metre of trench, can permit a substantially wider spacing and reduce the total cost considerably.**

> **The limit is the practicable depth of trenching — beyond 1.5 to 2 m the excavation becomes expensive and the trench needs support — and the depth to the impermeable layer, below which there is no advantage.**

> **So the design is an optimisation between depth and spacing, and the two must be considered together rather than the depth being fixed first by convention.**

**THE HOOGHOUDT RELATION AND WHAT IT EMBODIES:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **The flow to a drain is partly HORIZONTAL, through the soil above the impermeable layer** ← | ← |
| **And partly RADIAL, converging on the pipe itself** ← | ← |
| **The radial convergence causes an extra head loss near the drain** ← | **Which Hooghoudt handled by an EQUIVALENT DEPTH, replacing the real depth to the impermeable layer with a smaller effective one** ← |
| **The equivalent depth device makes the problem solvable as a simple horizontal flow** ← | ← |
| **The relation then gives the spacing in terms of k, the equivalent depth, the drainage coefficient and the permitted water table height** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW'S DEVICE IS THE SAME KIND OF ENGINEERING SIMPLIFICATION MET IN KHOSLA'S METHOD AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING: an exactly solvable idealisation is corrected toward the real geometry by an equivalent parameter.**

> **The real flow field converging on a small pipe is complex; a purely horizontal flow to a fully penetrating drain is simple.**

> **So the complex geometry is represented by a reduced 'equivalent depth' in the simple solution, chosen so the answer comes out right.**

> **That is a very common technique and being able to recognise it makes such formulae intelligible rather than arbitrary.**

**AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT THE WHOLE DESIGN DEPENDS ON DESERVES A CLOSING WARNING: the hydraulic conductivity k.**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The spacing depends DIRECTLY on k, so an error in k is an error in the spacing** ← | ← |
| **k varies enormously — over orders of magnitude — between soils and within one field** ← | ← |
| **It must be measured IN THE FIELD, below the water table, by an auger-hole or piezometer test** ← | **A laboratory test on a disturbed sample measures something else entirely** ← |
| **And enough tests must be done to characterise the variation, not merely to obtain a number** ← | ← |
| **A system designed on a single k value from one hole is designed on a guess** ← | ← |

> **The third row is the point that distinguishes a competent investigation from a nominal one: hydraulic conductivity is a field property of the soil in place, including its structure, its cracks, its root channels and its layering.**

> **A sample taken to a laboratory has lost all of those, and the value it yields may be an order of magnitude below the field value.**

> **So the auger-hole test — which measures the rate at which water flows into a hole bored below the water table — is the appropriate method, it is simple and cheap, and its omission is the commonest reason a drainage system fails to perform as designed.**

examTip.trick: **Conductivity, depth to the impermeable layer, drain depth and the drainage coefficient** — related by Hooghoudt's equation.
examTip.trap: **DEEPER drains can be spaced WIDER**, and cost goes with pipe length per hectare — so depth and spacing must be optimised together, not the depth fixed by convention.
examTip.mnemonic: **Measure k in the FIELD by an auger-hole test, below the water table** — a laboratory test on a disturbed sample measures something else and reads an order of magnitude low.

questions.stem: A SURFACE drainage system for agricultural land differs from a SUBSURFACE system in that surface drainage:
options: Removes water that has already entered the soil profile
Is used only in humid climates
Requires no outfall
Removes excess water standing on or moving over the land surface
questions.solution:
**It removes EXCESS WATER STANDING ON or moving over the LAND SURFACE — by land shaping, field ditches and collector drains** — and therefore addresses PONDING and inundation rather than a high water table.

**The two systems compared:**

| Aspect | SURFACE drainage | SUBSURFACE drainage |
|---|---|---|
| **What it removes** | **Water standing ON the land** ← | **Water WITHIN the soil profile — it lowers the WATER TABLE** ← (option a) |
| **Components** | **Land grading and smoothing, field ditches, collector and main drains, outfall** ← | **Buried perforated laterals, collectors, a main and an outfall** ← |
| **Addresses** | **Ponding after rain, inundation, and runoff from adjoining land** ← | **A high water table, waterlogging of the root zone, and salinity** ← |
| **Cost** | **LOWER** ← | **Much higher** ← |
| **Interference with cultivation** | **The ditches occupy land and obstruct machinery** ← | **NONE — the pipes are buried below plough depth** ← |
| **Suited to** | **Flat land with heavy rainfall; soils of LOW permeability where subsurface drainage would need impracticably close spacing** ← | **Permeable soils with a high water table, and where salinity must be controlled** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CONTAINS THE TECHNICAL CRITERION THAT DECIDES BETWEEN THEM AND IT FOLLOWS FROM THE SPACING RELATION: in a soil of low permeability, subsurface drains must be placed impracticably close together to be effective.**

> **A heavy clay may require a spacing of 5 or 10 m, at which the pipe length per hectare — and therefore the cost — is prohibitive.**

> **So in such a soil the water cannot economically be removed from within the profile, and the practical objective becomes preventing it from entering: shaping the land so that rain runs OFF rather than standing, and providing ditches to take it away.**

> **That is surface drainage, and in a heavy soil it is not an inferior substitute for subsurface drainage but the appropriate technique.**

**THE COMPONENTS OF SURFACE DRAINAGE, IN ORDER OF IMPORTANCE:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **LAND SHAPING and SMOOTHING** ← | **Giving the field a slight continuous grade so water runs off rather than ponding in hollows — much the most important, and the most neglected** ← |
| **FIELD ditches (shallow, at the field's edge or within it)** ← | **Collecting the runoff** ← |
| **COLLECTOR drains** ← | ← |
| **MAIN drain and OUTFALL** ← | ← |
| **And CROSS-DRAINAGE where the drains meet roads, canals and embankments** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS WHERE MOST OF THE BENEFIT LIES AND IT IS WORTH ARGUING FOR: a field with hollows will pond in them however good the ditches at its edge, because the water in the hollow has no route to the ditch.**

> **Smoothing out the hollows so the whole field drains to its edge is a one-time earthwork operation, it improves the irrigation's uniformity at the same time, and it costs far less than any pipework.**

> **It is also the operation most often omitted, because it produces no visible structure and is easily deferred.**

> **A drainage scheme that installs ditches without land shaping treats the symptom and leaves the cause, and the hollows continue to pond.**

**AND THE OUTFALL, WHICH OPTION (c) DENIES AND WHICH IS THE PRECONDITION FOR BOTH SYSTEMS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Every drainage system must DISCHARGE somewhere** ← | ← |
| **The outfall must be LOWER than the drains, and available when they are flowing** ← | ← |
| **A river in flood is higher than the drains, so the outfall is blocked at exactly the time it is needed** ← | **Requiring a flap valve and, if the flooding is prolonged, PUMPING** ← |
| **In a flat command far from any river, there may be NO gravity outfall at all** ← | ← |
| **Then the whole scheme depends on pumped drainage, with its permanent cost** ← | ← |
| **And where neither exists, the land cannot be drained by any means** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE HARD CONSTRAINT AND IT SHOULD BE ESTABLISHED FIRST IN ANY DRAINAGE INVESTIGATION: before designing anything, find out where the water is to go.**

> **A great deal of drainage design has been done for commands with no viable outfall, and the resulting systems collect water and deliver it to a point from which it cannot leave.**

> **The outfall's availability, its level, and its condition when the drains are running are therefore the first questions, and if they cannot be answered satisfactorily the answer to the drainage problem may be a change of land use rather than a drainage scheme.**

examTip.trick: **Surface drainage removes water ON the land; subsurface lowers the WATER TABLE within it.** Different problems, different techniques.
examTip.trap: **In a heavy clay, subsurface drains would need 5-10 m spacing — prohibitive** — so surface drainage is the appropriate technique there, not an inferior substitute.
examTip.mnemonic: **LAND SHAPING gives most of the benefit and is most often omitted** — ditches cannot drain a hollow. And establish the OUTFALL before designing anything.

questions.stem: The LEACHING REQUIREMENT of an irrigated area is the:
options: Depth of water that must be applied to bring the soil to field capacity
Extra depth of irrigation water
Depth of water lost to deep percolation in a season
Quantity of gypsum needed to reclaim a sodic soil
questions.solution:
**The EXTRA depth of irrigation water, over and above the crop's needs, that must be applied and allowed to PERCOLATE THROUGH the root zone in order to carry away the salts brought in by the irrigation water itself** — so that the salt does not accumulate.

**Why a leaching requirement exists at all:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **ALL irrigation water contains dissolved salts** ← | **Even good quality water — perhaps 200 to 500 mg/l** ← |
| **The crop transpires the WATER and leaves the SALT behind** ← | **Transpiration is a distillation** ← |
| **So salt accumulates in the root zone, year after year** ← | ← |
| **Applying 1,000 mm of water at 300 mg/l delivers 3 tonnes of salt per hectare per year** ← | **Which is a substantial quantity and it does not go away** ← |
| **Unless EXTRA water is applied to wash it below the root zone** ← | ← |
| **That extra water is the LEACHING REQUIREMENT** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW MAKES THE PROBLEM CONCRETE AND IT IS WORTH COMPUTING ONCE, BECAUSE THE QUANTITY SURPRISES PEOPLE: three tonnes of salt per hectare per year, arriving with perfectly ordinary irrigation water.**

> **Over twenty years that is sixty tonnes per hectare, and the root zone's soil weighs perhaps 3,000 tonnes per hectare — so the salt content of the root zone would rise by two per cent, which is far beyond what any crop tolerates.**

> **This is why irrigated agriculture in arid regions has repeatedly destroyed the land it was practised on, over centuries, and why salinisation is described as the oldest environmental problem in civilisation.**

> **The mechanism is not mysterious and the remedy is not complicated — it is simply that the salt must be flushed out, and the flushing water must be able to leave.**

**THE LEACHING REQUIREMENT'S MAGNITUDE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **LR = EC_iw / (5 × EC_e − EC_iw), approximately** ← | **EC_iw being the irrigation water's conductivity and EC_e the maximum the crop tolerates** ← |
| **For good water and a tolerant crop, LR may be 5 to 10 per cent** ← | **A modest addition** ← |
| **For saline water or a sensitive crop, it can exceed 30 per cent** ← | **Which is a large addition, and it may make the irrigation uneconomic** ← |
| **And in a humid climate, the monsoon rainfall may provide the leaching free** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE REASON SALINITY IS A SMALLER PROBLEM IN NEPAL THAN IN THE ARID IRRIGATED REGIONS AND IT IS WORTH STATING: a monsoon delivering 1,500 mm of rain leaches the profile thoroughly every year, without anyone having to intend it.**

> **So the salt brought in by the dry-season irrigation is flushed out by the wet season's rain, and the balance is maintained naturally.**

> **That is a genuine advantage of a monsoon climate and it means the leaching requirement, which dominates irrigation design in arid regions, is largely academic in the Terai — PROVIDED the drainage allows the leached salt to leave.**

> **Where it does not — where the water table is high and there is no outfall — the monsoon's water leaches the salt down to the water table and the dry season's capillary rise brings it back, and the land salinises despite the rainfall.**

> **So even in a wet climate the requirement is DRAINAGE rather than water, and the salinity problem in the Terai, where it occurs, is a drainage problem rather than a leaching one.**

> **THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION IS THE SAME ONE REACHED FROM SEVERAL DIRECTIONS IN THIS SUBCHAPTER: the salt must have somewhere to go.**

> **Applying leaching water without a drainage outlet moves the salt from the root zone to the water table, raises the water table, and returns the salt by capillary action.**

> **So leaching and drainage are a single measure with two halves, and performing only the first half is worse than doing nothing — since it adds water to a waterlogging problem and achieves no lasting salt removal.**

verification.notes: 1000 mm at 300 mg/l = 10000 m3/ha x 0.3 kg/m3 = 3000 kg = 3 tonnes per hectare per year.

examTip.trick: **Extra water applied to wash the salt below the root zone** — because transpiration removes the water and leaves the salt behind.
examTip.trap: **1,000 mm of water at 300 mg/l delivers 3 TONNES of salt per hectare per year** — with perfectly ordinary irrigation water. It does not go away by itself.
examTip.mnemonic: **A monsoon leaches for free — but only if the salt can LEAVE.** Leaching without drainage moves the salt to the water table and capillary rise brings it back.

questions.stem: VERTICAL DRAINAGE — pumping from tube wells to lower a high water table — has an advantage over horizontal (tile) drainage in a suitable aquifer in that it:
options: Produces A usable supply of irrigation water as a by-product of the drainage
Requires no energy to operate
Works equally well in a clay soil
Produces no effluent requiring disposal
questions.solution:
**It PRODUCES A USABLE SUPPLY of irrigation water as a by-product of the drainage**, so the same operation both lowers the water table and augments the supply — provided the pumped water is of acceptable quality.

**The two drainage approaches compared:**

| Aspect | HORIZONTAL (tile) drainage | VERTICAL (tube well) drainage |
|---|---|---|
| **Method** | **Buried perforated pipes at 1 to 2 m depth** ← | **Tube wells pumping from the aquifer** ← |
| **Energy** | **NONE — gravity, if there is an outfall** ← | **CONTINUOUS pumping cost** ← (so option b is inverted) |
| **Suited to** | **Any permeable soil; the only option where there is no aquifer** ← | **Requires a TRANSMISSIVE aquifer beneath — useless in clay** ← (option c is inverted) |
| **Effluent** | **Must be disposed of — and it is saline** ← | **Also must be disposed of, OR used for irrigation if its quality allows** ← (option d) |
| **The pumped water's use** | **Not applicable** | **Its GREAT advantage — the drainage water becomes irrigation water** ← |
| **Capital cost** | **High — a dense network of pipes** ← | **Lower per hectare where an aquifer exists — a few wells serve a large area** ← |
| **Control** | **Passive and continuous** ← | **Active — the water table can be managed by adjusting the pumping** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE PROPERTY THAT MAKES VERTICAL DRAINAGE SO ATTRACTIVE WHERE IT IS POSSIBLE AND IT IS THE CONJUNCTIVE USE ARGUMENT ARRIVED AT FROM THE DRAINAGE SIDE: the same pumping that removes the excess water supplies the dry-season irrigation.**

> **A command suffering from a rising water table has, by definition, more water than it needs — stored in the ground beneath it.**

> **Pumping that water lowers the table, which is the drainage objective, and provides water in the dry season, which is the supply objective.**

> **So the two problems solve one another, and the cost of the pumping is offset by the value of the water.**

> **That is a genuinely elegant resolution and it is why vertical drainage has been favoured in the Indo-Gangetic commands, where the aquifer is transmissive and the water is generally of usable quality.**

**THE CONDITIONS IT REQUIRES, WHICH LIMIT ITS APPLICATION:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **A TRANSMISSIVE aquifer beneath the land** ← | **Sand or gravel of adequate thickness and permeability — a clay profile cannot be drained by pumping** ← |
| **Groundwater of acceptable QUALITY for irrigation** ← | **If it is saline, the pumped water cannot be used and must be disposed of — which removes the whole advantage** ← |
| **A reliable and affordable ENERGY supply** ← | **Which is the constraint in Nepal, as elsewhere** ← |
| **A hydraulic connection between the shallow waterlogged zone and the pumped aquifer** ← | **If an impermeable layer separates them, pumping the deep aquifer does not drain the shallow one** ← |
| **And an institutional arrangement for operating and paying for the pumping** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A TECHNICAL TRAP THAT HAS DEFEATED SCHEMES AND IS WORTH KNOWING: a command may be waterlogged in its shallow soil and underlain by a deep confined aquifer separated from it by a clay layer.**

> **Pumping the deep aquifer then lowers the deep piezometric level and does nothing whatever to the shallow water table that is causing the waterlogging.**

> **The wells produce water, the pumping costs are incurred, and the land stays wet — and the failure is attributed to inadequate pumping rather than to the aquifer's structure.**

> **So establishing the hydraulic connection between the waterlogged zone and the aquifer to be pumped is a necessary investigation, and it requires piezometers at more than one depth rather than a single observation well.**

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE OTHER COMMON DISAPPOINTMENT AND IT IS PARTICULARLY CRUEL: the areas most prone to waterlogging in an arid command are often those where the groundwater has become saline, precisely BECAUSE the water table has been high for a long time.**

> **So the places that most need vertical drainage are the places where its product cannot be used, and the pumped water becomes a disposal problem instead of a benefit.**

> **Vertical drainage is therefore best applied EARLY, while the groundwater is still fresh — which is to say, before the problem becomes severe, which is exactly when it is hardest to justify.**
tags: conjunctive use from the drainage side

examTip.trick: **The pumped drainage water becomes irrigation water** — so the same operation lowers the table and augments the supply. Conjunctive use from the drainage side.
examTip.trap: **It needs a TRANSMISSIVE aquifer and it costs energy** — options (b) and (c) are both inverted. And it produces an effluent too, unless the water is usable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the hydraulic CONNECTION between the waterlogged shallow zone and the pumped aquifer** — a clay layer between them means the pumping drains nothing that matters.

questions.stem: The DRAINAGE COEFFICIENT used in designing an agricultural drainage system is:
options: The ratio of the drained area to the total area
The hydraulic conductivity of the soil divided by its porosity
The depth of water, expressed in millimetres per day, that the system must be capable of removing from the whole area it serves
The proportion of rainfall that becomes runoff
questions.solution:
**The DEPTH of water, expressed in millimetres per day, that the system must be capable of REMOVING from the whole area it serves** — a design rate rather than a soil property.

**What it represents and how it is chosen:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is the design REMOVAL RATE, in mm/day** ← | **Equivalent to a discharge per unit area** ← |
| **It is NOT the rainfall, and NOT the excess water** ← | **It is the rate at which the system is required to remove water** ← |
| **Typical values are 3 to 10 mm/day for subsurface drainage** ← | **And considerably more for surface drainage, which must handle storm runoff** ← |
| **It is chosen from the crop's tolerance, the rainfall, and the value of the crop** ← | ← |
| **A HIGHER coefficient means a system that drains faster — closer spacing, larger pipes, and more cost** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW SHOWS THE ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO SYSTEMS' REQUIREMENTS AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT: a subsurface system removes water SLOWLY over days, and a surface system must remove it FAST.**

> **Subsurface drainage's task is to lower a water table, which is a matter of days — the crop tolerates a high table for a short period, and the design aims to bring it down within two or three days of a wetting.**

> **Surface drainage's task is to remove standing water, and a crop submerged for more than a day or two is often destroyed — so the removal must be within about 24 to 48 hours, and the drains must be sized for a storm's runoff rather than for a percolation rate.**

> **So the two coefficients differ by an order of magnitude, and using a subsurface figure for a surface system undersizes it drastically.**

**WHY THE COEFFICIENT IS AN ECONOMIC CHOICE RATHER THAN A TECHNICAL ONE:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A HIGHER coefficient gives better protection and costs more** ← | ← |
| **A LOWER one costs less and allows more frequent damage** ← | ← |
| **The optimum depends on the crop's VALUE and its SENSITIVITY** ← | **A high-value vegetable crop justifies a high coefficient; a tolerant fodder crop does not** ← |
| **And on the FREQUENCY of the wet conditions** ← | **A rare event may be more economically endured than protected against** ← |
| **So the coefficient is set by weighing the damage avoided against the cost** ← | **Exactly as a design return period is** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW MAKES THE PARALLEL WITH FLOOD DESIGN EXPLICIT AND IT IS WORTH DRAWING: choosing a drainage coefficient is the same kind of decision as choosing a design return period, and it should be made in the same way.**

> **Both trade cost against the frequency and severity of failure.**

> **Both are often made by convention — 'we use 5 mm/day' or 'we design for the 50-year flood' — when they should be made by comparing what the protection costs with what the damage would.**

> **And in both cases the conventional value may be right for the setting it was developed in and wrong for another — a coefficient developed for temperate European agriculture may be quite unsuited to a monsoon climate and a paddy-based cropping system.**

**THE PADDY CASE DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT INVERTS THE WHOLE SUBJECT IN THE TERAI:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Paddy is grown in PONDED water and requires the field to be flooded** ← | ← |
| **So drainage during the paddy season is not wanted at all** ← | **And a subsurface drainage system would drain away the water the crop needs** ← |
| **Drainage IS wanted for the rabi crop that follows** ← | **Which needs the profile drained within days of the paddy's harvest** ← |
| **So the requirement is SEASONAL, and the system must be capable of being SHUT OFF** ← | **By controlled drainage — a gate or a riser in the collector that holds the water table high during paddy and lowers it afterwards** ← |
| **A conventional always-on system is actively harmful in a paddy command** ← | ← |

> **The fourth row describes CONTROLLED DRAINAGE, and it is the appropriate form for a rice-based system: the drains are there, and their outlet level is adjustable, so the water table is held high when the paddy wants it and lowered when the wheat does.**

> **That converts drainage from a permanent removal into a management tool, and it also conserves water and reduces the leaching of nutrients — so it is better in several respects than continuous drainage as well as being necessary for the cropping pattern.**
tags: economic choice like a return period

examTip.trick: **The DEPTH per day the system must remove** — a design rate, 3-10 mm/day for subsurface drainage and much more for surface.
examTip.trap: **Subsurface drains a water table over DAYS; surface removes ponding within 24-48 HOURS.** The two coefficients differ by an order of magnitude.
examTip.mnemonic: **In a paddy command, drainage is SEASONAL** — an always-on system drains away the water the rice needs. Use CONTROLLED drainage with an adjustable outlet level.

questions.stem: In an irrigation command, the single most effective PREVENTIVE measure against waterlogging — as distinct from curing it once it has occurred — is:
options: Deep ploughing to break up any impermeable layer
Growing crops that tolerate a high water table
Installing pumps to lower the water table when it rises
Preventing the water from reaching the water table in the first place
questions.solution:
**Preventing the water from reaching the water table in the first place — by LINING the canals to stop seepage, and by managing the irrigation so that no more water is applied than the crop can use.**

**The measures, arranged as prevention and cure:**

| PREVENTIVE (stop the water arriving) | CURATIVE (remove it once it has) |
|---|---|
| **LINE the canals and watercourses** ← | **Subsurface (tile) drainage** ← |
| **Manage the IRRIGATION — apply the right depth at the right interval** ← | **Surface drainage** ← |
| **Improve the application EFFICIENCY, so less is lost to percolation** ← | **Vertical (tube well) drainage** ← |
| **Maintain the natural DRAINAGE lines — do not block them with embankments** ← | **Bio-drainage** ← |
| **Control the CROPPING pattern, limiting high-water-use crops where the risk is greatest** ← | **Pumped drainage where there is no gravity outfall** ← |
| **Provide adequate drainage capacity from the OUTSET, before the problem appears** ← | ← |

> **THE PREVENTIVE MEASURES ARE CHEAPER, MORE EFFECTIVE AND ALMOST ALWAYS DEFERRED, AND THE REASON IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: prevention must be paid for before the problem is visible.**

> **A new command has no waterlogging, so lining the canals to prevent it looks like an unnecessary expense.**

> **Twenty years later the water table has risen, thousands of hectares are damaged, and drainage works costing many times the lining are needed to recover land that need never have been lost.**

> **This is exactly the mitigation-against-response argument met in disaster management, and it fails for the same reason: the benefit of prevention is invisible, and the cost of the cure is unavoidable and therefore funded.**

**THE MAGNITUDE OF THE TWO PRINCIPAL SOURCES IS WORTH KNOWING, SINCE IT DIRECTS THE EFFORT:**

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **CANAL SEEPAGE** ← | **Often the largest single source in a command — a continuous line source, operating whenever the canal runs** ← |
| **FIELD percolation from over-irrigation** ← | **Distributed over the whole area, and it is what irrigation efficiency measures address** ← |
| **Rainfall** ← | **Unavoidable, and it is why the command's natural drainage must be preserved** ← |
| **Seepage from the RESERVOIR or the headworks** ← | **Local** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW MAKES CANAL LINING THE PRINCIPAL PREVENTIVE MEASURE IN MOST COMMANDS AND IT IS WORTH NOTING WHERE THE PRIORITY LIES: the largest seepage comes from the largest canals in the most permeable ground, and from the WATERCOURSES.**

> **Watercourses — the small unlined channels from the outlet to the fields — are numerous, are in the worst condition, are the least maintained, and account for a substantial share of the total conveyance loss.**

> **Lining the main canal is visible and is usually done first; lining the watercourses is dispersed, unglamorous and often more effective per rupee.**

> **So a lining programme that begins with the main canal because it is the obvious candidate may be addressing the smaller part of the problem.**

> **THE SECOND SOURCE — OVER-IRRIGATION — IS ADDRESSED BY MEASURES THAT COST NOTHING IN CONSTRUCTION AND EVERYTHING IN MANAGEMENT, WHICH IS WHY IT IS HARDER:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Irrigation SCHEDULING — the right depth at the right interval** ← | **Which requires knowing the soil, the crop and the weather** ← |
| **LAND LEVELLING, so the application is uniform and no part is over-watered to wet another** ← | ← |
| **Volumetric CHARGING rather than an area-based fee** ← | **So that using more water costs more — the incentive that area-based charging removes entirely** ← |
| **And WATER USER involvement in the distribution** ← | ← |

> **The third row is the measure with the greatest potential and the greatest political difficulty: where water is charged by the area irrigated rather than by the volume used, a farmer has no reason whatever to use less.**

> **The marginal cost of an extra irrigation is zero, so more is applied than the crop needs, and the excess goes to the water table.**

> **Volumetric charging changes that incentive at a stroke — but it requires measurement at every outlet, an administration to bill and collect, and a political willingness to charge for water that has historically been nearly free.**

> **So the technically obvious measure is the institutionally hardest, which is a pattern that recurs throughout irrigation management and is worth recognising as such rather than being surprised by it each time.**

examTip.trick: **Stop the water arriving — line the canals and do not over-irrigate.** Prevention is cheaper and more effective than any drainage cure.
examTip.trap: **Prevention must be paid for before the problem is visible** — so it is deferred, and the cure costs many times more. The same failure as mitigation against disaster response.
examTip.mnemonic: **WATERCOURSES leak more in total than the main canal** — numerous, unmaintained and unglamorous. And area-based charging removes every incentive to use less water.

questions.stem: A subsurface drainage system's MAIN DRAIN discharges into a river that is in flood for part of the monsoon, so that the outfall is submerged. The standard provision for this is:
options: A flap (non-return) valve at the outfall, which closes when the river is higher than the drain and opens when it falls
To raise the whole drainage system above the river's flood level
To discharge the drainage into the irrigation canal instead
To accept that the system cannot function and abandon it
questions.solution:
**A FLAP (non-return) valve at the outfall, which closes when the river is higher than the drain and opens when it falls** — with PUMPING provided where the submergence lasts too long for the land to tolerate the resulting ponding.

**The situation and its remedy:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The drain discharges by gravity when the river is low** ← | ← |
| **When the river rises above the drain's outlet, the flow would REVERSE** ← | **The river entering the drainage system and flooding the land it serves** ← |
| **A FLAP VALVE prevents that — it opens outward under the drain's pressure and closes under the river's** ← | ← |
| **But while it is closed, the drainage cannot discharge** ← | **So the drainage water accumulates behind it** ← |
| **If the closure is brief, the land tolerates the temporary ponding** ← | ← |
| **If it is prolonged, PUMPING is needed to lift the drainage over the closed outfall** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS CONTAIN THE PROBLEM'S ESSENCE AND IT IS AN UNFORTUNATE COINCIDENCE OF TIMING: the outfall is blocked exactly when the drainage is most needed.**

> **The river is in flood because it has been raining heavily; the land is waterlogged for the same reason; and the drainage cannot discharge because the river is high.**

> **So the system's capacity is unavailable at precisely the moment of demand, which is the opposite of what one would design if one had a choice.**

> **The flap valve prevents the situation from being worse — without it the river would flow INTO the land — but it cannot make the drainage work.**

> **That is why pumped drainage is so common in flat commands near large rivers, and why the pumping station's capacity is determined by the duration of the submergence rather than by the drainage coefficient alone.**

**THE DESIGN OF SUCH AN OUTFALL:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A FLAP valve, or a set of them for a large drain** ← | **Simple, automatic, and it needs no operator** ← |
| **A SUMP or storage behind it** ← | **To hold the drainage that accumulates while the valve is shut, so the land is not flooded immediately** ← |
| **A PUMP, where the storage is insufficient for the expected duration** ← | ← |
| **A DUPLICATE valve or a stop log** ← | **Since a flap held open by debris admits the river — the failure that matters** ← |
| **Protection against SCOUR at the outfall** ← | ← |
| **And ACCESS for clearing debris from the flap's seating** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES THE FLAP VALVE'S CHARACTERISTIC FAILURE AND IT IS THE ONE TO GUARD AGAINST: a branch, a rag or a stone lodged on the seat holds the flap slightly open.**

> **The river then flows steadily into the drainage system throughout the flood, and the land the system was built to protect is flooded by its own outfall.**

> **The failure is invisible from the land side, and the water arriving is attributed to rainfall or to the river's overtopping.**

> **So a duplicate closure — a second flap, or a stop log that can be dropped in — is a cheap and worthwhile provision, and access to clear the seating before each flood season is a maintenance item worth specifying.**

**THE PUMPED DRAINAGE OPTION DESERVES ITS OWN ASSESSMENT AS A CLOSING POINT, SINCE IT IS A PERMANENT COMMITMENT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A pumped outfall works whatever the river's level** ← | ← |
| **But it costs energy, permanently, and it is needed most during a monsoon power failure** ← | **The two coinciding as usual** ← |
| **It requires an institution to operate, fuel and maintain it** ← | ← |
| **And if the pumps fail, the land floods exactly as if there were no drainage** ← | ← |
| **So the storage behind the outfall should be sized to give TIME, not merely to bridge a normal closure** ← | **Long enough for a failed pump to be repaired or a generator brought** ← |

> **The last row is a design provision worth arguing for, and it is a form of graceful failure: storage buys time, and time is what converts an equipment failure into an inconvenience rather than a loss of the crop.**

> **Sizing the sump for a nominal closure only, on the assumption that the pumps will run, makes the whole command dependent on machinery in a setting where machinery is not dependable — which is a judgment about reliability rather than about hydraulics, and it is the one that determines whether the scheme works in the year it is tested.**

examTip.trick: **A flap valve to stop the river entering, plus pumping where the submergence is prolonged** — the outfall is blocked exactly when the drainage is most needed.
examTip.trap: **A flap held slightly open by debris admits the river continuously** — flooding the land through its own outfall, invisibly. Provide a duplicate closure and clear the seat each season.
examTip.mnemonic: **Size the storage to buy TIME, not just to bridge a normal closure** — long enough to repair a failed pump. Storage converts an equipment failure into an inconvenience.

questions.stem: MOLE DRAINAGE is a technique in which:
options: An unlined channel is formed in the subsoil by drawing a bullet-shaped plug through it behind a blade
Perforated pipes are laid in trenches at close spacing
A mole plough is used to break up a compacted layer without forming any channel
Vertical holes are bored to connect the topsoil to a permeable layer beneath
questions.solution:
**An unlined CHANNEL is formed in the subsoil by drawing a bullet-shaped plug through it behind a blade** — giving a cheap temporary drain that lasts a few years, and which is practicable only in a soil with enough CLAY to hold the channel open.

**How it is done and what it produces:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A MOLE PLOUGH consists of a narrow blade with a bullet-shaped 'mole' at its foot, and an EXPANDER behind the mole** ← | ← |
| **It is drawn through the subsoil at 400 to 700 mm depth** ← | **By a crawler tractor or a winch** ← |
| **The mole forms a CHANNEL of 50 to 100 mm diameter, and the expander compresses and smooths its walls** ← | ← |
| **The blade's slot above the channel also drains, and it cracks the soil laterally** ← | **Which is part of the benefit** ← |
| **The moles are drawn at 2 to 5 m spacing, across the slope's fall** ← | ← |
| **And they discharge into a piped collector or an open ditch** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN IMPORTANT PART OF THE MECHANISM AND IT IS EASILY OVERLOOKED: much of mole drainage's benefit comes from the CRACKING that the plough causes, not from the channel alone.**

> **Drawing a blade through a clay subsoil shatters it laterally for some distance either side, creating a network of fissures.**

> **Those fissures conduct water to the mole channel, so the mole drains a width far greater than its own diameter would suggest.**

> **This is why the operation is done when the subsoil is in the right condition — dry enough to crack rather than smear — and why moling a wet soil produces a smeared channel with no cracking and very little benefit.**

> **The timing is therefore critical and it is a matter of days: the topsoil must be moist enough for the tractor to work and the subsoil dry enough to fracture.**

**ITS ADVANTAGES AND ITS LIMITATIONS:**

| Advantage | Limitation |
|---|---|
| **VERY CHEAP — a fraction of piped drainage, with no materials at all** ← | **TEMPORARY — it lasts 3 to 10 years and must be redrawn** ← |
| **Rapid — a large area can be moled in a day** ← | **Only works in a CLAY soil with enough cohesion to hold the channel open** ← |
| **No trenching, so the land is barely disturbed** ← | **Useless in a sandy or unstable soil, where the channel collapses at once** ← |
| **It can be repeated as often as needed** ← | **Depth is limited to what a plough can reach — under a metre** ← |
| **And it complements a permanent piped collector system** ← | **It cannot serve as the collector itself** ← |

> **THE COMBINATION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE USUAL ARRANGEMENT AND IT IS THE ECONOMICAL ONE: permanent piped collectors at a wide spacing, with moles drawn between them at a close spacing and renewed periodically.**

> **The permanent element is the expensive one and there is little of it; the close-spaced element is the cheap one and it is replaced as it decays.**

> **That is a sensible allocation — permanence where it is costly to renew and impermanence where renewal is cheap — and it produces a system with the drainage intensity of close-spaced pipes at a fraction of the cost.**

> **THE CLAY REQUIREMENT IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE CONDITION THAT DECIDES WHERE THE TECHNIQUE IS USABLE, AND IT IS A HAPPY COINCIDENCE: mole drainage works only in clay soils, and clay soils are precisely the ones in which piped subsurface drainage requires impracticably close spacing.**

> **So the technique is available exactly where the alternative is most expensive, and unavailable where the alternative is affordable.**

> **In a heavy clay a piped system might need 10 m spacing and moles need 3 m — but the moles cost almost nothing per metre, so the close spacing is affordable in a way the pipes are not.**

> **That makes mole drainage the appropriate technique for heavy land, and it is widely used on clay soils in temperate agriculture for exactly this reason.**

examTip.trick: **An unlined channel pulled through the subsoil by a bullet-shaped mole** — cheap, quick, temporary, and only in clay that will hold the channel open.
examTip.trap: **Much of the benefit is the lateral CRACKING, not the channel** — so the subsoil must be dry enough to fracture rather than smear. The timing window is days.
examTip.mnemonic: **Permanent piped collectors, temporary moles between them** — permanence where renewal is dear, impermanence where it is cheap. And moles suit exactly the clays where pipes cannot.

questions.stem: An INTERCEPTOR DRAIN laid parallel to and a short distance from an unlined canal is provided to:
options: Carry the canal's surplus water away when demand falls
Provide a route for the canal's silt to be removed
Intercept the seepage emerging from the canal before it reaches and raises the water table over the wider command
Supply water to the fields nearest the canal
questions.solution:
**To INTERCEPT the SEEPAGE emerging from the canal before it reaches and raises the water table over the wider command** — dealing with the seepage at its source rather than draining the whole area affected by it.

**Why an interceptor is efficient:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Canal seepage is a LINE source — it enters the ground along the canal's whole length** ← | ← |
| **From there it spreads laterally, raising the water table over a wide band on either side** ← | ← |
| **Draining that whole band requires a full field drainage system over a large area** ← | ← |
| **An interceptor drain, laid parallel to the canal and deeper than it, catches the seepage close to its source** ← | ← |
| **So one line of drain protects a band many times its own width** ← | ← |
| **Which is far cheaper than draining the band itself** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ECONOMY AND IT IS SUBSTANTIAL: a single interceptor drain along a canal can protect a strip several hundred metres wide on that side.**

> **Draining the same strip by a conventional lateral system would require a pipe every 30 or 40 metres over its whole width.**

> **So the interceptor achieves comparable protection with perhaps a twentieth of the pipe, and it does so because it attacks the problem where the water is concentrated rather than where it has spread.**

> **That is a general principle worth carrying: intercept a source rather than drain its consequences, wherever the source is identifiable and accessible.**

**HOW AN INTERCEPTOR IS DESIGNED:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **It must be DEEPER than the canal's bed, or the seepage passes beneath it** ← | **Which is the commonest reason an interceptor fails to work** ← |
| **It must be close enough to catch the seepage before it spreads** ← | **But far enough not to undermine the canal's bank** ← |
| **It needs its own OUTFALL, at a level below the drain** ← | ← |
| **It may be an open ditch or a buried pipe** ← | **An open ditch is cheaper and takes land; a pipe takes none and costs more** ← |
| **And it should be on the side where the ground FALLS away** ← | **Or on both sides where the canal is in a cutting or on level ground** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE CRITICAL DIMENSION AND ITS OMISSION IS THE CLASSIC FAILURE: a drain laid at the usual field drainage depth of 1.5 m alongside a canal whose bed is 2 m deep will intercept nothing.**

> **The seepage leaves the canal at and below its bed level, so it is already below the drain when it passes.**

> **The drain then collects a little shallow water and the seepage travels on beneath it, and the interceptor appears to have been provided while achieving nothing.**

> **So the depth relationship between the canal's bed and the drain's invert is the design's essential dimension, and it must be established from the canal's actual profile rather than from a standard drainage depth.**

**AND THE INTERCEPTOR'S PLACE AMONG THE ALTERNATIVES DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE, SINCE IT IS A SECOND-BEST MEASURE:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **LINE the canal** ← | **Prevents the seepage entirely — the first-best measure** ← |
| **INTERCEPT the seepage** ← | **Accepts the seepage and catches it — second best, and cheaper** ← |
| **DRAIN the affected area** ← | **Accepts both the seepage and its spread — the most expensive** ← |

> **THE ORDER IS THE PREVENTION-OVER-CURE HIERARCHY AGAIN, AND THE INTERCEPTOR SITS IN THE MIDDLE: it does not prevent the loss of water, so the canal still loses its seepage and the command still loses that supply.**

> **It merely prevents the seeped water from doing damage.**

> **So where the water itself is valuable — which in an irrigation command it is — lining remains preferable, and the interceptor is the measure adopted when lining an existing canal is unaffordable or when the seepage is discovered after construction.**

> **A useful compromise where funds are limited is to line the REACHES that pass through the most permeable ground or the most vulnerable land, and to intercept elsewhere — which directs the expensive measure to where it earns most, and is a more defensible allocation than lining uniformly from the head until the money runs out.**
tags: canal seepage as a line source
one drain protects a wide band

examTip.trick: **Catch the seepage at its source, before it spreads** — one line of drain protects a band many times its width, at a fraction of a full field system's cost.
examTip.trap: **It must be DEEPER than the canal's bed** — otherwise the seepage passes beneath it and the drain intercepts nothing while appearing to be provided.
