examTip.mnemonic: **Line > intercept > drain the area** — prevention over cure. And an interceptor saves the land but not the water, which lining does both.

questions.stem: OBSERVATION WELLS installed across an irrigated command are the basic instrument of drainage work because they:
options: Provide an emergency water supply during a drought
Measure the depth to the water table and its variation with time
Measure the soil's salinity directly
Allow the aquifer's yield to be tested
questions.solution:
**They measure the DEPTH TO THE WATER TABLE and its variation with time** — which is the quantity that defines waterlogging, cannot be judged by eye, and is the only way to establish whether the problem is developing, stable or being cured.

**What a network of observation wells tells you:**

| Reading | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **The DEPTH to the water table at each point** ← | **Whether that point is waterlogged by the critical-depth criterion** ← |
| **A CONTOUR MAP of the water table, from many wells** ← | **Where the high spots are, and therefore where the recharge is coming from** ← |
| **The DIRECTION of groundwater flow, perpendicular to those contours** ← | **Which identifies the source — a canal, a reservoir, a particular reach** ← |
| **The TREND over years** ← | **Whether the table is rising, stable or falling — the single most important fact about a command** ← |
| **The SEASONAL fluctuation** ← | **Which distinguishes a monsoon rise that recedes from a permanent rise that does not** ← |
| **And the RESPONSE to a drainage intervention** ← | **Which is how the intervention's effectiveness is judged** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE DIAGNOSTIC USE THAT MOST JUSTIFIES A NETWORK AND IT IS OFTEN NOT EXPLOITED: a water table contour map shows where the water is coming from.**

> **Groundwater flows perpendicular to the water table's contours, from high to low, exactly as surface water does.**

> **So a ridge in the water table along a canal's alignment identifies that canal as the source; a mound beneath a particular reach identifies that reach; and a general rise across the command points to field percolation rather than to any single source.**

> **That distinction determines the remedy — lining a reach, or improving the irrigation practice — and it cannot be made without the map.**

> **A command that is waterlogged and has no water table map is being treated without a diagnosis, and the treatment chosen will be whichever one the agency is accustomed to providing.**

**THE FOURTH ROW DESERVES ITS DESCRIPTION AS THE MOST IMPORTANT FACT, AND IT IS WORTH EXPLAINING WHY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A water table rising at 0.3 m a year is a command that will be waterlogged within a decade** ← | **Even if it is perfectly healthy today** ← |
| **A stable water table at 4 m depth is a command with no problem and none developing** ← | ← |
| **The two look IDENTICAL from the surface today** ← | ← |
| **Only the TREND distinguishes them, and a trend requires records over years** ← | ← |
| **Which means the wells must be installed and read BEFORE the problem appears** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL DIFFICULTY AND IT IS THE SAME ONE THAT AFFLICTS ALL PREVENTIVE MEASURES: the monitoring must begin when there is nothing to see.**

> **A network installed after the waterlogging appears can measure the present condition and cannot establish how fast it developed or what caused it.**

> **So the wells should be installed with the irrigation scheme, read from its first year, and their records kept — which costs very little and is almost never done, because a scheme's completion report has no line for it.**

> **A recommendation worth making on any new command is that a baseline water table network be installed and read monthly from commissioning, and that its records be a required annual return — because ten years of readings is what allows the problem to be caught while it is still cheap to fix.**

**A NOTE ON THE INSTRUMENTS, SINCE THE TERMS ARE DISTINGUISHED:**

| Instrument | Measures |
|---|---|
| **OBSERVATION WELL** ← | **The water table in an unconfined aquifer — it is open over its length and reflects the general water level** ← |
| **PIEZOMETER** ← | **The pressure head at ONE SPECIFIC DEPTH — sealed except at its tip** ← |
| **A NEST of piezometers at different depths at one location** ← | **Reveals the VERTICAL gradient — whether water is moving up or down, which an observation well cannot show** ← |

> **The third row is the arrangement that answers the question raised earlier about vertical drainage: whether the shallow waterlogged zone is hydraulically connected to the deeper aquifer.**

> **A nest of piezometers shows the pressure at each depth, and hence whether they are in continuity or separated — which an observation well, averaging over its open length, cannot distinguish.**

> **So the choice of instrument follows from the question being asked, and installing observation wells where piezometer nests are needed produces readings that cannot answer it.**

examTip.trick: **They measure the depth to the water table and its TREND** — the quantity that defines waterlogging and cannot be judged by eye.
examTip.trap: **A water table CONTOUR MAP identifies the source** — groundwater flows perpendicular to the contours, so a ridge along a canal indicts that canal. No map means no diagnosis.
examTip.mnemonic: **A rising table and a stable one look identical today** — only years of records distinguish them. Install and read the wells from commissioning, before there is anything to see.

questions.stem: The MAIN DRAIN of an agricultural drainage system should preferably be aligned:
options: Along the shortest straight line to the outfall
Parallel to the irrigation canal that serves the command
Along the boundaries of landholdings, to avoid dividing any field
Along the natural drainage line
questions.solution:
**ALONG the NATURAL DRAINAGE LINE — the lowest ground, which the land already drains toward** — so that the collectors can reach it by gravity and the excavation is least.

**Why the natural line is the right alignment:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The land already SLOPES toward it** ← | **So every collector can reach it by gravity, from both sides** ← |
| **It is the LOWEST ground, so the drain is shallowest there** ← | **Minimising the excavation, which is the main cost** ← |
| **A natural channel often already exists** ← | **Which can be improved rather than excavated afresh** ← |
| **And the outfall is at the natural line's own outlet** ← | **Which is where the land's water has always gone** ← |
| **So the whole system works with the topography rather than against it** ← | ← |

> **THE CONTRAST WITH AN IRRIGATION CANAL IS INSTRUCTIVE AND IT IS WORTH DRAWING EXPLICITLY: a canal is aligned along the RIDGE and a drain along the VALLEY.**

> **A canal must be HIGH, to command the land by gravity, so it seeks the watershed.**

> **A drain must be LOW, to receive the land's water by gravity, so it seeks the depression.**

> **They are therefore aligned on opposite features of the same topography, and an irrigation and drainage system laid out together forms an interlocking pattern of canals on the ridges and drains in the hollows, each serving the land between.**

> **That pattern is worth being able to picture, because it explains why the two networks must be planned together — and why planning the irrigation first and the drainage afterwards, which is what usually happens, leaves the drains with whatever alignments the canals have not taken.**

**THE CONSEQUENCE OF NOT PLANNING THEM TOGETHER, WHICH IS THE COMMON SITUATION:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **Canals are built across the natural drainage lines** ← | **Blocking them, unless cross-drainage is provided** ← |
| **Roads and spoil banks do the same** ← | ← |
| **So the land's natural drainage is obstructed before any drainage system is contemplated** ← | ← |
| **And by the time drainage is needed, the natural lines are broken and their outlets are blocked** ← | ← |
| **Restoring them then costs far more than preserving them would have** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ARGUMENT FOR PLANNING THE DRAINAGE AT THE OUTSET EVEN WHERE IT IS NOT YET NEEDED, and it is a modest requirement: the drainage lines must be IDENTIFIED and PRESERVED, with cross-drainage provided wherever anything crosses them.**

> **The drains themselves need not be built until they are needed.**

> **What must be done at the outset is to ensure that the routes remain available and unobstructed, which costs the price of some culverts and some restraint in tipping spoil.**

> **A command in which that has been done can be drained when the need arises; one in which it has not requires the obstructions to be removed first, and many of them are roads and canals that cannot be removed.**

> **So the phrase worth using is that drainage should be PROVIDED FOR at the outset even if it is not provided — and the distinction between the two is the difference between a modest foresight and a large later cost.**

**AND THE PRACTICAL POINT ABOUT LANDHOLDINGS IN OPTION (c) DESERVES AN ANSWER, SINCE IT IS A REAL CONSIDERATION:**

> **A drain along the natural line will inevitably cross some holdings and divide some fields, and the landowners will object.**

> **Aligning it along the boundaries instead means it does not follow the lowest ground, so parts of the command cannot reach it by gravity and the excavation is deeper.**

> **The usual resolution is to follow the natural line for the MAIN drain, where the hydraulic requirement is strict, and to follow the boundaries for the FIELD drains and the collectors, where there is more latitude.**

> **That gives the hydraulics what it needs at the few places it matters most, and accommodates the landholding pattern everywhere else — which is a reasonable compromise and is usually acceptable to the landowners when the alternative is explained.**
tags: canals on ridges and drains in valleys

examTip.trick: **Along the natural drainage line — the lowest ground** — so collectors reach it by gravity and the excavation is least.
examTip.trap: **Canals seek the RIDGE and drains the VALLEY** — opposite features of the same topography. So the two networks must be planned together, not one after the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **Drainage must be PROVIDED FOR at the outset even if not provided** — identify and preserve the routes with cross-drainage. Restoring blocked lines later costs far more.

questions.stem: In reclaiming land that has become both WATERLOGGED and SALINE, the correct order of measures is:
options: First establish drainage, then apply any chemical amendment needed, then leach
First leach, then drain, then amend
First amend, then drain, then leach
Leaching alone is sufficient in every case
questions.solution:
**First establish DRAINAGE, then apply any chemical amendment needed, then LEACH** — because leaching before the drainage exists merely moves the salt to the water table, from which capillary rise returns it.

**The sequence and the reason for each step's position:**

| Step | Why it comes where it does |
|---|---|
| **1. DRAINAGE** ← | **Without an outlet, the salt has nowhere to go; and until the water table is lowered, capillary rise will return whatever is washed down** ← |
| **2. AMENDMENT (gypsum) if the soil is SODIC** ← | **A dispersed sodic soil is impermeable, so leaching water cannot pass through it — the permeability must be restored first** ← |
| **3. LEACHING with good water** ← | **Now the water can pass through, and the salt it carries can leave the area** ← |
| **4. Establish a tolerant CROP, then progressively less tolerant ones** ← | **Beginning with barley, rice or a salt-tolerant grass, and improving the soil's structure and organic matter as the crops grow** ← |
| **5. Maintain the drainage and the leaching thereafter** ← | **The salt continues to arrive with every irrigation, so the maintenance is permanent** ← |

> **THE FIRST STEP'S PRIMACY IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION AND IT CANNOT BE OVERSTATED: every other measure depends on it.**

> **Leaching without drainage adds water to a waterlogged profile, raises the water table further, and returns the salt within a season.**

> **Gypsum without leaching displaces the sodium into solution and leaves it in the soil, where it does the same harm.**

> **And a crop planted without either fails.**

> **So the sequence is not a preference but a dependency chain, and performing the steps out of order wastes the effort of each.**

**THE FOURTH STEP DESERVES ITS OWN ATTENTION BECAUSE IT IS BIOLOGICAL RATHER THAN ENGINEERING AND IS FREQUENTLY OMITTED FROM AN ENGINEER'S CONCEPTION OF RECLAMATION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A reclaimed soil is structureless, low in organic matter and biologically dead** ← | **Even once its salt has gone** ← |
| **Growing a tolerant crop begins to restore it** ← | **Roots open the soil, residues add organic matter, and the biology returns** ← |
| **Each season's crop improves the soil for the next** ← | ← |
| **So the reclamation continues for several years after the engineering is finished** ← | ← |
| **And a green manure or a leguminous crop accelerates it considerably** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHY RECLAMATION IS MEASURED IN YEARS RATHER THAN SEASONS AND IT IS WORTH SETTING EXPECTATIONS ACCORDINGLY: a scheme that installs drainage, applies gypsum and leaches, and is then judged on the first season's yield, will appear to have failed.**

> **The salt may have gone and the soil may still be unproductive, because its structure and its biology have not recovered.**

> **Three to five years is a realistic period for a badly degraded soil to return to full production, and the intervening seasons need tolerant crops and patience.**

> **A project whose evaluation is scheduled for its second year will record a failure that a fifth-year evaluation would record as a success, and the difference is in the timing of the assessment rather than in the work.**

**AND THE ECONOMIC QUESTION DESERVES A CLOSING WORD, SINCE IT DETERMINES WHETHER RECLAMATION IS ATTEMPTED AT ALL:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reclamation is EXPENSIVE — drainage, gypsum, leaching water and several years of reduced yield** ← | ← |
| **The land recovered is often of modest productivity even when reclaimed** ← | ← |
| **So the benefit-cost ratio can be marginal** ← | ← |
| **Whereas PREVENTING the degradation would have cost a small fraction** ← | ← |
| **Which is the argument for the preventive measures, made once more and from a different direction** ← | ← |

> **The fourth and fifth rows close the subchapter on the point it has returned to repeatedly: preventing waterlogging and salinity costs a fraction of curing them, and the cure may not even be economic.**

> **Land that has been allowed to salinise may be cheaper to abandon than to reclaim, which is a conclusion nobody wishes to reach and which the arithmetic sometimes supports.**

> **So the case for lining the canals, managing the irrigation and installing the drainage at the outset does not rest on the cost of the eventual cure — it rests on the possibility that there will be no economic cure at all.**

examTip.trick: **Drain, amend, leach, crop** — in that order. Each step depends on the one before, so doing them out of order wastes them all.
examTip.trap: **Leaching without drainage returns the salt within a season** — it moves to the water table, which rises, and capillary action brings it back.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reclamation takes 3-5 years** — the salt goes first and the structure and biology recover slowly. A second-year evaluation records a failure the fifth year would call a success.

questions.stem: Among the materials used for buried subsurface drain laterals, CORRUGATED PERFORATED PVC pipe has largely displaced clay tiles chiefly because it:
options: Withstands greater external soil loads than clay
Has a larger internal diameter for the same trench width
Comes in long coils that can be laid continuously by a trenching machine
Requires no envelope or filter material
questions.solution:
**It comes in LONG COILS that can be laid CONTINUOUSLY by a trenching machine** — eliminating the many joints of short tiles, which are the points where roots enter, silt enters and alignment is lost.

**The two materials compared:**

| Aspect | CLAY (or concrete) TILES | CORRUGATED PERFORATED PVC |
|---|---|---|
| **Form** | **Short lengths, 300 to 600 mm, butted end to end** ← | **A continuous coil, hundreds of metres long** ← |
| **Water entry** | **Through the JOINTS between tiles** ← | **Through machine-cut PERFORATIONS distributed along the pipe** ← |
| **Number of joints** | **Two or three per metre** ← | **Almost none** ← |
| **Laying** | **By hand, each tile placed and aligned** ← | **By a MACHINE that opens the trench, lays the pipe and backfills in one pass** ← |
| **Speed** | **Slow** ← | **Very fast — hundreds of metres an hour** ← |
| **Root and silt entry** | **At every joint** ← | **Through the perforations, which are smaller and are protected by the envelope** ← |
| **Weight and transport** | **Heavy and fragile** ← | **Light, and a coil carries hundreds of metres** ← |
| **Strength under load** | **STRONGER in crushing** ← (so option a favours clay) | **Flexible — it deflects rather than breaking, and it depends on the surrounding soil for support** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE WHAT ACTUALLY CHANGED THE PRACTICE AND THE POINT IS ECONOMIC RATHER THAN TECHNICAL: the coil made MACHINE LAYING possible.**

> **A drainage machine trenches, lays and backfills in a single continuous pass, controlled to grade by a laser.**

> **That reduces the cost per metre by a large factor and it makes large-scale drainage economically feasible where hand-laid tiles were not.**

> **So the material's advantage is not chiefly in the pipe's own properties but in the METHOD it permits, which is a common pattern in construction — a material is adopted because of how it can be installed rather than because of how it performs once installed.**

**THE FLEXIBILITY IN THE LAST ROW IS BOTH AN ADVANTAGE AND A REQUIREMENT AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A corrugated PVC pipe is FLEXIBLE — it deflects under load rather than cracking** ← | ← |
| **So it tolerates ground movement and settlement that would break a rigid tile** ← | ← |
| **But its load capacity depends on the SUPPORT of the soil around it** ← | **A flexible pipe carries its load by deflecting until the surrounding soil resists** ← |
| **So the BEDDING and the SIDEFILL must be properly placed and compacted** ← | **A flexible pipe in a poorly filled trench deflects excessively and may collapse** ← |
| **Which is the same requirement as for any flexible pipe, and the same one met with sewers** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS STATE THE ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCE BETWEEN RIGID AND FLEXIBLE PIPE BEHAVIOUR AND IT IS WORTH CARRYING GENERALLY: a rigid pipe resists the load itself, and a flexible pipe borrows the soil's strength.**

> **So a rigid pipe in a badly filled trench is over-stressed and cracks; a flexible pipe in the same trench deflects and, if the fill is bad enough, collapses.**

> **Both fail, but for opposite reasons — one because it had to carry the load alone and one because its partner was absent.**

> **And the remedy differs accordingly: a rigid pipe needs a stronger class, and a flexible pipe needs better sidefill, which is generally the cheaper answer.**

**AND OPTION (d) REQUIRES AN ANSWER SINCE IT IS A COMMON MISCONCEPTION: the ENVELOPE is required regardless of the pipe material.**

> **The envelope's function is to prevent the surrounding soil entering the pipe and to improve the flow into it, and that requirement follows from the SOIL rather than from the pipe.**

> **A perforated PVC pipe's holes are, if anything, more vulnerable to fine soil entering than a tile's joints, because they are distributed and cannot be individually protected.**

> **So PVC pipe is supplied with a pre-wrapped geotextile or coir envelope for exactly this reason, and laying it bare in a fine soil results in the pipe silting up along its length — which cannot be corrected, since the pipe cannot be cleaned effectively once its perforations are blocked from outside.**

examTip.trick: **Long coils allow continuous MACHINE laying** — the economic change, not a property of the pipe itself. Tiles need two or three joints per metre.
examTip.trap: **Clay is STRONGER in crushing; PVC is FLEXIBLE and borrows the soil's strength** — so it needs properly compacted sidefill or it deflects and collapses.
examTip.mnemonic: **The envelope is required whatever the pipe** — its need comes from the SOIL. Bare perforated pipe in a fine soil silts up and cannot be cleaned from outside.

questions.stem: In assessing the economic justification for a drainage scheme, the benefit that is usually LARGEST and is most often overlooked is:
options: The value of the drainage water itself, which can be sold
The avoided future loss
The employment created during construction
The increase in the land's market value
questions.solution:
**The AVOIDED FUTURE LOSS — the production that would have been lost as the waterlogging and salinity continued to spread** — which must be compared against a 'without project' case of CONTINUING DETERIORATION rather than against present conditions.

**Why the comparison must be against a deteriorating baseline:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A project's benefit is the difference between WITH the project and WITHOUT it** ← | **Not between with the project and today** ← |
| **In a deteriorating command, the 'without project' case is WORSE than today** ← | **The water table continues to rise and more land is lost each year** ← |
| **So the benefit includes both the RECOVERY of what has been lost and the PREVENTION of further loss** ← | ← |
| **Comparing against present conditions counts only the first and omits the second** ← | ← |
| **Which can understate the benefit by a large factor** ← | **Particularly where the deterioration is rapid** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES AN ERROR THAT IS ROUTINELY MADE AND IT SYSTEMATICALLY UNDERVALUES PREVENTIVE AND PROTECTIVE PROJECTS OF EVERY KIND: the baseline is taken as the present state, and the present state is not what will happen.**

> **A drainage scheme in a command losing 200 hectares a year to salinity is not merely recovering the land already lost; it is preventing the loss of 200 hectares a year for ever.**

> **Over a thirty-year appraisal period that is 6,000 hectares of avoided loss, which may dwarf the recovery benefit entirely.**

> **And the same error affects flood protection, slope stabilisation, erosion control and maintenance of every kind — all of which are valued against a static baseline when their real benefit is preventing a decline.**

> **So the first question in appraising any protective work is: what happens if nothing is done? — and the answer is rarely 'things stay as they are'.**

**THE FULL SET OF BENEFITS FROM A DRAINAGE SCHEME, FOR COMPLETENESS:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Increased yield on land currently under-producing** ← | ← |
| **RECOVERY of land gone out of cultivation** ← | ← |
| **AVOIDED future loss** ← | **Usually the largest, as above** ← |
| **A change to more valuable CROPS, now that the land will support them** ← | **Often a large benefit — from paddy alone to a paddy-wheat rotation, or to vegetables** ← |
| **A longer growing SEASON, since the land dries earlier after the monsoon** ← | ← |
| **Improved TRAFFICABILITY for machinery and cultivation** ← | ← |
| **Better health, from reduced standing water and its mosquitoes** ← | **Real, and hard to value** ← |
| **And improved efficiency of the IRRIGATION, since the drainage permits proper leaching** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS FREQUENTLY THE LARGEST OF THE PRODUCTION BENEFITS AND IT IS WORTH LOOKING FOR: drainage does not merely raise the yield of what is grown, it changes what CAN be grown.**

> **A waterlogged field can grow paddy in the monsoon and nothing afterwards, because it is too wet to cultivate in November.**

> **Drained, it grows paddy and then wheat, which doubles its cropping intensity — and the wheat is a rabi crop of substantial value.**

> **So the benefit is not a percentage improvement in an existing yield but the addition of a whole second crop, and valuing it as the former badly understates it.**

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MECHANISM BEHIND THAT AND IT IS WORTH STATING SEPARATELY: what prevents the rabi crop is not the waterlogging in the monsoon but the field being too wet to PREPARE at sowing time.**

> **A field that drains a fortnight earlier can be ploughed and sown a fortnight earlier, and in a rabi season that fortnight can be the difference between a good crop and a poor one, because the crop must mature before the pre-monsoon heat.**

> **So the TIMING benefit of drainage — bringing the land into workable condition sooner — is a distinct benefit from the yield benefit, and on a rice-wheat system it is often the more valuable of the two.**

examTip.trick: **Compare against a DETERIORATING 'without project' case, not against today** — the benefit includes preventing further loss, not just recovering what has gone.
examTip.trap: **This error undervalues every protective work** — flood defence, erosion control, maintenance. Ask first: what happens if nothing is done?
examTip.mnemonic: **Drainage changes what CAN be grown, not just the yield** — a second rabi crop, enabled by the field drying two weeks earlier and being workable at sowing time.

questions.stem: In the Terai, waterlogging in the monsoon frequently arises less from a rising groundwater table than from:
options: Excessive irrigation during the monsoon season
Seepage from lined canals
Salinity of the groundwater
Drainage congestion
questions.solution:
**DRAINAGE CONGESTION — the natural drainage lines being obstructed by roads, railway and canal embankments, and by the aggrading, embanked rivers themselves** — so that rainfall cannot escape and ponds on the land.

**Why the Terai's problem is congestion rather than a rising table:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **The rainfall is INTENSE and concentrated in four months** ← | **So a great deal of water must leave in a short time** ← |
| **The land is very FLAT, so the natural drainage is slow even unobstructed** ← | ← |
| **The rivers are AGGRADING, so their beds rise and their capacity to receive drainage falls** ← | **The Chure sediment, arriving where the slope breaks** ← |
| **Those rivers are EMBANKED, so the land beside them cannot drain into them at all except through sluices** ← | ← |
| **And the whole plain is crossed by the EAST-WEST HIGHWAY, its feeder roads, the railway and the irrigation canals** ← | **Every one an embankment across the drainage** ← |
| **So the water arrives quickly, moves slowly, and meets a series of barriers** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ACCUMULATED EFFECT OF DECADES OF INFRASTRUCTURE AND IT IS NOBODY'S RESPONSIBILITY IN PARTICULAR, WHICH IS THE HEART OF THE PROBLEM: each embankment was built by a different agency for a good reason.**

> **The highway department built the road, the railway the railway, the irrigation department the canals, and the flood control programme the river embankments.**

> **Each provided some cross-drainage, sized for the drainage it could see at the time.**

> **The cumulative effect — a plain subdivided into compartments by embankments, each compartment draining through a few culverts — is the product of all of them and the design of none.**

> **And the culverts, sized decades ago for a catchment that has since been urbanised and whose runoff coefficient has doubled, are now inadequate.**

> **So the flooding worsens without any single decision having caused it, which is a cumulative-impact problem of exactly the kind that project-by-project assessment cannot address.**

**WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE REMEDY, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL POINT:**

| If the cause is | The remedy is |
|---|---|
| **A rising GROUNDWATER table** ← | **Subsurface drainage, canal lining, irrigation management, tube well pumping** ← |
| **DRAINAGE CONGESTION** ← | **Restoring and enlarging the SURFACE drainage — clearing the natural lines, enlarging the culverts, providing sluices through the embankments, and removing obstructions** ← |

> **THE TWO REMEDIES ARE ENTIRELY DIFFERENT, AND THE DIAGNOSIS THEREFORE MATTERS A GREAT DEAL: installing subsurface drainage in a command whose problem is congestion achieves nothing, because the water it collects has nowhere to go either.**

> **The observation wells discussed earlier are what distinguish the two: a command suffering congestion has a water table that rises sharply during the monsoon and recedes afterwards, while one with a rising table shows a trend across years.**

> **And congestion shows itself as SURFACE ponding in the compartments between embankments, with the ponding pattern following the embankments rather than the topography.**

> **That pattern is visible on a satellite image or an aerial photograph after a heavy rain, and it identifies the obstructions directly — which is a cheap and quick diagnosis that is well worth doing before any drainage design is contemplated.**

> **THE INSTITUTIONAL REMEDY IS HARDER THAN THE PHYSICAL ONE AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD: enlarging a culvert under a highway requires the highway department to agree, to fund it and to close the road while it is done.**

> **The benefit accrues to the farmers whose land is flooding, not to the highway department.**

> **So the works that would relieve the congestion are in the gift of agencies that gain nothing from them, and they are consequently not done — which is the upstream-downstream incentive problem, appearing again in a different form.**

> **Resolving it requires the drainage to be planned at the level of the whole plain, by a body with authority over all the obstructions — which is precisely what integrated basin management proposes and precisely what is hardest to establish.**

examTip.trick: **Obstructed natural drainage — roads, railway, canals and embanked aggrading rivers** — so the monsoon rain cannot escape and ponds.
examTip.trap: **Subsurface drainage achieves nothing against congestion** — the water it collects has nowhere to go either. Diagnose which problem it is before designing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ponding that follows the EMBANKMENTS rather than the topography** is the signature of congestion, visible on an aerial image after heavy rain. Cheap diagnosis, done first.
